(2015) found no enrichment in the initial targeted ASD screen; combined datasets showed a nominal signal for all coding C-terminal regulatory-domain variants (P = 0.03), but not nonsynonymous variants alone (P = 0.31), with different sequencing pipelines limiting interpretation. This does not remove the measured chloride-clearance defect, but keeps its experimental origin and autism relevance distinct.

##### 6.3.1 Additional candidates for local recovery and developmental reserve

The receptor, sterol, matrix and metabolic examples developed in the later mechanism-specific sections remain relevant beyond the fixed-cohort selection. Further pathway candidates for membrane stability, ion–water handling and recovery reserve are listed below; they are not additions to the frozen 42/102 count:

Sterol trafficking and membrane reserve: NPC1 and NPC2 (intracellular cholesterol mobilisation), ABCA1 (cholesterol export), APOE (lipid delivery), and CAV1 (membrane organisation). Table [35.1](#ss_p10_table_35_1) separates measured variant effects from pathway candidates.

Astrocytic ion–water coupling: AQP4 (water flux speed), GJA1 (Connexin-43 spatial buffering), SNTA1/DTNA (anchoring of perivascular end-feet).

Osmolyte recovery: SLC6A6 (taurine), SLC6A12 (betaine), SLC5A3 (myo-inositol), LRRC8A (volume-regulated anion channel \[VRAC\]-mediated loss).

Barrier integrity: CLDN5, OCLN (tight-junction resilience), MFSD2A (lipid support).

Mitochondrial and autonomic reserve: PPARGC1A (recovery capacity), SOD2 (redox buffering), ADRA2A (sympathetic termination).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_6_4"></a>

#### 6.4 Interpretive Conclusion

Genetic variation can therefore determine where instability begins and which restorative step becomes limiting. The hypothesis considers intrinsic neural or glial disruption alongside reduced renal, vascular and energetic reserve. These are possible causal entry points, not merely modifiers of a prior maternal disturbance. The proposed shared contribution is a local ionic or volume-recovery disturbance that alters neural development. Convergence remains subject to the causal boundary in Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2).

Bell's frozen phenotype-first classification makes these candidate entry points explicit: 42 of the externally fixed Satterstrom-102 genes each cleared one strict primary gate across ten heterogeneous endpoint families (Bell, 2026c). Fifteen qualify through current, receptor or GABA-related endpoints: 12 in direct ion transport and excitability and three in chloride/GABA-related function. Their neuronal location is consistent with an ionic mechanism, but neither identifies its developmental cost nor establishes altered chloride gradients in all 15. The remaining families concern physiological support, control and recovery. This is component evidence within the proposed architecture. Classification asks whether an endpoint meets the stated rule; enrichment asks whether such endpoints occur more often than in comparable genes; mediation asks whether the specified local recovery disturbance carries a developmental effect. Universality is a further question. No matched-set enrichment or shared developmental mediation was demonstrated, and the classification paper's subset formulation cannot establish the parent's universal conjecture.

Two examples show both the signal and the next missing measurement. In Celf4+/− mouse cortical layer-V pyramidal neurons, persistent sodium current and axon-initial-segment NaV1.6 abundance were increased (Sun et al., 2013). This is a measured sodium-current endpoint in a heterozygous model, not merely a functional annotation. Whether it increases pump work, delays sodium or chloride recovery, or changes maturation through those costs remains unmeasured. In HEK293 receptor-expression experiments, the human de novo GRIA2 A643V variant slowed AMPAR deactivation and reduced desensitisation; deactivation was approximately sevenfold longer in homomeric GluA2(Q) receptors (Coombs et al., 2022). Prolonged cation entry supplies a concrete test of duration-dependent recovery demand, although neuronal ATP use and recovery were not measured. The variant was identified in a child with epilepsy and developmental delay; it cannot stand for every GRIA2 allele or the exact variants ascertained by Satterstrom. These examples preserve the proposal that altered signalling can become altered restoration work, while locating the untested joint precisely.

Genetic routes into developmental chloride regulation are experimentally concrete. In male Fmr1-null mice, He et al. (2014) found delayed chloride-reversal maturation in layer-IV somatosensory neurons and increased cortical NKCC1 protein at postnatal day 10; KCC2 protein was unchanged at the sampled ages, and the reversal-potential difference was no longer detected at day 15. In human neurons derived from Rett patients carrying MECP2 Q83X or N126I variants, Tang et al. (2016) found deficient KCC2 and a delayed hyperpolarising GABA-reversal shift during 1–3 months of culture. IGF1 treatment increased KCC2 and restored that electrophysiological endpoint. These findings support direct genetic entry into chloride regulation without requiring a preceding maternal sodium–volume episode. They identify distinct candidate import and extrusion routes, rather than a requirement that every lesion increases NKCC1. Neither study measured restoration after a matched chloride load, and reversal-potential rescue is not a complete behavioural or clinical rescue.

The intrinsic worked example in Section [4](#ss_p10_sec_4) draws on dynamic recovery measured in a defined genetic model. Tang et al. (2019) reported that the KCC2-expression enhancer KW-2449 accelerated chloride extrusion in human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons, shortening the SuperClomeleon recovery time constant towards the isogenic wild-type value. This supplies a positive precedent for measuring local recovery beyond a resting chloride value or transporter abundance. It does not establish osmotic initiation, impaired cell-volume recovery or a common mechanism across autism. KCC2 also has structural functions in synapse development, and the drug acts on other signalling processes; improved recovery and morphology under the same treatment do not by themselves identify chloride recovery as the developmental mediator.

WNK3 adds a human genetic example of an intrinsic developmental route into cation–chloride regulation. Küry et al. (2022) identified six maternally inherited hemizygous variants in 14 males from six families with intellectual disability/developmental delay; autistic features were reported in one individual. An earlier report of two brothers with autism and intellectual disability involved a deletion encompassing PHF8, FAM120C and WNK3, so it could not attribute autism specifically to WNK3 (Qiao et al., 2008). The single-gene evidence supports a rare X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder, rather than an explanation of autism’s population sex ratio. Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7) considers the direction-specific functional findings and the proposed recovery question. WNK3 is discussed outside the frozen 42/102 analysis, whose membership and classifications remain unchanged.

The Shank3B counterexample and negative human bumetanide trials constrain generalisation (Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7)), which also distinguishes normal WNK-dependent restoration from delayed recovery. Sections [29](#ss_p10_sec_29) and [31](#ss_p10_sec_31) connect recovery to developmental protein production and the relative timing of interacting cell populations. Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) compares the recovery claim with immune, metabolic and developmental-signalling explanations. A shared endpoint does not decide which causal route produced it.

Calibration of the map remains incomplete. In the frozen companion audit, review was not blind to the hypothesis, an independent matched comparison set was not analysed, and background phenotype extraction was unfinished (Bell, 2026c). One intended no-change control retained a strict count of zero while generating additional non-counting routes, leaving the specificity of route generation unresolved. A second control and an equal-depth IMPC comparison had not been completed. These limitations affect calibration of the classification; they do not erase the reported component findings.

Enrichment depends on comparable evidence-search depth and assay coverage; untested endpoints are not negative findings. Even demonstrated enrichment would leave developmental mediation unresolved (Section [7](#ss_p10_sec_7)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_7"></a>

### 7 Intrinsic and Direct Molecular Entry into Sodium-Handling Burden

Intrinsic molecular initiation provides another possible local entry into the recovery problem introduced in Section [4](#ss_p10_sec_4), without preceding systemic sodium–volume disturbance. The functional examples below complement the genetic evidence in Section [6](#ss_p10_sec_6). No majority allocation to systemic or maternal routes across autism is assumed.

Reduced gradient-maintenance or energetic capacity could lower the demand at which recovery fails; altered channels or receptors could instead increase demand. A direct developmental effect with preserved relevant recovery remains an alternative, not an instance of the common process by definition.

One route is insufficient mitochondrial support for Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase during actual demand. If compensation meets that demand, reduced reserve need not impair extrusion or deplete ATP. Otherwise sodium recovery could fail locally, with developmental significance only if that recovery constraint carries an effect.

A substrate-specific energetic constraint is demonstrated in AGC1 deficiency. Homozygous SLC25A12 Gln590Arg abolished AGC1 transport in reconstituted liposomes and accompanied severe developmental disease with hypomyelination. Muscle-mitochondrial ATP production was markedly reduced with glutamate-based substrate pairs, while respiratory-chain enzyme activities were normal (Wibom et al., 2009). This preserves a substrate-dependent energetic route alongside aspartate/N-acetylaspartate supply. It does not equate biallelic AGC1 disease with ASD association or establish deficient neural recovery reserve.

Direct pump dysfunction is distinct from inadequate ATP production. In cultured rat hippocampal neurons, α3-preferring ouabain inhibition slowed dendritic sodium clearance after transient potassium-free loading; separate pump-current recordings supplied excess ATP (Azarias et al., 2013). In COS cells expressing the neurological-disease-associated ATP1A3 D923N variant, reduced sodium affinity accompanied higher intracellular sodium than with wild-type α3 (Toustrup-Jensen et al., 2014). These findings make intrinsic transport limitation a concrete local entry route, without implying that every variant lowers transport or causes ATP depletion. Its proposed developmental role still requires impaired neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery to mediate the specified developmental change.

A third route is impaired chloride extrusion through reduced KCC2 (SLC12A5) function, arising from genetic variation, altered developmental regulation or changes in membrane organisation. Reduced effective extrusion can constrain restoration of an age-appropriate chloride state during repeated loading; Table [6.2](#ss_p10_table_6_2) supplies variant-specific recovery findings. This does not by itself establish increased NKCC1 inward flux, sodium accumulation or additional pump work; those quantities require separate measurements under the prevailing gradients (Section [23.2](#ss_p10_sec_23_2)).

Membrane scaffolding supplies a measured component of this route. In mature rat hippocampal cultures, gephyrin knockdown reduced KCC2 clustering and weakened chloride extrusion assessed from the somatodendritic GABA-reversal gradient during an imposed chloride load. The surface-to-total ratio of recombinant KCC2 did not change significantly (Al Awabdh et al., 2022). This connects a scaffold perturbation with functional chloride handling. KCC2 also has structural effects on excitatory synapses that are separable from its transport function (Gauvain et al., 2011; Section [28](#ss_p10_sec_28)). The proposed developmental extension requires the specified molecular change to impair local chloride recovery and that difficulty to alter circuit development. Such an intrinsic entry need not begin with a systemic sodium–volume disturbance.

Environmental compounds can also act directly: §[14.8](#ss_p10_sec_14_8) and Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1) include increased neuronal sodium influx and impaired astrocytic volume recovery. Whether these effects occur at relevant developmental exposures and mediate lasting change is distinct from exposure–ASD association or an effect on pumps or actin.

Intrinsic initiation may bypass systemic stress while still acting through recovery. A well-characterised recovery-independent route to the neurodevelopmental features of autism would challenge universal scope. The intermediary cannot be reassigned after the result, and peripheral findings cannot substitute for a failed neuronal prediction.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_8"></a>

### 8 Developmental Anatomy and Endocrine Regulation

Primary developmental abnormalities can alter endocrine and water-regulatory capacity. In a holoprosencephaly cohort, diabetes-insipidus severity was associated with hypothalamic non-separation (Hahn et al., 2005). This illustrates a possible causal direction from developmental anatomy to water-regulatory dysfunction; it does not establish a sodium-mediated cause of the anatomical abnormality.

Human OTX2 variants are associated with variable pituitary phenotypes, and patient-derived organoids demonstrate a role for hypothalamic OTX2 in pituitary development (Gregory et al., 2021; Matsumoto et al., 2020). These primary developmental mechanisms should be distinguished from the later extracellular OTX2 signalling discussed in Sections [30](#ss_p10_sec_30) and [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4). They do not demonstrate sodium–volume mediation, and craniofacial morphology is not used here as supporting evidence for the hypothesis.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_9"></a>

### 9 Calibration Inputs to the Sodium–Volume Defence Axis During Fetal and Early Perinatal Development

During fetal life and the early perinatal transition, repeated defence and recovery may shape later sodium–volume regulation. Persistent recalibration here means an exposure-related change in threshold, gain or recovery that remains after the initiating conditions resolve, assessed under comparable current physiology and developmental stage. Ordinary recruitment supports the current challenge and subsides as conditions recover (Sections [4.3](#ss_p10_sec_4_3) and [39.3](#ss_p10_sec_39_3)). Maternal physiology contributes through placental fluid, perfusion, nutrient and endocrine conditions; the developmental input is the fetal exposure and response history that results, rather than a single maternal analyte.

In Guyton’s systems physiology framework, total body sodium and extracellular fluid volume are coupled through renal–vascular feedback: changes in sodium balance affect volume, pressure and renal excretion. Plasma tonicity instead describes effective extracellular osmoles, chiefly sodium salts, relative to water and governs transcellular water distribution. These distinct variables interact, linking circulatory filling, tissue perfusion, renal handling and cellular hydration.

At birth, placental exchange ends, pulmonary flow increases with lung aeration and sodium–volume regulation shifts towards autonomous neonatal control. The hypothesis proposes that demand across fetal life and this transition can alter receptor responsiveness, transporter regulation or neural thresholds. Maternal regulatory activity is not transmitted intact: placental transformation and the fetus’s own response connect maternal conditions to any persistent recalibration.

The fetal regulatory environment includes its own tonicity trajectory, perfusion and oxygen delivery, renal handling and endocrine responsiveness. Maternal and placental inputs interact with intrinsic fetal capacity; maternal sodium alone cannot describe that environment.

During fetal and early perinatal development, calibration inputs arise through multiple interacting domains. The inventory below separates the variables and signals involved; Section [10](#ss_p10_sec_10) then follows the maternal contribution through placental transformation and the fetus’s own regulation.

**A. Osmotic and Electrolyte Inputs**

• Maternal extracellular sodium relative to water, chloride availability and other contributors to tonicity  
• Maternal osmoreceptor recruitment and the resulting changes in water balance  
• Fetal extracellular composition after placental exchange  
• Placental and fetal cellular osmolyte handling, measured separately from maternal osmotic signalling

**B. Volume, Pressure, and Perfusion Inputs**

• Maternal effective arterial blood volume, assessed alongside maternal RAAS and AVP recruitment  
• Maternal arterial pressure, vascular tone and uteroplacental perfusion  
• Fetal pressure, filling and oxygen delivery after placental exchange  
• Fetal regional redistribution, including brain-sparing responses during circulatory stress

**C. Endocrine and Receptor–Ligand Inputs**

• Maternal AVP recruitment and water balance as indirect inputs to fetal exposure and endogenous fetal defence, including fetal AVP pulsatility and V1a/V1b/V2 responsiveness (Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3))  
• Maternal RAAS-dependent sodium conservation and vascular effects, distinguished from local placental and fetal angiotensin signalling and AGTR1 response gain  
• Fetal cortisol exposure after placental metabolism, interpreted with fetal mineralocorticoid/glucocorticoid receptor (MR/GR) expression, enzymatic gating and coupling  
• Maternal thyroid status and resulting fetal hormone exposure as possible influences on metabolic and transport development, including thyroid support of Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase

**D. Stress, Cytokine, and Sympathetic Inputs**

• Maternal inflammatory signals acting on placental metabolism and vascular function  
• Maternal sympathetic activity influencing maternal resistance, renin recruitment and adrenal output  
• Fetal autonomic and endocrine responses to the resulting changes in oxygenation, perfusion and composition, with any lasting threshold change tested in the fetus; metabolic and mitochondrial activity are additional determinants of tissue response capacity

**E. Neural and Vascular Threat-Interpretation Inputs**

• Maternal arterial and cardiopulmonary afferents regulating the maternal circulation  
• Candidate fetal arterial and cardiopulmonary afferent inputs, distinguished from local endothelial flow responses  
• Fetal brainstem and hypothalamic integration of circulatory and chemical inputs  
• Candidate afferent routes through the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), with their contribution defined by stimulus, species and gestational stage

Fetal integration permits coordinated defence without one afferent route carrying every response. In late-gestation fetal sheep, bilateral cervical vagosympathetic section altered circulation during slow haemorrhage without significantly changing AVP, ACTH, cortisol or plasma renin activity increases (Wood et al., 1989). Repeated fetal integration, rather than transfer of maternal neural traffic, is the proposed calibration input.

These inputs interact. Water handling, membrane transport, barrier permeability or inflammation may first disturb tonicity; underfilling or impaired delivery may initiate a circulatory route. Where pooling or containment failure demonstrably reduces central filling, defence can respond to a real deficit despite adequate sodium intake; this is distinct from a sensing error. Sensory or regulatory disturbances can instead exaggerate, blunt or mistime defence, so impaired sensing implies no uniform AVP or RAAS direction. Disproportionate free-water retention can lower sodium concentration. Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) separates actual filling/delivery disturbances from sensing/regulation disturbances while allowing their interaction.

Hormone concentration alone does not define signalling strength. For AVP, RAAS ligands, cortisol, oxytocin and FGF-23, available ligand, receptor abundance and downstream coupling influence the response at a specified tissue. Steroid-specific controls act at additional steps: adrenal zonation and steroidogenic programmes shape production, while 11β-HSD-dependent metabolism modifies local glucocorticoid availability (Sections [10.1](#ss_p10_sec_10_1) and [34](#ss_p10_sec_34)). Production, local metabolism and receptor responsiveness therefore require separate interpretation.

Cortisol-biased signalling could involve glucocorticoid responsiveness, MR/GR balance, local 11β-HSD activity or adrenal architecture (§[34](#ss_p10_sec_34)). Normal or low serum cortisol neither excludes nor establishes that state. The proposal requires a greater specified response at comparable exposure, or independently demonstrated prolonged exposure, with the proposed developmental consequence.

Stable osmotic, volume and autonomic inputs permit calibration under relatively consistent conditions. Maternal dehydration or inflammation, placental perfusion instability and intrinsic fetal transport or receptor variation can instead impose competing cues. The hypothesis is that repeated adjustment under those constraints leaves shifted thresholds, receptor balance, endocrine recruitment or cellular recovery kinetics.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_10"></a>

### 10 Maternal-Fetal Signal Transformation and Calibration of the Sodium-Volume Defence Axis

Placental transport, peptide metabolism and vascular regulation transform maternal changes into fetal exposures. The fetus’s endocrine and renal responses then shape its history of defence and recovery. Recirculating fluid compartments could prolong that history, but amplification is a prediction rather than an automatic consequence of circulation through a loop (Section [10.4](#ss_p10_sec_10_4)). The account below follows peptide availability and transport kinetics, fetal endocrine recruitment, renal and amniotic-fluid feedback, and developmental timing.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_10_1"></a>

#### 10.1 Maternal-Fetal Partitioning and Enzymatic Barriers

Within this placental interface, local RAAS balance, endothelial sensing and perfusion modify how maternal sodium–water balance and endocrine activity become fetal exposures. Transport, peptide metabolism and endocrine filtering determine different aspects of that transformation. Water–solute balance, nutrient and oxygen delivery, vascular resistance and glucocorticoid availability therefore require joint interpretation when defining the fetal exposure.

Maternal and fetal fluid and peptide environments are coupled through different processes. Water and small-solute exchange can change fetal osmotic or metabolic stimuli without equivalent transfer of the maternal AVP response. Human placental perfusion experiments support substantial AVP metabolism and limited detectable transfer under the tested conditions, rather than an absolute barrier (Landon et al., 1988). These perfusion findings do not map every gestational stage or define a frequency-specific filter. Placental 11beta-HSD2 separately limits maternal cortisol exposure by converting cortisol to cortisone (Stirrat et al., 2018). Fetal hormone concentrations therefore depend on fetal secretion and removal as well as maternal contributions. This partitioning provides a possible route to different maternal and fetal endocrine states; lower fetal effective tonicity or discordant osmotic and circulatory cues must be established separately. Oxytocin and desmopressin require peptide-specific assessments of transfer and metabolism.

Normal gestation establishes a lower osmotic reference for thirst and AVP release. Longitudinal human studies found lower plasma osmolality and lower osmotic thresholds during pregnancy; basal AVP in late pregnancy could remain similar to postpartum values (Davison et al., 1984, 1988). This coordinated reset is a normal adaptation, distinct from additional hypotonicity, impaired effective circulating filling or glucose-related changes in tonicity. A proposed disturbance must therefore be defined against gestational stage and, where possible, the individual's baseline. Lower osmolality alone does not establish deficient AVP. Lower sodium during hyperglycaemia likewise does not establish lower effective tonicity; the glucose-first and subsequent recovery phases are considered separately in Sections [10.2](#ss_p10_sec_10_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_10_1_1"></a>

##### 10.1.1 Gestational Peptide Clearance and Compensatory Capacity

Peptide exposure reflects secretion and active removal, while its physiological effect also depends on tissue responsiveness. In five women studied longitudinally, maternal AVP metabolic clearance at 7–8 gestational weeks was similar to the preconception value, and circulating vasopressinase was undetectable. Clearance was approximately 3–4-fold higher at 22–24 and 36–38 weeks, alongside increased plasma vasopressinase. Basal plasma AVP remained similar, so Davison et al. (1989) inferred increased production to offset disposal; secretion was not directly quantified. Similar urine osmolality at matched plasma AVP supported preserved renal responsiveness under the study conditions. Normal hormone concentrations can therefore coexist with substantially increased hormone turnover.

Changes in clearance can be offset by secretion. The proposed disturbance arises when that compensation is insufficient to preserve appropriate exposure or water handling; the normal gestational rise in clearance does not demonstrate failure.

The underlying enzyme is placental leucine aminopeptidase (P-LAP), also called insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP), encoded by LNPEP; vasopressinase and oxytocinase describe its peptide-degrading activities. Purified human placental enzyme can hydrolyse both AVP and oxytocin (Tsujimoto et al., 1992). Tissue expression, access of substrate to membrane enzyme, soluble enzyme released by shedding, and native-peptide degradation are different measurements (Ito et al., 2004; Vear et al., 2023). They should be linked experimentally before a change in one is assigned to altered hormone exposure. Reproducible parity associations could motivate such measurements, but parity is not a measurement of enzyme burden or compensatory capacity. Neither parity nor enzyme abundance alone specifies maternal water balance, fetal dilution or the direction of the fetal AVP response.

Maternal peptide turnover therefore changes across gestation. Undetectable circulating vasopressinase early in pregnancy does not establish absent placental tissue activity or passage of intact maternal AVP into fetal blood. The clearance study did not measure that transfer, and the placental perfusion findings in Section [10.1](#ss_p10_sec_10_1) do not map it across gestational ages. These observations do not establish a period of maternal AVP supply followed by a discrete fetal takeover. Fetal AVP development follows its own timetable (Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3)).

MIA adds molecular passage, placental relay and circulatory routes to this interface (Sections [18.5](#ss_p10_sec_18_5) and [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6)). Their distinct intermediaries connect maternal conditions to fetal exposure and possible local recovery disturbance. Maternal dependence does not establish molecular transfer, and maternal concentration alone identifies neither fetal dose nor response.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_10_2"></a>

#### 10.2 Placental Transport Asymmetry and Exposure Kinetics

Placental transport asymmetry is kinetic and regulatory rather than absolute. Glucose and water exchange do not imply identical sodium transfer kinetics. In human term placental preparations, Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase protein and activity occur in both the maternal-facing microvillous and fetal-facing basal syncytiotrophoblast membranes (Johansson et al., 2000). Na⁺/H⁺ exchange supports trophoblast pH recovery; Speake et al. (2005) found predominantly NHE1-mediated activity on the microvillous side, with no detectable basal-membrane NHE activity under their assay conditions. These are measured components of placental ion handling, not a complete map of net maternal-to-fetal sodium flux. The proposed exposure mechanism is that their regulation, together with water and nutrient exchange, changes the time course of fetal composition after a defined maternal input.

Transport asymmetry does not itself establish fetal hypotonicity, swelling, a fixed equilibration lag or an anti-hyponatraemic response. Recurrent glycaemic excursions and low-solute fluid loading are separate inputs: their fetal gradients, composition and timing determine the proposed sodium–water consequence (Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)). Maternal and fetal concentrations may change at different rates; sodium concentration must be interpreted alongside glucose and other effective osmoles.

Organic osmolytes add a further layer of placental regulation. Perfused term human placentas actively transferred taurine and sustained a fetal-to-maternal concentration ratio of 1.38 ± 0.14 (SEM) in six preparations (Hibbard et al., 1990). Myo-inositol has a different supply pattern: stable-isotope measurements in seven uncomplicated term pregnancies indicated that less than 10% of fetal plasma inositol came from maternal plasma, consistent with substantial endogenous production (Staat et al., 2012). Nuclear factor of activated T cells 5 (NFAT5/TonEBP) protein and SMIT transcripts are present in term human trophoblasts (Shin et al., 2012). Together these findings support a regulated osmolyte environment, while requiring transfer, local synthesis and intracellular redistribution to be distinguished. The hypothesis proposes that altered regulation of this environment changes fetal buffering and recovery; fetal brain osmolyte restoration is a separate endpoint from placental abundance or cord concentration.

Placental processing leads to fetal exposure, defined by composition, oxygenation, filling and perfusion.

Fetal exposure leads downward to the fetus’s own responses. Recruitment of AVP–RAAS–cortisol depends on cues and maturity. A solid arrow connects these responses to renal and fluid handling, which includes stage-dependent salt–water regulation and amniotic exchange, with a cross-reference to Figure 10.2. <a name="ss_p10_sec_10_3"></a>

#### 10.3 The Fetal Endocrine Readout: The AVP–RAAS–Cortisol Defence Triad

The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad names complementary protective roles: AVP supports water balance and circulatory defence; RAAS supports sodium conservation and effective circulating volume; cortisol provides stress and metabolic support. Their recruitment has different triggers and timescales, so the architecture does not require all three to rise together. The developmental hypothesis concerns how repeated defence or incomplete recovery during sensitive periods might alter maturation. With sufficient reserve, appropriate withdrawal and recovery, compensation may leave no lasting functional impairment.

Human fetal pituitary samples contained immunoreactive AVP at 11–19 gestational weeks (Skowsky and Fisher, 1977), with continued maturation of hypothalamic and pituitary hormone content (Burford and Robinson, 1982). These ages establish neither first synthesis, mature secretion or renal responsiveness, nor a maternal-to-fetal supply handover. Earlier maternal or placental disturbance could affect neural and endocrine formation before fetal AVP matures; a mechanism requiring fetal AVP persistence instead depends on secretion, clearance and target-organ competence at the relevant stage (Section [36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5)).

Osmotic and volume inputs interact within AVP regulation. In unanaesthetised rats, hypovolaemia increased the sensitivity of the osmotic AVP response and, with greater depletion, lowered its threshold (Dunn et al., 1973). This provides a physiological basis for interacting cues; fetal response thresholds and the developmental consequences of repeated defence require their own evidence.

When fetal hypotonicity coexists with a filling, perfusion or oxygen-delivery threat, osmotic suppression of AVP can compete with nonosmotic recruitment. The mixed-cue prediction is delayed recruitment or a smaller response than under a comparable circulatory challenge without hypotonicity. These are distinct predictions: AVP may still rise, and appropriate suppression during uncomplicated dilution is not failed defence. RAAS and cortisol responses need not form a fixed hormonal profile. Adequately demonstrated absence of delay or attenuation would oppose the corresponding prediction; absence of a proposed concurrent RAAS or cortisol response would limit that additional conjunction. A mixed-cue response can reflect appropriate cue integration without harmful mismatch.

In near-term fetal sheep, maternal DDAVP plus water loading shifted the threshold for increased AVP immunoreactivity from 17.5% to 22.5% of estimated blood volume withdrawn during haemorrhage. Plasma immunoreactivity rose in both groups: the published abstract describes similar increases, whereas the full Results and Discussion report differing response slopes and a lower peak in treated fetuses (Desai et al., 2003a). These are withdrawal thresholds, not measurements of the net circulating deficit. Assay cross-reactivity with DDAVP and differing volume restoration limit attribution to osmotic inhibition alone. Renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone and cortisol were not measured together to establish the full triad.

The intervention also relatively preserved fetal urine output. At the end of the 60-minute haemorrhage, after withdrawal of 30% of estimated blood volume, urine flow was 0.35 mL/min in treated fetuses versus 0.12 mL/min in controls, approximately 2.9-fold higher. Flow fell in both groups. The authors proposed that preserved output could help sustain amniotic-fluid supply during haemorrhage; benefit to amniotic-fluid volume and later development was not demonstrated by this experiment (Desai et al., 2003a).

Experimental fetal physiology supports protective recruitment and changing endocrine relationships. In anaesthetised sheep, V1 antagonism reduced the hypoxaemia-associated rise in fetal cerebral blood flow (Eisenach et al., 1992). During prolonged reduced uterine flow in another sheep study, AVP rose early and then approached control levels while cortisol remained elevated despite continuing hypoxaemia (Hooper et al., 1990). This is phase separation during a continuing challenge, not complete recovery or evidence that near-control AVP is deficient. Fetal pituitary-adrenal stress responses mature with gestation (Rose et al., 1978); these preparations provide component evidence, not human midgestational thresholds or proof of developmental imprinting.

The corresponding birth-response prediction is lower cord copeptin with lower effective fetal tonicity under comparable nonosmotic stimuli and birth context (Section [18.1.9](#ss_p10_sec_18_1_9)). A positive association could reflect ordinary protective physiology, without harmful mismatch or developmental programming; an adequately precise null or opposite relation would weaken this prediction.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_10_4"></a>

#### 10.4 Fetal Renal Decoding and Amniotic-Fluid Re-exposure

The fetus is not a passive recipient of placental information, and its renal response changes as transport capacity develops. Human MAGED2-related antenatal Bartter syndrome provides direct evidence: impaired NKCC2 (sodium–potassium–2 chloride cotransporter 2) and NCC (sodium–chloride cotransporter) expression and function accompany severe fetal salt loss and polyhydramnios, yet the renal phenotype can resolve after birth (Laghmani et al., 2016). In human fetal kidney specimens, AQP1–3 expression, including collecting-duct AQP2, increased with gestational age while remaining below adult levels (Feng et al., 2019). These findings anchor stage-dependent salt and water handling; they do not establish adult levels of concentrating capacity. Macula densa–renin signalling, epithelial sodium channel (ENaC)–mineralocorticoid responsiveness and natriuretic counter-signals must likewise be assigned to the relevant stage. The hypothesis predicts that the same placental input can therefore produce different urine output, sodium conservation and endocrine recruitment as the fetal kidney matures.

Fetal urine changes amniotic water–solute balance; swallowing with gastrointestinal absorption and intramembranous transfer can return water and solutes to circulation. Fetal-sheep experiments demonstrate systemic osmotic effects after ingested or intraamniotic fluid, followed by recovery and regulatory fluid removal (Smith et al., 1986; Ross et al., 1991; Brace et al., 2004). The developmental extension is that residence and delayed return prolong or repeat a disturbance after a transient input. Direction and duration depend on composition, flows, compartment volumes, placental exchange and renal responses. Recirculation alone establishes neither amplification nor developmental harm. Polyhydramnios identifies neither fetal salt depletion nor hypotonic exposure by itself; urine production, swallowing and intramembranous return require separate assessment.

**Text description of Figure 10.2**

The diagram maps selected fetal fluid pathways using solid arrows. Its subtitle specifies that an increase in disturbance amplitude is not assumed.

At the top, a two-headed arrow connects ongoing placental exchange of water and solutes with fetal circulation. The circulation box states that composition reflects input, distribution and removal. A downward arrow leads from fetal circulation to fetal renal handling, identified as stage-dependent urinary water and solute output. A further downward arrow carries renal output to amniotic fluid, whose composition and volume reflect inflows and outflows.

Two return routes leave the amniotic-fluid box. One leads to swallowing and gastrointestinal absorption; the other leads to intramembranous transfer. Both connect to a shared pathway labelled “Water and solute return”, which points back to fetal circulation. Together these connections depict exchange and recirculation rather than a quantified balance of all flows.

A separate box with a dashed outline states the proposed re-exposure mechanism: delayed return may prolong or repeat a measured fetal disturbance. The same box states that regulation can restore stability and that recirculation alone establishes neither amplification nor harm. The legend identifies the solid arrows as component pathways and emphasises that only selected fluxes are shown; the diagram is not a complete fluid-balance model. The dashed outline marks a prediction about persistence or recurrence, rather than an established developmental consequence.

#### 10.5 Temporal Vulnerability: Skin-Barrier Maturation and Proposed NFAT5 Imprinting

Skin-barrier maturation provides a candidate window in which fetal fluid exchange and susceptibility change. Human fetal-skin experiments found lower tracer-water permeability as keratinisation progressed (Parmley and Seeds, 1970). Hardman et al. (1999) reported regionally patterned barrier initiation at 22–26 weeks menstrual age (20–24 weeks in their gestational convention), rather than synchronous whole-skin closure. These findings identify changing routes of exchange; they do not by themselves establish weaker whole-fetus osmotic buffering or larger tonicity excursions. The developmental proposal is that altered exposure kinetics can coincide with limited response or recovery capacity while control thresholds are being set. That prediction requires stage-specific exposure and response measurements, rather than assigning the endocrine behaviour of near-term sheep to a human midgestational window.

NFAT5 provides a candidate molecular connection between osmotic exposure, chloride regulation and endothelial recovery (Section [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)). Term placental NFAT5/SMIT localisation identifies an interface component (Shin et al., 2012), not fetal neural imprinting. Intracellular ionic strength, cell volume and extracellular tonicity remain distinct; hypertonic findings do not specify a hypotonic response. The 20–24-week anchor identifies regional skin-barrier initiation, not a measured NFAT5 calibration window.

#### 10.6 Integration with Later Control Systems

Placentally transformed exposure could influence later brainstem threat classification, hypothalamic AVP recruitment and sodium-conserving endocrine behaviour through the fetus’s own defence and recovery history. Repeated or incompletely resolved challenge may alter conditions while regulatory thresholds develop; successful recovery can leave no lasting impairment.

The proposed developmental input is the pattern of defence needed to maintain stability, shaped jointly by maternal physiology, placental processing and intrinsic fetal capacity. A single maternal sodium value cannot reconstruct that history, and compartment separation alone does not establish costly compensation. The core developmental test is whether that exposure impairs local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery, and whether the recovery disturbance carries a specified developmental effect (Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_11"></a>

### 11 The Intergenerational Sodium Struggle: Inherited Susceptibility and Developmental Programming

The intergenerational proposal connects two distinct routes: inherited susceptibility and developmental exposure. Genetic variants can constrain offspring transport, structural reserve or recovery directly (Section [6](#ss_p10_sec_6)), while maternal physiology can influence the gestational environment through the maternal–placental–fetal processes developed in Sections [9](#ss_p10_sec_9), [10](#ss_p10_sec_10), and [18.1](#ss_p10_sec_18_1). In the latter route, fetal tissues respond to the exposure that reaches them. A maternal receptor pattern is not transferred intact. Structural reserve and receptor responsiveness are candidate offspring outcomes to measure, not interchangeable signs of an inherited defence state.

For the developmental-exposure route, the proposed continuity must be traced from maternal physiology through a measured fetal exposure to a persistent offspring structural or response change. Section [32.6](#ss_p10_sec_32_6) supplies a specific renal-reserve example to test alongside inherited liability and shared environment. Its place in the common-process account still requires the defined local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty and its developmental effect (Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2)). Adequate gestational compensation and normal offspring recovery remain alternatives. Neither progressive loss of reserve across generations nor transmission of acquired receptor changes is assumed; familial recurrence alone cannot supply the missing links.

<a name="ss_p10_part_c"></a>

## Part C Candidate disturbances and evidence

<a name="ss_p10_sec_12"></a>

### 12 Converging Osmotic and Volume Pathways in Autism Contributing Factors

The defence weightings described in [Section 5](#ss_p10_sec_5) can arise through different initiating disturbances. The Sodium Struggle concerns both those disturbances and the cost of correcting them when solute, water, circulatory and cellular recovery operate on different timescales. Routes may begin with hypotonic dilution, hypertonic loading, altered renal transport, impaired effective filling or vascular signalling. Their proposed developmental significance depends on magnitude, duration, compensation and its withdrawal, particularly whether recovery finishes before another challenge.

The two contributor maps organise possible entry routes into the coupled physiology of §[3](#ss_p10_sec_3): extracellular tonicity, effective circulating volume, and vascular tone or containment. Table [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1) addresses cellular osmotic, ionic and volume-control difficulties. Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) addresses circulatory difficulties and altered defence, separating actual filling or delivery disturbances in Panel A from sensing or regulatory disturbances in Panel B. These maps organise overlapping routes; they do not assign a separate defended variable to each panel. Their proposed developmental convergence requires the recovery intermediary specified in §[2](#ss_p10_sec_2).

The maps use matching fields to connect a defined disturbance with its mechanism, representative contributors, candidate genes or systems, and claim-specific evidence. Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1) indexes the observed associations, measured components and hypothesized developmental links. Sections [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) and [16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9) distinguish actual vascular dysfunction from mechanical transmission, afferent encoding and regulatory interpretation; Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1) supplies supporting component evidence. Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) retain the glucose-related redistribution and proposed compensatory roles, distinct from hypotonicity.

#### 12.1 Neonatal Sodium Trajectories and Later Development

Measured neonatal sodium disturbances already have longitudinal developmental associations in humans. The relevant evidence concerns different exposures: a concentration minimum, a maximum, a range across days, or the number of days above a threshold. These measurements bring the question beyond component physiology, while separating an observed sodium history from the proposed cost of defending and recovering from it.

Gervais et al. (2022) studied 147 infants born before 29 weeks who survived the first ten days; 127 had ascertainable death or developmental outcomes. A larger first-ten-day range of glucose-corrected sodium was associated with death or developmental impairment at 18–21 months corrected age after gestational-age adjustment (linear-model coefficient B=2.10, 95% CI 0.16–4.04). With gestational age, neonatal illness score and NSAID use considered together, the estimate was B=2.03 (−0.30 to 4.37; p=.087); uncorrected sodium remained nominally associated (B=2.28, 0.01–4.56; p=.049). These are published linear coefficients, not risk ratios. The range was the maximum minus minimum of daily medians, with missing days interpolated; it did not measure oscillation count or recovery time. Glucose correction changed the analysed quantity but was not necessary to detect an association.

The high-sodium branch has a further human developmental signal. Murakami et al. (2026) analysed 272 followed infants born before 32 weeks. A first-week peak whole-blood sodium above 145 mEq/L was associated with composite neurodevelopmental impairment at 3–4 years (adjusted RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.08–2.84). In a supplementary analysis, sodium above 145 on at least two days was associated with RR 2.37 (1.39–4.02), compared with RR 1.07 (0.50–2.28) for one day, each relative to infants without hypernatraemia. This was not a direct statistical comparison between the two exposure durations. The days need not be consecutive, so persistent and recurrent disturbance remain distinguishable explanations. The composite combined developmental-quotient, motor and sensory impairments. Developmental-quotient impairment alone was not statistically significant in the main adjusted analysis, but was associated in the supplementary two-or-more-day comparison (RR 2.06, 1.17–3.63). Deaths were excluded and developmental data were available for 272 of 418 survivors, making selective follow-up an important limit.

Low sodium has been examined in a different clinical setting. Viitaharju et al. (2026) followed 269 infants born at or after 36 weeks with perinatal asphyxia for a median 11.2 years. A minimum sodium below 125 mmol/L in the first 72 hours was associated with death or a listed neurological or developmental diagnosis (adjusted OR 3.85, 95% CI 1.04–14.22). The below-130 threshold was associated with cerebral-palsy/paralytic, epilepsy and hearing outcomes, but the grouped psychiatric/developmental endpoint was not statistically significant (OR 1.51, 0.69–3.28). That heterogeneous category was not an autism-specific test, and its interval does not establish equivalence. This asphyxia cohort is neither a direct replication nor a refutation of the preterm sodium-range result.

Together, these findings justify testing the developmental consequences of sodium history in both directions. They do not yet establish a shared causal U-shaped curve, a safe middle band, compensatory overshoot from high to low sodium, or the proposed recovery intermediary. Prematurity, hypoxic injury, treatment and sampling can contribute to the associations; none of these cohorts measured the full defence-to-recovery sequence or an autism-specific outcome. The discriminating next step is to connect the timed exposure to independently measured physiological recovery and later development. This preserves the hypothesis’s central question: whether the history of maintaining stability matters beyond the laboratory value observed at one moment.

The maternal posture and gestational-load comparison is developed in Section [16.5](#ss_p10_sec_16_5), alongside regional filling and venous-return constraints.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_13"></a>

### 13 Osmotic Pathway Catalogue

This catalogue retains nine core routes into water–solute imbalance, altered transport or incomplete cellular recovery. Table [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1) also maps intergenerational programming, hyperglycaemic translocation and maternal salt loading as interacting contexts. The rows identify initiating disturbances, regulatory responses and recovery constraints at interacting causal levels, rather than mutually exclusive diagnoses. Not every route begins with hypotonicity or low serum sodium. Compensation can change the direction of disturbance; recurrence, overshoot and incomplete recovery are separate possibilities. Endocrine responses depend on phase, compartment and effective filling. The component studies cited below anchor particular steps; §[14](#ss_p10_sec_14) and Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1) distinguish those observations from proposed developmental mediation.

#### 13.1 Water-Balance and AVP Pathways

These pathways begin with altered water balance or AVP recruitment. Appropriate early conservation, excessive or persistent antidiuresis, and later dilution are distinguishable phases rather than one obligatory sequence.

##### 13.1.1 True dilution (low-TDS / free-water states)

True dilution reflects water retained in excess of effective solute and excretory capacity. Infant water-intoxication cases demonstrate an acute free-water exposure, not harm from low mineral content alone (CDC, 1994; §[14.1](#ss_p10_sec_14_1)). Appropriate AVP suppression favours water excretion; filling, renal function and concurrent stress determine whether that response suffices.

##### 13.1.2 Maternal antidiuresis / excess AVP action

Maternal antidiuresis, altered fetal water–solute exposure and the fetal response are separate steps. Renal drug action need not require maternal AVP excess: sertraline enhanced AQP2 signalling in rat renal preparations (Kim et al., 2021; §[14.2](#ss_p10_sec_14_2)). That component does not establish fetal dilution or ASD mediation; maternal peptide transfer is not required for a maternal water-balance change to matter.

##### 13.1.3 Fetal AVP recruitment, persistence and withdrawal

Fetal hypoxia can recruit AVP (Raff and Wood, 1992; §§[10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3) and [14.3](#ss_p10_sec_14_3)). A dilutional route additionally requires available water and antidiuretic action sufficient for water retention relative to solute; delayed withdrawal is one proposed mechanism. Acute recruitment does not demonstrate failed termination or developmental recovery impairment.

#### 13.2 Sodium-Balance Failure Pathways

These represent disturbances that weaken sodium retention or mineralocorticoid-mediated sodium conservation.

##### 13.2.1 Salt-wasting phenotypes

Net sodium loss occurs when losses exceed replacement and conservation. Preterm infants can have negative sodium balance despite renin and aldosterone recruitment (Sulyok et al., 1979; Al-Dahhan et al., 1984; §[14.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_4)). Sodium concentration and filling also depend on water balance; the neonatal balance findings do not establish the proposed local recovery or ASD connection.

##### 13.2.2 Inadequate RAAS support / possible control reassignment

RAAS support is inadequate only relative to a demonstrated conservation or circulatory need. A low hormone value alone does not show failed support: FGF23-treated mice retained sodium while aldosterone fell (Andrukhova et al., 2014). Where support is deficient, alternative endocrine or vascular contributions may be recruited. Sections [14.5](#ss_p10_sec_14_5) and [16.10](#ss_p10_sec_16_10) distinguish hormone direction, renal response and proposed control reassignment.

#### 13.3 Perfusion-Energetic Sodium Stress

These routes concern possible energetic constraints on sodium transport when oxygen delivery or ATP support is inadequate.

##### 13.3.1 High-RAAS impact / angiotensin-dominant constriction

Ang II impaired endothelial redox/NO signalling in cultured cells (Chalupsky and Cai, 2005; §[14.6.7](#ss_p10_sec_14_6_7)). The further route from excessive vascular action to constrained microvascular delivery and ATP-supported ionic recovery remains conditional. High circulating input and excessive tissue responsiveness are distinct possibilities; neither is identified by plasma renin alone.

##### 13.3.2 Hypoxia-induced sodium stress

Hypoxia enters this route when oxygen limitation prevents adequate ATP-supported transport despite available sodium and endocrine compensation. In cultured postnatal rat hippocampal neurons, intracellular sodium returned to baseline after reoxygenation, whereas Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase blockade prevented recovery (Sheldon et al., 2004; §[14.7](#ss_p10_sec_14_7)). Fetal hypoxic endocrine recruitment is a separate measured component (Raff and Wood, 1992). The proposed delivery-related transport and developmental effects require their own endpoints. Hypoxia or hormone recruitment alone does not establish progressive hypotonicity.

#### 13.4 Cellular Osmolyte-Control Failure

These routes concern regulatory volume decrease and proposed impairment of osmolyte recovery following cellular swelling.

##### 13.4.1 Cytoskeletal volume-control disruption (actin / osmolyte axis)

Actin perturbation delayed regulatory volume decrease (RVD) in human HT-3 cells (Shen et al., 1999; §[14.8](#ss_p10_sec_14_8)). A distinct ionic comparator is methylmercury-induced RVD inhibition in neonatal-rat astrocytes, with recovery restored by extracellular sodium substitution (Vitarella et al., 1996). These findings support cellular volume-control components, not a shared fetal lesion across the listed toxicants or genes. Altered osmolyte recovery and systemic endocrine amplification require additional measurements linking local disturbance to the relevant response.

#### 13.5 Renal Sodium-Redistribution Pathway

This pathway asks whether proximal phosphate disposal and distal sodium conservation become insufficiently coordinated under a specified load.

##### 13.5.1 Dietary inorganic phosphate load

Phosphate loading engages absorption, renal phosphate transport and FGF23/Klotho regulation. A five-day human loading study raised FGF23 without detected changes in serum or urinary sodium, urine volume or weight; sodium matching was imperfect (Scotti Gerber et al., 2025; §[14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). Timing and compensating transport determine balance; phosphaturia alone does not establish salt wasting or developmental recovery failure.

Table [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1) maps each disturbance to its physiological mechanism, representative contributors, candidate genes or systems, and claim-specific evidence. Contributor cells distinguish ASD-associated exposures from physiological comparators and untested candidates; they do not assign every listed item an ASD association. Volume appearance is phase-dependent. Table [13.2](#ss_p10_table_13_2) retains the conditional endocrine patterns; §[14](#ss_p10_sec_14) and Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1) provide the fuller evidence and its limits.

Evidence key: \[E\] marks the stated empirical observation or association; \[S\], a measured physiological component; \[H\], a proposed response or mediation, as in Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1). These are claim roles, not a strength ranking. Gene names retain candidate correspondences. ASD genetic relevance and measured variant effects are separate claims, limited to individually sourced findings in §[6](#ss_p10_sec_6) and Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1); neither establishes assignment to this row. The proposed local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery link remains \[H\] unless directly measured. Physiological systems imply no ASD genetic association. This chart does not change the frozen genetic classification.

<td><p>Gene candidates [H]: SCN2A, SCN1A, SLC12A2, SLC12A5, ATP1A3, AVPR1A</p>
<p>Systems: AVPR1A (V1a), Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, NKCC1 / KCC2, endothelial surface layer</p></td>
<td>[E] Offspring behavioural differences after parental high-salt exposure in mice (Afroz et al., 2021, corrected 2022). [H] The fetal osmotic / recovery sequence; sodium and osmolality were unmeasured, and the study did not establish autism (§<a href="#ss_p10_sec_18_4">18.4</a>).</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Table [13.2](#ss_p10_table_13_2) separates the initiating state from conditional maternal and fetal responses. Its entries are working physiological predictions, not validated diagnostic signatures or obligatory stages. Renin, angiotensin action and aldosterone are not interchangeable measurements of RAAS; copeptin informs secretion-related activity rather than intact AVP clearance. Maternal and fetal values must be aligned by phase rather than assumed to move together. The proposed persistence depends on incomplete recovery, not on the presence of a transient response.
