<a name="ss_p10_sec_14"></a>

### 14 Mechanisms of Osmotic Pathways

The nine core mechanisms below develop the systemic and cellular routes mapped in Table [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1); its additional contexts are developed in §§[11](#ss_p10_sec_11), [18](#ss_p10_sec_18), and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7). Exposure associations and molecular findings support different claims; listed genetic correspondences remain candidates until variant-specific function is linked to the proposed route. Developmental mediation requires an identified disturbance of local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery in the relevant compartment and window (§[2](#ss_p10_sec_2); Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_1"></a>

#### 14.1 Mechanism — True Dilution

##### 14.1.1 Initiating condition and the canonical low-AVP geometry

True dilution is the reference case of water intake exceeding excretory capacity relative to solute availability. Low-mineral water alone does not establish that imbalance. Falling tonicity appropriately suppresses AVP, although underfilling or renal constraints can oppose water excretion. RAAS follows filling and renal signals; cortisol recruitment is a separate stress response. Copeptin reflects secretion rather than AVP clearance.

Reverse osmosis can substantially reduce mineral content, but it does not prescribe one final ionic concentration. In point-of-use dispensers studied by Sacchetti et al. (2015), mean total dissolved solids fell from 311 ± 45 mg/L in the incoming water to 43 ± 38 mg/L in unchilled RO output; mean output calcium and sodium were 7.0 and 4.0 mg/L. These are measured concentrations in that installation sample, not universal RO specifications, and dissolved-solids mass alone is not osmolarity. A dilutional signal still requires retained water in excess of the capacity to maintain solute–water balance; the treatment label alone does not demonstrate that state.

##### 14.1.2 The core mechanism — movement toward hypo-osmotic stress

Falling extracellular tonicity drives cellular swelling and volume-regulatory work, including changes in chloride and organic osmolytes. AVP suppression and renal water excretion normally restore the extracellular state; underfilling or limited renal capacity may prolong it. A cortisol-dominant response is a conditional extension, not the defining physiology of dilution.

##### 14.1.3 Water composition and developmental outcomes

Zeng et al. (2014) compared five drinking waters across rat reproduction and offspring development. Purified water produced the lowest pup survival at lactation day 21, whereas unfiltered tap water was associated with longer maze-learning latencies than the other four waters. In the memory probe trial, filtered tap water produced more platform-location crossings than tap water. The day-21 survival result followed day-4 litter standardisation, and earlier survival differences did not follow a simple mineral-content gradient. The purified product had very low dissolved solids, but the paper does not establish that it was distilled or processed specifically by reverse osmosis. Selected contaminants were measured alongside minerals. Their co-variation leaves pollutant, mineral-nutrition and maternal or lactational mechanisms unresolved. Maternal serum zinc correlated positively with offspring memory, without establishing a causal nutrient effect. Maternal and pup blood sodium and osmolality were not reported in the main study. Better maze performance among purified-water survivors does not explain the mortality finding; survivor selection is a possibility, not a demonstrated bias. The experiment raises a substantive question about water composition and early-life outcomes, while leaving osmotic mediation and any relevance to autism untested.

Human evidence distinguishes excess free-water exposure from low mineral content itself. The CDC infant cases involved water given in addition to or in place of formula, including tap water; they do not establish harm from correctly prepared formula made with low-mineral water (CDC, 1994). The German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment found no adverse effects warranting avoidance of very-low-mineral water with a balanced diet and normal drinking quantities, while acknowledging evidence gaps and the importance of total calcium and magnesium intake during pregnancy and lactation (BfR, 2020). The relevant osmotic exposure is the balance of water intake, dietary solute and excretory capacity, rather than the treatment label alone.

Contaminant exposure, nutritional contribution and net free-water balance are distinct questions. Water labels or survival and behavioural differences alone cannot identify a dilutional developmental mechanism. Geographic prevalence variation does not establish a water-chemistry cause. Across 16 US surveillance sites, identified autism prevalence in eight-year-olds ranged from 9.7 to 53.1 per 1,000 in 2022, alongside substantial differences in identification and service practices (Shaw et al., 2025). Apparent alignment with geological or hydrogeologic boundaries remains a hypothesis requiring measured exposure and physiological consequences, with ascertainment, population structure and correlated exposures distinguished.

##### 14.1.4 Secondary interactions — solvent effects and cytoskeletal vulnerability

Low mineral content and contact-material toxicants are separate exposure questions: total dissolved solids do not specify a toxicant dose. A combined route requires demonstrated water–solute imbalance alongside a specified toxicant effect on recovery or regulation (Sections [14.8](#ss_p10_sec_14_8) and [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). Actin-related recovery and phosphate handling provide possible additional amplifiers (Sections [14.8](#ss_p10_sec_14_8) and [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)), not consequences of low TDS alone.

##### 14.1.5 Scope clarification of true dilution and solute-driven water redistribution

Non-remineralised household or municipal water can provide little solute, whereas some products supply substantial salt. Neither label establishes the physiological state: total diet, final feed composition and retained water matter. Solute-loading and glucose-related routes are distinguished in Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7).

##### 14.1.6 Peripartum and early-infancy analogues

Peripartum fluid loading can produce dilutional hyponatraemia; in a prospective labour cohort, total fluid volume, but not oxytocin administration, remained independently associated with this outcome (Moen et al., 2009). Oxytocin nevertheless has a demonstrated antidiuretic action: human infusion reduced urine volume and free-water clearance and increased urinary AQP2 excretion in healthy volunteers and patients with central diabetes insipidus (Joo et al., 2004). V2-receptor dependence and increased apical AQP2 trafficking were demonstrated separately during five-day oxytocin infusion in male AVP-deficient Brattleboro rats (Li et al., 2008). These findings support a water-retention component while distinguishing the human exposure from the experimental renal mechanism. AVP, RAAS and cortisol responses then depend on tonicity, filling, renal function and labour-related stress.

Hypotonic intravenous fluids or peripartum free-water loading enter this route when net delivery exceeds excretory and solute-handling capacity. In infant feeding, the relevant exposure is the final feed and water–solute balance, not preparation-water mineral content alone.

##### 14.1.7 Endocrine adaptation and cortisol-dominant imprinting

Maternal and fetal responses depend on their own filling and tonicity. Appropriate AVP suppression remains protective; a cortisol-weighted developmental response is a further hypothesis.

Prenatal steroid biology provides a relevant observation, but the measured compartment matters. In amniotic-fluid samples from 128 males later diagnosed with autism and 217 controls, a shared steroidogenic factor spanning cortisol and four sex steroids was elevated (Baron-Cohen et al., 2015). This was not a measurement of maternal cortisol, dilution or cortisol-mediated sodium defence, and it did not identify which maternal, placental or fetal source generated the difference. It supports investigating the prenatal steroid environment without assigning the sodium–volume route in advance.

**Hypothesis.** During a demonstrated sodium–volume challenge, glucocorticoid-dependent support could preserve circulation while changing the balance of renal and vascular regulation. Whether it expands effective volume or suppresses renin depends on the exposure and tissue response; these effects do not establish increased fetal cortisol. In five isolated term human placentas, inhibition of 11β-HSD activity increased cortisol transfer to the fetal circuit, demonstrating a regulated transmission step (Stirrat et al., 2018). The proposed chain therefore requires both altered maternal physiology and a measured change in fetal exposure, rather than an assumed loss of placental protection.

A lasting fetal change would involve altered receptor availability, occupancy or downstream responsiveness after the initiating disturbance resolves. It need not imply changed receptor identity or permanent cortisol dominance; later water, clearance or glycaemic challenges could reveal the proposed altered response.

True dilution begins with net water excess. Appropriate AVP suppression and water excretion can restore balance; the developmental proposal concerns constraints that prolong the disturbance or leave cellular recovery incomplete. This provides the comparator for the subsequent osmotic routes.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_2"></a>

#### 14.2 Mechanism: Maternal Antidiuresis and Excess AVP Action

##### 14.2.1 Initiating condition and maternal–fetal exposure asymmetry

Maternal antidiuresis, from AVP or a drug-induced renal action (Section [14.2.3](#ss_p10_sec_14_2_3)), may change fetal water–solute conditions through placental exchange. Placental metabolism and limited peptide transfer separate maternal AVP from fetal dose: the exposure need not involve maternal hormone crossing. The fetus responds to its own conditions, so suppression during dilution can be appropriate; persistent exposure–response mismatch is the additional developmental hypothesis.

##### 14.2.2 The core mechanism — signal mismatch and compensatory recruitment

Maternal and fetal endocrine states can diverge because their filling, tonicity and regulatory capacity differ. Fetal RAAS or cortisol recruitment requires fetal need, not merely maternal AVP excess or fetal AVP suppression. Where fetal hypotonicity coexists with circulatory threat, Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3) supplies the mixed-cue AVP prediction.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_2_3"></a>

##### 14.2.3 Empirical support: distinct pharmacological disturbances of water–sodium balance

Drugs can disturb sodium and water handling through distinct renal mechanisms, including actions that do not require increased AVP. In adults, oxcarbazepine reduced water-load excretion without an accompanying rise in circulating AVP (Sachdeo et al., 2002). Oxytocin produced V2-mediated antidiuresis in AVP-deficient rats (Li et al., 2008), and sertraline increased AQP2 abundance and trafficking through V2R–cAMP–PKA signalling in rat collecting-duct preparations without AVP stimulation (Kim et al., 2021). Thiazides affect renal sodium transport and water excretion; a hydrochlorothiazide–amiloride rechallenge caused a greater sodium fall in susceptible patients without a greater measured AVP response than in controls (Friedman et al., 1989). These are distinct mechanisms and experimental settings, not a common maternal hormone signature. Their relevance to this fetal pathway depends on a maternal water–solute disturbance producing a corresponding fetal exposure. This preserves a concrete convergence claim: different perturbations may place similar demands on defence and recovery, even when the initiating hormone profiles differ.

The ASD inference faces a separate test. In 1,580,629 Swedish offspring, Sujan et al. (2017) found that the first-trimester SSRI association fell from an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.66 (95% CI 1.46–1.89) to 0.81 (0.58–1.14) in sibling comparisons. For all antidepressants, the sibling estimate was 0.83 (0.62–1.13). Timing-of-exposure and paternal comparisons also supported familial confounding, while analyses using different exposure definitions yielded a consistent pattern. These findings weaken a causal interpretation of the population association. They do not negate sertraline’s experimental renal action, but that action cannot establish maternal dilution, fetal exposure or ASD mediation. The hypothesis therefore requires a measured physiological intermediary, rather than medication use as its proxy. Section [18.1.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_1_2) distinguishes this pregnancy-exposure contrast from the separate maternal-baseline proposal and explains the relevant design limitations.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_2_4"></a>

##### 14.2.4 Proposed secondary amplification: acetaminophen and AVP persistence

Impaired termination of an appropriate antidiuretic response is a possible point of amplification. AVP is a disulfide-bridged nonapeptide; rat proximal-tubule studies suggest a reduced-glutathione-dependent reduction step before further peptide cleavage, and human renal brush-border experiments demonstrate glutathione-sensitive AVP degradation (Carone et al., 1987; Fjellestad-Paulsen & Lundin, 1996). Once AVP has been filtered from plasma, slower luminal degradation could increase intact urinary peptide without prolonging its circulating action. Renal removal is nevertheless broader than filtration: isolated perfused rat kidneys cleared immunoreactive AVP at 1,145 ± 47 µL/min against a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 515 ± 37 µL/min (mean ± SE), indicating a substantial peritubular component (Rabkin et al., 1979). That experiment did not establish the component’s reduced-glutathione (GSH) dependence or whether loss of immunoreactivity equalled loss of biological activity. The proposed persistence mechanism requires reduced net removal of biologically active circulating AVP, assessed separately from tissue degradation or urinary peptide recovery.

Therapeutic-dose human studies supply a measured glutathione component. In a randomised crossover study enrolling 12 healthy adults, two 15 mg/kg acetaminophen doses six hours apart lowered plasma GSH on a sulfur-amino-acid-free diet (paired n = 9), but not on the adequate diet (n = 10; Mannery et al., 2010). A separate 24-person crossover reported decreased whole-blood GSH after 1 g four times daily for four days with N-acetylcysteine placebo, whereas GSH was maintained with N-acetylcysteine (Pickering et al., 2019). Both arms of the latter study received acetaminophen. These findings support context-dependent GSH effects, but measured neither renal-site availability nor AVP clearance. They do not establish the proposed sequence in pregnancy.

Reduced local GSH could constrain renal AVP processing, but prolonging intact circulating AVP also depends on other clearance pathways and compensatory secretion. Antidiuresis and dilution additionally require renal responsiveness and available water. Therapeutic acetaminophen producing this sequence remains unestablished; illness, oxidative stress and dosing are candidate modifiers. Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) distinguishes GSH-sensitive processing from zinc-dependent LNPEP/IRAP cleavage and systemic GSH depletion. Neither clearance route is established as the physiological bottleneck in this setting.

Acetaminophen epidemiology constrains this proposal. Among 2,480,797 Swedish children, the adjusted association with autism was small (hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 1.02–1.08) and was absent in sibling comparisons (0.98, 0.93–1.04; Ahlqvist et al., 2024). Exposure measurement did not resolve every dose, duration or developmental window, and the study did not measure AVP clearance. The proposed clearance mechanism requires evidence that a therapeutic exposure prolongs active AVP action. A developmental contribution additionally requires a consequential disturbance and altered local recovery; the epidemiological measurement limits supply no evidence for either step. Postnatal findings are separate: Bittker and Bell (2018) reported an acetaminophen association in a retrospective parent survey; the estimate remained positive but did not reach statistical significance in a model also including ibuprofen. Exposure reports were not independently verified, and the study did not measure AVP or recovery mediation.

D’Antonio et al. (2026) likewise found no association with autism in their sibling-comparison synthesis, which was dominated by the same Ahlqvist cohort and therefore provides overlapping synthesis rather than an independent replication.

###### ***14.2.4.1 Neonatal randomised evidence and the formulation question***

PreParaS randomised 48 infants born before 32 weeks to early intravenous paracetamol or placebo. The regimen began within 24 hours of birth with 20 mg/kg, followed by 7.5 mg/kg every six hours for four days (Härkin et al., 2016). The trial registry identifies Perfalgan 10 mg/mL (EudraCT 2013-001842-33). At two years, 44 infants were assessed: Griffiths developmental results were similar between groups and no signs of autism were reported (Juujärvi et al., 2019). The five-year parental survey included 39 children and found neurological or neuropsychiatric symptoms uncommon, without an adverse pattern in the paracetamol group (Juujärvi et al., 2022).

Perfalgan product information lists mannitol among its excipients (Bristol-Myers Squibb, 2010). This identifies a formulation variable, not an established protective effect. Whether the excipient altered water or electrolyte handling in PreParaS requires confirmation of the administered mannitol dose and measured effects under that neonatal regimen. A concentration reported for another intravenous paracetamol product cannot establish the trial’s excipient exposure.

These small follow-ups constrain developmental-harm claims for the neonatal regimen studied; they do not provide a precise ASD-specific risk estimate or test prenatal exposure. An unmeasured mannitol effect cannot explain away their reassuring findings. The proposed persistence mechanism still requires direct evidence of altered active AVP exposure and consequential recovery disturbance. Neither this proposal nor the observational medication associations justify changing indicated treatment to prevent autism.

##### 14.2.5 Hypothesis-level extension: endocrine imprinting during repeated defence

**Hypothesis.** Repeated discordant fetal osmotic and circulatory cues, or incomplete recovery, could alter receptor responsiveness, stress-axis reliance or later regulatory thresholds. The proposed imprint concerns function after the initiating exposure resolves, rather than maternal hormone concentration or appropriate acute fetal suppression alone.

Maternal antidiuresis is an upstream water-balance exposure; fetal mismatch is a further step. Maternal water retention may change fetal water–solute conditions, but fetal response and recovery determine whether developmental recalibration follows. Maternal and fetal hormone concentrations cannot substitute for one another.

<a name="ss_p10_table_14_1"></a>**Table [14.1](#ss_p10_table_14_1). Pharmacological disturbances of water–sodium balance and conditional fetal exposure**

| **Mechanism**                                                   | **Examples**                                                                 | **Possible consequence and missing link**                                                                                                     |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Drug-specific impairment of water excretion or sodium transport | Oxcarbazepine; oxytocin; thiazides; sertraline (renal experimental evidence) | Possible maternal water–solute disturbance; fetal exposure requires evidence of transmission. AVP excess does not follow from exposure alone. |
| Teratogenic comparator                                          | Valproate                                                                    | Sodium–volume mediation unestablished here; receptor and osmotic intermediates require direct evidence.                                       |

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_3"></a>

#### 14.3 Mechanism: Fetal AVP recruitment, persistence and withdrawal

##### 14.3.1 Initiating condition: fetal AVP recruitment

Fetal AVP recruitment is a measured response to challenge: acute hypoxaemia increased AVP in chronically instrumented sheep fetuses, with gestational-age and pressure dependence and without a concurrent rise in plasma renin activity (Raff and Wood, 1992; Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3); Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1)). This recruitment is distinct from the proposed failure to terminate antidiuretic action after its stimulus resolves. Maternal sodium loading alone does not establish fetal hypertonicity; the osmotic branch requires a demonstrated fetal stimulus.

##### 14.3.2 The core mechanism — time-lagged equilibration and delayed dilution

A dilutional rebound requires antidiuretic action to persist while the initial solute stimulus declines and water remains available. Its timing depends on AVP secretion and clearance, renal responsiveness and maternal–fetal exchange; neither salt loading nor a glucose fall makes rebound automatic.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_3_3"></a>

##### 14.3.3 Endocrine response: conditional responses during recovery

RAAS responses differ between expansion and underfilling, while cortisol follows additional stress inputs. The proposed sequence therefore has phase-dependent endocrine responses rather than one fixed hormone signature.

Adult experiments show that volume-regulatory sodium excretion can accompany continuing antidiuresis. After oral water loading in three patients with SIADH and five healthy participants given intranasal desmopressin, plasma atrial natriuretic factor and urinary sodium excretion increased during water retention, with a later aldosterone decrease (Cogan et al., 1988). A separate saline-loading experiment in eight healthy adults on a low-sodium diet found natriuresis with RAAS suppression without increased mean arterial pressure, GFR or ANP (Rasmussen et al., 2003). The recruited effectors therefore depend on the challenge. Paired water and sodium balances distinguish corrective excretion from net depletion; these adult component findings do not establish a fetal sequence or developmental effect.

##### 14.3.4 Candidate endocrine imprinting after incomplete recovery

Hypothesis. Repeatedly mistimed AVP action or additional endocrine recruitment could change later renal V₂ responsiveness, osmotic thresholds or sodium–volume defence activation. The proposed imprint arises from unstable recovery dynamics rather than brief compensated dilution and must persist beyond the initiating episode.

##### 14.3.5 Testing AVP recruitment and recovery

Cord copeptin could contribute to testing fetal AVP secretion, interpreted alongside sampling time, fetal tonicity, filling and birth-related stress. It does not by itself establish a preceding salt exposure, distinguish all proposed pathways or measure intact-AVP clearance. A diagnostic signature for this proposed recovery mechanism has not been established.

This route concerns a mismatch between a resolved osmotic stimulus and continuing antidiuretic action. When available water permits subsequent dilution and recovery remains incomplete, repeated episodes could recalibrate later responses; timely termination and full recovery interrupt the proposed sequence.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_4"></a>

#### 14.4 Mechanism — Salt-Wasting Phenotypes

##### 14.4.1 Initiating condition: sodium loss exceeding conservation

True salt wasting is net sodium loss beyond replacement and conservation. Unlike dilution, it removes solute; associated volume loss depends on water balance. The defence triad may respond appropriately without every component reaching a maximum or closing the deficit.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_4_2"></a>

##### 14.4.2 Core physiology — coupled electrolyte loss and impaired recovery

Salt-wasting can combine sodium depletion with potassium or magnesium disturbance, but the coupling is specific to the cause. In sodium-depleted rats, concurrent potassium depletion prevented the usual ENaC activation, despite increased abundance of upstream sodium transporters (Frindt et al., 2011). This is a trade-off between conservation tasks, not a rule that potassium deficiency abolishes sodium reabsorption. At the cellular level, TauT/SLC6A6 transports taurine with sodium and chloride (Uchida et al., 1992). The proposed recovery problem is that impaired gradients or transporter regulation could delay replenishment of osmolytes lost during defence. A specific magnesium-dependent TauT defect and its effect in developing neurons or astrocytes require direct evidence. The retained prediction is coupled recovery demand: restoring circulating balance and rebuilding cellular osmolyte reserves may impose different constraints after the same episode.

Infant urinary infection and uropathy provide a defined renal salt-wasting initiator. Six infants aged nine days to seven months with E. coli urinary infection and urinary tract abnormalities developed hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis, with increased fractional sodium excretion despite markedly elevated aldosterone ([Rodríguez-Soriano et al., 1983](#ss_revsyn1_ref_RodriguezSoriano1983)). This clinical pattern supports transient tubular aldosterone resistance, termed secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism. Treatment largely normalised the measured disturbances. A later four-infant series, including two girls and two boys, documented recurrence with infection after previously observed hydronephrosis had resolved in one infant, supporting an infection-associated contribution without persistent obstruction ([Nandagopal et al., 2009](#ss_revsyn1_ref_Nandagopal2009)). These selected cases establish a clinically important phenotype, not its frequency among all infants with UTI.

The proposed sequence is conditional: impaired renal sodium conservation can increase replacement and circulatory-defence demands; persistent depletion, altered water balance or recurrent episodes could then constrain local neural or glial ionic and cell-volume recovery during a sensitive interval. Timely treatment and successful renal recovery could interrupt the proposed sequence. The clinical reports establish neither molecular ENaC blockade nor a male distal-reserve deficit, and the hyperkalaemic phenotype must be kept separate from the potassium-depletion/ammoniagenesis branch in Section [33.1.2](#ss_p10_sec_33_1_2). Existing clinical records and longitudinal cohorts could distinguish the salt-wasting subgroup from uncomplicated infection using paired electrolyte, renal and recovery trajectories, followed by developmental observations. Normal serum chemistry alone would neither demonstrate nor exclude compensatory work; the proposed developmental contribution still requires the local recovery intermediary, rather than treating peripheral renal dysfunction as its substitute.

Infection histories provide a separate epidemiological question. In a record-based comparison of 403 children with ASD and 2,100 controls, first-month infection diagnoses were more frequent in the ASD group (22.6% versus 18.7%), while genitourinary diagnoses were more frequent across the first two years despite fewer children having any recorded infection over that whole interval ([Rosen et al., 2007](#ss_revsyn1_ref_Rosen2007)). The neonatal comparison concerned any infection, not specifically UTI; the genitourinary finding concerns a different exposure interval.

The Danish cohort analysed hospitalised perinatal/neonatal infection from birth through 28 days separately, with adjusted ASD HR 1.16 (95% CI 0.97–1.39). Childhood infection began after 28 days, and its first age stratum extended from 29 days to 17 months. Childhood UTI estimates were 1.14 (0.87–1.49) overall, 1.13 (0.82–1.58) in boys and 1.10 (0.70–1.74) in girls, without a demonstrated sex interaction (p = .76). Broad childhood-infection associations also showed no significant modification across the tested age strata (p = .46). Noninfectious somatic admission was associated with ASD diagnosis, HR 1.76 (1.68–1.86), keeping illness selection and ascertainment among the alternatives ([Atladóttir et al., 2010](#ss_revsyn1_ref_Atladottir2010)).

The narrower renal hypothesis concerns a documented salt-wasting episode and its recovery during a specified developmental interval. The nine-day to seven-month range in the [Rodríguez-Soriano et al. (1983)](#ss_revsyn1_ref_RodriguezSoriano1983) series spans both Danish exposure windows; early infancy was not simply omitted. Those broad categories did not isolate tubular aldosterone resistance, sodium balance or neural recovery. A comparison of infants with UTI and measured salt wasting against similarly ill infants with preserved sodium conservation could test the proposed distinction using existing records or cohorts. Age pooling does not demonstrate a hidden effect, and the sex-specific estimates do not support an older-girl dilution explanation. Maternal pregnancy infection remains a separate exposure (Section [18.5](#ss_p10_sec_18_5)).

##### 14.4.3 Clinical archetype — hyperemesis gravidarum (HG)

Hyperemesis can combine sodium and water loss with potassium or magnesium disturbance and metabolic stress. The resulting state depends on losses, intake, replacement and renal compensation, rather than a compulsory joint AVP–RAAS–cortisol rise.

##### 14.4.4 Mechanistic spectrum — causes of true sodium loss

Table [14.2](#ss_p10_table_14_2) separates mechanisms of net sodium loss from dilution and redistribution comparators. Depletion develops when replacement and available conservation cannot close the loss.

| **Mechanism / Context**                                     | **Primary Driver**                                                                                                 | **Conditional response in the affected individual**                                                                                                                                | **Clinical consequences and fetal inference**                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Hyperemesis gravidarum**                                  | Vomiting → Na⁺ & volume loss                                                                                       | Unreplaced losses can recruit AVP and RAAS as effective filling falls, if the axes respond; cortisol is assessed separately.                                                       | Maternal depletion may occur when losses exceed replacement; fetal stress requires independent fetal evidence.                                                  |
| **Renal tubular loss** *(e.g., Bartter/Gitelman analogues)* | NaCl transport defects; Mg²⁺ loss                                                                                  | Renin and aldosterone can rise despite ongoing renal loss; defect, treatment and developmental phase matter. No fixed AVP/cortisol direction (Laghmani et al., 2016).              | Fetal renal polyuria can cause polyhydramnios in antenatal Bartter disease; maternal tubular disease does not imply the same fetal phenotype.                   |
| **Adrenal insufficiency: specify the deficient hormone(s)** | Mineralocorticoid deficiency can impair sodium conservation; glucocorticoid deficiency can impair water excretion. | In primary disease, renin can rise despite deficient aldosterone; AVP can remain active during hypotonicity when cortisol is deficient (Oelkers et al., 1992; Kamoi et al., 1993). | Sodium loss, water retention or both are possible; identify lesion, balance and replacement before inferring fetal effects.                                     |
| **Prematurity: neonatal renal adaptation**                  | Immature reabsorption                                                                                              | High renin/aldosterone can coexist with neonatal sodium loss; renal effectiveness and timing matter (Sulyok et al., 1979). No fixed AVP direction.                                 | Deficient sodium intake relative to losses can impair growth; assess balance and concentration separately (Al-Dahhan et al., 1984).                             |
| **Iatrogenic causes**                                       | Separate diuretic sodium loss from retained hypotonic-fluid dilution.                                              | Responses depend on drug, filling and tonicity; hyponatraemia alone does not establish increased AVP (Friedman et al., 1989).                                                      | Maternal or neonatal depletion, dilution or overlap must be distinguished; a fluid load is not itself net sodium loss.                                          |
| **Proposed placental/amniotic redistribution**              | Redistribution may change exposure without net fetal sodium loss; total compartment balance is decisive.           | Fetal AVP and RAAS responses depend on demonstrated changes in tonicity and filling, not an isolated amniotic concentration.                                                       | Amniotic concentration can rise while solute leaves the cavity (ovine experiment: Brace et al., 2004); polyhydramnios alone does not establish fetal depletion. |

##### 14.4.5 Endocrine consequence — persistent activation and receptor drift

**Hypothesis.** Severe or recurrent salt loss with incomplete recovery could leave altered conservation thresholds, receptor responsiveness or autonomic tone after balance is restored, potentially favouring stress-weighted defence. Normal post-recovery regulation would oppose persistence despite substantial acute compensation.

Salt wasting distinguishes net loss despite conservation from antidiuretic action that outlasts its stimulus; both can coexist. Continued or recurrent depletion may impose recovery costs, while a lasting stress-weighted response remains a hypothesis about regulation after the acute deficit resolves.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_14_5"></a>

#### 14.5 Mechanism: Renal handling and adequacy of RAAS support

##### 14.5.1 Initiating condition: inadequate support relative to need

RAAS support is deficient only relative to a measured conservation or circulatory need. Low renin alone may instead reflect volume expansion or effective downstream retention. Control reassignment is proposed where alternative responses compensate for genuinely inadequate support.

##### 14.5.2 Core mechanism: altered renal sodium handling and candidate alternative support

Phosphate–FGF23/Klotho effects on NCC do not imply uniform renin suppression or failed sodium conservation (Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). Cortisol-weighted support and redox-dependent vascular regulation are distinct candidate modifiers (Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8)).

##### 14.5.3 Environmental and clinical candidates for altered RAAS recruitment

Environmental and physiological contributors may alter RAAS recruitment through different routes. The proposed maternal thyroid-related pathway, for example, requires separate assessment of maternal cardiac output, renal water handling and fetal response; it does not establish one shared maternal–fetal hormone pattern.

<a name="ss_p10_table_14_3"></a>**Table [14.3](#ss_p10_table_14_3). Candidate changes in RAAS support: measured responses and developmental questions**

| **Scenario and evidence status**                                       | **Mechanism or directional evidence**                                                                                                                                                | **Cortisol interpretation**                                                                          | **Developmental implication and boundary**                                                                                                            |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Measured component: phosphate / FGF23**                              | Recombinant FGF23 in adult mice: NCC-mediated Na⁺ retention; aldosterone decreased, plasma renin activity unchanged (Andrukhova et al., 2014).                                       | Separate candidate support, not established cortisol substitution.                                   | Altered maternal sodium handling could change fetal exposure; the mouse experiment does not establish human dietary or fetal mediation.               |
| **Candidate extension: low-TDS / RO water**                            | Retained water relative to total solute intake and renal clearance determines the proposed challenge; processing method alone assigns no RAAS direction (§[14.1](#ss_p10_sec_14_1)). | Low mineral content does not establish cortisol recruitment.                                         | The candidate route depends on maternal imbalance and a consequential fetal exposure.                                                                 |
| **Candidate extension: cortisol excess and persistence**               | Effects depend on dose, renal receptor action, volume balance and distinct renin/aldosterone responses.                                                                              | Functional support during exposure differs from altered responsiveness persisting after recovery.    | Maternal cortisol excess alone establishes neither transmitted exposure nor persistent fetal mis-tuning.                                              |
