<a name="ss_p10_sec_16"></a>

### 16 Mechanisms of Volume Pathways

These ten mechanisms concern actual filling, regional delivery or their sensing and regulation, as organised in the two panels of Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1). Each retains its own intermediary: actual underdelivery does not require low total volume or sensory error, and a sensing defect need not occur with adequate circulation. The proposed developmental convergence is impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery (§[2](#ss_p10_sec_2)), not a uniform hormone pattern.

The sections distinguish evidence for an initiating exposure from the additional claim that it alters placental delivery, endocrine regulation or early-life recovery. Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1) collects the exposure evidence.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_1"></a>

#### 16.1 Mechanism — True Volume Loss

True volume loss removes sodium-bearing fluid. Extracellular reserve and arterial filling fall when losses exceed replacement and buffering. Maternal depletion may threaten uteroplacental delivery; fetal oxygenation, pressure and filling remain separate consequences to establish.

Baroreflex and renal conservation can defend circulation while replacement proceeds, with stress-axis support depending on severity and capacity. Redistribution may protect vital delivery but cannot replace lost fluid; absolute depletion distinguishes this route from containment or signalling failure.

Major entry points include haemorrhage, hyperemesis gravidarum, diarrhoeal illness, burns, adrenal insufficiency, renal tubular salt loss, and other states in which sodium and water leave the body faster than recovery systems can replace them.

Hyperemesis illustrates combined fluid, sodium and potassium loss with metabolic stress. Its endocrine pattern depends on losses, replacement and regulatory capacity (Section [14.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_4)).

Recorded maternal HG was associated with offspring disability-service use for neurodevelopmental disorders in a population cohort; the authors reported that most outcome associations did not persist in exposure-discordant sibling analyses (Pont et al., 2025). HG therefore remains a model of possible maternal fluid loss rather than an established ASD determinant.

Haemorrhage and salt-wasting crises are timing-dependent delivery threats whose significance depends on severity, recurrence, recovery and maternal–fetal buffering.

Reduced filling can recruit non-osmotic AVP and renin–angiotensin support. Aldosterone additionally depends on potassium and adrenal capacity; cortisol follows stress and developmental context. Fetal recruitment follows fetal disturbance, not maternal hormone values. The defence triad protects perfusion without requiring all outputs to rise together (Table [10.1](#ss_p10_table_10_1)).

Hypothesis. Recurrent depletion with incomplete recovery may lower later thresholds for perfusion defence. The proposed imprint is altered response or recovery after filling is restored, not persistent hyponatraemia or lasting recalibration inferred from the diagnosis alone.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_2"></a>

#### 16.2 Mechanism — Volume Redistribution

Redistribution reduces effective filling when fluid accumulates outside the compartments supporting arterial supply. Total water may remain normal or increased: the deficit is centrally available fluid rather than absolute loss.

Third-spacing, interstitial oedema and serosal sequestration can reduce central availability. Unlike primary barrier failure, this spatial route does not require endothelial leak or loss of oncotic support as its initiating lesion.

Inflammatory oedema and ascitic or serosal trapping are representative settings. Adiposity, gestational diabetes and insulin resistance enter this route only where altered distribution or return is demonstrated.

Reduced lymphatic clearance, compliant interstitium and slow return from third spaces can prolong underfilling.

Observational associations of maternal body mass index in early pregnancy, gestational weight gain or diabetes with offspring ASD do not identify redistribution as the mediator (Gardner et al., 2015; Xiang et al., 2018). The proposed bridge is measured interstitial trapping or impaired return, potentially alongside metabolic inflammation and endothelial stress; placental, metabolic and direct developmental routes remain alternatives.

Redistribution can recruit non-osmotic AVP and renin despite overall fluid abundance when effective filling falls. Aldosterone and cortisol retain their additional controls (Table [10.1](#ss_p10_table_10_1); Section [15](#ss_p10_sec_15)). Oedema can therefore coexist with genuine arterial scarcity without prescribing a fixed endocrine profile.

Hypothesis. Recurrent oedematous underfilling may recalibrate later volume defence so that it is recruited too readily even after effective filling recovers. The initiating disturbance remains actual fluid mislocation, not fluid abundance alone.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_3"></a>

#### 16.3 Mechanism — Barrier / Oncotic Failure

Barrier or oncotic failure reduces intravascular retention. Total fluid can increase while effective filling falls because plasma water escapes or oncotic support cannot retain it.

Endothelial junction opening, glycocalyx injury, inflammatory vasoplegia or reduced oncotic pressure can compromise effective filling. The defining lesion is retention failure rather than redistribution alone. Section [35.1](#ss_p10_sec_35_1) distinguishes vascular surface injury from cellular bilayer oxidation and their possible convergence.

Severe endothelial inflammation, hypoalbuminaemia, nephrotic protein loss and hepatic synthetic failure can impair retention. Maternal infection, autoimmunity or specified particle exposures qualify through demonstrated permeability, albumin or filling effects; fever or exposure detection alone does not identify a leak state.

Weak junctional resilience, high VEGF tone, limited lymphatic rescue or low albumin reserve may prolong oedematous underfilling.

Maternal infection raises a specific question: does it alter maternal or fetal barriers, effective filling or placental delivery? This route may interact with direct immune effects on the developing brain, but an exposure association does not distinguish them or demonstrate leakage.

Maternal autoimmune associations are more heterogeneous and vulnerable to bias. They motivate a possible endothelial-leak route rather than a uniform ASD determinant.

Neonatal illness supplies component evidence. Among 47 term newborns, suspected infection was associated with less continuous skin microvascular flow without shock or severe sepsis; flow often improved as inflammatory indices declined (Alba-Alejandre et al., 2013). Of 196 septic neonates in a retrospective study, 59 had clinically classified capillary leak; oedema began a median three days after admission and lasted a median five days in survivors (Cao et al., 2025). Permeability was not directly measured. Glucose was higher in the leak group, but its adjusted association with leak was not significant. These findings establish neither glucose causation, brain hypoperfusion nor necessarily failed recovery.

Loss of effective filling can recruit AVP and sodium-conserving RAAS support. Renin, aldosterone and cortisol additionally depend on renal, potassium, adrenal and inflammatory conditions (Table [10.1](#ss_p10_table_10_1); Section [15](#ss_p10_sec_15)). The defining state is oedema with measured underfilling, not endocrine scarcity or a fixed hormone pattern.

Hypothesis. Recurrent oedematous underfilling may lower later thresholds for non-osmotic AVP and stress-weighted perfusion defence, even after retention recovers. The proposed recalibration links repeated retention failure to subsequent regulation.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_4"></a>

#### 16.4 Mechanism — Vascular Containment Failure

In vascular containment failure, excessive venous capacitance or weak recoil reduces central filling despite near-normal intravascular volume. The fluid has neither left the body nor entered a third space.

Excessive compliance or insufficient venous tone leaves more blood in capacitance vessels and reduces return to the heart. This is a broad containment problem, distinct from expansion of one regional reservoir.

Candidate contexts include connective-tissue laxity, pregnancy, prolonged standing, heat, deconditioning and orthostatic intolerance. These contexts enter the proposed pathway only where altered venous capacitance, recoil or constriction demonstrably reduces central return.

Hypermobility provides a clinically motivated context, but joint laxity alone does not establish excessive venous capacitance. The relevant intermediary is reduced recoil or altered venous mechanics that compromises central filling.

Csecs et al. (2022) compared 109 adults with autism, ADHD or Tourette syndrome, including co-occurrence, with 57 controls; 30 participants had autism. Hypermobility and self-reported orthostatic symptoms were elevated. Mean orthostatic scores were 24.2 versus 5.1 out of 120, and Beighton scores correlated with symptoms (Spearman r = 0.39).

Neither joint examination nor symptom scores measured venous mechanics or central filling; statistical mediation cannot establish that intermediary. The findings motivate a defined containment subgroup, not hypermobility as a universal autistic feature.

Sufficiently reduced central filling can recruit non-osmotic AVP. Renin and aldosterone depend on renal perfusion, potassium, posture and adaptation; cortisol-mediated tone support is a further candidate response (Table [10.1](#ss_p10_table_10_1); Section [15](#ss_p10_sec_15)). The proposed burden is maintaining central availability of otherwise present volume.

Hypothesis. Recurrent containment failure could recalibrate volume defence so that posture, heat and ordinary stressors recruit it more readily after the initiating disturbance. Successful recovery remains an alternative to persistent defensive regulation.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_5"></a>

#### 16.5 Mechanism — Splanchnic Pooling / Reservoir Shift

Splanchnic pooling sequesters intravascular volume in a regional reservoir, reducing central availability despite preserved total volume. It differs from generalised containment failure because the rest of the vascular container may remain competent.

Mesenteric capacitance vessels can retain substantial blood. Excessive expansion after meals or with histamine-linked vasodilation is a candidate route to reduced central filling without external fluid loss. In ten supine healthy men, passive heating increased cutaneous vascular conductance while reducing central and hepatic blood-volume estimates (Crandall et al., 2008). Heat can therefore challenge central filling through a different regional redistribution pattern; it does not by itself identify mesenteric sequestration.

Postprandial pooling, large carbohydrate loads, mast-cell or histamine states, dysautonomia, and cirrhosis-like reservoir expansion are representative drivers.

Slow splanchnic emptying, unstable mesenteric sympathetic tone or hypermobility-linked visceral dysregulation could prolong sequestration.

Autonomic and orthostatic findings in subsets of autistic individuals, particularly with hypermobility, motivate this reservoir hypothesis (Section [16.4](#ss_p10_sec_16_4)). They do not locate the reservoir or establish sequestration; recurrent measured pooling, rather than the diagnosis, defines the proposed subgroup.

Pooling can recruit non-osmotic AVP when central filling falls sufficiently. Renal, potassium, postural and adaptive inputs determine renin and aldosterone; cortisol-linked support is an additional hypothesis (Table [10.1](#ss_p10_table_10_1); Section [15](#ss_p10_sec_15)). The physiological deficit is central availability, not total body volume.

Hypothesis. Repeated meal- or posture-linked reservoir shifts could bias subsequent regulation toward anticipating central scarcity during ordinary autonomic transitions, particularly when recovery is incomplete.

##### 16.5.1 Maternal posture and gestational load

Maternal posture and mechanical venous-return constraints provide a related filling comparison, separate from demonstrated splanchnic pooling. Gestational weight gain is an epidemiological lead, not a measurement of circulatory load. Gardner et al. (2015) reported a U-shaped population association with offspring ASD; the excessive-gain sibling estimate among women with normal baseline BMI was OR 1.48 (95% CI 0.93–2.38). The interval leaves uncertainty, while the study measured neither venous pooling nor sodium–volume mediation. The hypothesis therefore treats weight gain as a candidate exposure marker whose physiological meaning must be established.

Pregnancy couples volume expansion to vascular and cardiac adaptation, but greater weight gain does not automatically mean lower preload. In 1,752 women followed across pregnancy, greater gestational gain was associated with higher stroke volume and lower peripheral resistance; the authors cautioned that gains were modest and their findings could not be extended to excessive gain (Ling et al., 2022). A separate mechanical signal is more direct: among 40 women studied in four postures from 20 weeks to term, upright pelvic-vessel compression was accompanied by reported reductions of 22% in stroke volume and 11% in cardiac output despite a compensatory heart-rate rise (Schneider et al., 1993). That establishes a posture-dependent filling challenge in the studied setting, not a weight-gain-to-pooling relationship. The proposed amplifier is the measured disturbance in filling or recovery, rather than body mass alone.

Within this hypothesis, a gestational load that demonstrably destabilises venous return or effective filling could increase the frequency or magnitude of compensatory recruitment. The resulting RAAS, vasopressin, autonomic and glucocorticoid responses would depend on the actual filling and tonicity changes and their timing, rather than on weight gain alone.

Excessive gestational load is therefore considered a candidate amplifier, not evidence that ordinary pregnancy adaptation is pathological. Its contribution would be established by recurrent circulatory disturbance or incomplete recovery during a developmentally susceptible window.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_6"></a>

#### 16.6 Mechanism — Microvascular Flow Failure

Microvascular maldistribution makes tissue delivery heterogeneous, shunted or intermittently obstructed despite adequate central flow. The problem is deployment of available circulation where oxygen and sodium-dependent work are needed.

Failed capillary recruitment, endothelial dysfunction, microthrombi or placental maldistribution can restrict local delivery with a functioning pump and preserved central volume. This does not itself establish systemic underfilling or a false filling signal (Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8)).

Preeclampsia, diabetes, antiphospholipid and microthrombotic states, severe inflammation, oxidative endothelial stress, and placental villous malperfusion all fit this pathway.

Limited capillary recruitment and NO buffering can magnify the delivery effect of a modest change in vascular tone.

Preeclampsia and maternal diabetes supply separately studied ASD-associated contexts (Wang et al., 2021a; Xiang et al., 2018). Their proposed convergence is patchy tissue-level oxygen or nutrient delivery during sensitive windows, rather than any diagnosis establishing vascular mediation of autism.

Local underdelivery may constrain recovery without systemic AVP or RAAS recruitment. Renal perfusion and non-osmotic inputs determine whether broader defence follows (Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8)); the defining mismatch is central flow versus tissue delivery, not one hormone value.

Hypothesis. Recurrent maldistribution may expose developing tissue to focal oxygen and ionic-recovery constraints without sustained circulatory collapse. Developmental mediation remains a further step, while endocrine recruitment depends on the affected signals.

##### 16.6.1 Oxygen content and compensatory flow

Anaemia is a different constraint: oxygen content can fall while output rises. In 32 resting adults, acute isovolaemic haemodilution increased heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac index (Weiskopf et al., 1998). Anaemia therefore belongs in a low-output branch only when pump failure is demonstrated; otherwise the question is whether compensation maintains oxygen delivery.

A separate developmental signal concerns the timing of diagnosed maternal anaemia. In 532,232 Swedish children, diagnosis at or before 30 gestational weeks was associated with ASD (adjusted OR 1.44, 95% CI 1.13–1.84), including in sibling comparisons (OR 2.25, 95% CI 1.24–4.11); later diagnoses were not (Wiegersma et al., 2019). This supports investigating an early nutritional or oxygen-delivery constraint, without identifying its mechanism. The register diagnoses did not distinguish iron deficiency from every other cause, measure tissue hypoxia or establish local ionic recovery impairment.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_7"></a>

#### 16.7 Mechanism — Cardiac Output Limitation

Cardiac output limitation restricts forward delivery despite intravascular fluid being present. Effective filling can fall because the pump cannot provide sufficient flow, rather than because fluid is absent or sequestered.

Insufficient forward flow may constrain renal and uteroplacental delivery, with venous congestion alongside arterial underfilling. This differs from microvascular maldistribution downstream of adequate central flow; the affected maternal, fetal or postnatal circulation must be specified.

Maternal cardiomyopathy, haemodynamically significant arrhythmia, structural heart disease, myocarditis or a hypothyroid low-output state can enter this route when forward flow is limited.

Limited stroke-volume reserve may amplify the constraint; renal underfilling and endocrine recruitment depend on its magnitude and timing.

Two positive findings address different compartments. In 209 pregnant women with congenital heart disease (CHD) and 70 healthy controls, maternal cardiac function was associated with abnormal uteroplacental Doppler patterns (Pieper et al., 2013). This supports a maternal cardiovascular–placental component; Doppler resistance indices do not directly measure volume flow or fetal ionic recovery. Separately, a study of 8,760 autistic children and 26,280 controls found an adjusted association with the child’s CHD (OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.10–1.59; Sigmon et al., 2019). Shared genetics, fetal haemodynamics, hypoxaemia and perioperative exposures remain distinct candidate explanations; this association does not establish maternal placental underfilling.

Low forward flow can recruit AVP and renin through reduced filling or renal perfusion; aldosterone and cortisol depend on additional controls. The fetal response follows its own circulation and gestational capacity (Table [10.1](#ss_p10_table_10_1); Section [15](#ss_p10_sec_15)).

Hypothesis. Recurrent low output could influence development through reduced delivery, altered pulsatility and circulatory defence even without persistent electrolyte abnormality. This route requires impaired local neural or glial ionic/volume recovery; adequate recovery despite compensation opposes it. Maternal, fetal and postnatal routes remain distinct.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_8"></a>

#### 16.8 Redox-Dependent Vascular Regulation and Filling-Signal Integrity

##### 16.8.1 Initiating condition and volume geometry

Redox-dependent vascular changes may initiate or prolong defence by reducing delivery or altering regulatory information. Adequate total volume can coexist with insufficient recovery support. A false-deficit signal requires inappropriate defence despite adequate relevant filling; false adequacy under-reads a real deficit and can prevent needed recruitment. Normal total volume alone demonstrates neither error. Vascular tone, osmotic tonicity and cardiovascular sensing are distinct variables.

Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1), Panel A, maps actual disturbances of filling and delivery, including microvascular underdelivery (§[16.6](#ss_p10_sec_16_6)); Panel B maps sensing and regulatory disturbances. Altered vessel mechanics can also change strain at sensory endings for a given pressure; peripheral encoding concerns afferent response to matched local input; central interpretation concerns regulatory response to characterised afferent input (§[16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9)). Endothelial shear responses and renal pressure feedback occupy different local control sites. Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1) in Section [16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9) supplies the supporting component evidence; compliance, flow dilation and whole-body baroreflex measures cannot individually localise a neural false-filling defect.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_8_2"></a>

##### 16.8.2 Redox mechanisms and the sensory boundary

Reduced NO signalling can arise through impaired production, accelerated consumption or reduced responsiveness of its target. Oxidation of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), with a less favourable balance against its competing oxidation product BH2, can uncouple endothelial NO synthase (eNOS), shifting its output from NO towards superoxide (Crabtree et al., 2008). Impaired BH4 recycling supplies another route: Ang II-induced loss of dihydrofolate reductase can compromise this system (Chalupsky & Cai, 2005). A separate redox modification, eNOS S-glutathionylation, can reduce NO generation and increase superoxide even when BH4 is present (Chen et al., 2010a). Oxidation or loss of the haem group in soluble guanylyl cyclase can impair the response to NO downstream (Stasch et al., 2006). These mechanisms can reduce vasodilatory reserve, but they are not interchangeable measurements of one lesion.

Limited cysteine could constrain local glutathione synthesis, but cysteine availability, GSH concentration, GSH/GSSG balance, protein S-glutathionylation and BH4 status are distinct. The relevant susceptibility is a functional redox defect affecting vascular support or sensory signalling under demand, not any one marker standing for the entire corridor.

Membrane-peroxide demand could enter this corridor if local antioxidant use exceeds regeneration or synthesis (Section [35.1](#ss_p10_sec_35_1)). eNOS S-glutathionylation and hypoxia/reoxygenation-induced BH4 depletion demonstrate routes to reduced NO and increased superoxide (Chen et al., 2010a; De Pascali et al., 2014); lipid-peroxide removal producing those states is the additional hypothesis. Absolute GSH and GSSG pools, BH4/BH2 and eNOS function remain distinct, and conjugation can lower GSH without raising GSSG. Concurrent renal, endothelial and neural constraints involve separate pools, potentially connecting limited AVP processing (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)) with reduced vascular support. Klotho modifies some endothelial responses (Section [33.3](#ss_p10_sec_33_3)); abnormal afferent encoding remains a further step.

A separate skeletal preparation links sodium availability to antioxidant support. In murine RAW 264.7 preosteoclasts adapted to reduced extracellular sodium, radiolabelled ascorbate uptake fell; at 112 mmol/L sodium, oxidant-sensitive fluorescence was higher than at 136 mmol/L during a 30-minute assay with normalised osmolality (Barsony et al., 2011). This supplies a sodium-sensitive redox comparison alongside the skeletal findings in Section [48](#ss_p10_sec_48). The corresponding effects on endothelial NO regulation and neural developmental recovery remain compartment-specific questions.

Human neonatal intestinal vessels provide a functional example of impaired endothelial regulation. In arterioles resected for necrotising enterocolitis, eNOS protein remained detectable, but acetylcholine failed to stimulate NO release or dilation, and increased flow failed to evoke dilation. Responses to the external NO donor S-nitroso-N-acetylpenicillamine and to papaverine remained present (Nowicki et al., 2007). This separates impaired endothelial NO-dependent regulation from complete loss of smooth-muscle dilator capacity. It does not identify biochemical eNOS uncoupling, a glucose-mediated lesion or an isolated shear sensor defect. Vessel responsiveness, mechanical transmission to sensory endings and afferent encoding remain separate measurements.

A20 (TNFAIP3) manipulation altered eNOS expression through ERK5/KLF2 in human coronary endothelial cells, including protection against inflammatory downregulation (Angolano et al., 2021). Glucose-associated A20 protein loss (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)) therefore supplies a candidate route through enzyme availability alongside coupling defects; the complete glucose–NO–filling-signal sequence remains unestablished.

The sensory direction cannot be read from NO abundance alone. Antioxidants improved carotid baroreceptor activity in atherosclerotic rabbits, supporting a redox-sensitive component (Li et al., 1996), whereas local NO or S-nitrosocysteine suppressed activity in a rabbit carotid-sinus preparation (Matsuda et al., 1995). These experiments support testing redox-dependent sensory changes while opposing a universal low-NO-to-low-firing rule. A pressure–diameter comparison also does not fully resolve the strain experienced by a sensory ending.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_8_3"></a>

##### 16.8.3 Environmental and clinical contributors

Tobacco smoke and traffic-related pollution provide experimentally grounded candidate exposures. In chronic adult smokers, BH4 administration improved endothelium-dependent forearm vasodilatation (Heitzer et al., 2000). In a controlled crossover study of healthy men, diesel exhaust impaired several vasodilator responses without changing resting forearm blood flow (Mills et al., 2005). These findings support altered vascular reserve; they do not demonstrate prenatal BH4 depletion, baroreceptor error or inappropriate volume defence.

Exposure, tissue and timing matter. Acute diesel exposure increased rather than impaired acetylcholine-induced aortic relaxation in mice heterozygous for Gclm, despite a more oxidised plasma glutathione state (Weldy et al., 2013). Mould and mycotoxins remain candidate exposures requiring agent-, dose- and route-specific evidence. They should not be grouped with smoke and traffic as established causes of this vascular-sensing pathway. Residential proximity to a major road is an exposure proxy, not a measurement of a particular toxicant or mechanism.

Maternal redox conditions could affect fetal supply through placental vascular function without requiring an oxidised molecule to reach fetal membranes. In perfused human placental cotyledons, an experimental 100 µmol/L t-butyl hydroperoxide challenge increased vascular resistance from 14 ± 2 to 25 ± 3 mmHg·min/mL (mean ± SE); aspirin or thromboxane-receptor blockade prevented the constriction (Walsh et al., 1993). Separate experiments found stimulated placental peroxide secretion greater towards the maternal than fetal effluent (Walsh & Wang, 1993). These results identify the placenta as an active source and target of redox effects. They do not establish transfer of a specified maternal oxidised lipid, fetal membrane injury or a physiological maternal exposure threshold.

Neonatal nutrient preparations provide a separate, measurable exposure question. In an in-vitro tube-feeding study, light exposure increased lipid peroxidation in infant formula but not in human milk under the tested conditions (van Zoeren-Grobben et al., 1993). Intravenous lipid exposure bypasses intestinal processing: Neuzil et al. (1995) measured mean triglyceride hydroperoxide concentrations of 40 µmol/L in Intralipid solutions at the end of 24 hours of clinical infusion without phototherapy and 97 µmol/L with phototherapy. Experimental foil shielding prevented hydroperoxide formation. These are preparation concentrations, not infant plasma concentrations or cumulative tissue doses. The enteral and intravenous routes therefore cannot be combined into one exposure estimate.

Human intervention evidence is mixed. In an 80-infant randomised parenteral-nutrition study, photoprotection reduced urinary peroxides at 48 hours and a secondary analysis suggested less chronic lung disease (Bassiouny et al., 2009). A larger trial including 590 infants born before 30 weeks found no significant reduction in the composite endpoint of bronchopulmonary dysplasia or death: 77% versus 72% at 28 days and 30% versus 27% at 36 weeks corrected age, protected versus exposed, respectively (Laborie et al., 2015). Photoprotection changes the chemistry of the nutrient admixture, not only its lipids. Neither study tested lasting neural recovery or the proposed autism mechanism.

The proposed exposure must reduce membrane protection or recovery reserve (Section [35](#ss_p10_sec_35)). Product concentration, duration, flow and route determine delivery, while absorption, distribution and clearance determine internal dose. At steady flow, mean tubing residence time is internal volume divided by flow; continuous delivery is not itself a bolus. Enteral and intravenous PUFA preparations cannot be treated as one exposure.

##### 16.8.4 Autism associations and competing explanations

CHARGE case–control associations with freeway proximity and estimated traffic pollution (Volk et al., 2011, 2013) did not measure NO, afferent or endocrine mediation. Vascular, placental, immune and direct developmental routes remain alternatives, alongside correlated exposures and social or environmental confounding.

Maternal-smoking associations with autism attenuated in Danish family-based analyses (Kalkbrenner et al., 2020). Smoking-related vascular effects therefore do not establish autism causation, and smoking, traffic proxies and mould cannot be assigned one established mechanism.

##### 16.8.5 Endocrine responses and direct NO-sensitive branches

Low NO does not prescribe a single AVP–RAAS–cortisol profile. In nineteen healthy adults, acute systemic NO-synthase inhibition reduced urinary sodium and water excretion and raised blood pressure, while plasma renin fell, aldosterone remained unchanged and AVP did not rise (Al Therwani et al., 2014). Thus, a renal conservation response can occur without the predicted joint endocrine activation. Preserved or restored pressure and filling can oppose further conservation; the location, duration and background state of NO impairment matter.

Direct renal and central effects provide additional branches. NO reduced renal thick-ascending-limb Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter activity in isolated rat tubules (Ortiz et al., 2001). In water-loaded rats, central NO-synthase inhibition increased AVP and reduced urine volume while increasing sodium excretion (Reis et al., 2007). These are distinct preparations, not evidence for peripheral false filling. Renal NKCC2 must remain separate from neural NKCC1, and AVP secretion must remain separate from peripheral peptide termination and renal responsiveness (Sections [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) and [21.2](#ss_p10_sec_21_2)). Sodium and water outputs need not move together.

##### 16.8.6 Developmental hypothesis and interpretive limits

Hypothesis. Recurrent vascular underdelivery or inappropriate filling signals could prolong defence and burden developmental recovery. Either redox dysfunction or impaired perfusion may initiate the route: severe hypoxia/reoxygenation depleted BH4 and modified eNOS in cultured endothelium (De Pascali et al., 2014). Osmotic swelling is not required. Restored delivery, pressure feedback and metabolic support can interrupt amplification; persistence means dysfunction beyond continuing exposure or ordinary recovery lag under matched present conditions.

Normal afferent encoding and appropriate downstream output under characterised filling and mechanics would oppose false filling despite vascular dysfunction. Systemic BH4 rescue alone cannot localise the mediator.

> *The disturbance must precede and affect development. Genetic, immune and neural redox routes remain alternatives or interacting mechanisms; recovery and OTX2 accounts in Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23), [24](#ss_p10_sec_24), and [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4) do not supply the missing vascular-to-developmental link.*
>
> Maternal inflammation offers a prenatal context (Sections [18.5](#ss_p10_sec_18_5) and [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6)). Placental–cardiac disturbance and preserved estimated delivery have occurred in different preparations; neither inflammation nor abnormal Doppler indices establish neural ATP limitation. Local immune initiation can operate without the proposed delivery–energy–recovery sequence.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_9"></a>

#### 16.9 Mechanism — Volume Mis-Sensing

The sensing and regulatory routes in Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1), Panel B, distinguish biased estimates of need, altered response gain, mistimed recruitment or termination, shifted references and discordant integration. False deficit means adequate relevant filling is represented as insufficient; false adequacy means a real deficit is under-read. Reduced gain does not establish response delay or either bias, and resetting is not necessarily pathological. Central misinterpretation is one possible site; altered mechanical transmission, afferent encoding and renal pressure feedback require separate localisation (Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1)). Endocrine effector inadequacy can also occur with accurate sensing (§[16.10](#ss_p10_sec_16_10)).

Baroreflex resetting, ANP–BNP discordance, altered interoception or post-stress threshold drift are clues, not localisation. Central misinterpretation requires an abnormal regulatory response to characterised afferent input after actual filling and peripheral mechanics are addressed. A whole-reflex change can arise from vessel mechanics, sensory encoding, central integration or effector responsiveness.

##### 16.9.1 Candidate sites of impaired cardiovascular sensing

Evidence key: \[E\] identifies the stated empirical observation or association; \[S\], a measured physiological component. These are claim roles, not a strength ranking. Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1) supplies component evidence for Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1), especially Panel B; it is not a separate contributor catalogue. Most evidence comes from animal preparations studied in adulthood, with human functional or associative comparisons. The cardiac row adds a volume-related challenge endpoint alongside arterial pressure, local flow and renal feedback. None of these experiments establishes ASD mediation or developmental calibration by the proposed exposures. The developmental preterm comparison remains in Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) and Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1).

<a name="ss_p10_table_16_1"></a>Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1). Candidate sites of impaired cardiovascular sensing and signal interpretation

| **Candidate site or factor**           | **Measured component and evidence context**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | **Interpretive boundary**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Pressure-to-stretch transmission       | \[E\] Human association. In 47 healthy adult men, carotid compliance was associated with cardiovagal baroreflex sensitivity; changes also covaried after exercise (Monahan et al., 2001).                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Compliance was measured at rest and reflex sensitivity during Valsalva. Neither causation, a sensory-neuron lesion nor fetal susceptibility was established.                                                                                                                                                                       |

Combined Piezo1/Piezo2 deletion abolished tested pressure-evoked aortic nerve activity and reflex bradycardia; single deletions did not (Zeng et al., 2018). Electrical nerve stimulation retained cardiovascular responses after double deletion (Min et al., 2019).                                                                                 | The bypass result supports preserved downstream reflex function under the tested conditions. Phox2b-Cre is not baroreceptor-specific; this does not assign the mouse double-deletion effect to every human variant or establish developmental mediation.                                                                           |

The evidence labels apply to measured components, not complete developmental mediation. Redox effects, A20/eNOS regulation, NEC vessels and pollutant exposures retain their accounts in §§[16.8.2](#ss_p10_sec_16_8_2) and [16.8.3](#ss_p10_sec_16_8_3); glycocalyx and membrane distinctions remain in §[35.1](#ss_p10_sec_35_1). Impaired vasodilation does not establish central mis-sensing or a redox-induced PIEZO lesion. Arterial pressure, cardiac filling-related responses, renal pressure feedback and macula-densa salt signalling are distinct endpoints. The CUL3 renal comparison does not replace its intrinsic neural mechanisms or establish a shared allele-specific route. Every proposed route must impair local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery and thereby alter development.

##### 16.9.2 Adaptation and tests of persistence

Recent pressure history can alter the relationship between pressure and cardiovascular responses. Rabbit experiments demonstrated rapid shifts in baroreceptor firing and heart-rate reflex curves during rising and falling pressure (Burke et al., 1986). In 14 healthy adults, cardiac vagal hysteresis involved interacting mechanical and neural components and varied between trials (Studinger et al., 2007). Such history dependence does not establish permanent imprinting. After two months of experimental renal hypertension in rats, pressure normalisation produced substantial reversal of threshold resetting within two hours, while depressed gain recovered by 90–120 minutes (Moreira et al., 1990). A retained alteration must therefore be distinguished from continuing exposure or reversible adaptation.

Developmental controller differences provide a separate comparison. Prenatal dehydration was followed by altered Ang II-evoked reflex and pressor responses in young male rats despite similar resting pressure (Guan et al., 2009; Section [18.1.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_1_6)). That integrated response does not locate the retained defect or supply a full resetting curve, and reduced maternal food intake remains a confound. Section [39](#ss_p10_sec_39) therefore retains a distinct question about the substrate and duration of proposed vascular imprinting.

Dysautonomia, recovery from chronic illness, repeated dehydration or pooling, vascular stiffness and natriuretic-peptide differences motivate investigation. They may instead change actual filling or peripheral transmission; low baroreflex gain or altered vagal response cannot alone establish persistent central error.

Autonomic and interoceptive differences in autism are heterogeneous and nonspecific. They motivate a subgroup hypothesis about repeated circulatory misclassification, but establish neither false deficit nor its developmental origin.

Central misinterpretation could sustain AVP or RAAS despite adequate filling, or fail to recruit defence during real deficit. Each output, including cortisol, must be judged against the actual state and characterised input. Hormone variability alone cannot distinguish mis-sensing from changing distribution or peripheral transmission.

Hypothesis. Repeated false-deficit signalling could lower later thresholds for orthostatic, thermal or illness-related volume alarms; false-adequacy states could delay needed recruitment. Persistence requires an altered response after the initiating disturbance has resolved, with relevant current inputs characterised. Its developmental significance additionally requires that altered delivery or defence impair local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery and carry the specified developmental effect. Acute misclassification or increased regulatory effort with adequate recovery is insufficient.

> Section [47.1](#ss_p10_sec_47_1) connects this interpretive question to interoceptive-learning models while separating actual bodily input, detection, confidence and the weight assigned to a signal.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_10"></a>

#### 16.10 Mechanism — Endocrine Volume Mis-Regulation

##### 16.10.1 Initiating condition and volume geometry

Unlike mis-sensing, reassignment can occur with accurate perception of need but inadequate or more costly effector support. Endocrine control reassignment begins with inadequate support for a measured sodium-conservation or filling need. Alternative endocrine or vascular contributions may preserve volume and pressure; developmental vulnerability lies in their timing, burden or incomplete recovery. Section [14.5](#ss_p10_sec_14_5) details initiating renal and receptor disturbances; the present section considers the resulting pattern of support and the thyroid recovery mechanisms below.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_16_10_2"></a>

##### 16.10.2 The core mechanism

Low renin, altered FGF23 signalling, thyroid dysfunction, mineralocorticoid interference and glucocorticoid exposure do not define one loss of regulatory precision. In the FGF23 mouse experiment, enhanced renal sodium retention coexisted with lower aldosterone and unchanged plasma renin activity; the hypothyroid water-load study instead demonstrated impaired water excretion and absent AVP suppression (Andrukhova et al., 2014; Ota et al., 1994). The proposed common question is whether a specified disturbance leaves sodium conservation, water clearance or circulatory recovery inadequate, requiring additional support.

That AVP pattern is not obligatory: Iwasaki et al. (1990) studied eight patients with untreated myxoedema, including five who underwent water-loading tests; two had impaired urinary dilution despite appropriate AVP suppression. Impaired water excretion therefore does not by itself identify failed AVP suppression or reduced clearance.

Thyroid antioxidant capacity supplies a possible entry into this response heterogeneity. Hormone synthesis uses spatially controlled hydrogen peroxide, making peroxide production and removal complementary functions. Cultured human thyrocytes rapidly removed extracellular peroxide and had high basal selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase activity, with further activity increases after peroxide exposure (Ghaddhab et al., 2019). A distinct protective system has a demonstrated recovery function: during continued excess-iodide exposure, inhibiting or silencing thioredoxin reductase prevented recovery of sodium–iodide symporter activity in rat PCCl3 thyroid cells over the studied 72-hour interval (Leoni et al., 2011). This is evidence for antioxidant-dependent recovery of thyroid iodide transport, not for GPX4 as the exclusive thyroid defence.

Hypothesis. Oxidative burden or limited local reducing capacity could prolong thyroid recovery and alter support during a later water or circulatory challenge. This requires changed thyroid output and downstream function, not low GSH alone. Neither experiment establishes GSH depletion as the cause of Hashimoto’s disease or anti-TPO formation. Thyrocyte, renal and endothelial redox pools remain distinct. If thyroid output changes, water handling and the candidate T3–Klotho connection provide downstream routes (Section [33.3](#ss_p10_sec_33_3)).

##### 16.10.3 Environmental / clinical drivers and amplifiers

Specified FGF23/Klotho, thyroid, glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid-receptor disturbances enter through their physiological effects, not exposure labels (Table [14.3](#ss_p10_table_14_3)).

Altered mineralocorticoid selectivity or increased RAAS responsiveness could amplify later challenges. A transition from weak support to overshoot remains a tissue-specific prediction, not an obligatory exposure effect.

##### 16.10.4 Empirical support and ASD-relevant contributors

Developmental associations with thyroid dysfunction and endocrine disruptors are mixed and context dependent. The proposal is therefore physiological mediation in defined settings, not uniform ASD causation.

The FGF23 finding above illustrates the distinction: lower aldosterone accompanied sodium retention and expansion, not failed conservation (Andrukhova et al., 2014). Altered later response gain or recovery is the further developmental claim.

##### 16.10.5 Endocrine response

Alternative support may increase where sodium conservation or circulation is inadequate. AVP follows osmotic and non-osmotic inputs, while renin, aldosterone and cortisol vary by phase. A cortisol-weighted response is one possible configuration; short-term stability can still differ in recovery cost and timing.

##### 16.10.6 Developmental implication and synthesis

Hypothesis. Repeated reliance on cortisol-weighted or other reassigned support may leave stress-maintained normotension with less precise regulation, increasing later susceptibility to overshoot, dilutional overlap or autonomic cost. Restoration without persistent change remains the alternative.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_17"></a>

### 17 Lithium as a Renal and Environmental Comparison

The comparison below keeps therapeutic renal findings separate from the question raised by environmental exposure. Section [19.1](#ss_p10_sec_19_1) provides the broader framework for interactions among initiating disturbances.

#### 17.1 Lithium: Dose-Specific Renal Effects and an Environmental Association

Lithium provides a dose-specific example of altered water handling. In adults receiving therapeutic lithium, Bedford et al. (2008) documented impaired urinary concentrating responses and lower urinary AQP2 and cAMP responses with longer treatment exposure. In a small crossover trial, amiloride improved concentrating ability. This is evidence for reduced renal responsiveness to antidiuretic signalling, rather than a general lithium-induced state of water retention. It does not establish the same renal effect at trace drinking-water concentrations or during fetal development.

An interaction with reverse-osmosis or desalinated water requires measured composition and absorbed dose. Processing labels establish neither selective lithium retention nor biologically important enrichment or reduced sodium activity. Total diet, water volume and renal clearance determine any proposed low-solute interaction.

Lithium enters the hypothesis only where the relevant dose impairs sodium–water regulation, ionic recovery or developmental signalling. Serum sodium alone cannot identify that effect, and a fixed AVP-high, low-RAAS, cortisol-weighted sequence is not established.

There is a relevant environmental association. In Denmark, Liew et al. (2023) compared 8,842 children with ASD with 43,864 controls using estimated residential drinking-water lithium concentrations of 0.6–30.7 µg/L. The adjusted odds ratio for the highest versus lowest exposure quartile was 1.46 (95% CI 1.35–1.59). Exposure was modelled from waterworks measurements, rather than measured maternal intake or internal dose; geographically correlated constituents and residual confounding remain possible. This finding motivates replication and physiological exposure studies. It does not establish a desalination effect, sodium mimicry, antidiuresis or sodium–volume mediation of autism.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18"></a>

### 18 Maternal Exposures and Metabolic and Immune Pathways

This section follows maternal regulatory, metabolic and immune exposures into fetal development, alongside local cellular comparisons that do not require an initiating systemic episode. Sections [9](#ss_p10_sec_9) and [10](#ss_p10_sec_10) provide the general maternal–placental–fetal framework. Excitatory or metabolic challenges can disturb cellular volume regulation without true hyponatraemia or a measurable fall in serum sodium, while still involving sodium transport. The proposed developmental link is incomplete ionic or volume recovery that alters neural differentiation or circuit maturation; swelling or increased transport work alone does not establish it.

In second-passage astrocytes from newborn rat cortex, 1 mM glutamate over 1–48 hours increased cell perimeter, a morphological index of swelling; mGluR5 manipulation and AQP4 silencing implicated receptor–water-channel signalling (Shi et al., 2017). This local-exposure result cannot be assigned exclusively to ionotropic receptors or extrapolated to dietary monosodium glutamate. Swelling does not establish intracellular hypotonicity or impaired recovery. Ammonia, infection and hypoxia supply other candidate entry conditions, whose exposure and recovery effects remain preparation- and stage-dependent.

Glucose has a different initial direction: an effective extracellular rise favours outward water movement, while its decline permits return towards baseline volume. Neither phase alone establishes osmolyte depletion or developmental failure. Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) develop this metabolic route; Section [18.3](#ss_p10_sec_18_3) considers other non-electrolyte compounds.

Incomplete recovery from swelling, altered ionic gradients or extracellular-space organisation could change the conditions for neural differentiation and circuit maturation. Candidate consequences include delayed maturation, unstable dendrites, altered synapse retention and impaired pruning, depending on cell type, developmental window, severity and duration. Swelling does not make these outcomes automatic or imply a universal shrinkage transition before differentiation (Section [31.4.1](#ss_p10_sec_31_4_1)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_1"></a>

#### 18.1 Intergenerational Sodium–Volume Defence Programming

Intergenerational Sodium–Volume Defence Programming proposes that maternal water–solute handling, vascular regulation and endocrine responses shape fetal development through altered tonicity, delivery, nutrient or hormone exposure. Overt maternal hyponatraemia is not required. Fetal sensors and tissue capacities determine the response; the transmitted influence is a physiological exposure, not a copy of maternal interpretation.

##### 18.1.1 Maternal Sodium–Volume Instability: Definition

Clinical hyponatraemia is defined by serum sodium below 135 mmol/L. AVP control also integrates plasma volume and arterial baroreceptor signals: inadequate effective filling can recruit AVP without an osmotic deviation.

Maternal sodium–volume instability denotes recurrent misalignment among extracellular tonicity, effective arterial volume and vascular containment that recruits compensatory defence. It differs from a single low sodium concentration and from a transient disturbance followed by complete recovery.

A maternal defence bias is a proposed persistent weighting towards more readily recruited AVP-mediated water retention, AGTR1-linked vascular support, cortisol-supported compensation or slower recovery. Its fetal influence would pass through maternal water–solute balance or placental delivery.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_1_2"></a>

##### 18.1.2 Maternal Regulatory History and Fetal Exposure

Maternal regulatory history can shape AVP thresholds, RAAS sensitivity, adrenal zonation, thyroid–metabolic coupling, inflammatory tone, sympathetic gain and cortisol utilisation. Genetic susceptibility, early-life imprinting, autoimmunity, metabolic strain, chronic stress and previous pregnancies are candidate contributors, including when routine maternal measurements are normal.

Changes in maternal water–solute balance, thyroid or glucocorticoid availability, pressure and placental perfusion can alter the environment in which fetal osmoregulatory organs mature. Placental processing and endogenous fetal responses transform these inputs. The proposed programming signal is the resulting fetal exposure and response history; normal maternal chemistry neither excludes nor demonstrates it.

The maternal-baseline proposal concerns a persistent regulatory phenotype that could influence fetal exposure across pregnancies. A within-mother comparison of pregnancies differing in a recorded exposure, such as medication or infection, does not estimate the main effect of a maternal characteristic that remains constant across those pregnancies. If that characteristic influences both the recorded exposure and offspring development, it can confound their association even while being biologically causal itself. Its interaction with a pregnancy-specific exposure is not automatically removed by a sibling comparison. Changes in maternal physiology between pregnancies must instead be measured as varying exposures; they cannot simply be assigned to a shared baseline.

Sibling comparisons remain useful for controlling influences shared by the compared siblings. Their interpretation also depends on exposure validity and causes that differ between pregnancies or children. Analytical and simulation work shows that random exposure error can produce greater attenuation within siblings, while nonshared confounding can be magnified ([Frisell et al., 2012](#ss_revsyn2_ref_Frisell2012)). These possibilities require study-specific evaluation, rather than an assumed correction factor or a default explanation of a null result. The reported sibling estimates therefore constrain broad exposure claims without directly estimating every proposed maternal physiological route; they supply no affirmative evidence for the baseline proposal.

Evaluation of this proposal requires repeated maternal physiological measurements, validated pregnancy exposures and complementary within- and between-family analyses in existing cohorts or suitable archived material. The prediction is that the specified maternal phenotype precedes and predicts a measured fetal exposure or recovery difference, followed by the required neural or glial recovery intermediary and developmental consequence. Successful buffering and complete recovery remain comparators. Failure of sufficiently informative measurements to support that prespecified pathway would weigh against the proposed maternal contribution, rather than being reclassified as hidden compensation.

Table [18.1](#ss_p10_table_18_1) maps maternal phenotypes onto candidate osmotic, metabolic and vascular routes. Maternal-line associations do not distinguish genetic susceptibility, shared environment and gestational exposure; this non-Mendelian proposal requires a physiological maternal-to-fetal bridge and a developmental effect.
