##### 18.1.3 Fetal Exposure and Developmental Timing

Section [9](#ss_p10_sec_9) groups the osmotic, circulatory, endocrine, inflammatory and cellular inputs that define fetal exposure. Fetal AVP competence has its own developmental timetable (Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3)), distinct from the timing of a maternal exposure.

Mixed osmotic, circulatory and stress cues can be integrated successfully. The proposed calibration effect arises when recurrent demand, response mismatch or incomplete recovery during a susceptible window changes developmental conditions and later regulation—not from mixed cues alone.

Exposure timing must be separated from hormone maturation. In 419,425 children, gestational diabetes diagnosed by 26 weeks was associated with ASD, whereas later diagnosis was not (Xiang et al., 2018; estimates in Table [18.1](#ss_p10_table_18_1)). Diagnosis did not measure fetal exposure onset, duration or magnitude. First-trimester and later-only valproate prescription estimates were similar in another cohort, but the later group contained only 67 children and had a wide interval (Christensen et al., 2013). Neither finding establishes a universal earlier-is-worse rule or an AVP-defined 11–19-week susceptibility window.

##### 18.1.4 Maternal and Fetal Regulation in Specific Exposure Routes

Sections [9](#ss_p10_sec_9) and [10](#ss_p10_sec_10) distinguish maternal regulation of the input from the fetus’s response to placentally transformed exposure. The examples below concern vascular delivery, endocrine filtering and fetal cue integration; the exposure’s magnitude, recurrence and completeness of recovery remain the proposed influences on later thresholds and osmoregulatory behaviour.

###### ***18.1.4.1 Placental Vascular and Endocrine Examples***

Maternal peptide concentration cannot substitute for fetal exposure. Sections [10.1](#ss_p10_sec_10_1) and [10.1.1](#ss_p10_sec_10_1_1) separate placental transfer, metabolism and maternal turnover; Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3) describes fetal AVP competence and its distinct timetable.

Maternal glucose and water–solute perturbations require measured fetal concentration and timing; transport asymmetry alone does not specify the direction or duration of fetal exposure (Section [10.2](#ss_p10_sec_10_2)). Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) develop the metabolic route.

Maternal uteroplacental perfusion can influence fetal oxygen and nutrient delivery without maternal peptide transfer. Maternal and fetal placental vessels remain separate compartments: isolated human fetoplacental arterial branches contracted to AVP, but pre-eclamptic branches had lower responsiveness and AVPR1A expression (Gao et al., 2019; Section [14.6.3](#ss_p10_sec_14_6_3)). This opposes a uniform gain increase and locates the proposed bridge in altered delivery and endogenous fetal defence.

The resulting fetal exposure may also be prolonged or repeated by renal and amniotic-fluid feedback. Section [10.4](#ss_p10_sec_10_4) distinguishes the established fluid pathways from that persistence prediction during a sensitive window.

A consequential fetal disturbance could occur without recognised maternal pathology, while infection, fever or dehydration alone does not establish programming. Intrinsic genetic constraints can also initiate fetal ionic or recovery demand without passing through this maternal route.

###### ***18.1.4.2 Fetal Cue Integration***

Fetal cue integration is tested against the matched challenge in Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3). A smaller AVP response can be appropriate; the proposed adverse branch requires a consequential exposure or recovery disturbance.

Three relationships distinguish the proposed branches:

**Osmotic and water–solute timing: establish the fetal tonicity trajectory rather than inferring it from maternal sodium or a presumed transport lag (Section [10.2](#ss_p10_sec_10_2)).**

**Perfusion and dilution: establish both fetal hypotonicity and the filling or oxygen-delivery constraint; their interaction need not prescribe one hormone direction (Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3)).**

**Endocrine response: assess fetal secretion, removal and tissue responsiveness separately from maternal hormone values (Sections [10.1.1](#ss_p10_sec_10_1_1) and [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3)).**

Hypoxia can strongly recruit fetal AVP, including during mixed cues. The protective AVP–RAAS–cortisol triad can restore stability without its components rising together. Developmental calibration predicts a later functional change after the disturbance resolves; complete recovery without that change would oppose the persistence branch (Section [21.1](#ss_p10_sec_21_1)).

##### 18.1.5 Mechanistic Pathways: Receptor-Level Divergence and Axis Decalibration

Candidate calibration changes include easier AVPR1A-mediated vascular recruitment, stronger AVPR1B-linked ACTH responses and greater AGTR1 support after recurrent demand. A related neural branch predicts relatively stronger AVP signalling or weaker oxytocin modulation in specified circuits and windows. These are proposed functional directions, not signatures inferred from maternal concentrations. Renal AVPR2, MR/GR balance, adrenal development and thyroid support are additional modifiers (Sections [21.4](#ss_p10_sec_21_4) and [21.6](#ss_p10_sec_21_6)).

AGTR1 provides a developmental vascular example: deletion in human kidney organoids delayed VEGF-A production and prevented day-14 engraftment beneath the kidney capsule of immunodeficient mice, while day-24 mutants engrafted and matured. Induced VEGF-A rescued day-14 engraftment (Pode-Shakked et al., 2023). This renal-transplantation result does not establish the proposed extension that repeated fetal dilution-underfilling increases reliance on AGTR1 and later Ang II responsiveness.

Thyroid signalling connects endocrine state with water handling and neural maturation through different evidence. Hypothyroid adults showed impaired water-load excretion and absent AVP suppression despite normal serum sodium, reversible with replacement (Ota et al., 1994; Table [18.1](#ss_p10_table_18_1)). In embryonic-day-16 rat cortical cultures, 15 nM T3 increased KCC2 and accelerated loss of muscimol-evoked calcium responses in non-GABAergic neurons at 15–18 days in vitro; the measured GABAergic subgroups did not show that acceleration, and NKCC1 also increased (Westerholz et al., 2013). Thus thyroid-dependent timing does not imply uniformly lower NKCC1 or altered cell volume. Maternal status, fetal exposure and local recovery remain separate; direct thyroid-dependent developmental effects are an alternative to recovery mediation.

Maternal thyroid hormone and thyroid-directed IgG are also distinct exposures. T4 was detected in human embryonic coelomic fluid at 6–11 weeks, and maternal contribution was demonstrable at term when fetal synthesis was absent (Contempré et al., 1993; Vulsma et al., 1989). Anti-TPO transfer alone establishes neither fetal thyroid dysfunction nor neural pump inhibition; stimulating and blocking TSH-receptor antibodies have separate functional evidence (Table [18.4](#ss_p10_table_18_4)). Thyroid antioxidant and water-handling modifiers are developed in Section [16.10.2](#ss_p10_sec_16_10_2).

The proposed result is a changed relationship among ionic, volume, perfusion and stress signals: previously exposed tissue recruits a response more readily, sustains it longer or recovers less completely. Uniform hypo-osmolality is not required.

These directions remain tissue-specific. Reduced AVP responsiveness in pre-eclamptic placental vessels (Gao et al., 2019) cannot settle the fetal neural prediction, just as renal hormone–WNK–SPAK coupling cannot establish neural chloride effects.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_1_6"></a>

##### 18.1.6 Fetal Osmotic Set-Point Formation Under Threat-Biased or Conflicting Signals

The defensive-calibration branch predicts later recruitment of water or circulatory support at a lower threshold, a longer response or slower recovery under comparable conditions. A single hormone value cannot distinguish it from normal gestational resetting or temporary successful compensation.

Prenatal maternal water restriction shifted neonatal AVP thresholds upward in lambs, but they remained hypertonic and hypertensive at assessment and maternal nutritional restriction accompanied dehydration (Desai, Guerra, Wang and Ross, 2003b). This supports altered calibration after exposure ended, not persistence after complete physiological recovery or the lower threshold proposed for hypotonic or mixed cues. A stored imprint requires the specified later difference after the disturbance resolves; its adequately precise absence would oppose that branch.

After three days of maternal water deprivation from gestational day 18, rat fetal sodium rose from 124.29 to 129.45 mmol/L and osmolality from 288.86 to 324.67 mOsm/kg, alongside increased fetal Ang I and Ang II (Guan et al., 2009). At 7–8 weeks, exposed male offspring had greater pressor responses to intravenous Ang II and reduced baroreflex sensitivity without a detected resting-pressure difference; five offspring from different litters were compared per group. This demonstrates a later regulatory difference without requiring a low-sodium phase. Reduced maternal food intake lacked a pair-fed control, and AVP/corticosterone mediation, neural recovery and autism-related behaviour were not established.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_1_7"></a>

##### 18.1.7 Developmental Consequences: Ionic Handling, Volume Vulnerability, and Delayed Inhibitory Maturation

Fetal changes in intracellular chloride, KCC2 trafficking or expression, NKCC1 activity, WNK–SPAK signalling or metabolic support could prolong recovery and alter inhibitory maturation. Maternal defence alone does not establish these tissue effects; Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23), [26](#ss_p10_sec_26), and [27](#ss_p10_sec_27) develop their ionic, calcium and energetic consequences.

The proposed chloride-retentive branch links the following candidate findings, each requiring direct evidence:

- NKCC1-dominant cation–chloride transport

- elevated intracellular chloride (Cl⁻)

- secondary intracellular sodium burden (secondary Na⁺ burden) arising from coupled Na⁺ entry with NKCC1-mediated chloride loading

- increased Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase demand, required to continuously extrude the sodium loaded alongside chloride

- reduced extracellular space volume fraction (ECS compression)

- sustained energetic constraint (energy constraint), as ATP demand rises to maintain ionic gradients precisely when mitochondrial support may be limited by perfusion variability

Cellular water gain can compress extracellular space and raise local concentrations at fixed solute content; altered diffusion or removal is a separate effect. Limited oxygen or substrate can impair gradient restoration when ATP supply and reserve no longer meet demand. Repetition could establish a chloride-retentive, high-work recovery pattern, whereas adequate reserve permits successful recovery.

In embryonic mouse medial ganglionic eminence-derived cortical interneurons, KCC2 manipulation changed the transition from GABA-driven migration to a stop response through membrane voltage and L-type calcium-channel transients (Bortone and Polleux, 2009). This links chloride handling to migration timing in a defined population. The proposed extension is that impaired chloride recovery alters this timing and later circuitry; delayed KCC2 expression alone does not establish it. Depolarising GABA can retain shunting inhibition (§§[23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [26](#ss_p10_sec_26)), and hypoxia or swelling findings must be matched to the relevant cell and stage.

Delayed KCC2-mediated maturation could consequently affect circuit refinement that depends on precise interneuron timing, including parvalbumin (PV) networks. The chloride disturbance and its circuit effect remain distinct causal steps.

PV interneurons connect this proposal to network function. Optogenetic PV inhibition suppressed prefrontal gamma oscillations in mice, while PV feedback generated gamma-frequency rhythms in slices (Sohal et al., 2009). In 7–10-month-old mouse prefrontal slices, ten minutes of oxygen–glucose deprivation and fifteen minutes of reoxygenation allowed recovery in 1/7 PV interneurons versus 6/8 pyramidal neurons under current clamp; the difference was not significant under voltage clamp (Povysheva et al., 2019). This is preparation-dependent vulnerability, not a developmental ranking. In mice with impaired glutathione synthesis, degradation of mature perineuronal nets increased PV susceptibility to oxidative challenge and altered fast synchrony (Cabungcal et al., 2013). These studies support recovery and extracellular redox protection as candidate influences on PV function without establishing the developmental sequence.

The predicted consequence is delayed inhibitory maturation and less stable oscillatory recruitment when ionic, volume or energetic disturbance burdens rapidly firing interneurons. Slower KCC2 maturation, altered PV function and impaired refinement are separate endpoints; their persistence after serum sodium normalises must be demonstrated.

The proposed maternal-to-neural sequence is therefore:

maternal sodium–volume demand → placentally transformed fetal exposure → defence and recovery during a sensitive window → altered receptor, transporter or recovery function → possible chloride loading, sodium-extrusion work or extracellular-space change → altered inhibitory maturation, PV function or circuit refinement. Successful restoration can interrupt this sequence; intrinsic fetal constraints can enter without a maternal trigger.

##### 18.1.8 Developmental Effects Without Obligatory Sodium Loss or Dilution

Altered developmental calibration could reproduce specified ionic imbalance, chloride vulnerability or reduced volume resilience without sodium loss or extracellular dilution. Such a phenocopy would concern the specified endpoint, not independence from sodium transport. Maternal exposure must connect to a fetal defence/recovery response and later functional change. The imprint is altered response to demand, not obligatory lifelong hyponatraemia or hormone abnormality; intrinsic transporter constraints provide another entry.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_1_9"></a>

##### 18.1.9 Labour-Phase Sodium–Volume Perturbation

Labour adds a further interval in which maternal metabolic conditions may reduce physiological reserve. In pre-labour myometrium from 40 women with diabetes (18 type 1; 22 gestational) and 68 controls, absolute contractility was lower in diabetes (Al-Qahtani et al., 2012). At 10 nmol/L oxytocin, six diabetic and seven control samples showed proportional stimulation that did not differ significantly, although diabetic absolute force remained lower. Reduced calcium signals, channel expression and muscle content offered downstream explanations; OXTR abundance and affinity were unmeasured, so the single dose did not establish equivalent receptor function. The proposed osmotic–metabolic route concerns reduced contractile reserve or delayed recovery.

Exogenous oxytocin can also affect maternal water handling. Human infusion experiments demonstrate antidiuresis when the urinary concentrating mechanism is preserved, while V2-receptor involvement has been demonstrated in vasopressin-deficient rats (Joo et al., 2004; Li et al., 2008). These findings support a water-retention route without making oxytocin physiologically interchangeable with AVP or desmopressin.

Labour combines changes in fluid balance, contractions and fetal oxygenation. Of 61 women receiving more than 2.5 L of oral plus intravenous fluid, 16 (26%) developed postpartum sodium ≤130 mmol/L; about two-thirds of cohort fluid intake was oral (Moen et al., 2009). Umbilical arterial sodium correlated with maternal postpartum sodium. Total fluid volume remained associated with hyponatraemia after adjustment, whereas oxytocin was not independently significant. This supports a maternal–fetal fluid link without isolating oxytocin or establishing augmentation-related fetal injury.

Cord copeptin varies with delivery mode, acid–base state and gestational age; arterial and venous samples must remain distinct (Wellmann et al., 2010; Schlapbach et al., 2011). It reflects secretion-related activity, with kinetics distinct from intact AVP, not clearance, IRAP function or central release (Fenske et al., 2018). We predict relative attenuation with lower fetal effective tonicity under comparable birth and nonosmotic stimuli, rather than obligatory low copeptin. A low value during stress does not identify dilution, and a birth snapshot cannot establish earlier exposure or persistent calibration.

Reduced contractile reserve could increase augmentation needs, while fluid-balance and contraction-related perfusion changes could alter fetal exposure or recovery. However, in 1,362,950 Swedish births, the induction–ASD association fell from HR 1.19 (95% CI 1.13–1.24) to 0.99 (0.88–1.10) in sibling comparisons (Oberg et al., 2016). Induction is not an isolated oxytocin or fluid exposure. This result weakens causal attribution and supplies no support for an unmeasured osmotic subgroup; indicated augmentation is not intrinsically harmful.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_2"></a>

#### 18.2 Gestational hyperglycaemia and phase dependent osmotic stress

Glucose provides a distinct osmotic route within these metabolic exposures: an effective extracellular rise can draw water from cells and lower sodium by redistribution while tonicity rises. As glucose falls, this translocational component reverses when other balances are unchanged; neither phase establishes hypotonic hyponatraemia (Hillier et al., 1999). Table [18.2](#ss_p10_table_18_2) separates this physical sequence from pathological possibilities. Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) develops its quantitative limits and the proposed glucose–insulin recovery mechanism.

<a name="ss_p10_table_18_2"></a>***Table [18.2](#ss_p10_table_18_2). Glucose phase and the limits of osmotic inference***

| **Phase or condition**      | **Physical interpretation**                                                                                   | **Interpretive boundary**                                                                                                         |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Extracellular glucose rises | Water may move from cells to extracellular fluid; sodium may fall by dilution while effective tonicity rises. | Relevant compartment, glucose permeability and interval; sodium amount is not inferred from concentration alone.                  |
| Hyperglycaemia persists     | Glucose remains an osmotic contribution; glucosuria, if present, changes water and solute balance.            | Intake, urine losses, renal function and volume status determine net effects. No fixed AVP, RAAS or cortisol pattern is assigned. |
| Glucose declines            | Glucose-derived tonic support falls and the translocational shift can reverse.                                | Return towards baseline is distinct from overshoot, injury or true hypotonicity.                                                  |
| Recovery is incomplete      | Persistent imbalance is possible if additional processes delay restoration.                                   | Rebound requires a persistent water, solute, cellular or hormonal disturbance; glucose variation alone does not establish it.     |

##### 18.2.1 Circulatory and endocrine conditions that modify recovery

Impaired placental perfusion or persistent water imbalance could modify a glycaemic excursion. Translocational sodium lowering alone establishes neither a fixed AVP–RAAS–cortisol sequence, receptor fatigue nor fetal hypoperfusion. Redistribution into total extracellular water must also remain distinct from plasma expansion or effective filling.

##### 18.2.2 Maternal fetal transfer and developmental exposure

Maternal glucose and sodium do not specify fetal intracellular conditions; transport differences alone establish neither a sugar-rich, salt-deficient fetus nor low AVP with high RAAS/cortisol. Maternal diabetes–ASD associations do not establish that sequence or fetal recovery mediation (Xiang et al., 2018). Table [18.3](#ss_p10_table_18_3) separates the required causal links.

<a name="ss_p10_table_18_3"></a>**Table [18.3](#ss_p10_table_18_3). Causal links and boundaries of a maternal metabolic route to altered development**

| **Proposed link**        | **Required causal link**                                                                              | **Inference boundary**                                                                                        |
|--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Maternal metabolic state | A metabolic disturbance changes maternal tonicity or water–solute balance in its circulatory context. | Glucose included in calculated osmolality does not itself create an unexplained osmolal gap.                  |
| Fetal exposure           | A corresponding fetal exposure occurs during the relevant developmental interval.                     | Maternal values do not establish fetal cell volume, hormone direction or a fixed equilibration lag.           |
| Cellular recovery        | The exposure impairs local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery.                         | Initial hypertonic water loss and later return are not equivalent to hypotonic swelling or persistent injury. |
| Developmental mediation  | The recovery disturbance contributes causally to the susceptible developmental process.               | Association, transient illness or a later metabolic diagnosis does not establish this causal chain.           |

##### 18.2.3 Comparisons with other disturbances of water and solute balance

Low-solute intake, antidiuresis, placental disease and non-electrolyte exposure should not inherit the same fetal signature as hyperglycaemia. True hypotonic dilution, hypertonic translocational sodium lowering and analytical pseudohyponatraemia are distinct: the last is a measurement artifact, not a physiological dilution mechanism.

##### 18.2.4 Oncotic and nutritional modifiers as separate candidate mechanisms

Plasma proteins can alter intravascular–interstitial distribution without producing glucose-driven translocational dilution or low tonicity. Nutritional, placental and circulatory factors could amplify a metabolic disturbance through altered filling or fetal exposure, but their diagnosis does not prescribe a low-AVP, high-RAAS, high-cortisol state.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_3"></a>

#### 18.3 Artificial sweeteners and polyols and the limits of osmotic inference

Artificial sweeteners are not included as positive osmotic contributors in Table [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1) without evidence of sufficient exposure in the relevant compartment. In 19 late-pregnancy participants given 75 mg sucralose with other sweeteners, mean fetal plasma sucralose was 23.6 ng/mL (95% CI 16.7–30.5); the median intake-to-cord-clamp interval was 274 minutes (Leth-Møller et al., 2023). Using a molecular mass of 397.64 g/mol, this corresponds to a calculated ideal osmolar contribution of approximately 0.00006 mOsm/L, not a measured osmolality or tonicity. Placental transfer therefore does not support a material direct sucralose osmotic load at that sampled exposure. Earlier gestation, other doses and nonosmotic mechanisms remain separate questions. Polyols require their own compound-, dose- and compartment-specific evidence; the sucralose calculation neither excludes nor validates their effects. No sweetener-induced osmotic signal error or developmental recovery mechanism is established here.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_4"></a>

#### 18.4 Maternal Salt Loading

Maternal salt loading is an exposure trajectory, not a low-sodium endpoint. A measured fetal hypertonic excursion could recruit water conservation and cellular volume regulation. If effective solute subsequently falls while retention persists, a later hypotonic overshoot could follow, aided by continued nonosmotic drive, altered peptide removal or renal handling. Diet alone establishes neither fetal hypertonicity nor delayed AVP clearance; adult adipocyte and global-mouse IRAP findings do not establish fetal kinetics. Gestational peptide turnover and fetal AVP competence constrain this route (Sections [10.1.1](#ss_p10_sec_10_1_1), [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3), and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)).

In Afroz et al. (2021, corrected 2022), both parental C57BL/6 mice received 8% NaCl chow and 1% NaCl water from eight weeks before breeding through offspring weaning; controls received 0.1% NaCl chow and ordinary water. After offspring diet normalisation, exposed males showed more locomotion and marble burying at 8–10 weeks (77.14% versus 59.81% buried; p = 0.04). Significant social-chamber preference within controls but not exposed mice did not establish a between-diet social effect. Maternal, paternal, gestational and lactational contributions were unseparated, litter clustering was insufficiently described, and sodium, osmolality and recovery were unmeasured. Microbiome differences lacked demonstrated mediation. The study supplies a persistent behavioural signal, not autism or a demonstrated fetal hypertonic-to-hypotonic trajectory.

Cellular de-adaptation offers a different mismatch: adaptations established during hypertonicity might withdraw more slowly than extracellular tonicity normalises, leaving altered volume or ion gradients without plasma hypo-osmolality. This prediction is distinct from absolute hypotonic overshoot; one cannot substitute for a failed test of the other.

When hypertonicity recruits inward ion transport, including NKCC1 under permissive gradients, accompanying sodium entry can increase Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase work. The proposed cost arises only if restoration is constrained; persistent chloride elevation, inadequate ATP reserve and delayed recovery are not automatic. The mechanism is added restoration work, not simply pumping against higher extracellular sodium.

Salt-related endothelial or placental impairment could separately threaten filling or oxygen delivery and recruit protective AVP–RAAS–cortisol responses without one fixed hormone pattern. Maternal and fetal vessels, peptide exposure and renal balance remain distinct. Hypertonicity alone also does not establish cellular water gain or extracellular-space compression.

Altered nephrogenesis supplies another continuation without requiring dilutional rebound. Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32) reviews sodium experiments with differing nephron outcomes; the proposed enduring change in renal structure or regulatory reserve remains separate from its RAAS/perfusion mechanism and any later neural consequence.

Thus direct hypertonic challenge, later hypotonic overshoot, slow cellular de-adaptation, vascular constraint and altered renal development are distinguishable salt-exposure routes. Their developmental convergence remains a claim to establish, not a shared endpoint assigned in advance or a reason to substitute branches after a negative result.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_5"></a>

#### 18.5 Maternal Immune Activation and Placental Cardiovascular Responses

Maternal immune activation (MIA) could change the fetal environment and the demands placed on ionic and volume regulation through three overlapping routes: maternal molecular passage; placental or fetal production of mediators in response to maternal signals; and altered placental vascular function, fetal loading or oxygen/substrate delivery. Experimental support for these components and the pooled maternal infection/fever association (Tioleco et al., 2021) do not establish a general human infection-to-autism claim: the association in a large Swedish cohort attenuated in sibling comparisons (Brynge et al., 2022; Table [48.1](#ss_p10_table_48_1)).

Maternal urinary infection supplies a specific exposure for investigating this proposal. In a Swedish register study, a UTI diagnosis recorded during pregnancy hospitalisation was associated with an offspring inpatient autism diagnosis, adjusted HR 1.89 (95% CI 1.23–2.90; [Al-Haddad et al., 2019](#ss_revsyn1_ref_AlHaddad2019)). This was a hospital-recorded exposure, not an estimate for routine outpatient cystitis. Its adjustment for correlated sibling observations was not a within-family exposure comparison. Brynge et al. (2022) addressed a broader maternal-infection definition in a different population; its sibling attenuation therefore remains a relevant constraint without constituting a UTI-specific reanalysis. Maternal renal disturbance, fetal exposure and local recovery mediation were unmeasured in these associations. Section [18.1.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_1_2) explains the sibling-design limits and the distinct question of a persistent maternal physiological baseline.

Transfer depends on molecule and developmental stage. Term human placental perfusions disagree about IL-6 transfer (Zaretsky et al., 2004; Aaltonen et al., 2005), whereas mouse experiments support maternal IL-17A passage into fetal-associated compartments (Andruszewski et al., 2025). Neither defines early human fetal-brain dose: maternal concentration, amniotic-fluid detection and target-tissue exposure are distinct.

Placental relay is experimentally supported: trophoblast IL-6-receptor deletion prevented specified fetal-brain and later offspring abnormalities after mouse MIA (Wu et al., 2017). The mouse placenta also transiently supplies fetal forebrain serotonin from maternal tryptophan; poly(I:C) inflammation increased placental output and fetal forebrain serotonin, with altered serotonergic axon development (Bonnin et al., 2011; Goeden et al., 2016). These are active processing routes, alongside molecular transfer and circulation.

Inflammation can alter the placental glucocorticoid gate. In term human villous explants, IL-1β, IL-6 and TNF-α, each applied separately at 10 ng/mL, reduced 11β-HSD2 activity to about 23–25% of control by two hours, with further inhibition at 24 hours and unchanged mRNA (Kossintseva et al., 2006). Activity can thus change without reduced expression. If this occurred in vivo it could alter fetal glucocorticoid exposure and recovery; the explant finding does not establish that ordinary maternal stress produces it.

Acute cardiovascular effects were demonstrated after severe maternal intraperitoneal LPS (2.4 mg/kg) at mouse gestational day 14. At six hours, placental congestion and abnormal fetal Doppler measures were observed, with atrioventricular regurgitation in 15/23 surviving exposed fetuses versus 1/25 controls; three exposed fetuses died (Rounioja et al., 2005). The findings supported increased placental resistance and fetal afterload despite no significant induction of assayed fetal heart, lung and liver cytokine mRNAs. Those assays exclude neither transferred cytokine protein nor local inflammatory effects. This severe model establishes a cardiovascular possibility, not typical human infection effects or a later autism outcome.

Inflammation could also modify the maternal environment through renal handling. High-dose LPS in mice reduced blood pressure and GFR, increased fractional sodium excretion and lowered the expression of several sodium-handling transporters; supplementary glucocorticoid treatment attenuated both renal dysfunction and transporter downregulation ([Schmidt et al., 2007](#ss_revsyn1_ref_Schmidt2007)). This provides experimental component evidence, rather than a measurement in pregnant women with UTI. Increased fractional excretion during reduced filtration does not alone establish negative whole-body sodium balance, and pharmacological attenuation does not demonstrate an obligatory endogenous cortisol rescue. The proposed maternal branch applies where infection produces a consequential sodium or water disturbance that adds to placental or fetal recovery demands. Successful renal compensation and treatment remain alternatives, and the infant aldosterone-resistance phenotype in Section [14.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_4) is a separate clinical observation.

Compensation changes the developmental interpretation. In intra-amniotic-LPS sheep, reduced arterial oxygen content accompanied increased carotid flow, with no detected reduction in estimated cerebral oxygen delivery (Galinsky et al., 2013). A lower-dose maternal-LPS mouse model showed placental injury without detected uterine or umbilical Doppler-index changes (Fricke et al., 2018). Inflammation can therefore produce different delivery trajectories across preparations.

The proposed adverse branch begins when delivery falls below requirements despite compensation, or disturbances recur before local recovery completes. Developmentally competent fetal AVP–RAAS–cortisol and autonomic responses may preserve circulation. Where oxygen or substrate remains inadequate, ATP-dependent sodium/potassium maintenance could become constrained, affecting chloride regulation and volume recovery. The required link is impaired recovery during a susceptible interval; increased afterload alone does not establish a neural ATP deficit. Section [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6) develops the local neural alternative.

Antibodies provide cardiovascular comparators distinct from acute infection-triggered MIA. FcRn participates in human IgG transfer; fetal concentrations were relatively low at 17–22 weeks and rose substantially towards term (Firan et al., 2001; Malek et al., 1996). Heart-block-associated maternal IgG altered calcium currents and conduction in cardiac preparations (Boutjdir et al., 1997). Agonistic AT1 antibodies retained activity in human cord blood and produced placental/fetal effects in transfer experiments (Irani et al., 2009). Antibody-driven AT1 activation is not compensatory fetal RAAS recruitment, and convergence on impaired recovery remains proposed (see also Section [19.2](#ss_p10_sec_19_2)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_18_6"></a>

#### 18.6 Local Neural Effects and Maternal Brain-Reactive Antibodies

Alongside the placental and cardiovascular routes, inflammatory effects on transport, glial support or maturation could reduce local recovery capacity during a sensitive window. They may interact with restricted delivery or initiate the proposed process without systemic hyponatraemia, hypovolaemia or prior AVP recruitment. Their connection to the common process requires impaired ionic or cellular-volume recovery that changes development.

After mouse MIA, Corradini et al. (2018) found elevated neuronal chloride, altered chloride-transporter expression and delayed GABA maturation. Fernandez et al. (2019) found an abnormally depolarising hippocampal GABA driving force already at birth, acutely corrected by bath-applied bumetanide. These establish modifiable ionic state and developmental timing; the additional recovery claim is inadequate restoration after challenge (Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)), with possible consequences for inhibitory maturation (Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4)).

Systemic LPS impaired dentate granule-cell chloride regulation in adult mice 48 hours later: a reduced somatodendritic gradient under maintained somatic chloride load indicated weaker extrusion, alongside separate evidence of increased NKCC1 uptake (Kurki et al., 2023). This functional-demand result did not measure post-pulse return or development. We propose that inflammation persisting into recovery could prolong a similar constraint in immature tissue; glucose is a possible duration modifier (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)).

IL-17A increased cortical folding, thickness and neurogenesis in cerebroids derived from 11–14-week human fetal brain tissue, retaining microglia and vascular cells but lacking systemic circulation (Assir et al., 2026). This demonstrates local developmental susceptibility without establishing recovery mediation. Responses differ across stages and preparations: prenatal IL-17A contributed to cortical and behavioural abnormalities in mice (Choi et al., 2016), whereas IL-17A-dependent signalling transiently improved adult MIA-offspring sociability (Reed et al., 2020). The latter circuit effect is distinct from temperature-mediated fever responses (Section [46.2](#ss_p10_sec_46_2)).

Assir et al. (2026) also found sustained nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) p65 activation in separately studied human iPSC-derived neural progenitors; parthenolide co-treatment reduced cerebroid cortical and neurogenic abnormalities. Treatment during exposure does not demonstrate later reversal of established architecture. The mouse MIA-to-protein-production mechanism in Section [29.2](#ss_p10_sec_29_2) supplies another comparison. Neither establishes recovery mediation, and accelerated maturation, delayed differentiation and altered coordination remain distinct outcomes (Sections [29.3](#ss_p10_sec_29_3) and [31.4](#ss_p10_sec_31_4)).

The maternal autoantibody-related autism programme (MAR autism; MAR-ASD) concerns a distinct exposure. Maternal antibodies recognise developing-brain proteins including lactate dehydrogenase A/B (LDHA/LDHB), stress-induced phosphoprotein 1 (STIP1) and collapsin response mediator proteins 1/2 (CRMP1/CRMP2) (Braunschweig et al., 2013). Associated patterns were developed from postpartum samples (Ramirez-Celis et al., 2021) and later found in pregnancy samples (Ramirez-Celis et al., 2022), strengthening temporal order without yielding a universally accurate prenatal test. Selected maternal IgG altered brain growth and social behaviour in rhesus monkeys (Bauman et al., 2013); a maternal contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2)-reactive monoclonal antibody produced cortical and behavioural abnormalities in male mice (Brimberg et al., 2016). CASPR2 was not enriched in a separate human gestational ASD comparison (Coutinho et al., 2017), a different target from the multi-antigen profiles. Specificity, fetal dose and target access define each route; acute MIA need not generate these antibodies.

Folate-receptor antibodies measured in children identify another possible route: restricted substrate delivery at a brain interface (Ramaekers et al., 2005, 2007; Section [30](#ss_p10_sec_30)). These are not maternal brain-reactive IgG or prenatal MIA findings. Folate delivery could affect recovery or development through another mechanism.

Complement-associated synaptic handling offers another candidate local interaction. MIA preparations have produced increased or deficient microglial engulfment, so neither excess pruning nor maternal complement passage follows automatically from an offspring signal (Yan et al., 2024; Andoh et al., 2019; Section [48](#ss_p10_sec_48)).

The common-process conjecture predicts that immune routes contributing to the neurodevelopmental features of autism converge on the recovery constraint in Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2). A reproducible developmental effect with adequately demonstrated preserved relevant recovery would challenge that necessity; unmeasured recovery establishes neither convergence nor bypass. Direct developmental alternatives therefore remain part of the comparison (Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)).

Term studies provide no universal early-transfer threshold. EV, extracellular vesicle; NPC, neural progenitor cell. This is a bounded comparison, not an exhaustive catalogue.
