The proposed convergence concerns recovery and its developmental consequence, not identical intracellular changes or hormone responses. Sections [7](#ss_p10_sec_7) and [19](#ss_p10_sec_19) distinguish intrinsic initiation from interactions among routes.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_19"></a>

### 19 Convergence and Interaction Among Sodium–Volume Defence Pathways

The systemic and intrinsic routes considered separately above may converge on a shared recovery disturbance without occurring together. When they do interact, one route may increase or reduce the demand imposed by another, or alter ionic, volume or perfusion recovery. Triad discordance, joint intracellular Na⁺/Cl⁻ elevation, increased pump work and ATP depletion are distinct candidate findings, not obligatory features. Systemic and intrinsic routes converge on the proposed core only through a recovery disturbance that carries a developmental effect.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_19_1"></a>

#### 19.1 Convergence, Interaction and Hybrid States

Dietary, pharmacological, obstetric, infectious and environmental inputs can amplify, counteract or act independently of one another. Convergence means different initiating routes reaching a shared physiological endpoint; they need not occur together. The candidate combinations considered here involve disturbed water handling, hypotonic dilution, hypertonic redistribution, renal sodium handling, delivery threat or cellular recovery. An interaction changes the effect of one input in the presence of another. Adverse amplification is the more specific prediction that a defined combination produces a larger or longer relevant disturbance than its components under matched conditions. Neither a common hormone direction nor an intracellular signature is assumed.

Hybrid states combine pathways through layered or transient mechanisms. One candidate is a cytokine–phosphate/FGF23 sequence with an early RAAS response followed by reduced mineralocorticoid support and greater glucocorticoid contribution, interacting with sensory, energetic or distribution constraints.

The developmental claim concerns the timing and incomplete recovery of such compensation. Immune illness might produce high AVP with inadequate mineralocorticoid support and cortisol weighting, but the defence triad does not prescribe this sequence. “Hybrid” denotes pathway integration, not rarity or persistent hyponatraemia.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_19_2"></a>

#### 19.2 Maternal Alloimmunisation (Rh\[D\]) and Fetal Haemolytic Hypoxia

Maternal anti-Rh(D) IgG causes fetal haemolysis and anaemia, threatening oxygen delivery where circulatory compensation is insufficient. Inadequate oxygen/substrate support could then impair sodium extrusion or renal reclamation. Fetal AVP can support vascular tone and water conservation during hypoxia without increased renin activity (Raff and Wood, 1992); renin and aldosterone depend separately on renal perfusion, pressure, potassium and developmental stage.

The proposed energetic paradox is appropriate endocrine defence alongside inadequate ATP-supported transport: sodium-conserving signals cannot supply the energy to restore gradients. Additional antibody-mediated membrane effects remain a separate hypothesis, not a consequence of haemolysis alone.

Intrauterine transfusion changes fetal cardiac measures and rheology while the maternal antibody source persists (Herling et al., 2020; Welch et al., 1994). Because it changes oxygen carriage, haematocrit, viscosity, volume and loading together, it is not a selective volume rescue; anaemia itself is not hypovolaemia. This red-cell route complements the cardiac and brain-reactive antibodies in Sections [18.5](#ss_p10_sec_18_5) and [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6).

Recurrent hypoxic demand could also calibrate later AVPR1A vascular responsiveness, AVPR1B stress recruitment or AGTR1 support upward in specified tissues. A related branch predicts stronger AVP-linked neural signalling and weaker oxytocin modulation; AVPR2/AQP2 adaptation and AQP4 distribution are additional modifiers. Lasting changes after recovery could affect neurovascular support, stress or social-affiliative function. Acute AVP elevation or receptor expression alone does not establish that persistent functional imprint.

During mixed hypoxia and dilution, hypotonicity can restrain osmotic AVP drive without prescribing low AVP, quiet RAAS or cortisol substitution (Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3)). The defence triad responds to actual fetal signals; a shift towards cortisol support requires a changed need and response, not an inference from anaemia, energetic strain or phosphate exposure.

This route links maternal antibody exposure to haemolytic oxygen-delivery limitation, possible ATP-supported transport constraint and developmentally consequential defence or recovery. Successful restoration remains possible. An adequately precise absence or opposite direction of the specified later receptor or recovery difference after resolution would oppose the persistence branch.

#### 19.3 Mechanistic Convergence Across Initiating Routes

Impaired water excretion could combine with inadequate sodium conservation or perfusion. Hypothyroid water-load findings demonstrate impaired excretion with absent AVP suppression (Ota et al., 1994; Table [14.3](#ss_p10_table_14_3)), and additional free water could deepen dilution if supply exceeded clearance. Low mineral content alone does not establish that imbalance. Nor do low renin or preeclampsia establish failed conservation: downstream retention can remain effective, and maternal state does not specify fetal exposure.

Glucose–insulin physiology can initiate, amplify, oppose or modify recovery from a hydromineral disturbance (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)). Cortisol, inflammatory, renal and circulatory effects could change the trajectory. Glucose-associated sodium lowering remains distinct from hypotonicity, and IRAP–AVP termination supplies a separate candidate link.

Cellular reserve can modify the response to a systemic challenge. The compound-specific component findings and exposure limits are set out in Section [14.8](#ss_p10_sec_14_8) and Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1). A dose-relevant cytoskeletal, barrier or volume-recovery defect from a specified PFAS, phthalate or other exposure could amplify measured antidiuresis or hypotonic stress. One-carbon metabolism and betaine supply separate candidate influences on osmolyte reserve. NFAT5 participation and ionic transport direction remain to be established; no shared membrane–synapse effect is assigned to all compounds.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_19_4"></a>

#### 19.4 Endocrine Amplification and Feedback Locking

Inflammatory, endothelial and endocrine responses could prolong a disturbance through cytokine recruitment of AVP/HPA signalling, altered placental perfusion or permeability, and local glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid actions. Cytokine–endocrine coupling has component evidence: IL-6 infusion increased cortisol in healthy adults (Steensberg et al., 2003; Section [14.6.10](#ss_p10_sec_14_6_10)). The effects of these responses depend on the defended state: continued antidiuresis may impede dilutional recovery, whereas sodium conservation may restore inadequate filling. A raised osmotic threshold delays AVP recruitment, and MR engagement alone does not imply increased HPA output. Feedback locking requires the disturbance to sustain a response that in turn maintains the disturbance; overlapping hormones are insufficient. Persistence after normalisation is a further proposed change in receptors, thresholds or recovery capacity.

#### 19.5 Physiological Outcomes of Convergence

Convergence could combine greater ionic demand with less recovery capacity, changing later AVPR1A/AVPR1B responsiveness or local MR/GR signalling. A separate membrane branch predicts impaired OXTR surface organisation from cytoskeletal or microdomain disruption. Altered barriers might also change fetal exposure to maternal hydration or metabolic fluctuations. These functional effects, their persistence and their developmental consequences must be distinguished from circulating hormone levels. Chloride and GABA consequences remain cell- and stage-dependent (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [26](#ss_p10_sec_26)); the proposed lasting link is altered calibration after repeated challenge or incomplete recovery.

Preterm sodium loss supplies a measured component: in seven infants, negative sodium balance developed during the first two weeks despite high plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentrations (Sulyok et al., 1979; Section [14.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_4)). Its combination with antidiuresis or an additional epithelial or energetic constraint remains a hypothesis requiring measured effects on water–solute recovery. Prematurity alone does not establish that interaction.

#### 19.6 Clinical and Environmental Realism: Convergent Exposure Clusters

Candidate exposure clusters require distinct causal interpretation. Low-mineral water plus phosphate could alter water–solute balance, but low mineral content does not establish hypotonicity or antidiuresis and FGF23 promoted sodium retention in mice (Andrukhova et al., 2014; §§[14.5](#ss_p10_sec_14_5) and [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). Maternal illness plus acetaminophen must be separated from treatment indication; sibling comparisons weigh against the medication association as causal support (Ahlqvist et al., 2024; §[14.2.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_2_4)). Pollution plus a specified cytoskeletal disruptor remains a dose-specific barrier/recovery hypothesis (§§[14.8](#ss_p10_sec_14_8), [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8), and [21.5](#ss_p10_sec_21_5)). Co-occurrence alone establishes neither amplification nor a common AVP-high, cortisol-high state.

Preeclampsia supplies a vascular context, not a fetal hormone profile; hypoxia is a separate AVP stimulus (§[10](#ss_p10_sec_10)). Preterm renal losses and fluid practices can produce low, high or changing sodium (§[12](#ss_p10_sec_12)). Folate, choline and iron may modify osmolyte reserve, barriers or oxygen delivery, but those proposed contributions must be separated from their other nutritional functions.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_19_7"></a>

#### 19.7 Glucose as a candidate extracellular osmotic resource and insulin dependent recovery

Glucose metabolism could influence both the disturbance that recruits osmotic–volume defence and the course of recovery. We propose two separable contributions: temporary extracellular osmotic support from glucose during a hypotonic threat, and coordination of substrate handling, ionic responses and peripheral peptide termination during recovery. The second could operate without a preceding protective glucose rise. GSH-sensitive processing, relative oxytocin exposure and redox or inflammatory feedback provide additional conditional extensions. Each connection requires its own conditions; the section does not propose one obligatory metabolic sequence.

##### 19.7.1 Glucose as a candidate extracellular osmotic resource

We propose that endogenous glucose mobilisation or reduced disposal during a hypotonic threat can temporarily oppose cellular disturbance through glucose’s extracellular osmotic effect. Its physical action motivates the hypothesis. Demonstrating an emergency buffering benefit requires improvement under the relevant conditions beyond glucose’s contribution as fuel.

While glucose acts as an effective extracellular osmole across a specified membrane and interval, its rise can draw water from cells and lower extracellular sodium by redistribution without requiring sodium loss. This does not establish hypotonic swelling. In an acute human experiment, sodium fell as glucose rose and normalised with glucose (Hillier et al., 1999). Subsequent water return towards cells is ordinary recovery. Pathological overshoot requires an additional imbalance in water, effective solute, intracellular osmolytes, transport or hormonal duration; vascular tone, filling and local brain state remain separate endpoints.

The model also constrains the possible effect size. In the illustrative closed adult model (Bell, 2026a), 42 L total water is initially divided into 14 L extracellular and 28 L intracellular water, with extracellular sodium 140 mmol/L and glucose 5 mmol/L. Adding glucose without water, fixing other effective-osmole inventories and allowing redistribution gives, at glucose 10 mmol/L, sodium approximately 138.35 mmol/L, extracellular volume approximately 14.167 L and effective osmolarity approximately 286.71 rather than 285 mOsm/L. The net increment is therefore about 1.71 mOsm/L and the transcellular redistribution about 167 mL. Sodium dilution is already included. The calculation assumes extracellular glucose confinement and no metabolism, intake or renal loss. The 167 mL is neither measured plasma expansion nor water that the kidneys must excrete. A fetal estimate requires its own compartment proportions, solute inventories, permeability and timing; even the concentration increment cannot simply be transferred unchanged.

Epithelial transport helps determine glucose appearance and retention. Small-intestinal sodium–glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1; SLC5A1) couples luminal glucose uptake to sodium entry (§[43.1.6](#ss_p10_sec_43_1_6)). Renal SGLT2 (SLC5A2) supplies the major early proximal-tubule reabsorptive route, with SGLT1 reclaiming glucose further downstream. Expressed human SGLT2 and SGLT1 couple one glucose molecule to one and two Na⁺ ions, respectively (Hummel et al., 2011). In euglycaemic mice, downstream SGLT1 can reabsorb substantial additional glucose when SGLT2 is inhibited or absent (Rieg et al., 2014). Renal reclamation limits urinary loss; it is distinct from intestinal delivery, endogenous glucose production and glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4)-mediated tissue disposal.

Glucosuria can increase water loss without necessarily causing sodium depletion. Sglt2-null mice had glucosuria and increased fluid excretion, but sodium excretion was unchanged in clearance studies; greater drinking accompanied preserved blood pressure, haematocrit and plasma sodium (Vallon et al., 2011). Net effects therefore depend on intake and renal responses as well as filtered glucose and reabsorptive capacity. A fetal extension requires stage-specific evidence for filtration and tubular function, and cannot equate total glucose-reabsorptive capacity with SGLT2 alone.

A protective contribution must improve volume, tonicity or circulation through an osmotic effect, separately from fuel provision and counterregulation; persistent glucose or glucosuria could instead complicate recovery. Severe water intoxication in young mice produced hyperglycaemia with lower insulin (Thurston et al., 1978). In ten men, a 17-hour hypotonic protocol using desmopressin, water and hypotonic saline reduced clamp glucose clearance from 4.4 to 3.3 mL/kg/min (about 25%), with pre-clamp glucose of 4.9 mmol/L in the isotonic condition and 4.7 mmol/L in the hypotonic condition (Berneis et al., 1999). The final two-hour insulin clamp was imposed, not spontaneous recovery. These findings support hydromineral–metabolic interaction, including without glucose elevation, but do not establish protection.

In differentiated H9c2 cells engineered to overexpress intracellular angiotensin II, 40 minutes of hypotonicity reduced insulin-present glucose-analogue uptake and IRS-1 abundance. Losartan pretreatment or repeated hypotonic-medium replacement counteracted the uptake reduction (Gerena et al., 2017). This is a context-specific swelling–transport link; GLUT4 recruitment, redox mediation and benefit to cell integrity were not established.

A selective redox brake is another candidate. In 3T3-L1 adipocytes, 10 µM mitochondria-targeted paraquat for two hours reduced insulin-stimulated 2-deoxyglucose uptake and surface GLUT4 recruitment by about 26%, without detectable respiratory or Akt/TBC1D4 phosphorylation impairment; an inactive analogue did not reproduce it (Fazakerley et al., 2018). L6 myotubes retained AMPK-agonist responsiveness despite impaired insulin-responsive GLUT4 recruitment. Thus transport can be selectively impaired, although no osmotic challenge or IRAP measurement established the proposed sequence.

Osmotic redox inputs depend on challenge direction. In HEK293 cells, 16 hours at 500 rather than 290 mOsm/kg with NaCl increased NFAT5-dependent transcription; mitochondrial inhibitors implicated oxidant signalling, and oligomycin reduced the response without significantly lowering measured ATP (Zhou et al., 2006). This is not evidence of hypotonic GLUT4 restriction. In neonatal rat cardiomyocytes, diluted hypotonic medium increased oxidant signals and injury, while catalase improved volume recovery and survival (Díaz-Elizondo et al., 2006). Harmful redox injury therefore remains an alternative to protective uptake restriction.

After 72 hours at sodium 110–130 rather than 140 mEq/L, neonatal rat cardiomyocyte DCF oxidant-probe signals increased; lipid-peroxidation readouts and vulnerability to an added oxidant challenge increased at 110–120 mEq/L, without detected basal mitochondrial-potential change (Oniki et al., 2020). Mannitol adjustment did not abolish the oxidative changes. This supports an effect beyond low bulk osmolality, but identifies neither mitochondrial superoxide as the source nor selective glucose restriction as protective.

Reduced insulin responsiveness need not mean reduced total glucose entry. Severe hyperosmotic shock with 600 mM sorbitol increased GLUT4 recruitment and glucose transport in 3T3-L1 adipocytes while preventing a further insulin response and impairing Akt activation (Chen et al., 1999). Direction, magnitude and basal transport therefore constrain any extracellular-glucose-retention interpretation.

Epple and Brinn (1976) proposed dual osmoregulatory and intermediary-metabolic islet functions varying across vertebrates, followed by eel pancreatectomy work and a later synthesis (Epple and Miller, 1981; Epple and Brinn, 1987). The present protective-glucose hypothesis was developed independently before this work was identified. It supplies historical precedent, but whole-pancreas removal did not isolate insulin or establish the protective-glucose, IRAP or autism mechanisms proposed here. Useful present-day regulation also does not establish its evolutionary origin.

##### 19.7.2 Insulin and IRAP in AVP termination

The second proposal is that insulin-associated changes in peripheral AVP clearance help coordinate water handling with metabolic recovery. It can be evaluated independently of protective glucose support. Insulin recruits GLUT4 and insulin-regulated aminopeptidase (IRAP; encoded by LNPEP) from shared muscle/adipose compartments, increasing glucose-transport capacity and exposing IRAP’s catalytic domain extracellularly. This is surface deployment, not necessarily enzyme release or catalytic activation by GLUT4 transport. Insulin increased adipocyte vasopressin cleavage and accelerated disappearance of intact labelled AVP in mice through IRAP (Herbst et al., 1997; Wallis et al., 2007). Habtemichael et al. (2015) previously proposed TUG-dependent coordination of glucose uptake and AVP inactivation to dispose of oxidation-generated water and relieve vasoconstriction. The present extension concerns recovery as extracellular glucose’s tonic contribution falls.

Wallis et al. (2007) estimated intact labelled-AVP half-lives of about 1.5 minutes in wild-type mice, 1 minute after insulin, and 3 minutes in IRAP-null mice with or without insulin. Knockouts had about twice the circulating endogenous AVP but lower whole-brain AVP content and transcripts: consistent with cross-compartment compensation, not an acquired suppression sequence. Intact labelled oxytocin recovery at five minutes did not differ detectably (n = 5), despite lost N-terminal processing in isolated knockout tissues. Shared substrates therefore do not impose a fixed AVP–oxytocin clearance ratio, and peripheral kinetics cannot identify reduced neural production, altered development or release (Section [36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5)).

Insulin’s renal and glucose effects can also dissociate. In six water-loaded participants at maintained glucose, insulin reduced sodium excretion and raised calculated free-water clearance from about 10.6 to 13.0 mL/min, because osmolar clearance fell while urine flow remained unchanged (DeFronzo et al., 1975). This was selective solute handling, not increased urine-water output; AVP was unmeasured and plasma osmolality approximately stable. Insulin also retained substantial antinatriuretic action in obese adolescents with impaired glucose responsiveness (Rocchini et al., 1989). Neither result establishes IRAP-mediated recovery from hypotonicity.

“Insulin resistance” does not specify peptide processing. Human type 2 diabetic adipocytes had about 4.4-fold higher basal plasma-membrane-fraction IRAP despite impaired further recruitment, with GLUT4 reduced across fractions (Maianu et al., 2001). That fraction does not measure exposed catalytic activity. Insulin deficiency, hyperinsulinaemic resistance, trafficking impairment and catalytic IRAP defects therefore remain distinct states (Section [21.2](#ss_p10_sec_21_2)).

The shared cargos can dissociate. In rat adipocytes pretreated with high glucose plus insulin or glucosamine, insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation remained intact while gp160/IRAP recruitment to the plasma-membrane fraction was impaired (Filippis et al., 1998). Lower basal transport nevertheless reduced glucose uptake, and peptide cleavage was unmeasured. The finding establishes trafficking dissociation, not preserved glucose disposal with proven AVP-clearance failure.

Where glucose redistribution and AVP-mediated water conservation occur together, we propose that their relative timing contributes to recovery. The proposed metabolic–osmotic handoff couples falling extracellular glucose to appropriately adjusted water conservation. Net appearance, disposal and distribution determine the glucose trajectory; GLUT4 recruitment alone does not. Insulin and IRAP need not wait for a distinct late phase: IRAP surface recruitment had a half-time of about two minutes in insulin-stimulated 3T3-L1 adipocytes (Ross et al., 1997). The prediction concerns relative timing and magnitude, allowing overlap.

Appropriately timed IRAP termination could limit dilution if excess water retention otherwise continued as glucose fell. But water conservation may remain appropriate during underfilling or shortage. Insulin-dependent cellular hydration can coexist with improved extracellular water balance; the proposal does not require insulin to shrink cells. Benefit depends on the starting state and actual water, tonicity and cellular or perfusion response.

Pregnancy offers a setting for the proposed handoff. Its normal downward osmotic reset is not failed regulation (§[10](#ss_p10_sec_10)). Insulin sensitivity falls while increased secretion compensates; women developing gestational diabetes showed a lag in that increase (Catalano et al., 1993). We propose an additional, state-dependent sequence during hypotonic challenge: an early extracellular glucose rise supports tonicity, followed by insulin-dependent disposal and appropriately timed peptide termination. This glucose-first, insulin-later coordination is not an established purpose of pregnancy insulin resistance. Glucose-associated sodium lowering must still be distinguished from hypotonicity.

Cell-surface IRAP, placental LNPEP expression, shed circulating P-LAP/IRAP and intact-peptide degradation are not interchangeable. Köse et al. (2025) found lower serum IRAP by ELISA in 40 women with GDM versus 40 controls; Guleroglu et al. (2023) found no significant early difference in 109 pregnancies, 19 later meeting GDM criteria. Assay comparability requires clarification, and neither measured active AVP or oxytocin clearance. Stage, treatment, secretion, tissue access and catalysis matter beyond diagnosis.

Oxytocin studies further separate assay activity from clearance. In ten women assessed late in pregnancy and postpartum, metabolic clearance at the lower matched concentration was 5.7 ± 0.6 versus 1.3 ± 0.1 L/min (Thornton et al., 1990). In 14 pregnant, puerperal and nonpregnant subjects, Takeda et al. (1989) found no significant in-vivo difference despite much greater degradation in pregnant plasma in vitro. These findings constrain a universal multiplier and cannot establish a GDM-specific peptide imbalance or the LNPEP share of clearance. Compensatory supply remains distinct from removal (§[10](#ss_p10_sec_10)).

A separate observation links osmotic state with peptide-processing activity. In challenged rats, plasma osmolality correlated with plasma cystine aminopeptidase activity while measured CNS activity was unchanged (Silveira et al., 2001). This synthetic-substrate CAP assay cannot substitute for identified cell-surface IRAP or native AVP clearance. Osmotic and insulin regulation therefore remain a proposed convergence, not one demonstrated by combining different activity assays.

The systemic IRAP–AVP prediction is that reduced accessible active IRAP prolongs active peripheral AVP independently of input and delays water or tonicity recovery (Bell, 2026b). Copeptin cannot establish clearance: in 91 volunteers its initial decay during osmotic suppression differed from AVP, about 26 versus 12 minutes (Fenske et al., 2018). These are endogenous protocol-dependent kinetics, not tracer-clearance constants. Global IRAP-null mice showed impaired urinary dilution after a water load of 10% body weight (Zuchowski et al., 2023); this substantial challenge does not isolate acute muscle/adipose action from renal or developmental effects. Peripheral kinetics also do not specify CSF AVP or neural release.

Compensation may normalise concentration without normalising pulse removal. In a first-order model at constant distribution volume, proportionally lower secretion and clearance preserve steady concentration but slow decay of an identical added pulse at fixed subsequent input. This predicts kinetics, not hidden compensation from a normal AVP value. If secretion, alternative clearance or renal responsiveness prevents prolonged active exposure or impaired water recovery, the harmful-exposure bridge is absent.

##### 19.7.3 Conditional GSH and oxytocin extensions

GSH-sensitive processing provides a separate candidate route that could modify the consequences of restricted IRAP termination. Preparation studies demonstrate GSH-sensitive AVP degradation without identifying its relationship to IRAP-mediated clearance. In rat renal brush-border membranes and cortical lysosomal fractions, adding 1 mmol/L reduced GSH enabled AVP degradation measured by HPLC (Carone et al., 1987). GSH-sensitive processing has direct human-tissue support: renal microvilli degraded AVP with added GSH but not without it, whereas oxytocin still degraded without added GSH; crude liver preparations also degraded AVP (Fjellestad-Paulsen and Lundin, 1996). Perfused organs showed peritubular renal and hepatic removal of immunoreactive AVP without identifying either route’s GSH dependence (Rabkin et al., 1979, 1980). These demonstrate multiple removal opportunities, not their physiological shares in active circulating AVP clearance (Section [14.2.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_2_4)). The enzymes responsible in these older preparations were not identified as IRAP, and these experiments do not establish GSH as an IRAP cofactor.

IRAP separately contains active-site zinc. In CHO-K1 membranes, 40–100 µM added zinc restored chelator-inhibited cystinyl aminopeptidase activity, with renewed inhibition at higher additions (Hermans et al., 2015; Laeremans et al., 2005). The synthetic substrate and chelator-containing buffer define no dietary or serum-zinc threshold for native AVP clearance. IRAP hydrolyses peptide bonds rather than reducing disulfides; zinc-dependent catalysis and GSH-sensitive processing are distinct constraints, not an established serial pathway or demonstrated nutrient limitation in vivo.

Lipid-peroxide demand could weaken membrane protection and AVP termination together if it outpaced GSH recycling and replacement at a relevant renal processing site. Less GSH-sensitive processing might then reduce backup capacity during restricted IRAP termination; that compensatory role remains proposed. Neural, renal and extracellular pools are separate, and renal-preparation findings do not establish lipid-oxidation-induced slowing of active circulating AVP removal (Carone et al., 1987; Fjellestad-Paulsen and Lundin, 1996; Section [14.2.4](#ss_p10_sec_14_2_4)).

The issue is local availability, not presumed whole-body depletion by AVP disposal. Greater reliance on GSH-sensitive processing need not consume enough GSH to compromise GPX4. Low concentration, poor substrate access or slow regeneration could nevertheless constrain a renal site. For this systemic branch, the effect must reduce active circulating AVP removal, not only filtered-peptide degradation. Secretion adjustment, alternative clearance or renal responsiveness could preserve water balance despite one impaired route. The developmental proposal is that restricted IRAP deployment and limited GSH at a relevant renal processing site could jointly prolong compensation during combined metabolic and oxidative stress. Neonatal blood-cell or plasma findings do not measure that renal pool, and neither a sex difference in infant active-AVP clearance nor compensation for impaired IRAP has been demonstrated.

The substrate differences above motivate an additional compensation hypothesis: selective slowing of AVP removal could increase circulating AVP exposure relative to oxytocin without lowering oxytocin concentration. Reduced oxytocin secretion would require a further feedback step. In rats, AVP or desmopressin pretreatment altered the osmotic threshold for release from oxytocin neurones, inferred from circulating neurophysin measurements, without changing the response slope ([Cheng and North, 1989](#ss_ref_cheng_north_1989)). The authors inferred a largely V2-like feedback influence from the pharmacology. The experiment used administered peptides rather than impaired clearance, and circulating neurophysin measurements do not establish local brain oxytocin release.

This experimental feedback component motivates, but does not establish, a clearance-driven reduction in oxytocin recruitment. The proposed sequence requires reduced oxytocin secretion after demonstrably prolonged active AVP exposure, distinguished from changes in oxytocin clearance and in osmotic or effective-filling conditions. Preserved oxytocin recruitment under a matched challenge despite prolonged AVP exposure would weaken the suppression branch. Its consequences for water and sodium handling depend on the physiological state; a protective renal purpose is not assumed. Any neural extension requires evidence in the relevant circuit (Section [37.1.2](#ss_p10_sec_37_1_2)).

##### 19.7.4 Proposed feedback between glucose and water handling

One possible feedback loop combines glucose support, peptide termination and GSH-sensitive processing when their necessary conditions coincide. In this scenario, oxidative membrane disturbance increases volume-control difficulty. A sufficient extracellular glucose rise could temporarily oppose swelling without repairing the bilayer, followed by insulin-dependent recovery. Water-intoxication findings establish neither deliberate insulin suppression nor a general high-glucose/low-insulin rule (Thurston et al., 1978); absent GLUT4 recruitment alone does not make glucose impermeant. If inadequate recruitment or a selective IRAP defect delays peptide termination as glucose is disposed of, protection could be followed by a water-handling cost. Acquired insulin resistance is unnecessary, and GLUT4 and IRAP need not fail together (Filippis et al., 1998).

Concurrent GSH-sensitive processing limitation could reduce another AVP-removal opportunity. If active AVP then outlasts the need for conservation, water supply and renal responsiveness could permit antidiuresis to deepen dilution, renewing the challenge to vulnerable membranes. This is the proposed return connection, not an automatic effect of falling glucose. A further return through AVP–lipid-peroxide competition requires enough demand at a shared local site to limit both functions; neither low blood GSH nor separate component studies establishes it. Normal active AVP clearance and water recovery despite verified renal redox limitation would weaken this branch.

Feedback could resolve after prolonging recovery through a sensitive developmental interval, leaving a circuit consequence (Sections [29](#ss_p10_sec_29), [31](#ss_p10_sec_31), and [36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5)). Lifelong hyperglycaemia, low GSH or abnormal AVP is unnecessary, but normal later values do not prove an earlier episode. Slow recovery, thresholds and hysteresis alone do not identify this return connection.

##### 19.7.5 Glucose exposure and inflammatory persistence

Glucose could prolong inflammatory conditions independently of the proposed osmotic-support and IRAP sequence, or of insulin resistance. In vascular-cell cultures, high glucose reduced inflammation-induced A20 protein despite preserved early RNA induction; osmotic controls did not reproduce it. O-GlcNAc modification, ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation accompanied the loss (Shrikhande et al., 2010). Reduced A20 could weaken inflammatory restraint, but this experiment did not establish persistence after glucose withdrawal.

Duration has two different experimental precedents. In mouse BV2 microglia, 25 versus 5.5 mmol/L glucose prolonged LPS-associated NF-κB p65 phosphorylation and increased inducible NO synthase expression; high glucose alone did not reproduce the NF-κB response (Hung et al., 2022). Both exposures continued, so post-withdrawal recovery was not established. In aortic endothelial cultures, 16 hours at 30 mmol/L glucose preceded persistent p65-associated chromatin and gene-expression changes over six days at normal glucose (El-Osta et al., 2008). This demonstrates persistence after a substantial pulse, not a threshold for brief infant excursions.

Two proposed consequences could interact: longer neural/glial inflammatory signalling and reduced vascular delivery support. A20-dependent eNOS expression supplies a candidate connection to endothelial reserve (Angolano et al., 2021; Section [16.8.2](#ss_p10_sec_16_8_2)), distinct from inducible NOS, eNOS coupling or measured NO output. A20 loss has not been shown to explain the microglial or post-withdrawal findings, and these studies do not establish uniform glucose inhibition of TNFAIP3, NFKBIA and NFKBIE. A20 remains the specific experimental example.

Glucose exposure could become a recovery modifier if it extends inflammatory activity sufficiently to delay local ionic or cellular-volume restoration, whatever glucose’s initiating role. The magnitude and duration needed in developing tissue remain unknown. Persistent inflammation with adequate local recovery would limit this proposed route into the Sodium Struggle.

A bounded neonatal exposure can precede later structural change. Streptozotocin on rat postnatal day 1 lowered insulin and raised glucose to 11.9–13.4 mmol/L on days 3–6, with no significant glucose difference after day 7. Early delayed retinal vascularisation, inflammation and apoptosis preceded reduced neuronal-layer counts at day 14; superficial vessel density and Iba1-positive microglial/macrophage counts did not differ significantly at day 21 (Kermorvant-Duchemin et al., 2013). This separates exposure from outcome timing, but concurrent insulin loss prevents glucose-only attribution and ionic/volume recovery was unmeasured.

##### 19.7.6 Physiological benefit and developmental effects

Limited insulin supply, physical-state sensing, signalling or trafficking could precede developmental divergence; repeated demand might instead produce later metabolic impairment, with shared causes or independent comorbidity also possible. Maternal diabetes, post-diagnosis measurements and later type 2 diabetes address different timescales (§[48](#ss_p10_sec_48)). Early islet autoantibodies establish chronology in selected at-risk children, not insulin deficiency or IRAP impairment in autistic children (Ziegler and Bonifacio, 2012). The shared defence process remains the overarching conjecture; no protective glucose surge, insulin resistance, hyperinsulinaemia or IRAP defect is obligatory in every trajectory.

A developmental contribution requires the relevant exposure to impair local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery during a susceptible interval. Candidate disturbances include impaired astrocytic volume recovery or chloride-gradient restoration; altered extracellular-space conditions or inadequate energetic support could initiate or amplify those disturbances and their effects on inhibitory maturation (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)–[29](#ss_p10_sec_29), [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4), and [31](#ss_p10_sec_31)). The prediction is altered maturation or refinement during a sensitive interval, leaving an enduring circuit consequence. Adult peripheral findings establish neither fetal exposure nor PV dysfunction; direct genetic, immune, placental and vascular effects remain alternatives. None of these component studies demonstrates altered OTX2 production, secretion, delivery or capture.

The two principal proposals can fail separately. Adequate evidence excluding the proposed benefit of temporary osmotic glucose support in the specified state would require withdrawal of that adaptive claim. Evidence excluding a useful contribution from IRAP-associated peptide termination or its timing would require withdrawal of the corresponding coordination claim in the specified state. Neither result by itself decides the other. A systemic benefit without developmental mediation remains physiological context. Imprecise nulls are inconclusive, but an unspecified hidden subgroup cannot rescue a well-tested negative result.

These proposals do not justify raising glucose, restricting insulin, altering salt or water intake, or changing medication.

#### 19.8 Chapter synthesis

One disturbance may reduce the capacity to compensate for another, extending recovery into a susceptible developmental window. Endocrine recruitment, osmolyte supply, cytoskeletal integrity and transport capacity provide candidate interaction sites. Successful compensation may instead restore balance or counteract a second disturbance. Convergence on a shared endpoint, adverse amplification, additivity, synergy and threshold behaviour require distinct comparisons; coexisting exposures do not establish any one of them. Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) illustrates why temporary osmotic glucose support and insulin/IRAP-associated peptide termination must be tested separately, even where they could interact. Section [20](#ss_p10_sec_20) maps the component evidence, and Section [21](#ss_p10_sec_21) examines how a disturbance or its consequences could persist after initiation.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_20"></a>

### 20 Integrated Evidence Map: Contributors, Modifiers and Comparisons

Table [20.1](#ss_p10_table_20_1) provides claim-specific source context for the cellular and circulation contributor maps (Tables [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1) and [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1)). Eight groups identify primary roles in the argument; their roles can overlap, and placement establishes neither causality nor developmental timing. Evidence of a disturbance or recovery constraint can justify retaining a candidate initiating input without proof of the complete developmental route. \[E\] marks the stated empirical observation or association; \[S\], a measured physiological component; \[H\], proposed mediation or an untested response. Each code applies only to its named endpoint. Unless explicitly measured, the final-column connections remain hypotheses: association or component physiology establishes neither the adjacent endocrine pathway nor the required local recovery disturbance and developmental consequence. Rows retain exposure-specific limits and contrary findings; an \[H\]-only response is not demonstrated by its representative citation.

<a name="ss_p10_part_d"></a>

## Part D From a response to lasting change

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21"></a>

### 21 Developmental Canalisation and Hysteresis in Sodium–Volume Defence

The preceding sections map candidate developmental inputs through osmotic and cellular disturbances (Table [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1)) and through actual circulatory disturbance or altered sensing and regulation (Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1), Panels A and B). This section asks how a transient osmotic, circulatory, sensing/regulatory or intrinsic cellular-recovery disturbance could leave a lasting regulatory or structural consequence. Neither neonatal dilution nor hypovolaemia is required in every route.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_1"></a>

#### 21.1 Recovery, persistence and developmental history

The proposed middle layer is developmental canalisation: early stabilisation could change the physiology on which renal, vascular, endocrine and neuroglial development proceeds. Persistence may involve an acquired response bias, altered recovery capacity or a developmental consequence that remains after physiology returns to baseline. These are distinct outcomes, each requiring evidence beyond the initiating disturbance.

During development, repeated reliance on an immediately effective response could change later thresholds, gain or effector allocation. Candidate consequences include altered vascular tone, AVP-linked recruitment, renal handling and splanchnic redistribution. Their direction and persistence must be measured against age-appropriate responses to the same input; repeated recruitment alone does not establish high gain.

A lasting allocation bias could preserve normal resting sodium or pressure while requiring greater effort under demand. Alternatively, normal measurements may reflect complete recovery and ordinary homeostasis. The proposed persistent state is identified by altered response or recovery at matched inputs, not inferred from apparently normal headline values.

Intermittent disturbances could have lasting effects if they alter a regulatory or structural process during a sensitive period. Later normalisation need not erase an established developmental change, but persistence cannot be inferred from the original load.

Fast loops can preserve water balance and perfusion. A lasting transition is proposed when a disturbance or recurrent demand changes later reserve, recovery or effector response; increased transport or signalling alone does not establish it.

Beyond a change in a fast response, repeated demand may leave recovery unfinished or constrain regulatory reserve. The hypothesis proposes that slower structural and compartmental adaptations then assume some stabilisation work, preserving immediate stability while changing developmental conditions.

This requires a demonstrable transfer of work or altered capacity persisting beyond normal recovery, rather than inference from a tissue difference or normal resting sodium and pressure.

Slower anatomical, biochemical or receptor changes could then carry part of the work, supporting viability while reducing later flexibility. Repeated recruitment alone does not demonstrate such structural offloading.

The proposed physiological diversity follows from the interaction between initiating conditions, genetic constraints, available reserve and developmental timing. A shared causal process must be shown at the specified intermediary, rather than inferred from the diversity of possible outputs.

The following examples examine acquired metabolic change, immune training or tolerance, and AVP-linked effector allocation. Each asks whether a specified function changes after exposure and relevant physiological recovery; none defines an obligatory entry route. Slower tissue adaptations and the final cross-system read-outs then connect these examples to later organ and developmental questions.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_2"></a>

#### 21.2 Metabolic persistence and functional dissociation

Recurrent hydromineral demand could leave lasting metabolic consequences, with or without an initially protective glucose response. Early limitations in insulin supply, physical-state sensing, signalling or trafficking remain possible initiating routes. Glucose support and peptide clearance, proposed separately in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7), could participate in metabolic feedback; the question here is whether an acquired functional change persists after the initiating conditions resolve.

Additional gradient-restoration work could constrain metabolic reserve (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23), [26](#ss_p10_sec_26), and [27](#ss_p10_sec_27)), but chloride flux does not establish reduced glucose disposal. Vascular access provides another link: insulin recruited skeletal-muscle microvasculature before increased glucose uptake in rats, while NOS inhibition blocked recruitment and partly inhibited early uptake (Vincent et al., 2004). This component result does not establish developmental vascular mediation in autism.

Metabolic imprinting here means an acquired functional change persisting after exposure and relevant extracellular conditions normalise. It differs from repeated fully reversible excursions, incomplete recovery between challenges and independently sustained metabolic disease. Delayed osmolyte restoration or ordinary dysglycaemic fluctuations alone do not establish chronic insulin resistance or a persistently erroneous AVP sensor.

Hyperosmotic stimulation of glucose transport reversed after restoration of isotonicity in small Clone9-cell and 3T3-L1-adipocyte washout experiments (Barros et al., 2001). Thus acute coupling can resolve; persistence requires an additional explanation, and an earlier protective effect cannot be assumed to remain beneficial under later hypertonic conditions.

Selective impairment depends on which functions remain available. Substantial antinatriuresis despite reduced glucose responsiveness (Rocchini et al., 1989), and increased basal membrane-fraction IRAP in type 2 diabetic adipocytes (Maianu et al., 2001), oppose a single insulin-resistance signature. Receptor desensitisation and downstream trafficking are distinct possibilities, and impaired dynamic actin remodelling is not synonymous with weak actin bundles. Fractional abundance does not establish exposed enzyme activity or native-peptide clearance (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)).

<a name="ss_p10_table_21_1"></a>**Table [21.1](#ss_p10_table_21_1). Observed component finding and proposed functional comparisons**

| **Pattern and status**                             | **Glucose disposal**                                | **IRAP-dependent AVP processing**             |
|----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Observed human component comparison, Rocchini 1989 | Reduced insulin responsiveness in obese adolescents | Not measured                                  |
| Predicted glucose selective limitation             | Reduced                                             | Preserved despite reduced disposal            |
| Predicted shared trafficking limitation            | Reduced if GLUT4 deployment is affected             | Reduced if accessible active IRAP is affected |
| Predicted catalytic IRAP limitation                | Preserved if transport is unaffected                | Reduced despite preserved glucose transport   |

Table [21.1](#ss_p10_table_21_1) describes proposed functional dissociations, not autism subtypes. Significance for one response but not another does not establish dissociation. Glucose-selective impairment could prolong extracellular glucose without prolonging AVP, while an IRAP defect could prolong peptide exposure despite preserved disposal. Whether feedback worsens, compensates for or leaves recovery unchanged depends on secretion, renal response and the initial water–solute and filling state.

IRAP recruitment and peptide clearance remain distinct (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)). Hypertonic saline and urea inhibited serum synthetic-substrate hydrolysis directly in vitro (Roy et al., 1981, 1982), so assay change need not imply enzyme recruitment. Basal activity, stimulated activity and their increment differ; neither enzyme proxies nor substrate hydrolysis establish intact circulating AVP removal or oxytocin processing.

Applying these proposals to pregnancy requires maternal–placental–fetal exposure assessment: glucose-associated sodium lowering can coexist with higher effective tonicity. Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) distinguish these states and the physiological contributions to be tested.

Reduced glucose entry during redox stress may protect or harm cells depending on tonicity, fuel availability and recovery; it is not itself evidence of an osmotic shield (Sections [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)).

A receptor change that persists after ligand exposure and local physiological recovery could support developmental memory; one resolving with recovery supports continuing-state dependence. AVPR1A/AVPR1B and OXTR branches remain tissue- and window-specific, with function distinct from expression (Section [18](#ss_p10_sec_18)).

The conditional birth prediction is lower cord copeptin with lower effective fetal tonicity under comparable nonosmotic stress. A sufficiently precise null or opposite result would weaken it. One cord sample addresses magnitude, not recruitment delay, clearance or earlier gestation; even a positive result could reflect ordinary protection rather than developmental impairment (Sections [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3) and [18.1.9](#ss_p10_sec_18_1_9)).

Later metabolic disease cannot identify earlier developmental causation. Shared genetic, placental or inflammatory influences, independent risk and treatment remain alternatives; prospective changes during risperidone treatment illustrate the latter (Scahill et al., 2016). The proposed acquired route is repeated demand followed by altered recovery and metabolic feedback.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_3"></a>

#### 21.3 Immune memory: training, tolerance and recovery

Microglia provide a rapid recipient of local extracellular signals. P2Y12-deficient mouse microglia retained baseline motility but showed markedly reduced directional responses to extracellular nucleotides and early process recruitment toward cortical injury (Haynes et al., 2006). Signal concentration, spatial gradient and receptor responsiveness can therefore influence the immediate recruitment response. Extracellular-space compression could modify the initial concentration change for a fixed released amount (Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)); a lasting change in responsiveness requires an additional cellular mechanism.

An inflammatory history can leave such a persistent cellular record. In adult mice, the second daily peripheral lipopolysaccharide exposure amplified brain cytokine responses, whereas further exposures induced tolerance. Microglial deletion of Tak1 or Hdac1/2 largely prevented the amplified response. Cytokines returned to baseline within 24 hours in the tested cessation conditions, while distinct microglial enhancer profiles remained detectable six months after the initial exposure schedule (Wendeln et al., 2018). This supplies a precedent for transient exposure producing a retained response programme. Training and tolerance are different possible outcomes; repeated challenge need not progressively sensitise tissue.

We propose that recurrent ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty can influence this response history by changing the timing, localisation or repetition of purinergic exposure, with accompanying inflammatory signals recruiting a more persistent programme. Vascular delivery and cortisol timing could modify that response. During development, altered microglial responsiveness could then change the conditions under which circuits are refined. The prediction is a changed threshold, response magnitude or resolution time across a graded series of matched later challenges after the initiating exposure has ended and the relevant ionic and cellular-volume disturbance has resolved. Correcting the earlier recovery disturbance should reduce this later difference under comparable immune exposure. Measuring these response dimensions separately would distinguish sensitisation, tolerance and delayed resolution, and test whether the adult inflammatory-memory precedent extends to the developmental recovery route proposed here.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_4"></a>

#### 21.4 Effector Allocation Under a Single-Ligand Constraint

This worked example concerns effector allocation: the relative renal, vascular and endocrine outputs defending filling and tonicity. It does not imply rationing AVP molecules between organs or an obligatory reduction in one output when another increases.

##### 21.4.1 The single-ligand constraint

The single-ligand constraint concerns shared peptide identity, not a single uniform AVP pool. Circulating AVP can couple renal water handling to vascular responses, while pituitary regulation also depends on hypophysial-portal delivery and interactions with corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). In rats, haemorrhage increased portal AVP and other ACTH secretagogues, demonstrating coordinated but multifactor control (Plotsky et al., 1985). Local AVP release has its own calcium-store-dependent regulation, demonstrated in rat supraoptic neurones (Ludwig et al., 2005). Peripheral, portal and neural exposure histories must therefore be distinguished. Effector allocation remains a useful problem wherever multiple responsive targets encounter the same AVP signal.

Within a shared exposure compartment, AVP-responsive pathways have different thresholds and time constants. Helping one target can change another’s operating conditions, creating potential trade-offs. Local access, release, sensitivity and clearance can partly separate their outputs; developmental weighting need not imply simultaneous recruitment or a uniform global broadcast.

##### 21.4.2 Minimal receptor map: V2, V1a, and V1b

The multi-effector reach of AVP is implemented through three receptor pathways that are relevant here.

V2 receptors in collecting-duct principal cells support water conservation through aquaporin-2 (AQP2) delivery to the apical membrane. In isolated rat collecting ducts, AVP increased apical AQP2 and water permeability; both declined after AVP withdrawal (Nielsen et al., 1995). This reversible response supplies the renal component of the model. Its effect on urine concentration and serum sodium also depends on the medullary gradient, solute excretion and water intake.

Vascular V1a receptors provide a rapid route from circulating AVP to smooth-muscle contraction. In V1a-null mice, AVP-induced vascular contraction and pressor responses were lost, while circulating volume and baroreflex function also changed (Koshimizu et al., 2006). This supports V1a participation in pressure defence, but also shows why whole-body blood pressure cannot isolate vascular receptor sensitivity. Regional flow and filtration must be measured in the relevant vascular bed.

Pituitary V1b receptors contribute to ACTH release through AVP signalling that interacts with CRH. In V1b-null mice, AVP-stimulated ACTH release was impaired while the response to administered CRH was preserved (Tanoue et al., 2004). ACTH recruits adrenal glucocorticoid production, chiefly cortisol in humans and corticosterone in these mice. Portal AVP exposure, ACTH secretion and the adrenal response are separate steps; peripheral AVP concentration alone cannot identify the contribution of this endocrine arm.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_4_3"></a>

##### 21.4.3 Why neonatal context matters

Development changes the reserve against which a challenge acts. In rats, urine concentration after dehydration and renal AQP2 expression increased between postnatal days 10 and 40, with a marked transition around weaning (Yasui et al., 1996). In clinically stable human neonates studied during quiet sleep, cardiac baroreflex sensitivity increased with postmenstrual age across 28–42 weeks (Andriessen et al., 2005). These are distinct renal and cardiovascular developmental findings, not a single measure of global immaturity. They explain why adult responses cannot simply be assigned to a newborn and why comparisons must match developmental stage.

A response that works during development could become part of the later starting state. There is a measured precedent: after prenatal maternal water restriction, lambs studied at 23 ± 2 days had an AVP-release osmotic threshold of 290 ± 2 mOsm/kg, compared with 280 ± 2 in control singletons and 285 ± 1 in control twins (Desai et al., 2003b). Maternal nutritional restriction accompanied dehydration, limiting attribution to tonicity alone. The exposed lambs remained hypertonic and hypertensive at testing. This supports developmental change in a regulatory threshold, but not persistence after complete physiological recovery or persistent weighting of V2, V1a or V1b. That allocation hypothesis requires pathway-specific responses after the initiating exposure has ended.

##### 21.4.4 Allocation trade-offs and burden placement

Allocation can support effective arterial filling, sensor-site tonicity, microvascular fluid exchange and local cell-volume regulation through different combinations of renal, vascular and endocrine work.

A V2-weighted allocation relies more on renal water conservation to support filling. Dilution requires a positive water balance relative to exchangeable solute, not V2 activation alone. There is also direct evidence for a renal consequence beyond concentration: desmopressin increased urinary albumin excretion reversibly in rats and approximately threefold after acute infusion in healthy human subjects (Bardoux et al., 2003). The human experiment was pharmacological and acute; the rat reversibility argues against treating the response itself as permanent damage. These results justify testing a renal cost of sustained V2 recruitment, but concentrated urine alone establishes neither that cost nor a developmental consequence.

V1a-weighted vasomotor support can defend pressure and distribution. Persistent endothelial injury, glycocalyx loss or rarefaction would be additional costs, not consequences established by the receptor-specific contraction evidence above.

A V1b-weighted endocrine allocation requires a demonstrated AVP contribution to ACTH and glucocorticoid recruitment. Metabolic involvement is experimentally supported: V1b-null mice showed increased insulin sensitivity in a hyperinsulinaemic–euglycaemic clamp (Fujiwara et al., 2007). However, V1b also acts outside the pituitary, including pancreatic and adipose pathways, so that whole-body knockout cannot assign the effect to cortisol. Persistent metabolic expenditure or substrate-handling changes caused specifically by developmental pituitary V1b recruitment remain predictions.

##### 21.4.5 Stable allocation regimes and hysteresis

A candidate memory mechanism is altered receptor-pathway effectiveness or downstream function after exposure. Increased responsiveness, reduced responsiveness and delayed recovery are different predictions; receptor abundance alone cannot identify functional gain. Section [36](#ss_p10_sec_36) distinguishes these changes from current exposure, acute desensitisation and rebound.

An attractor-like allocation pattern would repeatedly re-emerge under specified conditions. Hysteresis additionally requires history-dependent responses at matched current inputs; persistence alone establishes neither an attractor nor a particular feedback dynamic.

##### 21.4.6 Illustrative allocation regimes

To make the allocation logic concrete without asserting fixed subtypes, two illustrative regimes can be outlined.

A V2-weighted regime predicts greater renal water conservation for a given perturbation, through greater AVP exposure, renal sensitivity or AQP2 trafficking. Dilutional cost additionally requires intake and solute balance to produce positive water balance; concentrated urine alone does not identify it.

A vascular/endocrine regime predicts greater V1a-linked vasomotor or V1b-linked ACTH/glucocorticoid responses to the same challenge. These arms can vary independently and need not displace renal conservation; reduced vascular flexibility or lasting metabolic cost is an additional proposed consequence.

These are proposed stabilisation regimes with potentially different long-term costs. The discriminating prediction is that a measured allocation pattern changes a specified developmental outcome under comparable demand and reserve.

The later organ sections develop how this allocation could affect nephron reserve, splanchnic recruitment, matrix sodium buffering, neuroglial microdomains and membrane restoration.

Its subtitle emphasises shared peptide identity with distinct exposure histories. Solid arrows connect exposures to component actions. Dashed arrows connect those actions to conditional consequences or proposed persistent costs.

- **Renal branch:** Circulating AVP points to renal V₂ action, AQP2 trafficking and water permeability. The supporting study label is Nielsen et al. (1995), isolated rat collecting ducts. The dashed continuation states that dilution pressure occurs only with excess water relative to solute and poses persistent renal cost as an open question.
- **Vascular branch:** The same circulating-AVP exposure box separately points to vascular V₁ₐ action, contraction and pressure support. The supporting label is Koshimizu et al. (2006), V₁ₐ-null mice. The dashed continuation asks whether persistent barrier injury or capillary rarefaction follows.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_5"></a>

#### 21.5 Secondary stabilisation: contributors and tissue layers

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_5_1"></a>

##### 21.5.1 Convergent upstream contributors as control stressors

AVP-dependent retention, epithelial barrier injury and altered vascular regulation could increase stabilisation demand through different routes. Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) evaluates smoke, traffic-related pollution and candidate mould exposures separately: impaired vasodilation alone does not identify permeability, underfilling or high-gain AVP control.

Early respiratory morbidity offers another possible source of non-osmotic AVP recruitment, with sex-associated exposure differences considered in Section [40.2](#ss_p10_sec_40_2). In twelve ventilated premature newborns with respiratory distress syndrome, AVP remained elevated despite normal sodium and osmolality, and recovery-associated diuresis occurred without AVP normalisation (Zanardo et al., 1989). In a separate series of twelve infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia, acute hypoxaemia and air trapping accompanied increased ADH; concentrations fell with respiratory improvement, while three infants developed hyponatraemia (Rao et al., 1986). Altered atrial filling was proposed in the latter study, rather than isolated as the causal mechanism. Respiratory distress, hypoxaemia, mechanical support and filling changes are distinct variables.

These observations support a respiratory route into compensatory demand while preserving successful adaptation. Elevated circulating AVP can coexist with normal chemistry; normal measurements alone neither establish pathological compensation nor exclude regulatory work. For the proposed neural developmental route, the additional requirement remains disturbed local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery and its developmental consequence. Parallel peripheral consequences require separate assessment and do not substitute for that intermediary. Neither respiratory illness nor raised AVP alone establishes persistent developmental mediation.

Antioxidant defence could also limit the initiating disturbance, before sustained osmotic–volume compensation is needed. The proposed GSH contribution spans three separable functions: peroxide and membrane protection, preservation of the endothelial glycocalyx, and support of GSH-sensitive AVP processing (Sections [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) and [35.1](#ss_p10_sec_35_1)). The neonatal observations in Section [40.4](#ss_p10_sec_40_4) motivate a sex-dependent modifier of injury and compensatory demand, independently of sodium stores. Demonstrating one component would not establish the others; successful protection and complete recovery remain possible outcomes.

Nephron endowment and transport allocation could also modify an initiating sodium–water or mineral disturbance and the demand for compensation. Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32) distinguishes this upstream role from renal responses to a disturbance originating elsewhere and from persistent changes that modify later episodes; Section [40](#ss_p10_sec_40) considers the sex-dependent developmental proposal.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_5_2"></a>

##### 21.5.2 Secondary stabilisation layers

###### ***21.5.2.1 Layer A: Tissue sodium buffering and matrix-level capacitance***

Tissue sodium partitioning is a plausible secondary stabilisation layer with experimental support. In adult female rats fed less than 0.1% or 8% NaCl for eight weeks, higher skin sodium accompanied increased glycosaminoglycan content and chondroitin-synthase mRNA, supporting matrix-associated storage without directly measuring its binding chemistry (Titze et al., 2004). Genetic disruption provides a functional link: mice with combined heterozygous Ext1/Ext2 loss had lower skin sodium and water, a thinner endothelial surface layer and higher plasma osmolality despite similar plasma sodium; impaired vasodilation was an alternative explanation for their pressure response to sodium loading (Olde Engberink et al., 2019). Matrix architecture can therefore participate in sodium–water homeostasis. Its water balance must be measured: in salt-loaded hypertensive rats, tissue sodium increases were largely accompanied by water and were consistent with extracellular expansion rather than hypertonic storage (Rossitto et al., 2020). Tissue sodium content, bound fraction, interstitial water and effective tonicity are distinct endpoints.

In rats, Schafflhuber et al. (2007) compared sodium per unit tissue mass: growth-associated changes involved bone and carcass, while a four-week dietary contrast (0.1% versus 8% NaCl) principally involved the estimated osmotically inactive skin pool, without lower endpoint serum sodium. Bone values used ash mass. These comparisons do not establish ordered recruitment from tissue exchange to osteoclastic resorption.

Lymphatic support also has a measured regulatory role: macrophage depletion or VEGF-C trapping increased interstitial volume retention and blood pressure during salt loading in rats (Machnik et al., 2009). The hypothesis proposes that matrix partitioning and lymphatic transport could redistribute stabilisation work during recurrent challenges. Calling this plasma buffering requires a smaller or shorter plasma sodium or tonicity excursion after a matched load, attributable to tissue exchange; a larger tissue sodium store alone does not show that benefit. The developmental extension is that sustained reliance changes matrix maintenance or recovery capacity sufficiently to affect the local neural or glial recovery process defined in the core hypothesis.

###### ***21.5.2.2 Layer B: Vascular and epithelial remodelling with endocrine decoupling under inflammatory load***

Repeated barrier strain could shift stabilisation work into slower vascular or epithelial remodelling. Glycocalyx integrity, junctional maintenance and microvascular tone jointly affect fluid retention; their proposed persistent cost is altered vasomotor work, capillary-filtration control or regional flow heterogeneity. This need not appear as a resting leak. Section [35.1](#ss_p10_sec_35_1) distinguishes the glycocalyx and bilayer contributions.

Inflammation can uncouple endocrine components without imposing a fixed low-renin/high-aldosterone sequence. TNF and IL-1 increased renin release from rat renal slices, whereas TNF inhibited renin transcription in mouse preparations (Antonipillai et al., 1990; Todorov et al., 2002; §[14.6.10](#ss_p10_sec_14_6_10)). Three cancer patients with high IL-6 instead had high renin and low aldosterone; in one, both normalised with successful treatment and became abnormal again with tumour recurrence (Chung et al., 1996). The proposed developmental concern is a mismatch between available support and sodium–volume need, whose direction remains tissue-specific.

Low baseline renin does not establish amplified downstream gain. The proposed distortion requires a measured inflammatory exposure and a disproportionate receptor or effector response under comparable sodium balance and haemodynamics. Under such conditions, mineralocorticoid receptors may experience sustained stimulation that is poorly informative about physiological need. A plausible developmental extension is that prolonged exposure drives durable changes in mineralocorticoid receptor availability and effective gain, including reduced receptor expression, altered nuclear trafficking, shifts in co-regulator balance, or changes in 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 support. The direction and persistence of these changes, and whether they protect cells while compromising systemic sodium–volume defence, remain to be established.

Acute inflammatory changes in MR availability have direct support. In adult mice given 15 mg/kg lipopolysaccharide, aortic MR and α1-adrenoceptor expression fell at 6 and 18 hours; aldosterone co-treatment preserved receptor expression and improved vascular responses. TNF-α also reduced MR expression in human vascular cells (Fadel et al., 2017). This severe acute model supports an inflammatory change in the machinery of vascular support, not persistent renal mineralocorticoid failure. The hypothesis predicts that, in an affected developmental route, reduced functional MR responsiveness remains after inflammation resolves, weakens sodium conservation under a matched challenge and increases reliance on glucocorticoid support. Such redistribution could preserve immediate stability while imposing wider metabolic costs. Persistence, sodium-conserving function and greater glucocorticoid dependence require separate evidence; receptor abundance during illness or normal resting electrolytes cannot establish the sequence.

###### ***21.5.2.3 Layer C: Neuroglial water–ion microdomain management***

Astrocytic and perivascular water–ion regulation could carry a third share of stabilisation work. Its proposed costs include intermittent swelling, clearance strain and altered perivascular dynamics when restoration remains incomplete. Sections [24](#ss_p10_sec_24) and [30](#ss_p10_sec_30) develop these local mechanisms and their energetic and structural demands.

###### ***21.5.2.4 Layer D: Membrane and lipid remodelling***

Membrane organisation supplies a fourth candidate layer. Cholesterol can modify permeability and mechanical protection; caveolae can rapidly release surface area without ATP, while rebuilding that reservoir requires ATP (Sinha et al., 2011). Section [35](#ss_p10_sec_35) develops the resulting separation between immediate protection and restoration before another challenge.

##### 21.5.3 The emergence of autism-associated physiology

Secondary stabilisation could connect successful immediate defence to altered developmental timing, precision or flexibility when the adaptation outlasts normal recovery. Its relevance to autism requires a link between that physiological change and the resulting neural effect.

##### 21.5.4 Heterogeneity as a function of burden placement

The burden-placement hypothesis predicts that initiating conditions and reserve profiles may recruit different combinations of matrix, membrane, vascular, endocrine and neuroglial responses. A prespecified allocation pattern should predict a corresponding tissue or developmental consequence. Diverse signatures alone cannot establish a shared process, and retrospective branch selection cannot rescue a failed test.

Section [47](#ss_p10_sec_47) distinguishes lasting developmental consequences from continuing physiological constraints and examines how cellular persistence could modify later expression.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_21_6"></a>

#### 21.6 Cross-system response and persistence read-outs

<a name="ss_p10_box_21_1"></a>**Box [21.1](#ss_p10_box_21_1) Candidate receptor-network read-outs of the proposed shared defence process**

AVP/OXT axis: candidate tissue-specific responses include AVPR1A/AVPR1B sensitisation, reduced AVPR2/AQP2-mediated antidiuretic response or reduced OXTR responsiveness after a defined exposure. These are distinct directional predictions; high or low AVP alone does not identify any of them.

MR/GR axis: a proposed shift in glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid signalling could alter AVP recruitment or OXTR response. Enduring calibration requires evidence that the specified change remains after exposure and local physiological recovery, not merely after serum sodium normalises.

RAAS cross-talk: candidate signalling and trafficking interactions require direct measurement of the specified osmotic exposure, receptor response and persistence. Component interaction does not establish RAAS imprinting.

Renal and endothelial persistence: collecting-duct escape from antidiuresis and altered endothelial MR/NO responses are distinct candidates. Antidiuretic escape alone does not establish cell-identity change or incomplete reversibility.

Timing: regional skin-barrier maturation is a candidate exposure window; NFAT5 programming and osmolyte debt require stage-specific measurements. Prenatal and postnatal routes need distinct tests.

The hypothesis proposes a shared sodium–volume–vascular defence process that can be entered through different disturbances and expressed through different receptor and cellular configurations. Neither insufficient sodium nor one AVP direction is required as the initiating observation. High- and low-AVP findings require compartment, timing and receptor-context measurements before a shared mechanism is inferred.

Section [22](#ss_p10_sec_22) maps the remaining applications. Their common question is whether a candidate stabilisation layer leaves altered capacity after recovery, and how that capacity changes subsequent development.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_22"></a>

### 22 From Physiological Responses to Developmental and Later Expression

This roadmap connects the general persistence account in Section [21](#ss_p10_sec_21) to local recovery, developmental change and later expression. Successful immediate sodium–volume compensation could alter later capacity if it changes organ development during a sensitive window. Reduced renal endowment may instead precede the physiological struggle or arise from a shared genetic cause; Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32) distinguishes these routes. None substitutes for the central requirement that impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carries a developmental effect.

## Part E Local recovery and developmental conversion

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23"></a>

### 23 Functional NKCC1 Bias, Chloride Recovery, and the Sodium-Driven Energetic Burden

#### 23.1 Scope: an adaptive defence that can become maladaptive

Impaired chloride recovery is a candidate local persistence layer after osmotic, perfusion-metabolic or redox threat. Increased NKCC1 import, reduced KCC2 extrusion or weakened potassium driving conditions may act separately or together. The proposed developmental endpoint is impaired restoration of an age-appropriate chloride state, not simply delayed maturation or a uniform whole-brain chloride abnormality.

During hypotonic swelling, regulatory volume decrease (RVD) can export ions and organic osmolytes, allowing water to leave. Volume adaptation during continuing exposure differs from restoration after that exposure ends. A return of cell volume alone does not show that ionic gradients and solute pools have recovered. Timely restoration of the relevant variables with adequate reserve is the successful comparator. Section [24](#ss_p10_sec_24) develops the full volume and osmolyte account.

AVP recruitment, RVD and transient transporter reweighting can each protect immediate stability. The proposed transition is incomplete local ionic or volume recovery carrying a developmental effect; repetition, osmolyte loss or additional work alone does not establish it.

NKCC1 abundance, phosphorylation, localisation and net flux are distinct; KCC2 failure can raise chloride without NKCC1 gain. Section [23.2](#ss_p10_sec_23_2) defines the import, extrusion and combined branches before the evidence is considered. Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) sets out their recovery comparisons and limiting results.

Astrocytic volume, potassium handling and metabolic support could influence neuronal recovery in a perivascular route. The order can also run from neuronal transport, mitochondrial or redox disturbance to greater glial demand; astrocyte-first initiation is branch-specific.

Systemic defence enters this account only where it changes CNS exposure or recovery conditions. A local chloride disturbance does not identify its origin; direct genetic, developmental or redox initiation remains possible.

The metabolic route in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) could constrain CNS recovery through altered exposure, substrate delivery or extracellular conditions. Peripheral GLUT4 or plasma/urine measurements cannot establish that neural bridge.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_2"></a>

#### 23.2 What “functional NKCC1 bias” means

“Functional NKCC1 bias” is reserved here for a demonstrable NKCC1 contribution to inward chloride transport under the measured ionic conditions. Such a contribution may be local, cell-type-specific and restricted to a recovery window without a uniform increase in total NKCC1 protein. A chloride-loaded phenotype alone is better described as impaired chloride recovery until import and extrusion have been separated.

This neuronal and astrocytic usage must not be transferred unchanged to choroid-plexus epithelium. Developmental stage and ionic gradients alter the meaning of NKCC1 flux; neonatal CSF potassium clearance and adult CSF secretion are separate endpoints (Xu et al., 2021; Fame et al., 2023; Jensen et al., 2025). Section [30](#ss_p10_sec_30) treats this epithelial compartment separately.

Three non-exclusive branches should be distinguished. The import-cost branch requires increased NKCC1-mediated inward flux and its associated sodium-handling demand; phosphorylation and surface availability are supporting regulatory measurements. The extrusion-failure branch requires impaired KCC2-mediated chloride removal because of altered transporter function, stability or driving conditions. The combined branch requires evidence for both. Astrocytic ionic loading or extracellular-space changes may influence these branches but do not identify the neuronal transporter responsible.

KCC2 does not directly consume ATP, but its usual outward KCl transport depends on gradients maintained indirectly by energy-dependent processes.
