Increased extracellular K⁺ or reduced intracellular K⁺ can weaken outward transport even when KCC2 protein is unchanged. Reversal can occur under suitable gradients and is not necessarily pathological; activity-dependent KCC2 reversal has been supported by hippocampal slice measurements and modelling (Byvaltcev et al., 2023). An extrusion defect can therefore support a chloride-recovery mechanism while falsifying an increased-NKCC1-import explanation for that particular phenotype.

The WNK-SPAK/OSR1 axis can regulate NKCC1 and KCC2 reciprocally, but the relevant phosphosites and functional consequences must be identified. Phosphorylation is not a single on/off state shared by both transporters. KCC2 surface loss can also follow oxidant-sensitive tyrosine dephosphorylation, whereas NMDA or interictal-like activity can engage calpain-mediated KCC2 cleavage in rat hippocampal preparations (Wake et al., 2007; Puskarjov et al., 2012). These distinct mechanisms offer several routes to reduced chloride extrusion.

Elevated extracellular K⁺ is a possible amplifier rather than a universal positive-feedback driver. For a given release and clearance pattern, a smaller extracellular volume can increase local K⁺ transients. Their effects on NKCC1 and KCC2 depend on the complete ionic gradients: stronger inward NKCC1 driving conditions may coexist with weaker outward KCC2 transport, but rising intracellular Na⁺ and Cl⁻, potassium clearance, volume recovery and regulatory feedback can limit the response. The proposed swelling–potassium–chloride loop would amplify only while those stabilising processes remain insufficient.

#### 23.3 Three initiating threats and the controller layer

Three initiating threats are distinguished: osmotic conditions that change CNS tonicity or volume; perfusion-metabolic supply or reserve insufficient for local demand; and excess oxidants or inadequate local buffering. Underfilling is not itself hypotonicity.

These threats may interact bidirectionally through volume, ionic gradients, mitochondrial function and perfusion. Redox strain can follow osmotic or metabolic demand, or initiate recovery difficulty independently.

Systemic entry involves distinct endothelial, arterial-baroreflex, cardiopulmonary and central responses to osmotic, filling, oxygen and stress signals. Endothelial dysfunction is not itself a neural report of underfilling; direct neural or glial initiation need not involve this controller sequence.

Non-osmotic AVP can add water-retention burden to a genuine pressure or filling threat when intake and handling permit it. Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) develops the vascular redox route; the bridge here is its effect on CNS delivery or recovery, not an assumed AVP rise or chloride load from reduced NO alone.

Angiotensin II or AVP could affect transport through cell-specific receptors or indirectly through pressure, perfusion and tonicity. Those routes remain distinct: elevated hormone or transporter phosphorylation alone does not establish inward chloride flux.

#### 23.4 Timescale and anatomical sequence

Acute defence, restoration and developmental consequences operate on different schedules. Water redistribution and vascular/redox responses may begin within minutes to hours; osmolyte and transporter reset may extend over hours to days; circuit effects may emerge later. These are proposed observation windows, not a universal timetable. Pump work accompanies entry as well as subsequent recovery.

This temporal distinction is essential: acute hypotonic swelling can recruit protective RVD and does not necessarily increase net NKCC1 influx. This recovery branch concerns repeated episodes after which the water threat may have resolved but osmolyte debt, chloride recovery pressure, ATP strain or incomplete transporter reset remains.

A vascular-perivascular route could reach neurons through end-foot function, potassium handling and extracellular conditions. Direct neuronal redox or transporter disturbance can reverse that order and increase support demands. PV cells may be recipients or initiating sites; neither astrocyte-first nor OTX2 involvement is obligatory.

#### 23.5 Immediate defence: swelling, RVD, perfusion triage, and redox buffering

Hypotonic swelling can recruit RVD through loss of KCl, water and organic osmolytes. This cell-specific protective response is not inferred from underfilling without a corresponding osmotic change (Section [24](#ss_p10_sec_24)).

Perfusion-metabolic threat can recruit flow redistribution, extraction and metabolic adaptation that preserve ATP supply. Increased glycolysis or lactate is not energy failure; recovery becomes constrained when this support cannot meet local demand.

Redox threat recruits antioxidant, repair and metabolic responses that may initially limit injury. If oxidant production exceeds local buffering, it could affect vascular regulation, mitochondrial support or transporter stability. A direct neural example is the loss of surface KCC2 and a depolarising shift in GABA reversal potential after hydrogen peroxide exposure in mature rat hippocampal cultures (Wake et al., 2007). This establishes a component mechanism in an in vitro injury context, not a low-BH4 mechanism, a universal WNK response or developmental mediation in autism.

The proposed pathology concerns incomplete or unstable recovery when defensive demand exceeds available reserve, rather than recruitment of defence in itself.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_6"></a>

#### 23.6 Recovery Time Courses After Hyponatraemia

Recovery asymmetry concerns differences in how quickly the components of a defensive response reset. In rats with severe chronic hyponatraemia, organic osmolyte reaccumulation lagged during correction; rapid correction also produced a brain sodium and chloride overshoot that was not seen with slow correction (Lien et al., 1991). This supports the possibility that ionic and organic-osmolyte recovery follow different time courses. It does not establish osmolyte debt after mild intermittent exposure, which must be measured rather than assumed.

Tejedor et al. (2026) provide an experimental starting point for the osmotic arm. Female Wistar rats received a low-sodium diet and daily desmopressin with water for seven days, with four animals per group. Serum sodium recovered 24 hours after the final dose, but plasma osmolality remained below baseline. Lower whole-brain ADC and increased grey-matter GFAP staining were reported. ADC measures water mobility rather than total brain water; the grey-matter ADC comparison was borderline (p = 0.054). The study therefore does not demonstrate persistent CNS dysfunction after complete systemic osmotic recovery.

The same study found no significant group difference in the measured caudate-putamen osmolytes and did not measure cell-specific chloride, sodium, transporter flux or ATP. Small groups, dietary and caloric differences, and the acknowledged lack of an unchallenged RIH histology control further limit mechanistic attribution (Tejedor et al., 2026). It does not prove an osmolyte deficit, an NKCC1-mediated recovery mechanism or an energetic mismatch during chloride recovery. On subsequent water challenge, the recurrently exposed rats showed a slower, less pronounced ADC decline than controls, contrary to the predicted increase in vulnerability. Recurrence therefore did not produce a uniformly amplified imaging response (Tejedor et al., 2026).

This model leaves persistent extracellular disturbance, delayed cellular recovery and lasting developmental change distinct. Normal serum sodium does not identify which has occurred.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_7"></a>

#### 23.7 Chloride Recovery and Energetic Demand

The relationship to the Ben-Ari–Tyzio programme is mechanistic continuity plus an additional causal claim: what limits restoration under demand, and does that recovery difficulty alter development? Comparable resting chloride can coexist with different recovery, while altered resting chloride need not mean recovery failure. Tang et al. (2019) measured a treatment-associated acceleration of chloride extrusion in human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons (Section [6.4](#ss_p10_sec_6_4)). This provides a positive dynamic recovery comparison without establishing recovery as the developmental mediator. Loading, extrusion, extracellular and supply constraints remain candidate causes of recovery failure.

##### 23.7.1 Transport regulation and energetic demand

During chloride replenishment, increased inward NKCC1 transport could add sodium-pump work when energetic reserve is limited. This is the proposed import-cost branch. After RVD, some cells may have a transient chloride deficit or incompletely restored organic-osmolyte pools. Existing transport systems can support rapid ionic recovery, but chloride is not intrinsically a cheaper osmolyte once accompanying cation movements and restoration of their gradients are included. Fast replenishment need not be low-cost replenishment.

Low intracellular chloride can relieve direct inhibition of WNK1, allowing downstream SPAK/OSR1 signalling to favour NKCC1 transport capacity and restrain KCC-mediated extrusion. Rising intracellular chloride provides a brake, rather than continuing to activate this sensor (Piala et al., 2014). In mature hippocampal cultures, chloride-sensitive WNK1 signalling also regulates KCC2 membrane stability (Heubl et al., 2017). Shrinkage-related molecular crowding can sustain WNK signalling despite an inhibitory ionic environment in experimental cell systems (Boyd-Shiwarski et al., 2022). These inputs need not change in the same direction.

Restoration of external tonicity can itself recruit another phase of volume regulation. Boyd-Shiwarski et al. (2022) observed WNK1 puncta in HEK-293 cells during a post-RVD manoeuvre: water-diluted medium at 240 mOsm was followed by sorbitol restoration to 300 mOsm, producing acute shrinkage. Their broader experiments connected crowding-sensitive WNK1 condensation with transport signalling and volume recovery. This supplies a direct cellular precedent for recovery-phase recruitment of the proposed import-cost branch. The post-RVD observation did not demonstrate pathological neuronal chloride overshoot.

Chloride amount and chloride concentration must therefore be distinguished. RVD can remove chloride, but subsequent water loss can raise its concentration while increasing molecular crowding; return to isotonicity does not necessarily release the chloride brake. A separate activation protocol used hypotonic buffer with NaCl and KCl replaced by gluconate salts, leaving approximately 1 mM extracellular chloride (Thastrup et al., 2012). That combined perturbation cannot stand for ordinary hypotonic exposure. The relative contribution of chloride inhibition and crowding requires paired concentration and volume measurements, with WNK isoform, phosphosite and opposing phosphatase effects specified.

The proposed developmental extension is a failure to coordinate or terminate replenishment in a defined neural population. A particular variant or pathway state could prolong inward transport or delay extrusion after restoration, leaving ionic or volume recovery incomplete during a maturation process. Normal replenishment is the essential comparator: increased WNK signalling with adequate recovery remains compatible with successful regulation. Developmental baseline also matters. WNK1-dependent inhibitory KCC2 phosphorylation contributed to chloride regulation in immature rodent neurons (Friedel et al., 2015); this does not assign mature-neuron KCC2 physiology to undifferentiated progenitors. The developmental claim is that impaired recovery changes maturation in cells expressing the relevant transport machinery at that stage. Sections [29](#ss_p10_sec_29)–[31](#ss_p10_sec_31) distinguish the relevant protein-production, cell-state and developmental-timing questions. A renal effect of a variant can motivate this neural comparison without establishing its result.

WNK3 provides a candidate intrinsic route into the coordination of chloride transport. In Xenopus oocyte coexpression experiments, kinase-active WNK3 stimulated NKCC1 and inhibited KCC2, whereas an engineered kinase-inactive construct produced the opposite effects ([Kahle et al., 2005](#ss_bridge3_ref_Kahle2005)). Human variant assays refine the direction: the three missense variants tested by [Küry et al. (2022)](#ss_bridge3_ref_Kury2022) reduced WNK3 abundance and inhibitory KCC2 Thr1007 phosphorylation in transfected HEK293T cells, while total KCC2 remained unchanged. This result concerns reduced inhibitory phosphorylation, not demonstrated impairment of chloride extrusion. Transport and post-disturbance recovery were not measured in that assay.

Neuronal experiments show that developmental context can change the outcome of WNK3 loss. [Lim et al. (2021)](#ss_bridge3_ref_Lim2021) introduced WNK3-targeting shRNA on the first day of embryonic rat hippocampal culture. At days 13–15, GABA reversal potential was more negative, membrane-fraction KCC2 Thr1007 phosphorylation was reduced, and total KCC2, total NKCC1 and NKCC1 phosphorylation were unchanged. No significant GABA reversal-potential difference was detected at days 6–8. Intrinsic excitability and synaptic excitation nevertheless increased in the mature cultures. This was knockdown across culture development, not an acute intervention begun in mature neurons, and a more negative GABA reversal potential did not imply uniformly reduced neuronal excitation.

A constitutive knockout produced a different combination of effects. In juvenile male mice, [Sinha et al. (2022)](#ss_bridge3_ref_Sinha2022) found a more positive GABA reversal potential in medial prefrontal layer V pyramidal neurons, alongside increased inwardly rectifying potassium conductance and reduced intrinsic excitability. Assayed cortical WNK1/SPAK/OSR1 and NKCC1/KCC2 phosphorylation showed no significant differences. Thus, chloride-related responses and net excitability can move in different directions, and the hippocampal-culture and cortical-slice results cannot be collapsed into universal chloride loading or unloading. Neither study measured post-load chloride or cell-volume recovery, and neither established a male–female difference in the response to WNK3 disruption.

Renal findings demonstrate that preserved function is possible after WNK3 loss. [Oi et al. (2012)](#ss_bridge3_ref_Oi2012) found no significant difference in urinary sodium or potassium excretion in adult male knockout mice, including transitions between sodium diets, and no significant reduction in renal NKCC2 or NCC phosphorylation. Blood pressure was lower during sodium restriction, so the absence of salt wasting did not mean every physiological endpoint was unchanged. These excretion and phosphorylation findings constrain an obligatory renal-loss route; they do not infer compensatory work from normal serum chemistry. Shared expression or regulatory activity in kidney and brain does not establish renal mediation of the human neurodevelopmental phenotype.

The Sodium-Struggle proposal is that a specified WNK3 perturbation could alter the coordination or timing of local ionic recovery during development, either intrinsically or in interaction with a defined exposure. Appropriate experimental models would need to separate starting chloride, transport activity, potassium conductance and cell volume from recovery after matched loading, and relate any recovery defect to a subsequent developmental outcome. Preserved recovery during the relevant interval, or developmental effects independent of the proposed recovery change, would count against that route (Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)). Other WNK3-dependent neuronal effects remain alternatives. Any peripheral renal consequence would require its own measurements and could occur in parallel, rather than mediate the neural effect.

NKCC1 cotransports one Na⁺, one K⁺ and two Cl⁻ without directly hydrolysing ATP. Its net direction depends on the combined sodium, potassium and chloride gradients, not on phosphorylation alone. Rising intracellular sodium and chloride can oppose further inward flux, whereas increased extracellular potassium can favour it if the other gradients permit. Sodium entering through NKCC1 can increase Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase work during transport and recovery. Increased ATP turnover need not lower ATP concentration when supply compensates, and ATP depletion cannot be assumed to produce continuing inward NKCC1 flux. The proposed difficulty is a mismatch between transport-associated demand and available supply (Brumback and Staley, 2008).

Primary injury studies support components of this branch but also constrain it. In cultured embryonic mouse cortical neurons exposed to two hours of oxygen-glucose deprivation and reoxygenation, NKCC1 inhibition or deletion preserved sodium homeostasis and ATP, although reduced pump work was not isolated from other protective effects (Chen et al., 2010b). In P8–13 mouse neocortical slices, bumetanide reduced early swelling and chloride accumulation, but did not reduce swelling and worsened chloride accumulation during prolonged deprivation (Takezawa et al., 2023). These findings support context- and time-dependent transporter involvement. They do not demonstrate a self-sustaining mismatch between transport-associated demand and energetic supply after mild recurrent developmental stress.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_7_2"></a>

##### 23.7.2 Developmental exposures and perinatal signalling

Early experience can also change the developmental trajectory of chloride regulation. In male C57BL/6J mice, maternal separation on postnatal days 1–21 delayed the hippocampal GABA transition assessed through calcium imaging and reduced the developmental increase in membrane-associated KCC2. Reduced KCC2 persisted into adolescence, when behavioural differences were also reported ([Furukawa et al., 2017](#ss_bridge2_ref_Furukawa2017)). This provides an exposure-to-transport-development precedent; calcium responses and protein localisation are distinct from recovery after a matched chloride load, and the male-only experiment supplies no sex comparison.

Prenatal hypoxia supplies a different, region-specific precedent. Following maternal exposure to 10% oxygen on gestational days 5–20 and subsequent normoxia, rat pups had lower pontine membrane KCC2 at postnatal days 3–4, but not days 0–1. Between-group NKCC1 abundance and NKCC1/KCC2 ratios did not differ significantly. Transporter blockade altered fictive breathing in isolated brainstem preparations, while GABA-A blockade increased respiratory frequency in both groups at days 3–4 ([Caravagna et al., 2022](#ss_bridge2_ref_Caravagna2022)). Thus, reduced KCC2 coexisted with continuing net GABAergic restraint in that assay. These neonatal respiratory findings do not measure cortical recovery or adolescent behaviour.

Stress effects need not point towards delayed inhibition. In a different rat protocol, saline-injected pups separated for six hours daily on postnatal days 4–6 showed more hyperpolarising CA1 GABA responses in both sexes. KCC2 immunoreactivity increased in males only, while the bumetanide-sensitive transport contribution decreased in both sexes ([Galanopoulou, 2008)](#ss_bridge2_ref_Galanopoulou2008). This is a protocol-dependent contrast, not a direct replication of the longer mouse separation experiment.

The proposed connection is that an exposure could change chloride regulation during a sensitive window and thereby alter recovery under subsequent demand. Testing that sequence requires distinguishing transporter abundance, membrane localisation and phosphorylation from chloride extrusion, recovery kinetics, GABA driving force and net network inhibition. The studies above motivate this developmental comparison without establishing AVP or renal mediation. A systemic route and a local metabolic route remain alternatives, and preserved recovery after an appropriately matched load would count against the proposed recovery contribution (Sections [3.3](#ss_p10_sec_3_3), [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13), and [40.5](#ss_p10_sec_40_5)).

[Tyzio et al. (2006)](#ss_p4_ref_Tyzio2006) reported a transient inhibitory GABA shift near delivery in fetal and neonatal rat hippocampal preparations. Maternal oxytocin-receptor blockade prevented this shift, while separate chloride-imaging experiments supported an oxytocin-sensitive reduction in neuronal chloride. Receptor blockade also shortened the latency to anoxic depolarisation during oxygen–glucose deprivation in isolated E21 hippocampi. These findings support a protective birth-window mechanism in that preparation; they do not establish a universal mammalian switch or a human developmental outcome.

Positive developmental intervention evidence comes from two distinct rodent models. In valproate-exposed rats and Fmr1-null mice, Tyzio et al. (2014) reported altered CA3 GABA driving force, excitatory GABA responses and increased glutamatergic activity. Maternal bumetanide given one day before delivery shifted juvenile GABA responses toward inhibition and attenuated early vocalisation and network abnormalities. Maternal oxytocin-receptor blockade in otherwise unexposed animals produced related abnormalities. Following criticism of neonatal vocalisations as an autism proxy, the same group reported improved adult social approach in male valproate rats and reduced excess grooming in male Fmr1 mice (Bambini-Junior et al., 2014; Eftekhari et al., 2014). These experiments support a lasting developmental effect of a brief perinatal intervention. They did not measure systemic sodium–volume defence, recovery after matched ionic loading or a selective neuronal mechanism. The original study disclosed commercial and patent interests; independent replication remains important.

The result does not establish a universal birth-associated GABA defect. Shank3B-null mice had increased CA3 glutamatergic activity with preserved GABA driving force and inhibitory action at the tested ages (Chiesa et al., 2019). Independent work found continuing depolarising GABA in normal perinatal rats and AVP-mediated suppression of hippocampal network events through V1a-dependent interneuron activation in rats and neonatal guinea pigs (Spoljaric et al., 2017). Rat GABA driving force was unchanged by AVP. At the tested 10 nM concentration, oxytocin did not suppress rat network events; this dose and endpoint differ from the 2006 chloride experiments. The findings challenge a universal birth-associated inhibitory switch and support a potentially protective AVP mechanism, although protection from injury was not directly tested. This is not a direct replication of the valproate/Fmr1 intervention. Together these findings require model-specific tests of the ionic intermediary and selective rescue, with litter, sex and developmental stage specified. Rodent vocalisation, grooming and social-approach measures are experimental outcomes, not diagnoses of human autism.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_7_3"></a>

##### 23.7.3 Intervention limits and target engagement

Two phase 3 trials found no broad clinical benefit from bumetanide in established ASD. SIGN 1 (ages 7–17) and SIGN 2 (ages 2–6) each enrolled 211 participants, 422 combined. Neither met its week-26 CARS2 primary endpoint, and secondary results did not establish consistent efficacy. SIGN 1 nevertheless reported more Clinical Global Impression responders with bumetanide (22.7% versus 12.4%). Thirst, polyuria and hypokalaemia were more frequent with treatment (Fuentes et al., 2023). These results constrain therapeutic claims. Prenatal initiation and local chloride-recovery and ATP trajectories were not endpoints and require separate mechanistic tests; their omission supplies no evidence that an early recovery disturbance occurred.

Neuronal NKCC1 and renal NKCC2 actions require separate exposure measurements. Bumetanide inhibits human NKCC1A and NKCC2A expressed in Xenopus oocytes ([Lykke et al., 2016](#ss_revsyn5_ref_Lykke2016)); mouse experiments implicate restricted passive entry and active blood–brain barrier transport in low brain accumulation ([Römermann et al., 2017](#ss_revsyn5_ref_Romermann2017)). Renal diuresis and potassium loss can coexist with uncertain neuronal engagement. Animal brain-tissue measurements do not establish unbound neuronal exposure in treated children. NKCC1 also operates outside neurons, including in the choroid plexus (Section [30](#ss_p10_sec_30)). Section [3.3](#ss_p10_sec_3_3) adds blood-facing endothelial NKCC1 as another potential site of action, distinct from neuronal target engagement. Renal effects could modify compensatory demand depending on losses, intake and downstream conservation; SIGN adverse events do not identify RAAS, AVP or ammoniagenesis as mediators of failed efficacy.

NKCC1 inhibition can change resting chloride and the load to clear, so bumetanide does not selectively distinguish chloride-state from recovery accounts; negative trials do not favour the latter. Appropriate experimental models can test predicted neuronal chloride changes with verified target engagement alongside predicted renal salt, water or potassium handling changes, measuring net balance and compensatory demand separately. Selective interventions with matched initial ionic loads could distinguish recovery kinetics from starting chloride or systemic support. Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) separates adequate recovery during the causal interval, prevention of the proposed mediator and later downstream rescue.

##### 23.7.4 Metabolic regulation and vascular recovery

Endothelin-1 is a candidate vascular-to-glial signal. Metabolic strain might also impair KCC2 or its potassium driving gradient without increased import. Lactate elevation identifies neither that transport effect nor the direct oxidant-sensitive KCC2 changes described above.

NFAT5 provides an experimentally grounded connection between metabolic stress and chloride handling. In cultured hippocampal neurons, oxygen–glucose deprivation reduced NFAT5 and increased NKCC1; NFAT5 knockdown under normal culture conditions also increased NKCC1 and reduced chloride-sensitive MQAE fluorescence, consistent with increased intracellular chloride. Neuronal binding assays and promoter-reporter experiments in PC12 cells implicated opposing HIF-1α and NFAT5 regulation of NKCC1 (Yang et al., 2019). This supports a molecular connection, not a measured recovery-time defect: the fluorescence was not an absolute chloride calibration, and a selective NKCC1 rescue of the knockdown’s chloride effect was not reported. Experimental separation of NFAT5 ionic-strength sensing from WNK1 volume/crowding responses further shows why intracellular salt content, concentration and cell size need separate assays (Khandwala et al., 2025). Neither experiment establishes the proposed fetal imprint or its direction under mild recurrent dilution.

Because Yang et al. (2019) jointly removed oxygen and glucose, the experiment does not isolate hypoxia. It supplies a local metabolic route without prior systemic sodium–volume disturbance; recovery mediation and systemic initiation remain separate additional claims (Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)).

A separate vascular experiment makes recovery after challenge particularly relevant. Conditional endothelial Nfat5 deletion in adult mice impaired post-ischaemic reperfusion and reduced arterial Kir2.1 expression despite relatively unremarkable baseline findings (Kunze et al., 2024). This supports testing vascular reserve beyond resting measurements. It does not transfer the injury model to ordinary social demand or establish a fetal sodium-mediated pathway; neuronal and endothelial NFAT5 effects require their own causal tests.

#### 23.8 Why a cortical chloride bias matters disproportionately

A cortical chloride disturbance could intersect with KCC2 maturation, glial support, perfusion/redox conditions and the precision demands of inhibitory circuits. The argument concerns developmental timing rather than the highest absolute NKCC1 expression.

Cortical chloride extrusion changes during development, but GABA depolarisation and inhibition are not opposites. KCC2 contributes to chloride regulation, while the functional effect of GABA depends on reversal potential, conductance, location, resting voltage and firing threshold. Depolarising GABA can remain inhibitory, as demonstrated in neonatal neocortex and adult hippocampal parvalbumin interneurons under the respective experimental conditions (Kirmse et al., 2015; Otsu et al., 2020). Recurrent chloride loading or impaired extrusion could therefore alter the timing of inhibitory maturation where the resulting physiological change disrupts circuit control during a specified developmental window.

Perivascular astrocytic water, potassium and metabolic support supply a further interface. Where cellular expansion reduces ECS, fixed K⁺ or glutamate release can produce larger transients during neuronal chloride maturation (Sections [24](#ss_p10_sec_24) and [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)).

Together, these conditions could alter sensory precision, oscillatory timing or stability under load while circuits are refined.

The developmental timing of this intersection matters, but there is no single fetal-to-toddler switch shared by all cortical neurons or species. KCC2 regulation, the effect of GABA and PV-circuit maturation must be matched to the region, cell type and developmental stage studied. The proposed ASD relevance is a lasting alteration of circuit calibration during a susceptible window, which cannot be inferred simply from overlap between broad developmental timelines.

#### 23.9 Consequences for inhibitory polarity, calcium duty cycle, and PV-interneuron vulnerability

A chloride rise shifts E<sub>Cl</sub> positively and can shift E<sub>GABA</sub>, which also reflects bicarbonate permeability. As above, shunting may preserve inhibition; loss of timing precision requires a functional effect, not transporter abundance or reversal potential alone.

An altered excitation–inhibition ratio can itself help preserve circuit output. Antoine et al. (2019) examined somatosensory cortex in Fmr1, Cntnap2, 16p11.2-deletion and Tsc2 mouse models. Feedforward inhibition onto layer 2/3 pyramidal cells was reduced more than excitation, increasing the conductance ratio, yet synaptic depolarisation and spiking were largely preserved. Conductance modelling indicated that the paired changes stabilised depolarisation near spike threshold; whisker-evoked spiking was not increased in the in-vivo comparisons. This is a concrete example of protective compensation within an autism-relevant circuit. It supports distinguishing a changed regulatory setting from failed function, without establishing either an ionic-recovery defect or hidden developmental injury in those preparations.

The additional prediction is that incomplete recovery after repeated demand reduces fidelity or alters development despite initially maintained output. A developmental effect with recovery preserved throughout its causal interval would challenge that mediation; returning a compensatory excitation–inhibition ratio to control need not improve function.

Calcium entry could increase when GABA-related depolarisation reaches the activation range of available voltage-gated channels or relieves Mg²⁺ block at ligand-bound NMDA receptors during excitation. Strong shunting may instead reduce or leave entry unchanged. Shifting EGABA at fixed conductance differs from comparing excitation with and without GABA; Section [26](#ss_p10_sec_26) develops these distinct branches and their evidence (Owens et al., 1996; Kirmse et al., 2015; Staley and Mody, 1992).

PV interneurons are plausible high-demand recipients of local ionic and metabolic stress, but can also be an initiating site of redox dysfunction. In mice, PV-cell-targeted Gclc deletion reduced PV and perineuronal-net labelling and prolonged visual cortical plasticity into young adulthood (Morishita et al., 2015). That experiment provides a direct cellular redox route without requiring prior astrocytic failure. It did not establish chloride, sodium-pump, BH4 or ATP mediation, and reduced PV immunoreactivity should not be equated with PV-cell death.

Intrinsic PV dysfunction and altered glial support are separate routes to fast-spiking timing differences. Either could affect oscillatory precision, sensory gain or load-dependent stability; astrocytic, ionic and metabolic contributions remain conditional.

Oligodendrocytes can likewise be affected through their own recovery, calcium or metabolic support, or initiate a genetic disturbance themselves. Section [23.10](#ss_p10_sec_23_10) distinguishes developmental myelination from ongoing axonal support.

The local-support mechanism proposed here can coexist with the extracellular OTX2 mechanism in Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4). Evidence for altered inhibitory timing does not identify whether ionic recovery, signal supply, recipient capture or an independent developmental process was responsible.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_10"></a>

#### 23.10 Network-level consequences of chloride-weighted physiology

If reduced local reserve persists, its functional consequences could appear in inhibitory timing, axonal support or vulnerability to hyperexcitable transitions. These are the network-level extensions of the preceding cellular account.

PV interneuron vulnerability and gamma timing. PV-mediated inhibition provides a concrete link to network coordination: optogenetic PV inhibition suppressed prefrontal gamma activity in mice, while PV feedback generated gamma-frequency rhythms in slices (Sohal et al., 2009). The preparation-dependent metabolic-challenge recovery and extracellular redox-protection findings in Section [18.1.7](#ss_p10_sec_18_1_7) further support testing PV function under constrained local support (Povysheva et al., 2019; Cabungcal et al., 2013). The proposed consequence is impaired inhibitory precision during repeated demand when ionic or metabolic recovery is inadequate. Impaired local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery must mediate the developmental circuit change. A positive EGABA shift may remain inhibitory, and a larger extracellular potassium excursion depends on release, space and clearance together (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [26](#ss_p10_sec_26)).

Oligodendrocyte maturation and axonal support. Oligodendrocyte-lineage NKCC1 expression and calcium-sensitive maturation motivate two distinct possibilities: altered myelin construction and impaired adjustment of metabolic support to axonal demand. A recovery disturbance could affect conduction timing through either route, but neuronal GABA responses do not establish oligodendroglial calcium loading, and uniform demyelination is not required.

A genetic initiating route is demonstrated by Cho et al. (2023). Anks1b-deficient mice showed impaired oligodendrocyte maturation and myelination. Oligodendrocyte-lineage deletion reproduced social-preference and sensory-reactivity phenotypes that were not reproduced by the tested neuronal deletions. Rac1 signalling was dysregulated, and prolonged Rac1 stimulation restored myelin basic protein expression in cultured mutant oligodendrocytes. Clemastine treatment improved social preference and callosal myelination in adult mutant mice. The lineage restriction supports glial initiation; the later rescue shows that some measured outcomes remained modifiable. Neither result establishes an earlier ionic or cellular-volume recovery defect as the developmental mediator, and the drug result is not a treatment inference for human autism.

Looser et al. (2024) identify a different, physiological connection. In adult mouse optic nerves, activity-related extracellular K⁺ signalling through oligodendroglial Kir4.1 coupled axonal firing to glial calcium responses, glycolysis and axonal lactate support. Oligodendrocyte-specific Kir4.1 deletion reduced resting and activity-evoked axonal lactate and altered glucose metabolism. In approximately three-month-old mice, basal axonal ATP and initial ATP-recovery rates were comparable between genotypes, but rebound was modestly incomplete after glucose deprivation with mitochondrial inhibition or after high-frequency stimulation. Adjustment of conduction speed during recovery was also impaired. Bumetanide did not suppress the activity-evoked calcium response in adult oligodendrocytes under the tested conditions. This support mechanism therefore cannot be assigned to NKCC1-mediated loading, and an ATP-recovery result is not itself a measurement of ionic or cellular-volume recovery.

These studies make glial initiation and activity-dependent support concrete but distinct. The proposed intersection is that local recovery difficulty leaves restoration, metabolite supply and axonal conduction out of step after demand. During myelination, that mismatch could alter how activity is supported while circuits are assembled; neither study establishes this developmental sequence.

Neither study shows ANKS1B regulation of Kir4.1 or obligatory metabolic mediation. Direct cytoskeletal or maturation effects could change demand before recovery becomes impaired. Oligodendroglial Kir4.1 deletion also differs from the astrocytic gain-of-function alleles in Section [6.3](#ss_p10_sec_6_3); shared channel names do not imply shared dysfunction. Protein production is another possible intermediary (Section [29](#ss_p10_sec_29)).

Preserved relevant recovery during the developmental effect would limit this glial route. Upstream genetic or pleiotropic drug rescue cannot identify recovery mediation, and late rescue does not establish initiation.

Seizure vulnerability. Weakened GABAergic control, larger potassium or glutamate transients, or delayed recovery could reduce reserve against hyperexcitable transitions. A positive E<sub>GABA</sub> shift alone does not establish these conditions. The proposed consequence is greater vulnerability under load in relevant subsets, not universal, autism-specific or continuous seizures.

#### 23.11 Candidate Mechanisms of Persistent Recovery Difficulty

Persistence can reflect continuing exposure, delayed repair, developmental regulation or self-maintaining feedback. Candidate amplifiers must outlast normal termination through restored tonicity/perfusion, chloride-sensitive WNK inhibition, potassium-gradient recovery, transporter reset, osmolyte replenishment and antioxidant buffering.

BDNF/TrkB, cytokine and calcium-dependent pathways remain possible modifiers whose effects depend on developmental and injury context. Calpain-mediated KCC2 cleavage provides an experimentally supported component (Puskarjov et al., 2012). A loop in which a measured chloride and conductance state increases calcium entry, calcium activates calpain and KCC2 cleavage further impairs extrusion is plausible, but the complete loop and its persistence have not been demonstrated by those component experiments.

Other proposed persistence modifiers include delayed KCC2 maturation or membrane stabilisation, PNN disruption, thyroid and glucocorticoid signalling, AVP-related water-handling responses, oxidant burden and recurrent network activity. They need not act together or in the same direction at every age.

Either excess import-associated demand or impaired extrusion could interact with glial volume, extracellular potassium, calcium and transporter stability. The branches defined in Section [23.2](#ss_p10_sec_23_2) remain distinct even if they converge on delayed chloride recovery.

Energy-first, redox-first and KCC2-first paths remain possible. Prolonged recovery alone establishes neither hysteresis nor a self-maintaining state; persistence requires an identified sustaining mechanism after the initiating exposure and relevant extracellular abnormalities have ended. A lasting circuit alteration after physiological recovery is a separate developmental consequence.

#### 23.12 Modifiers of Recovery Thresholds and Persistence

Constitutional factors could modify threshold or persistence within the three-threat route; primary genetic or developmental mechanisms remain alternatives.

Candidate modifiers include antioxidant and mitochondrial reserve, endothelial/glycocalyx or autonomic function, AVP responsiveness, WNK–SPAK/OSR1 susceptibility, KCC2 regulation and maturation, thyroid/glucocorticoid effects, and PV/perineuronal-net resilience. Sex-dependent perfusion defence, stress-hormone escalation, vascular regulation, WNK plasticity and early buffering could modify entry, persistence or recovery without a sex-specific initiating pathology.

Within this proposed recovery route, chromatin and transcriptional-state regulators are considered as gain-and-reset modifiers; primary regulatory effects remain alternative explanations. Where a chloride and conductance change demonstrably raises calcium entry or duty cycle, repeated calcium signals could interact with chromatin state to influence transporter, cytoskeletal or developmental programmes. This would provide one route to heterogeneity of persistence without making chromatin the origin of the chloride change in that route.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_13"></a>

#### 23.13 Recovery mediation and interpretive limits

The distinctive claim concerns what fails to recover and how that changes development. This cellular route proposes altered inhibitory maturation, circuit precision and calibration during sensitive windows; it does not equate autism with generic brain injury or a disease-specific chloride lesion. Similar chloride disturbances occur in other conditions. Their relevance here depends on the local recovery disturbance carrying a defined developmental effect, rather than merely accompanying a stress response.

The Ben-Ari–Tyzio programme already links perinatal signalling, chloride regulation and lasting neural outcomes (Tyzio et al., 2014), and Tang et al. (2019) measured chloride-recovery kinetics in human Rett-syndrome neurons. The present account adds a proposed convergence across initiating routes. Comparable resting chloride values can coexist with different recovery responses; altered resting chloride or failure to establish an age-appropriate gradient does not itself demonstrate impaired restoration. Failure of a later bumetanide trial does not favour this account over an earlier developmental chloride mechanism.

The proposed transport branches remain distinct. Increased NKCC1-dependent inward flux can increase sodium-pump demand; reduced KCC2-mediated extrusion or its potassium driving force can impair chloride restoration without increased influx. Organic-osmolyte loss and glial buffering can create other recovery constraints. Regulatory volume decrease during continued hypotonic exposure and restoration after return to isotonic conditions are different phases, and normal volume need not mean restored ionic composition. Serum or CSF ions cannot substitute for the relevant cellular state. Increased work with adequate recovery remains successful compensation.

Systemic initiation and local mediation are separate claims. Oxygen or substrate limitation can constrain local recovery, while a sodium–volume route additionally requires a contribution from tonicity, effective filling, delivery or their regulation. Yang et al. (2019) studied joint oxygen–glucose deprivation, not isolated hypoxia or post-challenge recovery kinetics. That component result cannot establish the entire systemic sequence. Conversely, direct genetic, immune or metabolic initiation need not first produce a systemic deficit.

The endothelial route predicts altered blood-to-brain ion transfer, changed local extracellular conditions and prolonged neural or glial recovery under specified conditions (Section [3.3](#ss_p10_sec_3_3)). Appropriate developmental models would measure net transfer, permeability, perfusion and recovery separately. Timely selective prevention of the transfer change, with target engagement and other intervention effects assessed, tests its proposed contribution. Preserved recovery despite the transfer change, or an unchanged recovery defect despite preventing that change, would count against the specified mediation. Cellular uptake alone cannot establish net transfer.

The timing proposal predicts different recovery trajectories when a defined exposure overlaps a specified maturation interval (Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7); Section [40.5](#ss_p10_sec_40_5)). Appropriate models would measure recovery after comparable initial ionic perturbations, separately from starting chloride, transporter regulation, GABA reversal potential and net excitability. A sex-modifier claim requires a prespecified sex-by-exposure comparison of recovery trajectories. An adequately precise estimate excluding the predicted sex difference would constrain that modifier; developmental effects despite preserved relevant recovery would instead challenge recovery mediation.

WNK3 supplies an intrinsic comparison between recovery and other neuronal effects (Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7)). For a specified variant, cell type and developmental interval, appropriate models would measure the rate and completeness of chloride or volume restoration after comparable initial perturbations, alongside GABA reversal potential and potassium conductance. The predicted recovery change and its direction would be specified beforehand. Timely selective prevention of that change tests its proposed developmental role ([Table 2.1](#ss_p10_table_2_1)). Broad WNK3 rescue alone would not distinguish recovery mediation from its other cellular actions.

The clinical renal proposal predicts that documented salt wasting and its recovery contribute information beyond an infection diagnosis (Section [14.4.2](#ss_p10_sec_14_4_2); Section [46.3](#ss_p10_sec_46_3)). Within a prespecified developmental interval, existing records or cohorts could compare similarly ill infants with measured salt wasting against those with preserved conservation, using intake/replacement, output and serial blood/urine measurements where available. Prematurity, illness severity, treatment and sampling require consideration. A sufficiently precise comparison finding no added relationship between the prespecified physiological trajectory and developmental outcome would weaken that clinical prediction. A positive association would still require temporally relevant neural or glial recovery evidence to support the developmental intermediary; ear-fluid resolution remains a separate peripheral endpoint.

The immune comparison illustrates the distinction. Severe maternal inflammation produced fetal cardiovascular abnormalities in one model, whereas IL-17A altered human cerebroid development without systemic circulation (Rounioja et al., 2005; Assir et al., 2026). Failure of verified cardiovascular correction to restore recovery when local correction succeeds would weaken the specified cardiovascular intermediary while leaving local immune initiation possible. Antibody target specificity identifies an initiating mechanism, not recovery mediation. Similarly, prolonged glucose-associated inflammation matters to this account only if it impairs local recovery; inflammatory persistence alone is insufficient (Sections [18.5](#ss_p10_sec_18_5), [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6), and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)).

Persistent-defence and metabolic-signalling accounts provide important antecedents, including Naviaux’s cell danger response (Section [26.7](#ss_p10_sec_26_7)). Protein production, glial maturation, folate delivery, sterol signalling, channel-associated cytoskeletal effects and neuromodulation offer interacting or independent explanations (Sections [23.10](#ss_p10_sec_23_10), [26.9](#ss_p10_sec_26_9), [29](#ss_p10_sec_29), [30](#ss_p10_sec_30), [35.4.4](#ss_p10_sec_35_4_4), and [47.1](#ss_p10_sec_47_1)). Recovery may be upstream, downstream or parallel to these processes. Their co-occurrence, or improvement after a broad upstream intervention, does not resolve that causal order. The proposed recovery contribution must explain something beyond a generic stress signature.

Calcium consequences are also conditional. A positive shift in GABA reversal potential need not abolish shunting inhibition or increase calcium entry. Greater entry relative to a more negative reversal potential is not the same comparison as greater entry than during excitation without GABA. Reduced entry under the relevant conditions limits the increased-entry branch, without deciding other ionic or volume routes. Later low calcium responses cannot be attributed to earlier overload without evidence for that earlier event (Section [26](#ss_p10_sec_26)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_23_13_1"></a>

##### 23.13.1 What would limit the hypothesis

A developmental effect despite adequately demonstrated preservation of relevant local recovery, or despite timely prevention of its necessary disturbance, counts against recovery mediation in that route. An inconclusive null does not establish preserved recovery. Absence of increased NKCC1 influx limits the import-cost branch; normal chloride recovery alone does not establish normal glial or volume recovery. The relevant compartment, developmental interval and claimed disturbance must be specified in advance, rather than reassigned after a negative result. A credible bypass of the required intermediary would challenge universal participation even if recovery contributes elsewhere.

A transient disturbance can leave a lasting developmental consequence after physiology normalises. Normal later biomarkers and failure of late treatment therefore do not settle an earlier causal question, but neither supplies evidence that an earlier disturbance occurred. Peripheral-cell recovery can characterise a peripheral phenotype without establishing neural development. Cell and animal findings must retain their preparation and developmental context when related to autism. These distinctions preserve a testable common-process conjecture without making any single exposure, AVP direction, transporter response or metabolic branch compulsory.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_24"></a>

### 24 Astrocytic osmotic imprinting: volume regulation, osmolyte debt, and extracellular-space constraints

<a name="ss_p10_sec_24_1"></a>

#### 24.1 Astrocytes as candidate volume responders in early sodium instability

Astrocytes bring several of these recovery processes together through ion, water and transmitter handling that links local activity to vascular support. The developmental proposal is that repeated recruitment leaves altered recovery or reserve on a different schedule from systemic defence; plasma sodium alone establishes neither the original brain exposure nor its recovery.

Astrocytes are not the only cells capable of reversible swelling. In acute mouse brain slices, Murphy et al. (2017) observed rapid swelling of hippocampal and cortical pyramidal neurons alongside astrocytes during substantial reductions in bathing-medium osmolarity; volume recovered when normal medium returned. AQP4 deletion did not abolish swelling. These conditions do not establish responses to mild fetal exposure, but they rule out the categorical premise that neurons cannot swell and astrocytes must accept water on their behalf. Cell type, developmental stage, exposure and compartment must determine the proposed allocation of volume stress.

Intrinsic transporter variation supplies a complementary local entry point. In mammalian expression systems, SLC1A2 Leu85Pro combined impaired EAAT2 glutamate transport with increased anion-channel function, whereas Gly360Ala, classified in that study as a variant of uncertain significance, primarily increased anion-channel function (Kovermann et al., 2025). These findings in a neurodevelopmental/epilepsy cohort make impaired clearance and altered glial ionic handling concrete candidate routes. Their effects on local recovery and ATP demand require separate measurement, as do any developmental effects relevant to autism.

Experimental hyponatraemia provides a physiological comparator. Fujisawa et al. (2016) found impaired gait and memory, reduced hippocampal long-term potentiation and higher extracellular glutamate in rats given desmopressin and a liquid diet, including a group with serum sodium around 121 mmol/L. Cultured mouse astrocytes showed reduced glutamate uptake under low-NaCl culture and assay conditions, with uptake comparable to controls after gradual medium correction. Corrected rats in a separate cohort also performed comparably to controls on gait and memory tests, consistent with possible recovery. Sodium, chloride and tonicity were not independently isolated, and glutamate mediation of the behavioural effects was not established. These results connect extracellular composition with glial transmitter handling. The developmental proposal is that such changes impair local neural/glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery enough to alter circuit formation; that sequence was not tested.

Human findings provide a functional comparison: gait and attention measures were better during normonatraemia in a small within-person study of adults with chronic hyponatraemia (Renneboog et al., 2006). Such later-life recovery does not determine whether exposure during a sensitive developmental interval can leave lasting effects.

The proposed cost is altered recovery or acquired susceptibility after an initially protective response, without requiring primary neuronal injury or chronic hyponatraemia.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_24_2"></a>

#### 24.2 Osmolyte-based volume regulation under hypo-osmotic stress

This branch concerns measured cellular hypotonic exposure: water entry depends on membrane permeability, intracellular solutes and concurrent transport. Plasma sodium or osmolality alone does not establish the local volume change.

Regulatory volume decrease exports intracellular osmoles, allowing water to leave after swelling. Inorganic ions, including K⁺ and Cl⁻, and organic osmolytes can contribute; organic export does not replace ionic efflux as a universal rule. In primary rat cortical astrocytes, LRRC8A knockdown slowed and reduced the tested volume recovery after hypotonic swelling (Formaggio et al., 2019). This establishes a functional role for the volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) in that preparation, not a fixed division of osmotic work in developing human cortex.

Organic-osmolyte release is nevertheless a concrete part of this mechanism. In primary rat astrocytes, LRRC8 subunit manipulations differentiated swelling-activated taurine and myo-inositol release from release of an acidic-amino-acid tracer (Schober et al., 2017). Channel composition therefore influences which solutes leave. Compatible intracellular osmolytes are not necessarily inert outside the cell, and volume regulation can itself alter extracellular signalling. The developmental proposal concerns the balance between protective solute loss, subsequent replenishment and the local consequences of those fluxes.

LRRC8A/SWELL1, an essential subunit of heteromeric volume-regulated anion channels, also participates in adipocyte insulin signalling and GLUT4 recruitment. β-cell LRRC8 chloride current contributes to glucose-stimulated activity and secretion (Zhang et al., 2017; Kang et al., 2018). These tissue-specific links motivate the metabolic susceptibility route in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7). The adipocyte signalling effect is not interchangeable with channel conductance or established cortical recovery physiology.

The proposed long-term cost begins where measured loss exceeds restoration before the next challenge. Protective volume recovery and complete biochemical recovery are different endpoints. Whether early repeated exposure separates them is the question addressed by osmolyte debt. Section [40.5](#ss_p10_sec_40_5) distinguishes brain-water adaptation during continuing hyponatraemia from restoration after its resolution.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_24_3"></a>

#### 24.3 Osmolyte debt as a developmental state variable

Osmolyte debt denotes a measured deficit in specified intracellular organic osmolytes relative to an appropriate cell-type and developmental reference after the external challenge has resolved. Content per cell, concentration and cell volume must be separated. A deficit may record previous defence without implying injury, but it must be distinguished from an adaptive steady state or an unrelated developmental difference. The proposed debt becomes functionally important if it predicts altered response or recovery on the next matched challenge. Its contribution to the core requires impaired ionic or volume recovery; a separate signalling effect with adequate recovery would not satisfy that criterion.

Lien et al. (1991) provide the severe-hyponatraemia precedent for slower organic than ionic restoration (Section [23.6](#ss_p10_sec_23_6)). In a separate acute rat experiment reducing plasma osmolality 15–20%, taurine moved from Purkinje cells towards glia. Saline normalisation reversed that redistribution while total cerebellar taurine remained low (Nagelhus et al., 1993). Cellular redistribution and tissue-pool restoration are therefore distinct. Neither exposure establishes the mild-intermittent developmental proposal; cumulative loss requires replenishment to remain insufficient, while adaptation or lower starting content could limit further loss.

Redox defence supplies a separate possible cost of osmotic adaptation. In male rats, total brain glutathione decreased during 72 hours of desmopressin-induced hyponatraemia and returned towards control after slow correction. Hypo-osmotic adaptation also depleted glutathione and taurine in rat C6 glioma and human SK-N-SH neuroblastoma cells; subsequent peroxide exposure increased cytolytic injury in SK-N-SH cells but not significantly in C6 cells ([Clark et al., 1996](#ss_p5_ref_Clark1996)). These findings connect adaptation with susceptibility to a further oxidative challenge. They do not isolate glutathione from concurrent solute changes or establish a sex difference in brain-water recovery.

Lower organic content need not increase swelling: starting volume, inorganic replacement, permeability and regulation determine the response. The proposed cost is increased restoration work or altered tolerance of renewed load, not ATP demand inferred from the deficit alone.

The prediction is reduced tolerance or slower recovery during repeated, matched challenges in the specified cells, even if resting function is adequate. Normal recovery with adequate measurement precision, or restoration of the proposed osmolyte deficit without the predicted functional improvement, would weaken this branch. Chronic swelling at rest is not required.

##### 24.3.1 Renal and local substrate modifiers

Systemic substrate availability could modify osmolyte restoration alongside local synthesis and transport. The conditional renal route in Sections [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) and [33](#ss_p10_sec_33) asks whether a specified acid-base or potassium disturbance increases renal glutamine utilisation enough, and for long enough, to change the substrate environment supporting neural or glial recovery. Renal extraction, circulating concentration, blood-brain exchange and brain-cell metabolism are successive, distinct links. A renal response could be fully accommodated by other tissues, leaving neural substrate availability and recovery intact. The nephron proposal therefore remains independent of a universal low-glutamine/high-glutamate/high-ammonia profile.

Human findings motivate compartment-specific investigation. [Shimmura et al. (2011)](#ss_chain_ref_Shimmura2011) found higher platelet-poor plasma glutamate and lower glutamine in 23 drug-naïve autistic boys and adolescents aged 8–17 years compared with 22 male controls. This selected sample had IQ scores above 70. These peripheral observations identify a substrate pattern to investigate, without measuring its renal origin or the substrate available to brain cells.

In a separate postmortem series spanning ages 8–29 years, seven autistic donors had 34% lower left anterior-cingulate kidney-type glutaminase (KGA) protein than 13 controls (p = .007). Absolute tissue glutamate (p = .75) and glutamine (p = .11) differences were nonsignificant, while the Glu/Gln ratio was lower (p = .022; [Shimmura et al., 2013](#ss_chain_ref_Shimmura2013)). Kidney-type names an enzyme isoform present in brain tissue, not a renal source. Protein abundance, metabolite pools and their ratio are distinct from enzyme activity and metabolic flux; neither study paired blood and brain measurements within the same participants.

The postmortem finding was selective among the proteins examined: glutamine synthetase, liver-type glutaminase, glutamate dehydrogenases 1 and 2, GFAP and neuron-specific enolase did not differ significantly. KGA did not correlate with age or postmortem interval, and excluding the donor treated with valproate and topiramate retained the group difference (p = .015; [Shimmura et al., 2013](#ss_chain_ref_Shimmura2013)). These checks narrow some alternatives without establishing equivalence or excluding agonal effects. Five of seven autistic donors died by drowning, compared with one of thirteen controls, and no donor tissue-pH control was reported.

The positive proposal is that reduced local glutamine breakdown could conserve substrate during altered ionic or substrate conditions. A similar protein pattern could instead reflect substrate-constrained metabolism or intrinsic regulation, with agonal hypoxia remaining a separate explanation. In appropriate experimental models, measuring glutamine supply, cell-specific utilisation and ionic or volume recovery together could distinguish successful adaptation from a limitation that delays recovery. Selective restoration of substrate availability would support a substrate-limited recovery mechanism if the predicted local recovery deficit also improved. Aggregate tissue concentrations alone neither demonstrate that compensatory work occurred nor exclude independently evidenced compensation. The renal-to-neural extension still requires the successive links specified above; lower brain KGA protein does not establish them.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_24_4"></a>

#### 24.4 AQP4 Abundance and Perivascular Localisation

AQP4 provides a second candidate interface between water movement and later vulnerability. It is enriched in astrocytic perivascular end-feet, where localisation can influence exchange geometry. Its expression, membrane distribution and contribution to water flux are distinct measurements. In mouse slices, AQP4 deletion did not prevent acute swelling, but increased astrocytic swelling when medium osmolarity was reduced by 40%, with no such difference at a 17% reduction (Murphy et al., 2017). AQP4 can therefore contribute to limiting swelling without being required for water entry; its role depends on the challenge.

AQP4 polarity denotes domain-specific enrichment and can change without reduced total abundance. Its effects on exchange geometry and recovery depend on function, not localisation alone.

Repeated swelling during end-foot maturation could leave altered AQP4 localisation and later function. Persistence of that exposure-to-redistribution link remains proposed.

Kir4.1-mediated potassium conductance supplies a related interface, but shared localisation with AQP4 does not establish obligatory functional coupling or impaired K⁺ clearance.

The hypothesis therefore predicts that altered AQP4 localisation could redistribute water movement and affect K⁺ clearance dynamics or the spatial precision of vascular signalling. These consequences require separate testing: experimental solute-removal effects depend on both the AQP4 perturbation and the tracer, and do not establish obligatory Kir4.1 dysfunction or altered OTX2 delivery (Bojarskaite et al., 2024).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_24_5"></a>

#### 24.5 Glial signalling and support during recovery

Glial buffering can connect local ionic or volume conditions with circuit function through metabolic support, extracellular signalling and vascular recruitment. ATP used to restore gradients and ATP available to receptors are distinct quantities. The proposed developmental connection is that impaired local recovery changes the support available during later demand, influencing circuit refinement when compensation is insufficient. Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)–[30](#ss_p10_sec_30) explain related component physiology; the following subsections connect the volume and osmolyte accounts above to testable later consequences.

##### 24.5.1 Purinergic signalling during recovery

Osmotic challenge can recruit extracellular ATP signalling. Cultured astrocytes exposed to a 20% reduction in osmolarity released more ATP after 15 minutes; Aqp4 deletion abolished that increase. Separate cortical-slice experiments implicated P2 receptors in part of the calcium response (Thrane et al., 2011). This supplies a measured connection between osmotic challenge and extracellular signalling, while leaving the relation between pump expenditure and ATP release to be established.

ATP availability reflects release, extracellular breakdown and accessible volume, while its effects depend on receptor responsiveness. Altered ATP or adenosine timing could consequently change support during recovery without an intracellular ATP shortage. Conversely, additional restoration work can be compensated without abnormal extracellular signalling. The proposed effect on refinement depends on how these changes alter local recovery and subsequent circuit activity.

##### 24.5.2 Glial buffering regime and ECS geometry

Purinergic signalling can support volume regulation. In adult mouse retinal Müller glia, ATP prevented barium-associated swelling during a substantial hypotonic challenge; P2Y1 antagonism or IP3R2 deletion removed that protection (Lipp et al., 2009; Section [26.7](#ss_p10_sec_26_7)). Cortical osmotic calcium responses also vary by astrocytic compartment and challenge magnitude (Eilert-Olsen et al., 2019). These experiments identify protective signalling and local responsiveness that could modify recovery capacity. Both neurons and astrocytes can swell, so the cell bearing the relevant work or water load requires identification (Section [24.1](#ss_p10_sec_24_1)).

Where measured neuronal or astrocytic water loading narrows extracellular space, a given local solute release can produce a larger concentration excursion. Its duration depends separately on diffusion, uptake and removal (Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)). A buffering constraint arises if restoration of volume or local solute handling remains inadequate before renewed activity; additional transport work alone establishes neither water loading nor reduced reserve.

Altered end-foot geometry or water handling could delay extracellular-space restoration. Coupling might spread that burden through a network, but neither reduced reserve nor a wider tissue-state change follows from one swollen cell.

ECS compression is a further possible consequence, with concentration amplification distinct from diffusion and removal changes (Dmytrenko et al., 2013; Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)).

##### 24.5.3 Astrocyte-neuron support coupling strain

A separate circuit experiment illustrates the importance of adequate purinergic support. IP3R2-deficient mice had lower extracellular ATP in medial prefrontal cortex, whereas cultured astrocyte intracellular ATP was not detectably reduced. ATP-directed rescue of social and inhibitory-transmission endpoints depended on P2X2 receptors; repetitive behaviours were not rescued (Wang et al., 2021b; Section [26.7](#ss_p10_sec_26_7)). This demonstrates a signalling contribution to circuit function in that genetic model, without an experimentally imposed osmotic challenge or a detected reduction in cultured astrocyte intracellular ATP.

The recovery hypothesis adds a specific connection: preceding ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty changes glial signalling, metabolic resupply or transmitter handling enough to constrain subsequent neuronal recovery. Replenishment after adaptive solute loss provides another possible demand on recovery capacity (Sections [24.2](#ss_p10_sec_24_2) and [24.3](#ss_p10_sec_24_3)). If compensation is insufficient, reduced support flexibility could limit synaptic maintenance during clustered use. The developmental extension requires that support change to carry an effect during the relevant circuit-building interval. The hyponatraemia experiments in Section [24.1](#ss_p10_sec_24_1) provide a related transmitter-handling comparator.

##### 24.5.4 Astrocyte-mediated constraints on neurovascular precision

The proposed changes in osmolyte replenishment and end-foot organisation become functionally consequential if unfinished astrocytic recovery reduces the spatial or temporal precision of support during subsequent demand.

Delayed K⁺ clearance, altered calcium-signal spread and impaired flow matching to neural demand are distinct candidate consequences; one does not identify the others.

Comparing brief and sustained demand can test the timing of vascular support.

Astrocytes can contribute selectively to vascular recruitment during sustained demand. In awake mice, suppressing astrocyte Ca²⁺ signals reduced late penetrating-arteriole dilation during 30-second whisker stimulation while sparing the response to 5-second stimulation (Institoris et al., 2022). This establishes a demand-duration-dependent vascular component. Altered end-foot geometry, compartment-specific calcium signalling or endothelial redox regulation could change that contribution and make delivery less well matched to repeated activity (Sections [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) and [24.4](#ss_p10_sec_24_4)).

The proposed lasting consequence requires this delivery change to impair local ionic or cellular-volume recovery during development. Where limited delivery combines with incomplete recovery, repeated activity could exceed local reserve and prolong the interval before normal function returns. Resting perfusion alone would not identify such a temporal mismatch, and the acute dilation experiment does not itself establish retained impairment.

Altered water handling without the predicted K⁺-clearance or vascular effect would weaken that functional extension. The proposed connection is that unfinished recovery constrains subsequent support, rather than every glial response representing lost precision.

##### 24.5.5 State-dependent unmasking and slow recovery

Clustered demands could expose reduced reserve that is inconspicuous at rest. The predicted signature is incomplete restoration of a specified local ionic or cellular-volume variable before the next challenge, accompanied by a changed response to comparable demand. A support change supplies a possible mechanism for that delayed restoration. Transport work and water loading can contribute through different routes; altered ATP signalling is a candidate contributor rather than a substitute for the recovery measurement.

Recovery can outlast fast synaptic signalling because gradients, cell volume, extracellular geometry and metabolic reserve follow different trajectories. “Ion-energetic debt” denotes additional restoration work relative to available capacity, not every chloride shift or purinergic response. Adequate compensation can restore prompt function. A persistent physiological imprint requires evidence that a specified disturbance or acquired support change survives the initiating episode. Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25) develops the physical extracellular-space gain mechanism, separating concentration amplification from changes in diffusion or removal.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_25"></a>

### 25 Extracellular-Space Compression as a Gain Mechanism

Net cellular water loading could add an extracellular consequence to the ionic recovery mechanisms in Section [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and the volume responses developed in Section [24](#ss_p10_sec_24). Increased transporter flux or ATP turnover alone does not establish such loading.

Where net intracellular osmole gain produces water loading, astrocytic or neuronal expansion can reduce accessible extracellular space (ECS). Astrocytes are central participants in ion and water handling, but a glia-first sequence is a candidate configuration, not a necessary consequence of increased ATP turnover. Mouse-slice experiments found rapid, reversible hypo-osmotic swelling of both pyramidal neurons and astrocytes (Murphy et al., 2017). The proposed gain mechanism therefore requires cell-specific volume measurements alongside extracellular volume fraction; it cannot assign the burden to astrocytes from plasma sodium or transporter expression alone.

For a fixed local amount of released solute, less accessible extracellular volume can increase concentration. Tortuosity and removal need not change in parallel: experimental extracellular-volume reductions have occurred without an increase in tortuosity (Dmytrenko et al., 2013). The proposed gain mechanism must therefore distinguish concentration amplification from altered diffusion, uptake or loss from the region. Its physiological consequence depends on the measured concentration time course and the solute involved.

Concentration amplification could feed back into the chloride–calcium sequence. Larger local K⁺ or glutamate excursions may favour depolarisation or NMDA-receptor recruitment, depending on the measured concentration and circuit state; ATP and proton transients have their own receptor and pH-dependent effects. A more concentrated fixed amount of solute does not automatically require more total transport work. The energetic amplification prediction requires additional flux, altered transport efficiency or recurrent activity to be demonstrated. This preserves extracellular-space compression as a possible gain stage while separating signal amplitude, signal duration and ATP cost.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_26"></a>

### 26 Calcium Signalling in a Chloride-Weighted Ionic Neighbourhood

This section separates voltage-dependent neuronal calcium entry, sodium–calcium exchange and extrusion, ER–mitochondrial handling, glial calcium and purinergic signalling, and intrinsic channel-associated developmental effects. The findings below are read by cell type, compartment, stimulus and developmental stage. Chloride-related entry and glial swelling-to-calcium routes have different conditions; neither establishes the other. Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)–[25](#ss_p10_sec_25) supply the chloride, cell-volume and extracellular-space foundations, while Section [27](#ss_p10_sec_27) develops energetic support.

#### 26.1 Calcium findings in autism research

Calcium regulation is one route by which impaired ionic recovery could affect developing circuits. Calcium findings in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) models are heterogeneous in direction, cellular compartment and developmental stage. Day-100 cortical excitatory neurons derived from three autistic NRXN1α+/− donors showed more frequent, longer and larger spontaneous Ca²⁺ transients than those from five control donors, alongside transcriptomic enrichment of voltage-gated calcium-channel pathways (Avazzadeh et al., 2019). In contrast, early cortical cultures from six idiopathic-ASD donors showed fewer spontaneous somatic calcium transients than five control lines, with reduced multielectrode-array spiking in most ASD lines (DeRosa et al., 2018). These are different preparations and endpoints, not opposite outcomes of one matched experiment. In 22q11.2-deletion-derived cortical neurons, reduced evoked calcium responses were linked to depolarised resting voltage and reduced calcium-channel availability (Khan et al., 2020; Section [26.4](#ss_p10_sec_26_4)).

A stage-dependent split is especially informative. In two idiopathic-ASD and two control iPSC lines, ATP-evoked peak calcium responses were larger before differentiation, whereas four-week differentiated neurons showed smaller responses to ATP but larger responses to KCl and the group-I metabotropic glutamate-receptor agonist DHPG (AlShawaf et al., 2025). The stimuli were 100 μM ATP, 25 mM KCl and 200 μM DHPG. This small-line study shows why developmental stage and stimulus must be specified; it does not identify chloride as the mediator.

Store-release studies identify another component. Primary skin fibroblasts from fragile X and TSC1/TSC2 syndrome donors showed depressed ATP-evoked and photoreleased-IP3-evoked calcium signals; elementary-event measurements in selected fragile X and TSC1 lines also showed impaired release (Schmunk et al., 2015). A subsequent screen found smaller ATP-evoked, ionomycin-normalised responses in most sporadic-ASD fibroblast lines, although some overlapped controls and one high-response outlier was excluded from the principal comparison (Schmunk et al., 2017). These peripheral-cell findings preserve a cross-diagnosis store-signalling signal without demonstrating the same defect in developing neurons.

Cultured astrocytes from TSC surgical tissue showed fewer calcium-responsive cells after ATP, glutamate or DHPG stimulation, reduced store-operated calcium entry, lower basal mitochondrial calcium and reduced ATP-evoked mitochondrial uptake (Romagnolo et al., 2024). Reserve respiratory capacity was also reduced, while ATP-linked respiration did not differ detectably. The calcium-culture comparison used TSC tissue from patients aged 3–26 years and control tissue from 12–16-week gestations. It therefore links glial calcium handling with metabolic reserve in this preparation, while age, epilepsy and culture context limit attribution specifically to autism.

Dopaminergic cells differentiated from deciduous-tooth stem cells from three autistic and three comparison children showed higher endoplasmic-reticulum (ER)-associated and lower mitochondrial calcium signals. During differentiation, 1 μM melatonin improved mitochondrial calcium, ATP and neurite-outgrowth endpoints; receptor and IP3R antagonism blocked relevant effects (Dong et al., 2023). This supplies a positive pharmacological bridge between organelle calcium distribution and cellular development in a small dental-stem-cell model. It does not establish prior sodium loading or clinical efficacy. Together, these studies make compartment-specific calcium regulation a strong testing ground for the proposed ionic-environment mechanism, without making opposite calcium directions evidence for a common cause.

#### 26.2 Alternative explanations and ionic conditions

Channel/excitability defects, receptor or ER-store pathology, mitochondrial dysfunction and primary calciumopathies can explain different findings. The additional question is whether altered ionic conditions change calcium machinery that is otherwise functional.

Incomplete chloride recovery, additional sodium handling or altered glial/extracellular conditions could change voltage histories and calcium clearance. A calcium phenotype might then arise from the ionic environment without an intrinsic channel lesion; weakened inhibition and increased entry are conditional intermediates.

#### 26.3 Calcium duty-cycle shift in a chloride-weighted ionic neighbourhood

The calcium-entry hypothesis concerns how long and how often a defined membrane compartment occupies states that permit calcium influx during matched activity.
