A positive shift in E<sub>GABA</sub> changes the voltage towards which GABA<sub>A</sub> current drives that compartment; it does not itself reduce GABA<sub>A</sub> conductance or remove shunting. Strong GABA conductance can stabilise a depolarised voltage below the relevant calcium-channel activation range and suppress excitatory excursions. Increased entry is predicted where the resulting voltage history, channel availability and timing of excitation favour additional calcium current.

Time spent in prespecified calcium-permissive membrane states is a voltage-based proxy for calcium duty cycle, not a measurement of calcium entry. Channel activation and availability are graded and time dependent, so the proxy requires channel-specific validation. Calcium current, integrated entry, concentration transients and clearance remain distinct endpoints. Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) summarises the conditional calcium interpretation and its limits.

In cultured hippocampal neurons, integrated calcium fluorescence during depolarising GABA paired with postsynaptic spiking exceeded that during hyperpolarising GABA but did not differ significantly from postsynaptic spiking alone (Balena et al., 2010). That result illustrates the need for the matched comparator; it does not demonstrate equivalence or an additional calcium burden relative to activity without GABA.

Earlier excess entry could recruit later changes in channels, extrusion or organelle buffering, but that compensatory sequence requires the earlier phase to be documented. Reduced responses can instead reflect shunting, channel inactivation, receptor/store defects, connectivity or a primary lesion. Opposite findings cannot retrospectively confirm one earlier burden.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_26_4"></a>

#### 26.4 Depolarisation-driven Ca²⁺ entry under altered GABA polarity

Depolarising GABA can recruit voltage-gated calcium entry in particular immature neuronal preparations. In embryonic and neonatal rat neocortical slices, GABA<sub>A</sub> receptor activation produced depolarisation and calcium rises through voltage-gated channels (Owens et al., 1996). This establishes a positive mechanism when GABA-driven voltage reaches an available channel activation range. In contrast, depolarising GABA inhibited network activity and recruited voltage-gated calcium signals inefficiently in P3–4 mouse neocortex in vivo under anaesthesia (Kirmse et al., 2015). Depolarising GABA conductance also suppressed an NMDA-mediated synaptic component in adult rat dentate granule cells, although calcium was not imaged in that experiment (Staley and Mody, 1992). The relevant question is whether local voltage, conductance, channel availability and coincident excitation jointly permit additional calcium influx.

The proposed chloride-to-calcium bridge consequently has opposing prospective predictions. Entry may increase when depolarisation is sufficient and the conductance permits the required voltage excursion; it may decrease when shunting suppresses excitatory recruitment or sustained depolarisation reduces channel availability. Spontaneous, KCl-evoked and DHPG-evoked calcium responses probe different processes and cannot independently establish this GABA-mediated sequence. In human 22q11.2-deletion neuronal models, depolarised resting voltage reduced evoked calcium responses through voltage-dependent channel inactivation, without a corresponding intrinsic defect in the measured voltage-clamped calcium-channel currents (Khan et al., 2020). That result supports an operating-voltage mechanism but does not establish chloride mediation or earlier calcium overload. A channel-inactivation explanation requires the measured voltage-dependent loss of availability, not a reduced response alone.

#### 26.5 Sodium gradients, NCX strain, and Ca²⁺ clearance

Calcium clearance provides a distinct conditional branch. Increased NKCC1-mediated inward transport adds sodium-handling work, but Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity may preserve the sodium gradient despite that added flux. An NCX consequence therefore requires a measured change in local sodium gradients, membrane voltage or calcium conditions. Where the electrochemical driving force for forward-mode NCX is reduced, calcium extrusion may slow; reversal requires the relevant combined gradients and voltage, not NKCC1 activity alone.

In reduced suprachiasmatic-nucleus preparations from 18–25-day-old rats, removing extracellular Na⁺ slowed the fast component of somatic calcium clearance after high-K⁺ depolarisation approximately threefold (Wang et al., 2015). In acute mouse slices, NMDA evoked sodium increases and local calcium signals in neocortical astrocyte processes; NCX blockers reduced the calcium signal, and modelling supported sodium-driven reversal. Hippocampal astrocytes lacked the corresponding NMDA-evoked sodium response (Ziemens et al., 2019). In solitary astrocytes cultured from neonatal rat visual cortex, mechanical stimulation increased sodium and calcium, while pharmacological results supported a contribution of reverse NCX to calcium signalling and glutamate release (Reyes et al., 2012). These are distinct, positive component mechanisms. Sodium-free substitution, NMDA application and mechanical stimulation do not establish NCX reversal after a modest developmental increase in NKCC1 flux. That extension requires the local sodium, calcium and voltage measurements specified above.

Where calcium flux increases, PMCA, SERCA and the sodium pump supporting exchange could add to ATP turnover. Slower clearance may instead reflect impaired transport. Calcium flux, pump work and ATP concentration therefore remain distinct; preserved sodium gradients with reduced calcium entry would not support the same energetic prediction (Section [27](#ss_p10_sec_27)).

#### 26.6 ER and mitochondrial buffering responses

Increased entry or reduced extrusion could shift handling towards ER and mitochondria, changing store filling, release or coupling. Primary receptor, ER and mitochondrial defects can produce similar endpoints, so a compensatory interpretation requires the preceding entry/extrusion change.

The proposed route links ionic-recovery difficulty to increased calcium-handling work and later organelle change. A subsequent ROS increase is another step; reduced mitochondrial calcium alone does not establish earlier overload.

After oxygen–glucose deprivation and reoxygenation in cultured astrocytes, NKCC1 inhibition or deletion reduced mitochondrial calcium accumulation and dysfunction; reverse-NCX inhibition attenuated a sustained calcium rise during a separate severe hypoxic challenge (Kintner et al., 2007). These injury results establish consequential transport-dependent loading, not the developmental sequence. A further neural/glial-to-vascular redox effect could constrain local support through the corridor in Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8), but altered pump work, ATP, ROS and cysteine remain separate steps.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_26_7"></a>

#### 26.7 Astrocyte calcium signalling and osmotic stress

Astrocytes provide a measured bridge from osmotic challenge to calcium signalling. In adult mouse cortical slices, reducing bath osmolarity from 300 to 240 mOsm/L increased Ca²⁺ activity most prominently in subpial and perivascular endfeet. IP3R2 deletion strongly suppressed those endfoot responses but spared the response in fine processes. Dystrophin deficiency, which disrupts AQP4 anchoring, attenuated endfoot responses. TRPV4 blockade reduced the relative increase in spike rate without reducing the increase in integrated calcium-fluorescence signal, and also altered baseline activity (Eilert-Olsen et al., 2019). The same study detected no difference between IP3R2-deficient mice and controls in brain water accumulation after water intoxication; a 10% reduction in bath osmolarity also failed to elicit the calcium response seen with the larger challenge. These findings identify a compartment- and exposure-dependent response, while calcium signalling and regulation of total brain water remain distinct endpoints. Whether astrocytes carry an earlier recovery burden than neurons must be established in the relevant developmental preparation.

A direct volume-regulatory result comes from retinal Müller glia. In slices from adult mice, a solution at 60% of control osmolarity left wild-type somatic size approximately stable for four minutes, whereas IP3R2 deletion or intracellular calcium chelation permitted rapid swelling. ATP prevented barium-associated swelling in wild-type preparations but failed in IP3R2-deficient cells (Lipp et al., 2009). Glial calcium can therefore participate in maintaining cellular volume during an osmotic challenge. The retinal soma-size assay and cortical endfoot calcium assay establish complementary components; they do not establish the same volume-recovery defect across brain regions.

The hypothesis is that recurrent swelling and incomplete recovery alter glial calcium recruitment, local purinergic signalling or transporter organisation in a defined ionic neighbourhood. Persistent changes in anchoring or transporter localisation remain proposed intermediates. A separate causal circuit result strengthens the case for testing this route: IP3R2-null mice and mice with astrocyte-specific deletion induced at postnatal day 60 showed reduced social approach and increased repetitive behaviours (Wang et al., 2021b). Extracellular ATP fell, whereas cultured astrocyte intracellular and total ATP showed no detected difference. ATP or its stable analogue improved social and inhibitory-transmission endpoints; P2X2-receptor knockdown prevented these effects, and repetitive behaviour was not rescued. Thus, impaired astrocyte calcium signalling can alter purinergic support of inhibitory transmission and behaviour without demonstrated intracellular energy depletion. The adult conditional manipulation establishes circuit influence, not prenatal osmotic initiation. Connecting this positive glial result to Sodium Struggle requires the specified local ionic or volume-recovery difficulty to precede and mediate the calcium–purinergic change; an IP3R2 signalling defect alone does not establish that sequence.

Naviaux’s CDR model emphasises extracellular ATP-related signalling and mitochondrial adaptation in persistent defence (Naviaux, 2026a,b). The IP3R2 result shows why excessive extracellular ATP is not a universal requirement. Cellular ATP supply and turnover, extracellular release/removal, receptor responsiveness and concentration changes from altered volume are distinct. Sodium Struggle additionally proposes recovery difficulty changing these signalling conditions, or purinergic change constraining recovery; a developmental effect with adequate relevant ionic and volume recovery throughout the causal interval would challenge obligatory recovery mediation.

This glial swelling-to-calcium route is distinct from neuronal GABA-to-calcium recruitment. Evidence for one does not establish the other, and a positive astrocytic finding cannot rescue a failed neuronal prediction in the same test.

#### 26.8 Extracellular-space compression and network Ca²⁺ dynamics

Net cellular expansion can amplify a fixed solute release by reducing accessible ECS. Altered tortuosity, removal or persistence is a separate consequence (Dmytrenko et al., 2013; Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)).

The positive physiological precedents are specific. In P4–7 rat hippocampal slices, extracellular volume fraction was 0.41 ± 0.01 in control conditions and 0.17 ± 0.02 after a 90-mOsm reduction. In low-Mg²⁺ solution containing 4-aminopyridine, reductions of 40 and 90 mOsm increased CA3 epileptiform-event frequency by approximately 24% and 40%, respectively (Kilb et al., 2006). In rat CA1, lowering osmolality caused or enhanced synchronous bursts despite blockade of chemical synaptic transmission (Dudek et al., 1990). This was conditional on the preparation: a later CA1 protocol with normal extracellular Ca²⁺ found that 10–20% dilution enhanced synaptic activity but did not generate nonsynaptic bursts (Bikson et al., 2002). In mouse CA1 slices, hypo-osmotic swelling recruited NMDA-receptor-dependent slow inward currents within about one minute. Increased event frequency was detected with a 5% osmolarity reduction in Mg²⁺-free recording solution; a separate 40% dilution experiment retained enhanced firing with Mg²⁺ present (Lauderdale et al., 2015). These acute experiments establish volume-sensitive excitability under defined conditions, not chronic calcium burden or a developmental pathway to autism.

Larger K⁺, glutamate or ATP transients could increase depolarisation, NMDA recruitment or burst-related calcium entry; their duration depends on transport and uptake. Repeated recovery difficulty could thereby alter synchrony and neuron–astrocyte coupling without a lesion in every calcium component. A glia-first order remains one candidate developmental extension of these acute findings.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_26_9"></a>

#### 26.9 Genetic effects on calcium signalling and interactions with an altered ionic environment

Calcium-pathway variants can initiate developmental changes directly or modify a separately demonstrated ionic disturbance. In Timothy syndrome, CACNA1C p.Gly406Arg markedly impaired voltage-dependent channel inactivation, sustaining inward calcium current; patient-derived cortical neurons also showed altered calcium signalling, activity-dependent gene expression and differentiation (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011). ASD-associated CACNA1D p.Ala749Gly and p.Gly407Arg produced gain-of-function gating in expression systems (Pinggera et al., 2015). These are allele-specific findings: other neurodevelopmental CACNA1C variants produced loss, gain or no detected change in the tested channel properties (Rodan et al., 2021). ATP2B2 encodes the calcium-extruding pump PMCA2. A seven-person series with rare heterozygous ATP2B2 variants included neurodevelopmental presentations with autism; expression of the identified variants altered calcium handling in both loss- and gain-of-function directions (Poggio et al., 2023). Increased entry and impaired extrusion are therefore important candidate mechanisms, but neither direction can be assigned from a gene name alone.

An ion channel can also influence dendritic development through its associated signalling machinery. Krey et al. (2013) observed activity-dependent dendritic retraction in Timothy-syndrome rodent models and patient-derived neurons. In rat neurons, the Timothy-syndrome CaV1.2 channel still promoted retraction when additional pore mutations prevented calcium permeation through that channel. Gem overexpression and inhibition of RhoA signalling prevented retraction in the tested preparations. These experiments identify a channel-associated route to cytoskeletal change that cannot be reduced to excessive calcium entry through the mutant channel. They do not establish independence from every ionic process, and they did not test the defined post-challenge recovery intermediary. The measured endpoint was dendritic development, not the complete human autism phenotype. This comparison strengthens the distinction between an ion-channel mutation and the particular physiological process through which it acts.

For this channel-associated route, the additional Sodium-Struggle claim is that impaired local recovery contributes to dendritic change. Retraction with adequate recovery throughout the causal interval would weigh against that mediation. RhoA-directed rescue alone cannot exclude an upstream recovery contribution; the presence of an ion-channel lesion does not identify the mechanism carrying its developmental effect.

Receptor-variant association and receptor function also need to be distinguished. OXTR R376G was found in 6/132 ASD participants and 2/248 controls in a Japanese study (OR 5.83, 95% CI 1.16–29.33; Ma et al., 2013). This small association sample requires replication. The variant-specific functional findings below provide genetic entry points into altered receptor modulation, but do not establish uniformly weakened oxytocin buffering, an AVP/oxytocin imbalance or impaired developmental recovery.

Receptor and store-release findings need the same precision. In transfected cells, OXTR R376G reduced the calcium response to 100 nmol/L oxytocin; its IP3 reduction was significant at 5–30 seconds but not across the complete three-minute comparison (Ma et al., 2013). Another rare variant, R150S, increased oxytocin sensitivity and calcium mobilisation in vitro (Liu et al., 2024). The RYR2 candidate signal from a 41-child ASD CNV study involved an inherited duplication containing additional genes, without a measured channel-function direction (Soueid et al., 2016). A 2025 preprint reported cardiac calcium leak and elevated resting neuronal cytosolic calcium in hiPSC-derived cells from one RYR2 R169P carrier with catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ASD. S107 improved the cardiac leak and resting neuronal cytosolic-calcium endpoints. Comparison with a separate healthy control, without a corrected R169P isogenic line, supports a preliminary signal but does not isolate variant causality, demonstrate clinical benefit or establish sodium–volume mediation (Colombani et al., 2025). Within a demonstrated altered ionic baseline, a functionally established gain-of-function calcium-channel allele could increase the consequence of a given depolarisation, a loss-of-function PMCA2 allele could reduce extrusion reserve, and allele-specific OXTR or RYR2 effects could change store recruitment. These are conditional interactions, not evidence that an ionic disturbance precedes the genetic effect. In 22q11.2-deletion-derived neurons, the measured link was from altered resting voltage to reduced calcium-channel availability, with a specific genetic contribution involving DGCR8 (Khan et al., 2020). Chloride elevation and a preceding high-calcium workload were not established. The strong genetic signal makes convergence testable; demonstrating the proposed recovery intermediary remains a separate requirement.

#### 26.10 Integrated physiological synthesis

The integrated proposal is that incomplete ionic or volume recovery changes the operating conditions of otherwise functional calcium machinery during maturation. Chloride-related voltage shifts can increase entry only when excitation, conductance and channel availability permit it; shunting may preserve inhibition or reduce entry instead.

Altered NCX clearance, organelle redistribution, glial calcium responses and ECS amplification are separate branches. Their conditions differ, so one positive result cannot explain every calcium phenotype or establish the others.

Adequate recovery during the developmental interval would challenge this intermediary. Primary calcium-pathway defects remain alternative or interacting causes; heterogeneous calcium findings do not establish common initiation.

**Text description of Figure 26.1**

The diagram, titled “Ionic recovery and conditional calcium pathways”, begins with A, “Measured ionic state and recovery deficit”. Dashed arrows lead separately to three branches:

- B, “Neuronal conditions”: the GABA reversal potential (E_GABA), GABA_A conductance, voltage history, excitation and channels.
- E, “NCX route”: measure Na⁺, Ca²⁺ and voltage, and test exchanger direction and clearance.
- F, “Glial route”: measure volume, Ca²⁺ and extracellular space (ECS).

Branch B divides through dashed arrows into contrasting outcomes. C is “Shunting / inactivation”, with Ca²⁺ entry unchanged or lower. D is “Available channels recruited”, with increased Ca²⁺ entry. Only D continues to G, “Additional transport / buffering work”, which is qualified by “Only when separately demonstrated”. Separate dashed arrows from E and F also reach G. C has no onward arrow to G. An accompanying instruction directs readers to the §23.13 comparator for alternative outcomes.

A dashed arrow from G, labelled “Reserve and timing”, leads to H, “Proposed developmental change or later adaptation”. H calls for tests of timing, mediation and selective rescue. A separate box, “Separately measured calcium-signalling change”, has its own dashed arrow directly to H, without passing through G. A note states that signalling mediation need not act through additional ATP cost.

- Kirmse (2015), postnatal day 3–4 anaesthetised mouse cortex in vivo: depolarising GABA leads to inhibition, with inefficient calcium-channel recruitment.
- Khan (2020), human 22q11.2-deletion neuronal models: depolarised resting voltage leads to reduced channel availability and reduced evoked Ca²⁺.

The final qualification distinguishes greater ATP work from gradient failure. NCX means sodium–calcium exchanger; ECS means extracellular space.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_27"></a>

### 27 Phosphate Reserve and ATP Turnover Under Chloride-Weighted Ionic Stress

Additional inward NKCC1 flux can increase sodium-pump work while extrusion keeps intracellular sodium stable. Section [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) distinguishes this transport cost from failure of the gradient; here the question is its effect on energetic and phosphate reserve.

In mouse hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, activity that generated global sodium elevations was accompanied by ATP decreases of approximately 0.1–0.6 mmol/L, whereas brief, spatially restricted dendritic sodium signals produced no detectable local ATP fall (Gerkau et al., 2019). This is a measured connection between sodium-handling demand and energy availability. The local result is consistent with protective buffering by ATP production and intracellular redistribution. The authors judged ATP unlikely to limit sodium-pump activity under the tested conditions. A transient ATP fall is therefore not itself failed recovery. The proposed developmental cost requires demand or reduced reserve sufficient to impair the defined ionic or volume recovery endpoint.

Increased calcium cycling could add PMCA/SERCA work and sodium-pump support of exchange (Section [26](#ss_p10_sec_26)). This demand can compound sodium extrusion, but slower clearance does not establish more work and effective GABA shunting may reduce calcium recruitment.

Higher ATP turnover requires faster recycling of ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) through ATP-regenerating pathways; it does not by itself establish a phosphate deficit or a need for proportionally greater net phosphate import. Sodium-coupled Pi transport provides a possible additional constraint. PiT-family transporters mediate sodium-dependent phosphate uptake in expression experiments (Ravera et al., 2007). If the relevant sodium electrochemical driving force is measurably reduced, phosphate entry through these transporters may become less favourable, depending on the other transport conditions. A double constraint is therefore a conditional branch: increased ion-transport work raises ATP demand while a demonstrated transport limitation restricts phosphate availability. The proposed neural link requires measurements of sodium driving conditions, phosphate flux and intracellular Pi alongside ATP turnover. Greater pump work alone establishes neither the gradient disturbance nor phosphate limitation.

Energetic reserve is the margin between ongoing demand and the capacity to sustain it. Combined sodium and calcium transport may narrow that margin without ATP depletion. Phosphate limitation could add a further constraint but requires independent evidence of availability, transport and ATP-regenerating capacity. Sections [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) and [33](#ss_p10_sec_33) distinguish systemic phosphate exposure and renal coordination from this local neural constraint.

Reduced energetic reserve could increase vulnerability to astrocytic ion–water loading if it compromises the relevant ionic or volume restoration. Where net cellular water loading reduces accessible ECS, Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25) distinguishes concentration amplification from altered clearance. Section [29](#ss_p10_sec_29) considers substrate supply and protein production as separate supports or developmental intermediaries.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_28"></a>

### 28 Extracellular Matrix and Cellular Scaffolds in Ionic Recovery

Extracellular matrix and cellular scaffolds could influence both the disturbance that initiates compensatory work and the response to subsequent ionic or volume changes. Heparan-sulphate-dependent synaptic organisation supplies one measured component of this proposal. An intrinsic matrix alteration could precede physiological stress, while an acquired alteration could modify later signalling or recovery.

#### 28.1 Scaffold localisation and persistence

Repeated volume, calcium or energetic perturbation could alter cytoskeletal or membrane-protein organisation and thereby later transport or signalling. This proposed persistence layer requires the structural and functional change to outlast the initiating exposure and ionic disturbance.

Component evidence shows why localisation matters. Suppressing KCC2 in cultured hippocampal neurons reduced postsynaptic AMPA-receptor aggregation and changed receptor diffusion; disrupting its cytoskeletal interaction reproduced effects that pharmacological inhibition of transport did not (Gauvain et al., 2011). KCC2 therefore has structural functions separable from chloride transport. This strengthens the scaffold question but prevents a structural synaptic finding from being counted automatically as evidence of impaired chloride extrusion. Astrocytic end-foot organisation and AQP4 localisation are a separate candidate interface (Section [24.4](#ss_p10_sec_24_4)).

A scaffold change would become consequential by altering the next response; persistent redistribution without functional effect would not establish this bridge from brief disturbance to later demand.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_28_2"></a>

#### 28.2 Heparan sulphate and synaptic organisation

Heparan sulphate (HS) consists of glycan chains attached to core proteins to form heparan-sulphate proteoglycans (HSPGs). At neural cell surfaces and in the extracellular matrix, these molecules help organise ligand interactions and synaptic signalling. Their effects depend on the core protein, chain configuration and sulphation pattern, so HS abundance, HSPG expression and functional activity require separate measurements (Allen et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2018).

Astrocyte-derived glypicans 4 and 6 promoted functional excitatory synapses in retinal ganglion-cell cultures through surface recruitment and clustering of GluA1 AMPA receptors. Gpc4 loss also reduced excitatory synaptic strength and GluA1 recruitment in the developing mouse hippocampus (Allen et al., 2012). These results establish a contribution to synapse formation and function. HS differs from the chondroitin-sulphate motifs involved in OTX2 capture and perineuronal-net maturation (Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4)).

Neurexins provide another direct connection between HS and synaptic organisation. Their HS chains participate in binding neuroligins and LRRTMs, and removing the HS attachment site from neurexin-1 impaired synaptic structure and function in mice (Zhang et al., 2018). The direction of effect depends on molecular context: the splice insert at neurexin-1 site 5 increased HS-chain number and was associated with reduced neurexin-1 protein abundance and glutamatergic release (Lu et al., 2023). More HS therefore cannot be assumed to strengthen transmission or reduce pruning.

Genetic perturbation also separates synaptic function from synapse number. Ext1 deletion beginning after the third postnatal week in mouse forebrain glutamatergic neurons reduced neuronal HS and amygdala excitatory transmission, with social-communication and repetitive-behaviour abnormalities. Synapse density and dendritic morphology in the examined amygdala region were not detectably altered. Separately, Ext1-null embryonic cortical-neuron cultures showed reduced surface and synaptic GluA2 localisation (Irie et al., 2012). This supports an HS-dependent functional route without making synapse elimination its necessary mechanism.

Human postmortem observations provide a regional reason to investigate this biology beyond groups selected for known HS-pathway mutations. Pearson et al. (2013) compared four autistic male donors with four age- and sex-matched controls. N-sulphated-HS immunoreactivity was lower in the lateral-ventricle subventricular zone in the three younger donor pairs, but not in the oldest pair. The authors noted that reduced staining could reflect under-sulphation rather than reduced total HS. This small series cannot establish prevalence or a whole-brain deficit.

A separate childhood hippocampal study found reduced SPOCK1 mRNA in bulk tissue from seven autistic boys and six controls aged 3–14 years, with confirmation by qPCR (Rexrode et al., 2024). SPOCK1 encodes a chondroitin/heparan-sulphate proteoglycan core protein. This extends the human expression observations beyond the ventricular niche, while measuring neither HS-chain abundance nor its sulphation pattern. Together, the human findings motivate compartment-specific investigation; they do not identify one uniform matrix change or its developmental cause.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_28_3"></a>

#### 28.3 Osmotic responses and developmental predictions

HS-dependent responses to osmotic disturbance have been measured in a vascular preparation. In bovine aortic endothelial cells, heparinase III treatment attenuated the responses to a 30% reduction in extracellular tonicity, including FAK phosphorylation, volume-regulated anion current, ATP release, calcium signalling and actin remodelling. Responses to exogenous ATP and lysophosphatidic acid were preserved (Oike et al., 2008). This places cell-surface HS upstream of several osmotic-sensing responses under those conditions; whether analogous changes alter neural or glial volume-recovery kinetics remains to be established.

The proposed developmental connection is that a defined HS or scaffold alteration delays or prevents complete local ionic or cell-volume recovery, thereby modifying circuit maturation during a sensitive window. Additional recovery work or cost belongs to this route only if it compromises that required restoration. A matrix alteration could constitute an intrinsic initiating constraint or arise after an earlier disturbance. In appropriate experimental models, the informative sequence would pair the specified matrix change with recovery trajectories and developmental endpoints, including selective correction of the matrix alteration. Preserved recovery despite a synaptic effect would support a synaptic contribution while constraining the proposed recovery-mediated route; restoration with adequate reserve would represent successful adaptation.

HS-dependent synaptic organisation provides a rationale for this question independently of the optional AVPR1A-to-HSPG branch considered in Section [36.5.6](#ss_p10_sec_36_5_6). Synapse formation, maintenance, transmission and elimination remain distinct from ionic recovery. The KCC2 scaffold findings above do not establish a direct HS-to-KCC2 mechanism, and peripheral matrix responses may occur in parallel without supplying the neural developmental intermediary.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_29"></a>

### 29 Recovery Constraints: Why Ionic Reset May Be Incomplete

Local ionic or cell-volume recovery is the required endpoint. Energetic capacity, substrate replenishment and protein production can support or constrain that recovery, or transmit its developmental effects. Ionic gradients, calcium handling, osmolyte content, cell volume and ECS geometry need not reset together. A near-normal membrane potential can coexist with a different residual disturbance, which must be identified rather than assumed.

Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)–[28](#ss_p10_sec_28) distinguish gradient-dependent transport, extracellular concentration amplification and scaffold-dependent reset. Their different recovery times could interact, but unequal restoration is a prediction rather than a property of every stressed cell.

The resulting constraint could impair inhibitory precision, strengthen extracellular coupling or raise metabolic cost, reducing reserve for repeated or high-frequency demand. Function might remain adequate at low demand while dyscoordination or bursting emerges earlier under load. This supplies a candidate lasting network change without compulsory hyperexcitability or structural injury.

#### 29.1 Recovery and developmental protein production

A recovery disturbance could also reach the developmental programme through protein production: persistent ionic or volume changes could alter amino-acid supply, intracellular conditions or stress signalling, and thereby the production of transporter, structural and synaptic proteins. Conversely, a primary production defect could constrain restoration. Either recovery-mediated order requires more than extra housekeeping work: the recovery disturbance must carry the developmental effect.

An experimentally demonstrated connection between osmotic adaptation and protein production comes from human corneal epithelial cells. During continued exposure to 500 mOsm medium, protein synthesis first fell and then partially recovered; at 600 mOsm it remained suppressed. Early inhibition at 500 mOsm occurred without increased phosphorylation of eIF2α, the α subunit of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2. Later recovery depended on sodium-coupled neutral amino-acid transporter 2 (SNAT2): transporter knockdown reduced amino-acid uptake and impaired the recovery of synthesis. This linked solute acquisition to the resumption of protein production, alongside regulation of mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), a controller of growth and translation (Krokowski et al., 2022). It was adaptation during an ongoing hyperosmotic challenge, not restoration after its removal. The corneal preparation and these osmolarities do not establish the same sequence after neural swelling or during fetal development.

The sodium-gradient branch requires altered sodium-coupled nutrient flux; chloride disturbance with an intact sodium gradient does not supply it. A volume branch instead concerns the effect of persistent volume deviation on translation. Protein production may recover later and extend a developmental consequence, but translational lag alone does not replace the required recovery intermediary.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_29_2"></a>

#### 29.2 Immune and genetic control of protein production

Maternal immune activation supplies a causal protein-production mechanism in developing brain. Following maternal poly(I:C) exposure at embryonic day 12.5, male mouse fetal cortex at day 18.5 showed increased phosphorylation of protein kinase R-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK) and eIF2α, with reduced nascent protein synthesis. This integrated stress response (ISR), which regulates translation during stress, depended on maternal IL-17A; the same ISR activation was not detected in female offspring. Genetic attenuation using an eIF2α S51A allele restored synthesis while PERK phosphorylation remained elevated, and protected specified later cortical-activity and behavioural outcomes (Kalish et al., 2021). This identifies an intervenable step between immune exposure and neural consequences. It does not identify impaired ionic recovery or ATP shortage as its cause. For the proposed recovery route, correcting the measured recovery defect must alter this translational response under comparable immune exposure. Section [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6) supplies the upstream immune alternatives.

Fragile X provides an instructive opposite direction. In Fmr1-deficient mice, eIF2α phosphorylation was reduced and general protein synthesis increased in mature excitatory neurons, with no equivalent change in the inhibitory neurons examined. The phosphorylation differences emerged during postnatal weeks 5–8 in the assessed regions. Elevated mTOR complex 1 activity contributed to ISR suppression. Restoring eIF2α phosphorylation selectively in excitatory neurons corrected excessive synthesis and improved specified synaptic and behavioural outcomes (Hooshmandi et al., 2023). This later, cell-specific result cannot be substituted for the fetal MIA result. The shared question is whether the appropriate pattern of protein production is maintained or restored, not whether ISR activation or total synthesis always moves in one direction. A translation-first contribution to Sodium Struggle would require the altered programme to produce a measured recovery constraint that then mediates the developmental effect.

Selective protein production also matters when bulk synthesis is unchanged. Deleting eIF4E-binding protein 2 (4E-BP2), a repressor of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E), increased neuroligin translation without a detected rise in bulk hippocampal protein synthesis. eIF4E overexpression likewise increased neuroligin production. In the 4E-BP2-null mice, reducing eIF4E-complex activity corrected reported synaptic and social endpoints; reducing neuroligin 1 partly rescued social behaviour, whereas reducing neuroligin 2 worsened it (Gkogkas et al., 2013). The identity of the proteins produced therefore has causal importance beyond the total synthesis rate. This established translational-synaptic route is a candidate intermediary or independent explanation. Its energetic requirements do not themselves demonstrate sodium–volume mediation. The proposed connection must identify the recovery disturbance that changes selective translation, or the translational change that impairs recovery, and test which effect carries the later outcome.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_29_3"></a>

#### 29.3 Causal order and developmental recovery

Recovery and protein production can influence development in either causal order. Impaired restoration may alter the required protein-production programme, or altered translation may constrain recovery. A genetic or immune exposure could also affect both in parallel. Co-occurrence, or correction of both by an upstream intervention, does not establish mediation. A recovery problem first observed after developmental divergence demonstrates later susceptibility, not its role during circuit construction.

A developmental effect with adequately preserved relevant recovery during the causal interval would challenge obligatory recovery mediation. Conversely, a later translation-directed rescue could bypass an earlier recovery contribution without showing that it never occurred. The distinction is between a causal developmental intermediary and a response that accompanies or follows the outcome.

Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) applies this causal-order comparison across the other interfaces. Protein production is one possible developmental bridge: glial support, channel-associated signalling or learning could provide other routes, without an assumed universal translational defect. Sections [30](#ss_p10_sec_30) and [31](#ss_p10_sec_31) develop the delivery, signalling and maturation contexts for these alternatives.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_30"></a>

### 30 CSF and Interstitial Physiology and Choroid Plexus Signalling

#### 30.1 Compartments and local exchange

The astrocytic and ionic-recovery mechanisms proposed in Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)–[29](#ss_p10_sec_29) could affect both the local conditions supporting developing circuits and the extracellular routes by which signals reach them. These routes occupy distinct compartments. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fills the ventricles and subarachnoid spaces; the brain interstitium is the extracellular compartment between parenchymal cells; and perivascular spaces surround blood vessels. The extracellular matrix is the molecular scaffold around cells, with specialised cortical forms considered in Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4). The choroid plexus (ChP), a vascular tissue covered by secretory epithelium within the ventricles, regulates CSF ions and water and supplies extracellular developmental signals.

Incomplete cellular recovery or altered end-foot organisation could change water exchange and fluid routing after systemic sodium normalises. Venous conditions, perivascular exchange and meningeal outflow are additional candidate influences. Fluid imaging alone does not identify osmolyte debt or establish this physiological-history sequence.

Matrix and membrane experiments provide component mechanisms for this proposal. Laminin–dystroglycan manipulations regulate the surface expression and turnover of the water channel aquaporin-4 (AQP4) in cultured neonatal-rat astrocytes (Tham et al., 2016). In adult mice, complete AQP4 deletion and loss of its perivascular localisation produced different, tracer-dependent effects on solute removal at two hours (Bojarskaite et al., 2024). These findings support distinguishing protein abundance, location and function. Redistribution could assist acute volume equilibration while altering the spatial confinement of later exchange, but that proposed trade-off and its effect on solute transport require direct testing. The experiments do not establish the sequence from repeated ionic stress to persistent end-foot changes or altered transport of a particular developmental signal.

#### 30.2 Choroid plexus ion and fluid regulation

ChP ion transport provides another potential point of physiological influence. The sodium–potassium–chloride cotransporter NKCC1 contributes to potassium clearance from neonatal mouse CSF, whereas adult mouse knockdown demonstrates a contribution to basal CSF secretion (Xu et al., 2021; Fame et al., 2023; Jensen et al., 2025). Developmental stage and ionic driving conditions therefore matter. Elevated CSF potassium after perinatal ChP knockdown was not accompanied by gross cortical disruption at the early postnatal-day-4 endpoint, leaving later consequences unresolved (Fame et al., 2023). Vasopressin reduced ChP perfusion and CSF production in anaesthetised rabbits; V1-receptor blockade attenuated the fall in production during haemorrhage in a separate experiment (Faraci et al., 1990; Maktabi et al., 1993). These results establish experimentally responsive ion/fluid regulation, not the developmental effects of ordinary hormone fluctuations or an inverse effect of low vasopressin.

Inflammation can directly recruit a secretory transport pathway in a defined injury model. After experimentally induced intraventricular haemorrhage in eight-week-old male rats, [Karimy et al. (2017)](#ss_revsyn5_ref_Karimy2017) found approximately threefold higher bumetanide-sensitive CSF secretion, involving ChP TLR4–NF-κB signalling, SPAK activation and NKCC1 phosphorylation. Genetic or pharmacological interruption of the pathway reduced hypersecretion and hydrocephalus. This supplies an experimental inflammation-to-epithelial-transport link; it does not establish the same response to ordinary osmotic fluctuations or in infant ASD. Its secretory direction must be interpreted alongside the neonatal potassium/fluid-clearance findings above, rather than assuming that more NKCC1 activity always increases CSF volume.

MIA also supplies direct evidence for altered CSF physiology: Sun et al. (2025) measured increased CSF production, slower cilia-driven transport and reduced tracer drainage in adult male mouse offspring following prenatal MIA, alongside choroid-plexus and ependymal abnormalities. These are positive fluid-transport findings in a compartment distinct from neural or glial post-challenge ionic and cellular-volume recovery. Whether that transport disturbance changes local recovery or carries the developmental effect remains a specific connection to test (Sections [18.5](#ss_p10_sec_18_5), [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6), and [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)).

#### 30.3 Developmental signals and nutrient delivery

Alongside ion and fluid regulation, the ChP supplies extracellular developmental signals. Orthodenticle homeobox 2 (OTX2) can regulate intracellular transcription and also act as an extracellular signal: ChP-derived OTX2 contributes to cortical plasticity in mice (Spatazza et al., 2013). Disrupting export machinery reduced CSF and cortical OTX2 without significantly reducing total ChP OTX2 protein (Park et al., 2023), separating secretion from abundance. Park implicated linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton (LINC) machinery; Lu et al. (2025) found LINC-dependent hypo-osmotic cell-state responses in mouse pluripotent cells, using Otx2 as a lineage marker. Their intersection suggests a possible osmotic connection to ChP OTX2 export; Lu did not measure secretion.

The metabolic route in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) could enter through changed brain exposure or support. An additional ChP-signalling effect requires a link to production, secretion or delivery; systemic recovery and matrix remodelling do not establish OTX2 availability or capture.

Folate transport supplies a nutrient-delivery counterpart to OTX2 signalling: availability in blood does not establish delivery to developing brain cells. Ramaekers et al. (2005) detected blocking folate-receptor autoantibodies in 25 of 28 children selected for cerebral folate deficiency, compared with none of 28 matched controls. In a later study of 25 autistic children selected for features of that syndrome, 23 had low CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5MTHF) despite normal serum folate, and 19 of those 23 had blocking receptor antibodies in serum (Ramaekers et al., 2007). These selected cohorts support an antibody-associated transport constraint, not an autism-wide prevalence estimate. The child's antibody measurements also do not establish maternal antibody transfer or prenatal MIA.

Grapp et al. (2013) identified a specific delivery mechanism. Human folate receptor α (FRα) expressed in rat ChP cells travelled with labelled folate from the blood-facing to the CSF-facing surface; receptor-bearing exosomes were also detected in human CSF. After intraventricular injection into adult mice, FRα-positive exosomes reached brain parenchyma more extensively than receptor-negative exosomes. Separately, neonatal mouse cortical cultures showed uptake of receptor-positive exosomes and associated labelled folate by astrocytes. These experiments distinguish epithelial transport, vesicle carriage and recipient uptake. They do not show that MIA disrupts this pathway, that all cerebral folate uses it, or that antibody-associated folate deficiency is a CSF-flow disorder.

Restricted folate delivery could limit the machinery needed for neural/glial ionic or volume restoration despite normal circulating folate. Alternatively, folate-dependent biosynthesis or methylation could alter development with adequate recovery. This transport lesion supplies an immune entry point and a comparison for the common-process conjecture, not a demonstrated recovery intermediary (Sections [29](#ss_p10_sec_29) and [31.4](#ss_p10_sec_31_4)).

Improved folate delivery alone would not identify which route carried the developmental effect; a later correction addresses reversibility rather than excluding an earlier recovery contribution.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_30_4"></a>

#### 30.4 PV Maturation, Circuit Refinement and Extracellular OTX2 Signalling

The distinction between lasting circuit organisation and current constraint directs attention to mechanisms of maturation. PV-interneuron maturation is a candidate intersection of local ionic recovery, energetic support and circuit refinement. Selective PV vulnerability and an obligatory shrinkage gate remain unestablished. In specified genetic PV and Shank mouse models, reduced PV immunoreactivity reflected lower expression in surviving cells (Filice et al., 2016). This supports altered cell state as one possibility, but staining alone cannot distinguish cell number, maturity or inhibitory function.

Extracellular OTX2 adds a signal-dependent route to this local physiological account. Founding experiments in mouse visual cortex showed that visual experience promoted OTX2 accumulation in PV cells through transfer from other cells, while cortical OTX2 delivery advanced PV-associated development and critical-period timing (Sugiyama et al., 2008). Perineuronal nets are specialised extracellular-matrix structures surrounding some neurons, including many PV interneurons, that can participate in recipient-specific capture of OTX2. Reducing choroid-plexus-derived OTX2 in adult mice changes cortical PV/net-associated measures and reopens visual plasticity; extracellular neutralisation also distinguishes juvenile maturation from adult plasticity maintenance (Spatazza et al., 2013; Bernard et al., 2016). These findings establish that a protein produced outside a recipient cortical neuron can influence its maturation or plasticity state. They do not establish that sodium–volume disturbance changes that signal.

Signal availability and recipient capture are separate steps. OTX2 recognises particular chondroitin-sulphate motifs, and interference with capture alters adult visual plasticity (Beurdeley et al., 2012). Genetic mislocalisation of Otx2 delays critical periods, windows of heightened experience-dependent plasticity, in several mouse circuits, while some maturation markers approach control values later (Lee et al., 2017a,b). Altered capture could therefore change when experience has its strongest influence on circuit refinement without necessarily causing permanent immaturity. Matrix abundance or total sulphation cannot predict the direction: changing the balance of 4- and 6-sulphation alters Otx2 accumulation and plasticity, and net staining does not directly measure accessible binding sites or uptake (Miyata et al., 2012). These mechanisms do not require a developmental rise in bulk CSF OTX2; approximately stable CSF measurements leave changing recipient capture as a separate possibility (Spatazza et al., 2013).

OTX2 and perineuronal nets can sustain reciprocal maintenance: OTX2 promotes PV/net-associated maturation, while nets support capture. Adult-mouse perturbations reopened visual plasticity, with associated markers recovering after washout (Beurdeley et al., 2012). A transient disturbance of this interaction could change subsequent maturation and recovery according to signal availability, net state and activity history. This supplies a candidate persistence mechanism, not evidence of irreversible lock-in or sodium-mediated hysteresis.

The autism-interstitium research identifies a specific experiment at this recipient step. In a small male paediatric postmortem hippocampal cohort, RNA sequencing identified increased OTX2 and CHST3 expression; qPCR supported the OTX2 increase, while the same-direction CHST3 increase had p = .08 (Rexrode et al., 2024). Neither result measures OTX2 protein uptake. Increased TTR and other choroid-plexus-enriched transcripts in the same dataset also warrant checking cellular source and tissue composition, without establishing contamination. CHST3 encodes chondroitin 6-O-sulfotransferase-1, the enzyme overexpressed in the mouse study by Miyata et al. (2012), in which altered chondroitin sulphation impaired normal net condensation and Otx2 accumulation and maintained visual cortical plasticity. This supplies a mechanistic reason to test the human CHST3 observation, not evidence that autistic tissue has the same glycan pattern or capture defect. Specific accessible binding motifs, rather than total matrix or sulphation, must be measured.

A separate fetal cerebroid interleukin-17A study reported matrix-related observations, but its insoluble-matrix protein signals did not survive multiple-testing correction and the chondroitin-sulphate staining comparison came from one donor per group (Assir et al., 2026). These findings suggest testing whether defined physiological or immune exposures change the accessible motifs on PV-associated nets and subsequent OTX2 uptake. They do not yet connect astrocytic recovery or general matrix remodelling to altered OTX2 capture.

The ionic MIA findings in Section [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6) provide a complementary entry into this maturation question. Altered neuronal chloride and GABA driving force make transport-dependent inhibitory timing a concrete link, while the cerebroid results show a local human developmental response to IL-17A. Their proposed convergence with matrix accessibility and maturation does not yet establish an OTX2-mediated sequence.

Primary developmental mechanisms remain alternatives. Choroid-plexus immaturity, reduced Otx2 expression, transient cortical PV-associated differences and behavioural changes occur together in the CAMDI choroid-plexus knockout mice studied by Tanabe et al. (2025), but OTX2 mediation was not demonstrated; broad rescue of several outcomes cannot identify the necessary mediator. Tanabe’s valproic acid (VPA) model showed no Otx2 mRNA change, so reduced expression was not shared by all tested models. These choroid-plexus measurements are also distinct from the increased bulk hippocampal OTX2 transcript reported by Rexrode et al. (2024); they do not establish one universal direction of OTX2 dysfunction. Nor is delayed maturation obligatory: MeCP2-null mice show accelerated PV-associated maturation and precocious visual critical periods (Krishnan et al., 2015). Matrix-dependent social-memory effects can also occur without a detected hippocampal Otx2 change (Huang et al., 2023a). Genetic, immune, activity-dependent and physiological mechanisms must therefore remain distinguishable.

Altered inhibitory timing could change activity-based synapse selection; PV cells would influence refinement rather than execute all pruning. Connections stabilised differently during a sensitive window might persist after the disturbance resolves, without increased neuron production. This could contribute to enduring circuit differences, but neither cortical overgrowth nor the sodium-mediated sequence follows from OTX2 results or later normality of one marker.

The two candidate routes are altered local physiological support and altered signal delivery or capture. Metabolic recovery could affect either, but no insulin/IRAP-to-OTX2 pathway or obligatory OTX2 disturbance in autism is established. Section [31](#ss_p10_sec_31) compares the developmental endpoints and timing of prenatal construction, PV maturation and activity-dependent refinement.

#### 30.5 Fluid observations and recovery tests

Prospective infant MRI provides an early fluid-space observation. Increased extra-axial CSF, the CSF surrounding the brain in the subarachnoid space, was reported in the UC Davis cohort (Shen et al., 2013). In the 343-infant IBIS replication, the 47 high-risk infants diagnosed with ASD at 24 months had 18% greater extra-axial CSF volume at six months than high-risk infants without ASD; the group difference persisted through 24 months (Shen et al., 2017). Later IBIS analyses associated perivascular-space status with extra-axial CSF trajectories measured in the same participants (Garic et al., 2023). A separate later-childhood study found no diagnostic extra-axial CSF difference, without establishing resolution in the earlier infants (Peterson et al., 2023). Extra-axial CSF volume, MRI-visible perivascular spaces, parenchymal extracellular-space fraction and solute clearance are different quantities. Extracellular-space fraction measures how much tissue volume is occupied by interstitial space; clearance measures solute removal. Neither enlarged spaces nor CSF volume identifies secretion, impaired drainage or OTX2 delivery. Diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS), an MRI-derived index, is also sensitive to white-matter geometry and cannot by itself quantify clearance (Schilling et al., 2025).

A separate pathological comparison comes from acute experimental pneumococcal meningitis in adult rats, in which DNase I treatment restored impaired CSF-tracer entry into brain and drainage to cervical lymph nodes at 24 hours after infection (Pavan et al., 2021). Human evidence is less specific: bacterial meningitis was associated with later psychiatric neurodevelopmental diagnoses, whereas no increase was detected after enteroviral meningitis and the infant bacterial-meningitis autism estimate was imprecise; a separate neonatal study found an association between sepsis and autism but uncertain meningitis-specific estimates (Graham et al., 2025; Andersen et al., 2025). These experimental and observational findings do not establish that altered CSF transport causes autism, that bacterial and enteroviral meningitis are equivalent, or that OTX2 mediates any association.

The proposed routes are altered local support, ChP release or extracellular delivery, followed by recipient capture (Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4)). CSF concentration, secretion, regional availability and uptake are distinct. Primary ChP, genetic, inflammatory, matrix or growth changes remain alternative or interacting causes; none alone establishes the shared developmental process.

The developmental proposal is that altered CSF composition or transport could change the environment in which neural or glial ionic and cell-volume recovery occurs. Appropriate models can distinguish increased secretion, impaired drainage and altered composition, then test whether selectively correcting the specified CSF change improves the predicted local recovery deficit. A fluid-transport change with preserved recovery under the prespecified compartment, exposure and developmental conditions would weaken that bridge. A developmental effect despite demonstrably preserved recovery throughout the specified causal interval would challenge the common-process thesis, rather than support it (Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)). Epithelial and fluid-space findings may instead remain parallel consequences.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_31"></a>

### 31 Cortical Architecture and Developmental Timing

#### 31.1 Physiological Influences on Cortical Development

Earlier oxygen-delivery or recovery constraints could alter developmental timing and leave lasting changes in cortical organisation. Intrinsic neural mechanisms remain alternatives, and cortical circuits can themselves change autonomic and endocrine recruitment. Lasting circuit organisation must therefore be distinguished from ongoing systemic impairment.

Upstream pressure or flow constraints could limit support for a developing cortical territory. Low regional flow alone cannot distinguish inadequate delivery from redistribution, local resistance or lower demand; Section [47](#ss_p10_sec_47) develops the anatomical and functional comparison.

#### 31.2 Oxygen as a Developmental Timing Signal

Oxygen availability can regulate developmental timing. In embryonic mice, vessel-specific Gpr124 disruption impaired cortical angiogenesis, maintained hypoxia and increased radial-glial expansion at the expense of differentiation. Increasing tissue oxygenation rescued the differentiation imbalance despite the vascular defect; HIF-1α and glycolytic manipulations helped identify the mechanism (Lange et al., 2016). This is experimental support for a vascular–metabolic influence on corticogenesis. The Sodium-Struggle extension is that a specified sodium–perfusion disturbance changes oxygen delivery sufficiently, at the relevant stage, to alter that balance. Mild exposure, regional asynchrony and later autism-related outcomes were not established by this experiment.

A genetic experiment connects this developmental interface to an autism-associated regulator. Conditional Foxp1 loss in mouse radial glia lowered HIF-1α protein while increasing several HIF-responsive genes, including Vegfa, and accelerated cortical vascular development. In separate Foxp1-deficient cortical spheroids, pharmacological HIF-1α stabilisation restored the balance of progenitors and differentiating neurons (Buth et al., 2024). This is a measured connection among a neural gene, vascular development and progenitor timing. It also shows that the direction can run from neural progenitors to their environment. Systemic sodium disturbance and ionic-recovery mediation were not demonstrated. The result supports testing this interface without treating neural genetic mechanisms as necessarily downstream of systemic defence.

#### 31.3 Association Cortex as a Candidate Timing-Sensitive Territory

Association cortex is a candidate where integrative development coincides with limited local support. Its network label does not identify a vascular borderzone: adult arterial maps vary and cut across functional labels, without measuring fetal delivery (D. E. Kim et al., 2019). Preferential vulnerability would require larger timing or synchrony effects where support is actually limited during the relevant window.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_31_4"></a>

#### 31.4 Developmental Timing and Lasting Architecture

A timing mechanism could leave lasting architecture after physiological recovery, including regional differences in progenitor expansion, differentiation or circuit refinement. Laminar patches and minicolumn spacing are not specific signatures of oxygen timing: migration, cell-intrinsic development, injury and other processes remain alternatives. A visible feature cannot retrospectively identify its developmental cause.

Extracellular developmental signalling provides a distinct genetic comparison. The de novo RELN Arg2290C variant identified in an autistic proband reduced Reelin secretion in expression assays; heterozygous neurospheres also showed increased PDIA1 (Lammert et al., 2017). This supplies a specific route from altered protein handling to extracellular developmental signalling. Heightened susceptibility to an osmotic or perfusion challenge, and mediation through impaired recovery, remain testable extensions rather than consequences of the RELN label.

In human cortical organoids, SUV420H1/KMT5B, ARID1B or CHD8 haploinsufficiency altered the relative development of GABAergic and deep-layer projection-neuron lineages, with donor-dependent effects and largely distinct molecular changes (Paulsen et al., 2022). ARID1B organoids combined premature GABAergic expansion with delayed projection-neuron differentiation. This asynchrony differs from uniform delay or altered cell allocation, and does not establish recovery mediation. The proposed connection is that a recovery constraint changes the relative availability or signalling of interacting populations during circuit assembly, even if they later reach their usual identities.

Chronological age and maturation state can diverge, leaving different cell proportions and normal ionic physiology at the same age. Matching maturation alone could conceal the timing effect. The proposed intermediary is a recovery deficit that changes a transition, with altered initial loading distinguished from impaired restoration.

Later architecture cannot establish an earlier recovery disturbance. Developmental effects with preserved relevant recovery throughout the causal interval challenge the common-process conjecture, whereas failed late correction does not settle initiation (Section [29.3](#ss_p10_sec_29_3)).

Sections [26.9](#ss_p10_sec_26_9) and [35.4.4](#ss_p10_sec_35_4_4) provide complementary tests: premature neurogenesis associated with sterol-derived signalling and activity-dependent dendritic retraction associated with mutant-channel signalling. Each requires its own developmental endpoint and causal recovery test.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_31_4_1"></a>

##### 31.4.1 Developmental processes and recovery tests

The developmental target is specific: a recovery disturbance that changes the timing or stability of a defined neural process. Autism research supplies several relevant observations, but they do not establish one sequence shared across autistic trajectories. A small post-mortem study found greater prefrontal neuron numbers, which does not directly measure excessive proliferation (Courchesne et al., 2011). Temporal-cortex samples showed increased spine density and a smaller age-associated decline; the human comparison was cross-sectional, whereas causal mTOR–autophagy tests were conducted in mice (Tang et al., 2014). Cell models from autistic donors selected for early brain overgrowth have also shown accelerated early developmental programmes, or increased progenitor proliferation alongside fewer excitatory synaptic puncta and weaker network activity (Schafer et al., 2019; Marchetto et al., 2017). These observations separate neuronal production, differentiation, synapse formation, elimination and functional maturation. The Sodium Struggle proposal predicts that failure of ionic or volume recovery during a susceptible window can alter one or more of these processes through a specified intermediary. The recovery failure and intermediary must both be demonstrated; excess proliferation, failed pruning and prolonged immaturity are not inferred as an obligatory chain.

A sustained ionic or volume-recovery disturbance could change precursor differentiation or circuit stabilisation. The proposal does not impose a universal shrinkage gate or infer excess proliferation, failed pruning or overgrowth from swelling.

Astrocytic recovery could affect these processes through glutamate clearance, potassium buffering, metabolic support and extracellular conditions. RVD impairment alone does not identify reactivity, maturation or pruning outcomes (Section [24](#ss_p10_sec_24)).

Protein production supplies another possible intermediary (Section [29](#ss_p10_sec_29)): recovery could alter the timing or identity of proteins needed for a transition. The immune and genetic experiments there establish manipulable production mechanisms, but not their dependence on recovery. Electrical or extracellular-signalling routes need not share this intermediary.

The chloride branch predicts delayed stabilisation where an extrusion deficit in pyramidal neurons weakens GABAergic control during an appropriate postnatal window. KCC2 supports the developmental chloride shift in experimental neurons (Rivera et al., 1999), but a positive reversal shift alone does not establish weaker inhibition. An astrocyte-first account additionally requires impaired glial potassium/glutamate clearance or extracellular-space recovery to precede the neuronal effect. Preserved chloride recovery, an opposite timing effect or failure of timely, verified correction of the recovery deficit to prevent it would limit this branch. Neuronal correction alone would not identify astrocytic initiation.

Clinical hyponatraemia is not required: hormonal, antidiuretic, excitatory, metabolic or inflammatory disturbances could alter recovery (Section [18](#ss_p10_sec_18)). These routes retain their exposure limits; cultured-cell glutamate application does not establish an equivalent dietary MSG brain exposure. An unrecorded transient episode remains possible but cannot supply evidence of its occurrence or developmental effect.

Genetic changes could initiate recovery difficulty, alter susceptibility or affect development independently. ‘Idiopathic’ autism does not imply absence of genetic or polygenic causation, and high heritability does not identify the intermediary. The frozen Section [6](#ss_p10_sec_6) classification maps component links without establishing universal sodium–volume mediation.

The timing-window proposal is that different genetic and environmental routes converge on impaired developmental recovery. Its organising value depends on that shared intermediary carrying the outcome, not simply on finding compatible component physiology. The candidate cross-system receptor and response read-outs are collected in Section [21.6](#ss_p10_sec_21_6) (Box [21.1](#ss_p10_box_21_1)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_31_5"></a>

Table [31.1](#ss_p10_table_31_1) maps cortical features to developmental processes, proposed perturbations and the observations needed to distinguish their causes. Table [31.2](#ss_p10_table_31_2) in Section [31.5.2](#ss_p10_sec_31_5_2) instead separates candidate cellular routes and component evidence from proposed recovery-mediated effects. These are maps of testable connections; neither assigns a cortical finding or mechanism to sodium struggle from its label alone.

##### 31.5.2 Candidate cellular routes and recovery mechanisms

Table [31.2](#ss_p10_table_31_2) extends the entry maps in Tables [13.1](#ss_p10_table_13_1) and [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) to candidate developmental consequences, separating component physiology from recovery mediation. Convergence requires impaired recovery during a susceptible window; neither inevitable effects nor autism mediation follows from the exposure label. Hypertonic translocational sodium lowering remains distinct from hypotonic hyponatraemia.

The phase-dependent glucose route remains separate: extracellular glucose elevation initially favours outward water movement, while its decline permits return towards baseline. Maternal hyperglycaemia alone does not establish fetal swelling, pathological rebound or a fixed fetal AVP response (Sections [18.2](#ss_p10_sec_18_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)).

The proposed common link is impaired local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery during development. Local physiological support and OTX2 signalling are distinct candidate connections to maturation (Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4)), compatible with direct genetic, immune, vascular and neural alternatives.
