| **Autonomic and endocrine imprinting**           | AVP, RAAS and cortisol responses depend on the measured stimulus, volume state and phase; no fixed triad is assigned.                                                                                                                                                | Shared endocrine patterns remain conditional on exposure and phase.                                                                                                                                  | Selected cohorts show lower CSF AVP without an OXT difference (§[36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5)). Cardiac autonomic and steroid responses vary with task and sampling context (§§[34.4](#ss_p10_sec_34_4) and [42](#ss_p10_sec_42)); these findings establish neither a common endocrine signature nor acquired imprinting. |
| **Macro-developmental trajectory**               | Low tonicity does not itself predict early overgrowth followed by plateau.                                                                                                                                                                                           | No common growth curve is assigned; the exposure-to-recovery-to-growth sequence remains proposed.                                                                                                    | Early surface-area expansion and subsequent brain-volume overgrowth occurred in a high-risk infant cohort; this does not establish a universal lifelong trajectory (Hazlett et al., 2017).                                                                                                                           |
| **Regional delivery and recovery vulnerability** | Proposed: a defined recovery disturbance has greater impact where independently measured local delivery reserve is low.                                                                                                                                              | Regional exposure and reserve differ; convergence on the same cortical territories is not assumed.                                                                                                   | ASD perfusion findings vary by region, direction and protocol (Jann et al., 2015; Yerys et al., 2018); they do not establish shared watershed vulnerability.                                                                                                                                                         |

#### 31.6 Developmental Architecture and Later Physiology

Earlier circuit organisation could alter later sensory integration, salience and endocrine or autonomic recruitment after exposure resolves. This feedback remains a proposed causal link, compatible with neural initiation as well as physiological influences on development.

Section [47](#ss_p10_sec_47) distinguishes enduring organisation from current physiological modulation and retains the task-comparison framework in Section [47.4.2](#ss_p10_sec_47_4_2) (Box [47.1](#ss_p10_box_47_1)).

<a name="ss_p10_part_f"></a>

## Part F Organ reserve and persistent regulation

<a name="ss_p10_sec_32"></a>

### 32 Nephron endowment, renal reserve, brain-sparing haemodynamics, and the renin paradox

#### 32.1 Physiological software and anatomical hardware

The kidney illustrates how regulatory flexibility depends on structural reserve: responses redistribute blood, sodium and water, while nephron endowment constrains the renal structure supporting them. Regulation can preserve output but cannot recreate a missed nephrogenic opportunity after formation ends. This software–hardware distinction is useful rather than absolute: regulation can persist, and structure includes more than nephron count.

The hypothesis proposes that when recurrent sodium–volume or perfusion challenges impair renal growth during nephrogenesis, immediate stability may be preserved at the expense of future renal reserve. This is a candidate instance of survival under constraint, not a claim that every defence episode sacrifices nephrons. Genetic developmental defects, placental disease, nutrition, toxic exposures and altered maturation can also change endowment; assigning an adaptive trade-off requires evidence connecting the challenge, the defence response and the developmental cost.

Reduced nephron endowment, impaired renal reserve and kidney injury are different propositions. A normal creatinine or whole-kidney GFR does not count nephrons, but neither is it evidence that compensation is occurring. The present proposal predicts a measurable structural or functional constraint beyond an otherwise normal baseline result; the distinction is developed in §[32.3](#ss_p10_sec_32_3).

Allocation describes where transport occurs within the functioning units. Both sexes use the proximal tubule, the thick ascending limb, the distal convoluted tubule and the collecting system. NHE3-dependent proximal reclamation and NaPi-mediated phosphate transport have different roles; NKCC2, NCC and ENaC identify distinct downstream sodium pathways. AQP2 concerns water permeability rather than sodium flux. Nephrons drain into a shared branching collecting system, so nephron number is not a count of independent collecting ducts ([Ganeva et al., 2011](#ss_p3_ref_Ganeva2011)). The proximal–downstream comparison is therefore a useful organising distinction, not two interchangeable compartments.

Transporter abundance, activation markers and membrane localisation describe components of this system. Actual transport, the additional transport recruitable during a specified disturbance, sodium already stored, net balance and recovery after withdrawal require separate measurements. After approximately one week of combined sodium and potassium restriction in rats, cortical collecting-duct ENaC current was almost absent, yet sodium excretion in final-day morning urine collections was no greater than during sodium restriction with adequate potassium (Frindt et al., 2011). Increased NHE3 and NCC abundance suggested compensation elsewhere without directly measuring those fluxes. This pooled-sex experiment illustrates successful adjustment; it does not measure a sex difference or unlimited reserve.

Renal function can modify an initiating disturbance as well as respond to one. Pre-existing nephron endowment, developmental transport function or allocation between segments could alter sodium–water or mineral balance and the compensation it recruits (Section [21.5.1](#ss_p10_sec_21_5_1)). Conversely, a disturbance originating elsewhere can change renal perfusion, hormonal recruitment and delivery between segments. Successful adjustment can restore balance; injury or a persistent regulatory change is a separate outcome. A downstream renal change could become an upstream modifier of a later episode only if it persists and changes that later response. These causal positions differ from proximal and downstream anatomical locations. The proposed neural developmental contribution still requires the specified local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery intermediary; parallel peripheral consequences remain distinct.

Renin–angiotensin signalling supports kidney development as well as pressure and sodium regulation. The same system can therefore have different consequences through its developmental and vascular targets; an emergency angiotensin-II concentration does not necessarily stop nephrogenesis.

Three candidate links organise that test: altered delivery to the developing kidney, altered developmental signalling, and a mismatch between metabolic demand and available resources. They can interact, but none should be inferred solely from the presence of hyponatraemia, a raised hormone concentration or a brain-sparing Doppler pattern.

##### 32.1.1 Brain sparing and renal growth: a conditional trade-off

A threat to effective circulating volume is not the same exposure as low plasma sodium concentration, and neither is interchangeable with fetal hypoxaemia. Each can recruit protective responses, but the renal consequence depends on the actual haemodynamics and oxygen supply. The proposed renal bridge requires evidence that the relevant defence state reduces growth-supporting delivery or otherwise disrupts nephrogenesis; cerebral prioritisation alone cannot supply that evidence.

A fetal experiment illustrates the distinction. During 48 hours of moderate isocapnic hypoxaemia without acidaemia in late-gestation sheep, redistribution favoured the brain, yet renal blood flow increased from 11.8 ± 1.6 to 15.6 ± 1.8 mL/min. Renal oxygen delivery was maintained on the first day and fell on the second despite the increased flow (Braaksma et al., 1999). Blood flow, oxygen delivery and tissue oxygen adequacy must therefore be distinguished.

Conversely, a developmental deficit can be measured after placental challenge. Umbilical–placental embolisation from gestational days 110 to 130 in sheep, compared with saline controls, reduced nephron number by 24% at day 130, with seven fetuses per group (Zohdi et al., 2007). That result supports vulnerability during nephrogenesis. It does not identify sodium disturbance, sympathetic renal vasoconstriction or an adaptive sacrifice as the mediator. The construction-site metaphor is useful only when the interruption itself has been established.

##### 32.1.2 Renin–angiotensin signalling: developmental support and candidate constraints

There is positive experimental evidence for angiotensin-dependent developmental signalling. In cultured ureteric-bud cells, angiotensin II increased branching across concentrations of 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁵ M (Iosipiv and Schroeder, 2003). In human kidney organoids, it promoted podocyte differentiation and maturation while reducing the podocyte precursor pool; losartan favoured a less mature state (Chung et al., 2025). These findings support a role in developmental timing and cell fate, not a demonstrated concentration threshold separating growth from arrest.

Vascular resistance, redox conditions and receptor context could change this developmental balance. Neither increased angiotensin II nor accelerated organoid maturation establishes pathological progenitor exhaustion or reduced in-vivo endowment.

In the embolised sheep studied by Zohdi et al. (2007), the nephron deficit occurred without detectable differences in renal renin, angiotensinogen, AT1 or AT2 receptor mRNA. This neither measures all angiotensin activity nor establishes an opposing hormonal mechanism. It shows why fewer nephrons cannot retrospectively prove a high-gain RAAS state.

##### 32.1.3 Metabolic allocation during nephrogenesis

The energetic version of the trade-off asks whether homeostatic work and developmental growth compete under a measured resource constraint. A rise in fractional sodium reabsorption does not automatically establish greater total transport work: the filtered load, reabsorbed amount and efficiency of transport also matter. Nor does reduced renal blood flow alone demonstrate that oxygen delivery has fallen below metabolic demand.

The specific prediction is that a defined developmental challenge creates a mismatch between available energy and the combined demands of transport, progenitor maintenance and differentiation, thereby constraining nephron formation.

An informative alternative is altered resilience without a detected structural deficit. Cargill et al. (2020) exposed C57BL/6 mice to 12% oxygen from embryonic day 10.5 through postnatal day 3. Adult baseline histology, glomerular counts in sampled sections and blood urea nitrogen did not differ detectably from controls, but susceptibility to subsequent cisplatin injury increased in male offspring. The section counts were not a stereological estimate of whole-kidney nephron endowment. The study supports investigating developmental changes in resilience without presuming nephron depletion as their mediator.

The section therefore proposes a testable conversion from physiological demand into structural constraint. It does not equate recruitment of the defence triad with nephrogenic arrest. Preserved endowment under a well-characterised challenge would count against the nephron-depletion branch, even if a distinct effect on later resilience remained possible.

Timing gives this branch its special importance. Human nephrogenesis usually ends around 34–36 weeks of gestation, but preterm delivery need not end it immediately. Once formation has ceased, later regulation cannot simply replace an endowment deficit by restarting the normal developmental programme. The relevant exposure window must therefore be defined by ongoing nephrogenesis, rather than by birth alone.

Carpenter et al. (2024) compared seven preterm infants surviving more than 40 postnatal days with eight postmenstrual-age-matched controls. Four preterm kidneys retained histological and molecular evidence of nephrogenesis; persistence was observed up to 62 days after birth. The small autopsy series also suggested earlier cessation and altered tubular growth. Prematurity thus creates a changed developmental environment, not an automatic stop to nephron formation; its association with autism does not identify renal mediation.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_32_1_4"></a>

##### 32.1.4 Developmental and hormonal regulation of renal transport

Human computational models allow the allocation hypothesis to be explored, but their sex-specific transport parameters substantially extrapolate from rodents; greater recruitable female proximal capacity was hypothesised and introduced into the simulations rather than measured in infants or women ([Hu et al., 2021](#ss_p3_ref_Hu2021)). Direction also depends on the disturbance. Adult-rat simulations predicted greater female natriuresis during combined proximal/thick-ascending-limb NHE inhibition or combined NKCC2/NCC/ENaC blockade, but a greater male response to isolated ENaC inhibition ([Hu et al., 2020](#ss_p3_ref_Hu2020)). These steady-state manipulations neither reproduce isolated physiological PTH action nor measure recovery speed. A modelled response to SGLT2 blockade likewise cannot establish an infant male distal deficit.

Development can change the relevant pattern. In mice, a broad proximal-tubule transcriptional sex programme emerged around puberty and was modified by androgen-receptor manipulations (Xiong et al., 2023). Those findings identify developmental regulation, not sodium flux, and do not exclude earlier differences in particular components. Adult hormonal patterns and computational assumptions therefore supply candidate mechanisms for investigation, while the human infancy and childhood extension remains open (Section [40.3](#ss_p10_sec_40_3)).

Minipuberty supplies a human postnatal hormone window for this question in both sexes. In the Copenhagen study, gonadotropins and testosterone peaked within the first month in healthy term boys, while Sertoli-cell markers peaked later ([Busch et al., 2022](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Busch2022)). Among 98 healthy term girls, normalised mean hormone curves were biphasic: early peaks occurred around the first month, followed by later peaks around four months for ovarian hormones, including oestradiol, and five to six months for LH and FSH ([Ljubicic et al., 2022](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Ljubicic2022)). These are population trajectories rather than a fixed schedule for every infant.

Gestational maturity also matters. Separate longitudinal studies found higher urinary LH and testosterone in preterm than term boys ([Kuiri-Hänninen et al., 2011b](#ss_revsyn3_ref_KuiriHanninen2011b)), and a stronger, more prolonged FSH rise in near-term/preterm than term girls ([Kuiri-Hänninen et al., 2011a](#ss_revsyn3_ref_KuiriHanninen2011a)). Comparisons therefore need both postnatal and postmenstrual age. In 189 term infants from the Copenhagen cohort, free testosterone was associated with faster linear growth, particularly in boys; statistical mediation analysis attributed part of that association to IGF-I ([Pridik et al., 2026](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Pridik2026)). This is observational evidence from overlapping cohort work, not an independent demonstration of androgen-driven renal phosphate retention.

The proposed renal extension is that hormone-dependent regulation during minipuberty could alter proximal reclamation or downstream adjustment, changing the workload of phosphate disposal while sodium balance is maintained. Hormone-linked growth and mineral demand provide a competing or coexisting explanation; vascular and antioxidant responses would be separate candidate routes. Whether these signals alter infant NHE3/NaPi-mediated transport, downstream recruitment or recovery remains to be measured. Paired hormone, growth, feeding and renal-handling measurements in existing cohorts or appropriate experimental models could distinguish growth-related demand from altered renal handling and assess whether either accompanies successful adaptation or prolonged recovery.

Gestational androgen exposure is a candidate modifier of renal development and regulation. Could unusually high maternal circulating testosterone during pregnancy alter the mother's renal sodium–volume control, offspring renal development, or both, and thereby change the coordination of phosphate disposal with sodium conservation? Maternal hormone concentrations, placental effects and fetal androgen exposure are separate variables. The specific Sodium-Struggle proposal is that altered proximal reclamation or downstream adjustment could modify the duration or intensity of compensation after a defined mineral or sodium–volume disturbance.

Both developmental programming and later hormonal regulation can contribute. Brief fetal testosterone deficiency in male mice reduced proximal-tubule proliferation and later proximal-tubule size; supplementation during that fetal window restored adult kidney weight ([Junnila et al., 2026](#ss_and_ref_Junnila2026)). This supports prenatal growth programming, but restoring deficiency does not establish an effect of excess testosterone or reduced distal capacity. Structure also remains partly adjustable: adult mouse tubular cell size depended on continued androgen exposure, and three months after human kidney transplantation, tubular cell size was greater in male than female recipients regardless of donor sex ([Laouari et al., 2022](#ss_and_ref_Laouari2022)). Together with the androgen-receptor-dependent gene regulation described above, these findings favour interacting developmental and current hormonal influences rather than a wholly fixed proximal–distal allocation. Downstream responses need separate measurement: testosterone increased distal/collecting-duct ENaC expression in orchidectomised adult male rats ([Loh et al., 2016](#ss_and_ref_Loh2016)), precluding a universal inference of distal suppression.

Adult hormone-treatment experiments support adjustable transport, with context-dependent functional outcomes. After two months of testosterone treatment, adult female rats had increased proximal NHE3 immunostaining and lower body-weight-normalised urinary sodium excretion, with no significant GFR change; NCC staining did not change ([Lichtenecker et al., 2025](#ss_and_ref_Lichtenecker2025)). A four-month study reported similar sodium excretion per gram of kidney in treated and control females, despite altered renal morphology and lower GFR ([Lichtenecker et al., 2021](#ss_and_ref_Lichtenecker2021)). The studies differ in duration and normalisation and establish neither phosphate transport nor distal reserve.

The maternal kidney is itself an experimentally supported target. Testosterone treatment during late pregnancy reduced maternal renal glutathione and nitric oxide and increased plasma urea and creatinine in rats ([Usman et al., 2021](#ss_and_ref_Usman2021)). This motivates investigating maternal renal regulation as a route to an altered fetal environment, although segmental sodium transport, phosphate surges and osmotic oscillations were not established. Maternal exposure need not produce a matching fetal testosterone rise: in another rat experiment, a dose that doubled maternal testosterone altered placental amino-acid transport without increasing testosterone measured in whole fetuses; a higher dose increased fetal testosterone in both sexes ([Sathishkumar et al., 2011](#ss_and_ref_Sathishkumar2011)). Direct fetal androgen action and indirect maternal or placental effects therefore require separate exposure evidence.

Offspring findings also support altered regulation as a possibility. At six months, female rats exposed prenatally to testosterone had higher angiotensin II, AVP and blood pressure, with lower aldosterone and no significant differences in measured plasma volume or serum/urine sodium ([More et al., 2016](#ss_and_ref_More2016)). The hormonal pattern provides indirect support for altered control of sodium–water handling. It does not locate transport within the nephron or establish whether the hormone changes maintained balance through compensation or reflected a separately programmed endocrine state.

The phosphate prediction is specifically greater or more persistent proximal phosphate reclamation at a matched filtered load, with altered downstream sodium adjustment during disposal. Hormone concentration, proximal-tubule size and NHE3 expression cannot substitute for that measurement. Existing pregnancy/offspring cohorts, archived samples and appropriate experimental models could distinguish maternal and offspring effects, quantify phosphate handling alongside sodium balance, and follow recovery. Preserved handling and recovery under the defined exposure would weigh against this branch. Any contribution to neural development still requires the local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery intermediary; maternal or offspring peripheral changes alone do not establish that contribution.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_32_2"></a>

#### 32.2 A U-shaped experimental pattern and its limits

Both low and high maternal sodium intake have reduced offspring nephron number in a controlled rat experiment. That finding preserves the important insight that more sodium is not necessarily protective. It does not establish a universal U-shaped relationship between human plasma sodium, dietary salt, perfusion and nephron endowment.

Development requires both organising signals (the “blueprint”) and adequate oxygen, substrates and capacity to use them (the “bricks”). Angiotensin is one signalling contributor; circulating hormones, maternal intake and whole-organ flow do not establish the local nephrogenic state.

##### 32.2.1 The positive dietary experiment

Koleganova et al. (2011) assigned pregnant Sprague–Dawley rats to diets containing 0.07%, 0.51% or 3.0% sodium through pregnancy and lactation. Offspring then received the intermediate diet after weaning. Glomerular counts were lower in both extreme groups at one and twelve weeks, and male offspring had higher mean arterial pressure from the fifth postnatal month. This is experimental evidence that the perinatal dietary environment can alter renal endowment and later pressure regulation.

The study also reported changes in developmental proteins and higher amniotic marinobufagenin with high sodium intake. Its findings do not establish the proposed binary mechanism of high RAAS with ischaemia at one extreme and suppressed fetal RAAS with adequate perfusion at the other. Exposure continued after birth during ongoing rat nephrogenesis, so prenatal and lactational contributions cannot be separated by this design.

##### 32.2.2 A contrasting gestation-only experiment

Seravalli et al. (2016) studied Wistar offspring within 24 hours of birth after maternal diets containing 0.15%, 1.3% or 8% NaCl during pregnancy. With six to eight newborns per group in the reported analysis, counts of mature glomeruli did not differ. Low salt reduced renal AT1-receptor protein in males and AT2-receptor protein in both sexes, rather than simply producing the high-RAAS developmental state assumed by the earlier formulation.

The newborn endpoint preceded completion of rat nephrogenesis, and the strain, doses and exposure duration differed from the pregnancy-plus-lactation experiment. The null result therefore does not erase the later positive findings. It does rule out treating a deficit at birth, or one fixed hormonal response, as an established consequence of either dietary extreme. Dietary sodium percentage and NaCl percentage must also remain distinct when comparing doses.

##### 32.2.3 Convergent endpoints require measured mechanisms

Similar nephron deficits can arise through impaired growth-supporting delivery or altered local developmental signalling. These are distinct routes; a shared endpoint does not identify the intermediary.

Adequate delivery and intact relevant signalling during the developmental interval would weigh against those respective routes. The hardware-debt proposal connects immediate physiological constraint to lasting renal limitation without assigning every renal deficit to the same cause.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_32_3"></a>

#### 32.3 Compensatory hypertrophy: maintained output, variable reserve

Whole-kidney GFR is the sum of filtration across functioning nephrons. A reduced population can therefore maintain substantial total filtration through greater average single-nephron filtration and enlargement of glomeruli and tubules. Normal creatinine or eGFR cannot establish nephron number, but neither establishes hidden hyperfiltration or depleted reserve. In 1,388 healthy kidney donors, Denic et al. (2017) estimated nephron number from cortical imaging and biopsy, then calculated mean single-nephron GFR by dividing measured whole-kidney GFR by that estimate. This distinction matters: whole-organ output, structural endowment and the response to additional demand are different measurements.

The proposed cost is concentrated workload: if fewer units carry the same filtration and transport demand, each carries more. How that load is accommodated depends on renal plasma flow, filtration surface and permeability, and the balance of afferent and efferent vascular resistance. Efferent angiotensin-mediated constriction is one possible contributor, not the obligatory mechanism of compensation. Increased single-nephron filtration does not by itself demonstrate damaging glomerular pressure, greater ATP expenditure or exhausted reserve.

Compensation can preserve function, become costly, or do both at different stages. The evidence requires those outcomes to be distinguished.

**A developmental model demonstrates the costly route.** Good et al. (2023) used late developmental Ret manipulation to produce mice with approximately 30–70% fewer nephrons. Glomerular and tubular hypertrophy was followed by fibrosis, inflammation and impaired renal indices; urinary albumin excretion was increased by 12 weeks. These findings support a path from low endowment to later injury in that model. They do not establish that every nephron deficit progresses, that fetal sodium–volume defence caused the deficit, or that renal injury mediates autism.

The segment-specific measurements refine that conclusion. The model showed proximal-tubule enlargement; neonatal gentamicin produced greater proximal injury with incomplete repair (Good et al., 2023). Distal sparing, equally impaired distal recovery and an altered sodium-recovery trajectory were not established. The developmental Ret manipulation is also distinct from the maternal dietary-sodium experiments in Section [32.2](#ss_p10_sec_32_2); fewer nephrons alone cannot identify which surviving segment is most constrained.

**Adult kidney donation provides an important constraint.** In 21 donors studied before donation and at median follow-ups of 0.8 and 6.3 years, Lenihan et al. (2015) found sustained adaptive hyperfiltration associated with increased renal plasma flow and hypertrophy; modelling argued against substantial glomerular hypertension, and no participant had micro- or macroalbuminuria at the study visits. Hypertension diagnoses and treatment increased, and the small study lacked non-donor controls. Adult removal of a developed kidney is not congenital underdevelopment, but it shows why increased workload must not be equated automatically with progressive injury.

Redistribution of transport can have a measured energetic cost while preserving sodium balance. Adult male claudin-2-null mice conserved sodium through compensatory thick-ascending-limb transport, but had greater whole-kidney oxygen consumption and lower outer-medullary oxygen tension; cortical oxygen tension was similar to controls, and imposed ischaemia caused greater injury ([Pei et al., 2016](#ss_p3_ref_Pei2016)). This connects a specified proximal defect with downstream work and susceptibility. It does not establish a general female energetic disadvantage or make all downstream segments oxygen-poor. In the proposed developmental pathway, transport and resource measurements must distinguish successful compensation from a limitation that delays recovery.

The renin paradox also requires compartment-specific evidence. Fisher et al. (1995) found that the renal vascular response to renin inhibition outlasted its effects in plasma, supporting a functional tissue component of angiotensin signalling. Such dissociation makes a plasma renin measurement an incomplete account of renal angiotensin action. It does not make low plasma renin evidence of concealed intrarenal excess. In the proposed low-endowment route, local signalling, sodium balance, pressure and filtration responses must establish whether a compensatory RAAS contribution is actually present.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_32_4"></a>

#### 32.4 Copy-number syndromes as tests of shared kidney–brain–metabolic mechanisms

##### 32.4.1 The renal blind spot in neurodevelopmental disorders

This section does not establish reduced nephron endowment in autism. Routine renal imaging, creatinine, eGFR and albuminuria answer different questions from direct nephron quantification, and neither normal nor abnormal results alone identify a developmental nephron deficit. An autism-specific structural claim needs a suitable comparison study rather than inference from the phenotype.

Prematurity and fetal growth restriction provide reasons to investigate renal development alongside neurodevelopment. Their co-occurrence with later developmental differences does not show that renal constraint mediates those differences: shared genetic, placental or neonatal causes can affect both. The informative test is whether a measured renal or hydromineral intermediary contributes beyond those shared causes.

##### 32.4.2 Distinguishing shared genetic causes from renal mediation

Copy-number variants offer natural comparisons because one genomic change can affect several developing organs. That co-occurrence establishes a shared genetic exposure, but the causal connections may run in parallel, interact, or include renal and metabolic mediation. The hypothesis asks whether reduced renal reserve or altered hydromineral recovery adds a measurable developmental effect beyond direct neural consequences of the same lesion.

**In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, the renal component has a defined genetic basis.** Lopez-Rivera et al. (2017) mapped kidney and urinary-tract defects to a smaller interval and identified CRKL haploinsufficiency as a major driver. This demonstrates developmental renal vulnerability within a multi-organ syndrome. It does not establish that kidney abnormalities cause the syndrome's neuropsychiatric features or that all carriers have reduced nephron reserve. Longitudinal comparison within a defined deletion class can ask whether measured renal, sodium–water or perfusion abnormalities predict developmental outcomes independently of other affected organs and genes.

**The 17q12 deletion is particularly informative because it includes HNF1B and additional genes.** Renal abnormalities, diabetes and neurodevelopmental phenotypes can occur within this syndrome (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2010), but the wider deletion must be distinguished from an intragenic HNF1B variant. Among 38 people with HNF1B-associated renal disease, Clissold et al. (2016) found a diagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder in eight of 20 deletion carriers and none of 18 intragenic-variant carriers. This small, selected comparison constrains a simple HNF1B or renal-disease-only explanation; it does not exclude a modifying effect of renal physiology. The useful test is whether a measured hydromineral exposure explains additional developmental variation within appropriately matched genetic groups.

TSHZ3 similarly links a human deletion syndrome with neurodevelopmental and urinary-tract features. Caubit et al. (2016) also demonstrated altered corticostriatal synaptic function in heterozygous mice. Those neural findings provide a direct developmental alternative that must remain visible. Urinary-tract abnormalities do not by themselves establish nephron depletion, altered sodium balance or mediation of the neural phenotype.

Together, these syndromes make the kidney–brain–metabolic question concrete: shared genetic injury can affect several organs, while sodium–volume mediation is an additional causal claim. A reliably demonstrated absence of the proposed renal or hydromineral intermediary during the developmental interval would favour parallel effects over that renal mediation route.

#### 32.5 Long-term consequence: susceptibility revealed by load

Lower nephron endowment can increase susceptibility to salt-dependent pressure changes, but fewer nephrons do not impose a fixed pressure requirement. In Ret-deficient mice, Serrano Herrera et al. (2026) reported similar baseline blood pressure to controls, followed by a larger systolic rise with high-salt feeding in both sexes; diastolic responses differed by sex. The informative observation is the measured response to a defined challenge, not an assumption that normal resting pressure conceals dysfunction. Tubular handling, vascular responses, body size and later exposures help determine whether a structural deficit becomes functionally limiting.

Reduced renal reserve could amplify defence work during repeated sodium–water or perfusion challenges despite adequate baseline function. Its proposed neurodevelopmental contribution requires the resulting endocrine, haemodynamic or recovery difference to add explanatory value beyond shared genetic and perinatal causes; it does not prescribe one autistic RAAS or sympathetic state.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_32_6"></a>

#### 32.6 A candidate intergenerational route through renal reserve

Maternal renal reserve and gestational haemodynamics could influence fetal conditions during nephrogenesis, providing a candidate developmental route across generations alongside inherited genetic effects. The proposed sequence requires maternal physiological constraint, a corresponding fetal exposure and altered offspring renal endowment to be demonstrated together. Maternal salt sensitivity or low reserve alone does not establish placental hypoperfusion or arrest of nephron formation.

Reduced offspring reserve could then increase later regulatory work: a developmental “hardware debt”, not an assumed generational decline. Adequate gestational compensation remains possible.

This candidate intergenerational route is not an established explanation for rising autism prevalence or familial clustering. It must fit the genetic constraints in Section [6](#ss_p10_sec_6) and the ascertainment evidence in Section [1](#ss_p10_sec_1), and predict offspring outcomes from measured maternal and fetal physiology beyond inherited liability and family-level confounding.

A population study provides a direct, if limited, renal–neurodevelopmental comparison. Harel et al. (2024) followed 89,677 Ontario children whose mothers had serum creatinine measured from 120 days before conception to 28 days afterwards. Maternal creatinine above 78 µmol/L, compared with values at or below 78, was not associated with ASD diagnosed at ages 24–48 months (adjusted RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.67–1.10). Values below 46 µmol/L, compared with 46–78, showed a borderline association (1.23, 1.00–1.52). Creatinine did not directly measure hyperfiltration or nephron number; muscle mass, clinically selected testing and unmeasured familial factors remain alternative explanations. These findings neither demonstrate the proposed renal mediator nor support a simple elevated-creatinine route.

Structural endowment, filtration reserve, tubular water–solute handling and injury are distinct dimensions of renal capacity. Kidney size and eGFR do not count nephrons, a protein-stimulated GFR response does not establish water clearance, and normal albumin excretion identifies neither nephron number nor concealed injury. Preserved responses under demand would weaken the proposed low-endowment-to-defence link. Renal abnormalities without the predicted developmental intermediary or outcome would limit the renal mediation branch, even if a separate kidney-health risk remained. Section [33](#ss_p10_sec_33) takes up the coordination question: how proximal phosphate disposal, downstream sodium conservation and circulatory support interact under a defined load.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_33"></a>

### 33 Endocrine-Mineral Interactions

#### 33.1 Phosphate–Sodium Coupling

##### 33.1.1 Rationale and Framing

Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) develops the exposure and proximal transport interface, and Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32) distinguishes structural reserve from segmental transport capacity. This section asks how phosphate disposal coordinates with sodium conservation, water handling and vascular support. Renal handling could modify an initiating disturbance or change in response to one; parallel endocrine effects are another possibility. Neither coexisting responses nor different response times alone establish instability.

Rapid phosphate disposal can recruit both proximal transport regulation and PTH, with their relative contributions depending on the exposure (Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). A direct phosphate-to-PTH link has experimental support: in freshly isolated human parathyroid cells, raising extracellular phosphate to 2 mmol/L increased PTH secretion by 56 ± 10%, with reversal within minutes after phosphate returned to 0.8 mmol/L. Receptor and mouse-gland experiments identified inhibition of the calcium-sensing receptor as the mechanism (Centeno et al., 2019). These high-phosphate preparations establish a sensing route, not the response to an ordinary meal. Nor is PTH the sole obligatory bridge: acute NaPi downregulation persisted in PTH-deficient mice with FGF23 signalling blocked (Daryadel et al., 2022). The proposed sodium–phosphate interaction therefore concerns how these responses combine with sodium conservation, rather than a fixed NaPi-IIa/PTH-first sequence.

The proposed proximal–distal dissociation is prolonged compensatory work or recurrent excursions caused by mismatched responses. It requires measurements of transport, net balance, filling and recovery; asynchronous hormone peaks alone are insufficient. PTH, FGF-23, RAAS, AVP and cortisol need not follow a fixed sequence, and successful coordination remains possible.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_33_1_2"></a>

##### 33.1.2 Proximal and Distal Coordination During Phosphate Disposal

Repeated or sustained phosphate exposure could recruit a different balance of endocrine and transport responses from an acute load. The distal sodium-conservation component has direct experimental support: recombinant FGF23 increased renal NCC abundance and sodium retention in mice, with lower aldosterone but unchanged measured plasma renin activity (Andrukhova et al., 2014). This supports segment-specific allocation. It does not establish that every dietary phosphate load follows a PTH-first/FGF23-later sequence or produces an oscillating whole-body state.

PTH effects on downstream sodium transport differ across preparations. In mDCT15 cells, 100 nM PTH reduced NCC-mediated sodium uptake after 15 minutes ([Hoover et al., 2016](#ss_p3_ref_Hoover2016)). In native mouse kidney slices, PTH increased NCC phosphorylation, an activity-related marker rather than a direct flux measurement; the tested concentrations were also above physiological circulating levels ([Penton et al., 2019](#ss_p3_ref_Penton2019)). These findings prevent assigning obligatory NCC suppression to an infant PTH response. The separate FGF23 experiment above demonstrates a sodium-conserving component, whose effect could be useful during underfilling or contribute to excessive retention in another setting.

Human infancy supplies evidence of mineral-regulatory differences without identifying separate male and female response pathways. Among 113 healthy infants in a vitamin D trial, intact FGF23 at three months was higher in girls than boys, 51 versus 26 pg/mL ([Holmlund-Suila et al., 2016](#ss_p3_ref_Holmlund2016)). Hormone concentration and subgroup correlations do not establish renal target action or a sex-by-disturbance interaction. C-terminal assays can detect intact hormone as well as fragments, so their results cannot be read as an antagonistic-fragment burden ([Holmlund-Suila et al., 2017](#ss_p3_ref_Holmlund2017)). These observations motivate developmental investigation of phosphate–sodium coordination; they do not demonstrate infant NCC activity, greater female sodium conservation or an obligatory male PTH-first response.

The adult phosphate comparison also concerns a different endpoint. After a 500 mg phosphorus load as oral sodium phosphate, women had a larger rise in urinary phosphate relative to creatinine over four hours, while changes in circulating phosphate were similar between sexes ([Turner et al., 2023](#ss_p3_ref_Turner2023)). The greater urinary phosphate response does not establish faster clearance from female blood or prolonged male vascular exposure. The fasting adult protocol cannot be transferred directly to infant feeding: chemical form, dose, accompanying sodium and calcium, water availability, growth and developmental stage must define the actual exposure (Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)).

Modifiers include vitamin D signalling, renal dopamine-mediated proximal phosphaturia, tubular feedback on distal delivery and afferent tone, and ANP or pressure natriuresis opposing volume expansion. Thyroid effects on phosphate transport and water excretion do not fix RAAS direction. These influences may permit successful coordination rather than a sustained loop.

Acid-base and nitrogen handling add a conditional metabolic branch to this coordination problem. A defined phosphate exposure could coincide with bicarbonate loss, potassium depletion or sustained acid demand, increasing the requirement for renal glutamine metabolism; phosphate can also facilitate proton excretion directly as titratable acid (Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). The balance among these routes determines whether glutamine utilisation rises and whether other tissues replenish it sufficiently. The proposed sequence then asks whether a persistent systemic substrate change alters local neural or glial recovery (Section [24.3](#ss_p10_sec_24_3)). This separates a plausible chain assembled from component evidence from a demonstrated developmental pathway. Successful acid disposal and preserved neural recovery are explicit alternatives.

#### 33.2 RAAS Branch States and Endocrine Feedback

Underfilling may recruit renin and aldosterone, whereas successful sodium conservation may reduce that need. The cited FGF23/NCC experiment found unchanged renin despite sodium retention and lower aldosterone. Thus low-, high- and mixed-renin configurations are distinct possibilities, not interchangeable evidence of phosphate-driven defence.

AVP or glucocorticoid support could enter where additional defence is required. Preserved pressure with incomplete recovery is one candidate outcome; stable filling and prompt recovery remain possible without recurrent hormonal recruitment or oscillation.

Thyroid status modifies components of phosphate and water regulation. In mice and renal-cell assays, T3 supported Npt2a-mediated phosphate handling through direct transcriptional control (Ishiguro et al., 2010). In five adults with untreated hypothyroidism, impaired water excretion and failure to suppress AVP after a water load improved with thyroid replacement (Ota et al., 1994). RAAS direction is context-dependent: early-life surgical and adult drug-induced hypothyroidism produced different aldosterone/renin patterns in rats (Montiel et al., 1984). These findings support a thyroid modifier without establishing an obligatory shift toward AVP and cortisol. Growth, diet and renal function likewise need to be specified when comparing phosphate responses (§[14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)).

**Text description of Figure 33.1**

The diagram, titled “Phosphate disposal and sodium conservation”, presents two parallel renal responses whose coordination must be tested over time. The left lane starts with a specified phosphate challenge. A solid downward arrow leads to proximal phosphate disposal through NaPi transporter adaptation, with PTH identified as one contributor. This component is labelled as mouse evidence from Daryadel et al. (2022).

The right lane starts with FGF23 signalling, conditional on its recruitment by the exposure. A solid downward arrow leads to distal sodium conservation through an NCC-dependent response whose timing depends on exposure. This component is labelled as mouse evidence from Andrukhova et al. (2014). No directional arrow connects the phosphate-challenge box to the FGF23 box.

Lines without arrowheads join the two response boxes to a common “Measure together” box: phosphate excretion, sodium and water balance, effective filling, tonicity and recovery. These connectors specify combined measurement, rather than a causal sequence between the lanes.

Two dashed arrows descend from the measurement box to alternative outcomes. The left outcome is a coordinated response with stable filling and adequate recovery. The right outcome is residual disturbance, described as underfilling or incomplete recovery. A further dashed arrow connects residual disturbance to additional defence, if recruited: RAAS, water or vascular support, with renin and aldosterone to be measured. A dashed feedback arrow returns from this additional-defence box to the joint-measurement box.

A separate note states that recurrent excursions require their own dynamic test and that different response clocks do not establish cycling. The legend distinguishes solid arrows, representing demonstrated components in the named preparations, from dashed arrows, representing conditional coupling or feedback to test, and arrowless lines, representing combined measurement.
