<a name="ss_p10_sec_33_3"></a>

#### 33.3 Vascular / Klotho Modifiers

Membrane α-Klotho, its shed soluble ectodomain and circulating Klotho measurements are related but distinct. Andrukhova et al. (2014) demonstrated Klotho-dependent FGF-23 effects on distal-tubule NCC: recombinant FGF-23 increased NCC phosphorylation at Ser71 in isolated wild-type distal tubules, whereas this stimulated increment was absent in Klotho-deficient tubules. This identifies a requirement for the tested FGF-23 response, not loss of all basal NCC activity. Chen et al. (2018) showed that the soluble ectodomain can also scaffold FGF-23 receptor signalling. This biochemical competence does not establish that circulating soluble Klotho alone controls NCC in vivo. A plasma concentration therefore cannot substitute for tissue Klotho, receptor-complex activity or transport measurements; the five-day dietary finding in §[14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) concerns circulating soluble Klotho.

Thyroid status offers a candidate connection between endocrine recovery and renal Klotho signalling. T3 treatment increased kidney-specific Klotho expression in cell and mouse experiments (Mohanty et al., 2024). In 4,614 NHANES participants aged 40–79, higher serum soluble α-Klotho was associated with higher free and total T3; pregnancy was excluded, and the cross-sectional design cannot determine causal direction (Dong et al., 2024). The proposed extension is that a defined loss of thyroid support reduces relevant tissue Klotho and FGF-23 responsiveness, altering sodium conservation under demand. Neither study establishes that sequence during gestation or in fetal kidneys. The opposing soluble-Klotho directions in the dietary trials in Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) further preclude treating phosphate exposure as equivalent to Klotho deletion. Thyroid output, tissue co-receptor function and net transport must therefore connect the endocrine change to any reassignment of defence in Section [16.10](#ss_p10_sec_16_10).

Klotho can modify vascular responses, but protection depends on the preparation. Soluble Klotho relaxed mouse aortic rings preconstricted with 2.0 mM phosphate through an endothelium- and NOS-dependent mechanism; alone it also induced contraction and increased smooth-muscle ROS (Six et al., 2014). In cultured human aortic endothelial cells, FGF-23 increased NO production; β-glycerophosphate loading or Klotho knockdown attenuated that response, and soluble Klotho did not restore it (Chung et al., 2017). In the same study, human brain microvascular endothelial cells lacked detectable endogenous α-Klotho and showed no FGF-23-induced NO or eNOS response. These experiments give the vascular-resilience branch a measurable basis while rejecting a universal low-Klotho → low-NO → high-tone sequence. Transfer to developmental perfusion requires the relevant vascular bed, exposure and response to be demonstrated.

A separate coronary-endothelial experiment identifies how Klotho could modify the balance of oxidant production and removal. In cultured human coronary artery endothelial cells, FGF-23 stimulated Akt–eNOS-dependent NO release, NOX2-associated ROS formation and antioxidant responses involving superoxide dismutase 2 and catalase. Klotho inhibition attenuated the NO and antioxidant responses while leaving the ROS-production response intact (Richter et al., 2016). This supplies a specific convergence with Section [16.8.2](#ss_p10_sec_16_8_2): reduced Klotho responsiveness could weaken endothelial support during a concurrent redox challenge. Klotho-supported NO generation still uses eNOS, so it cannot be treated as an independent bypass around eNOS dysfunction. These experiments do not establish a consequent BH4 change in the combined model. Together with the renal response above, the proposal is reduced flexibility of sodium conservation and vascular support; its developmental significance requires a resulting disturbance of local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery, rather than either endocrine finding alone.

Reduced bone mineral density in some autism cohorts is compatible with altered mineral handling during repeated phosphaturic and calcitriol-lowering states, but does not specifically identify a phosphate-driven endocrine mechanism. Relations between Klotho measures and autism likewise remain exploratory, rather than established biomarker evidence.

Prather et al. (2015) found lower serum Klotho in selected high-stress mothers caring for autistic children than in low-stress maternal controls; recruitment required at least one child aged 2–16. Brown et al. (2023) examined Klotho and telomere biology in the same cohort, not an independent prenatal sample. These postdiagnosis maternal findings establish neither gestational Klotho deficiency nor a child biomarker. The temporal question is whether maternal Klotho and thyroid changes measured before or during pregnancy precede altered sodium–water handling or vascular support, rather than appearing later alongside caregiving stress.

#### 33.4 Environmental and Population Modifiers

Phosphate additives and specified endocrine-active chemicals could modify the renal pathway, while vascular, receptor or hepatic lipid effects provide other candidate influences (Table [14.3](#ss_p10_table_14_3); Sections [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) and [35.7.5](#ss_p10_sec_35_7_5)). They could supply initiating disturbances or modify recovery from a defined challenge; a shared GR/MR imbalance would require separate evidence.

Population and developmental context should enter through measured physiology: renal maturity, growth, sodium and water intake, and stimulus-appropriate endocrine responses may modify phosphate or other challenges. Climatic or evolutionary interpretations require a specified genotype and physiological phenotype; ancestry, low renin and a blood-pressure association do not establish increased neural WNK signalling. A variant may affect renal handling, neural recovery, both or neither (Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7)). Historical erythrocyte transport does not measure neural pump reserve. This physiological lens does not displace social, diagnostic or other developmental explanations for group differences.

Lipid identity and challenge matter. In 29 normotensive adults, four weeks of borage oil augmented vasoconstriction during lower-body negative pressure, whereas fish oil increased post-ischaemic forearm flow; safflower oil was the third comparison (Mills et al., 1990). Such differences could modify compensation without implying underfilling or greater AVP/cortisol support. Dietary lipids must also remain distinct from the oxidised preparations in Section [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8).

#### 33.5 The Osmotic Pendulum: A Testable Dynamics Proposal

The Osmotic Pendulum proposes recurrent excursions when phosphate disposal, sodium conservation, water handling and vascular support become mismatched under specified loading. Its defining claim is coupled feedback with particular phase relationships, not merely several responsive hormones or asynchronous peaks.

Different response times can produce stable compensation, sustained displacement, monotonic recovery or damped oscillation. Protocol-dependent PTH/FGF-23 results in Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) constrain the proposal without demonstrating a loop. Decaying overshoots differ from sustained cycles and repeated externally driven responses; stable or monotonic recovery weighs against oscillation while preserving broader phosphate–sodium interaction.

An observed withdrawal response gives the timing proposal a concrete starting point. In 18 healthy adults, 36 hours of neutral sodium-phosphate loading followed by 84 hours of observation produced persistently increased renal phosphate clearance and a circulating phosphate undershoot after loading stopped (Scanni et al., 2014). Sex-pooled results establish neither a sex difference nor a sodium–volume oscillation. A dynamic model should first reproduce such measured time courses, then test whether differing mineral and sodium-conserving response times prolong a balance or filling disturbance. Identical initial restoration assumptions and exchange of proximal/downstream parameters would help avoid building slower male recovery into the model. No such recovery simulation has been run here.

#### 33.6 Synthesis

The endocrine-mineral bridge is segmental: proximal phosphate disposal and distal sodium conservation interact with circulatory regulation. Timing, renal maturity and compensatory success could produce different trajectories, but hormone patterns do not identify filling or vascular function. A developmental contribution requires the local neural or glial recovery difficulty defined in Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2); recurrent oscillation is one possible outcome, not a necessary consequence of mineral handling.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_34"></a>

### 34 Adrenal Zonation (ZG, ZF, ZR), Developmental Plasticity, and Steroid Allocation in the Sodium-Struggle Hypothesis of Autism

#### 34.1 Adrenal zonation as a coordinated, adaptable system

The adrenal branch turns from renal capacity to the allocation of hormonal support. The adult human adrenal cortex partitions steroid production among the zona glomerulosa (ZG), zona fasciculata (ZF) and zona reticularis (ZR). Aldosterone from the ZG supports sodium conservation and potassium balance; cortisol from the ZF supports vascular responsiveness, metabolism and the response to stress. The ZR produces dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and its sulphate (DHEA-S). Its developmental timing matters: human postnatal tissue shows age-related changes in the enzymes and cofactors supporting androgen synthesis, including increasing reticularis cytochrome b5 and decreasing 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase expression during childhood (Suzuki et al., 2000). The three compartments cannot be treated as equally mature from birth.

This adrenal branch asks whether repeated sodium–water, filling or metabolic defence changes zonal composition, steroidogenic programmes or later responsiveness. Initially protective AVP–RAAS–cortisol recruitment could leave less flexibility for subsequent demands. Cortisol bias is one candidate outcome, not an obligatory response or the core neural-recovery mechanism.

#### 34.2 Developmental plasticity of adrenal zonation: lineage conversion, adaptation and persistence

Freedman et al. (2013) traced aldosterone-synthase-expressing ZG cells in mice and showed that their descendants populate the ZF during postnatal development and regeneration. Five-week-old mice also regenerated ZF tissue after two weeks of dexamethasone suppression followed by three to five weeks of recovery. These findings establish a cellular route for cortical renewal. They do not show that ordinary ZG-to-ZF conversion depletes ZG reserve or that developmental sodium stress locks the human gland into cortisol dominance. In these mice the principal glucocorticoid is corticosterone; human cortisol and ZR androgen capacity require their own evidence.

Sodium intake can alter adrenal architecture directly. In six-week-old pigs studied for 14 days, Vohra et al. (2020) compared low- and high-sodium diets with three animals per group. Sodium restriction increased plasma aldosterone 43-fold relative to the low-sodium group’s baseline, and ZG thickness was approximately twice that in the high-sodium group. This small experiment supports adaptive mineralocorticoid remodelling under a sodium-conservation demand. It also shows why a sodium challenge cannot automatically be assigned to ZF expansion or cortisol substitution; persistence after dietary recovery was not tested.

Potassium also regulates steroidogenic capacity, but suppression of synthesis must be separated from loss of lineage. Müller et al. (1989) restored aldosterone-forming activity in cultured rat ZG cells using high-potassium medium, including cells from potassium-restricted, sodium-loaded rats. The experimental restoration used 31 mmol/L potassium, far above physiological plasma concentrations. It demonstrates recoverable biosynthetic capacity in that preparation, rather than a human treatment effect or proof that every developmental deficit reverses. The proposed low-potassium “ratchet” therefore requires evidence of persistence beyond the initiating conditions.

The developmental architectural hypothesis makes two distinct predictions:

● Functional persistence: a developmental exposure leaves altered adrenal responsiveness after exposure and acute physiology recover. A cortisol-biased branch predicts disproportionate glucocorticoid support relative to need, not merely high random cortisol.

● Structural persistence: a sustained change in zonal abundance, identity or regenerative capacity explains the altered response. Reduced CYP11B2 alone does not establish loss of ZG cells.

Reversibility is an observed competing outcome. Taylor et al. (2020) activated Gq signalling throughout the adrenal cortex of adult transgenic mice, inducing aldosterone synthase in ZF cells and increasing aldosterone and blood pressure. After seven days of activation, ten days without the activating ligand returned the measured steroidogenic pattern, aldosterone and pressure to baseline. This was a partial functional change toward a ZG-like phenotype, not proof of complete reverse lineage conversion. It nevertheless rules out treating adult zonal reprogramming as intrinsically irreversible.

The distinctive claim is carry-over: an effective earlier defence changes capacity for a later demand. Restoration of both zonal structure and challenge response would constrain this adrenal-persistence branch.

#### 34.3 Steroid allocation within differentiated compartments

Cortisol and DHEA synthesis share biochemical precursors, but the producing cells have different enzyme programmes. In separated adult human adrenal cultures, Endoh et al. (1996) found that ZF cells converted added pregnenolone predominantly toward cortisol, whereas ZR cells produced mainly DHEA(S), with substantially lower 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase expression. This supports compartment-specific allocation. It does not establish a single circulating or gland-wide pool from which greater cortisol production necessarily withdraws substrate otherwise destined for DHEA.

The 17-hydroxypregnenolone branch point depends on local enzyme programmes, cofactors, delivery and flux. Repeated defence could change steroid allocation through these determinants, but a cortisol:DHEA-S ratio cannot establish substrate competition, production rates or zonal mass.

Two candidate changes in androgen capacity should therefore be tested separately:

● Functional change: altered precursor delivery, enzyme activity, sulphation or turnover changes DHEA/DHEA-S output without necessarily reducing ZR cell number. Production, clearance and peripheral interconversion remain distinct.

● Structural change: altered development or maintenance of the human ZR limits capacity. Its maturation provides a substrate for this proposal (Suzuki et al., 2000); mouse ZG-to-ZF renewal does not establish loss of human ZR reserve.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_34_4"></a>

#### 34.4 ASD-relevant steroid patterns: baseline, challenge and developmental context

Steroid findings make altered endocrine allocation a concrete question in autism, but the informative signal is the pattern within a defined age, sex and sampling condition. The studies below measure different parts of that pattern. They do not yet establish that recurrent sodium–perfusion defence produced it.

Adult baseline findings.

Strous et al. (2005) reported lower plasma DHEA-S in 15 medication-free autistic adults than in 13 controls (p\<0.05). The autistic group comprised 11 men and four women, aged 23.6±4.2 years; controls comprised six men and seven women, aged 30.3±4.1 years. Participants had been medication-free for at least one year. This is a positive, cohort-specific observation, with age and sex imbalance, rather than a general adult endocrine signature. A low circulating DHEA-S value alone does not identify precursor diversion or loss of zona reticularis tissue.

Prepubertal girls.

Jansakova et al. (2024) profiled 64 plasma steroids in 16 autistic girls and 16 controls, with mean ages of 4.69 and 4.00 years. Medication use was an exclusion criterion, and morning samples were collected after diagnostic assessment. Their age-adjusted results retained a selective pattern:

DHEA-S was 101 versus 34.5 nmol/L (p=0.007), and 17-hydroxypregnenolone was 3.26 versus 1.39 nmol/L (p=0.002), for autistic girls versus controls. No difference was detected in unconjugated DHEA (642 versus 682 pmol/L; p=0.77) or 17-hydroxyprogesterone (p=0.734). These are age-adjusted mean estimates, not individual diagnostic thresholds.

The combination is evidence for selective steroid differences, not uniform adrenal overactivity. Cortisol also showed no detected difference (p=0.412). Importantly, the DHEA-S:DHEA ratio itself did not differ significantly (p=0.107); the higher sulphated concentration therefore does not establish increased DHEA sulphation flux or successful buffering. Unconjugated DHEA is also not a measurement of the protein-unbound fraction.

Challenge responses add a different observation. Croonenberghs et al. (2008) studied 18 autistic males aged 13–19 years and 22 controls using oral 5-hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP; 4 mg/kg) and placebo. The placebo-day cortisol:DHEA-S ratio was higher in the autistic group (p=0.02), but 5-HTP produced a larger DHEA-S response and a smaller increase in the cortisol:DHEA-S ratio than in controls. Thus, baseline balance and stimulated responsiveness can diverge. This pharmacological test does not identify a sodium–volume exposure, adrenal zonal loss or a developmental depletion sequence.

#### 34.5 DHEA sulphation as a candidate buffer of endocrine output

Sulphation has a demonstrated capacity to alter androgen allocation. In a family with PAPSS2 variants, Oostdijk et al. (2015) combined cellular assays with an oral DHEA challenge: impaired sulphation was accompanied by increased conversion toward active androgens in two affected brothers and their mother. This supports a functional gate between DHEA and androgen activation. It does not show that the higher DHEA-S observed in autistic girls is an adaptive response to cortisol recruitment.

Increased sulphation could restrain immediate androgen activation while maintaining a sulphated pool during recurrent demand. This proposed “buffered adrenal readiness” separates production from immediate signalling; it is not established by high DHEA-S alone.

Reserve additionally requires uptake, desulphation and conversion to support later demand. Slower clearance can raise DHEA-S without buffering; impaired sulphation can lower it while increasing androgen activation, as the PAPSS2 result illustrates.

#### 34.6 Sex and developmental timing: a longitudinal buffering hypothesis

The girls’ finding does not establish female-specific protection or a later decline. In a separate cross-sectional study, Corbett et al. (2025) examined morning salivary hormones in 112 autistic and 96 comparison girls aged 6–12 years and detected no diagnostic differences in the sampled DHEA-S, estradiol and testosterone profiles across age or pubertal stage. The different ages and sample matrix preclude treating this as a direct replication of the younger plasma cohort, but it constrains a general claim of elevated DHEA-S in autistic girls.

Directional prediction.

The proposed sex difference is that, at matched developmental stage and physiological demand, girls may route a larger fraction of DHEA into sulphation and show a smaller excursion in selected downstream androgen outputs than boys. This prediction requires both sexes in the same design. Comparing a young female sample with an older male sample cannot demonstrate it.

Age, pubertal stage and current exposure affect these ratios, which can change through either component without identifying developmental neurotoxicity.

The proposed developmental sequence is an initially increased sulphated pool followed by reduced output or diminished reserve if the relevant demand persists. Opposite findings in unrelated cohorts cannot establish that history; stable or increasing reserve despite persistent burden would weigh against it.

The longitudinal proposal therefore concerns defence history changing endocrine capacity beyond ordinary maturation and current stress; the observed between-cohort differences do not supply that history.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_34_7"></a>

#### 34.7 Steroid sulphatase: local steroid availability, OXTR and birth-window modifiers

Steroid sulphatase (STS) removes sulphate from steroid substrates and can thereby modify local steroid availability. This is distinct from DHEA sulphation and does not itself measure the proposed adrenal buffer. Human STS is X-linked, whereas its Y-linked homologue is a pseudogene (Yen et al., 1988). STS escapes X-chromosome inactivation, providing a basis for higher female dosage. Ordinary male hemizygosity, with one functional copy, is distinct from pathological STS deficiency. In freshly isolated term-placental cytotrophoblasts, STS activity was about 1.7-fold higher in female-derived cells and increased during culture only in those cells (Ugele and Regemann, 2000). Subsequent conversion of desulphated substrates requires other enzymes. Human lung tissue converted oestrone sulphate to oestrone and then oestradiol, whereas cultured pulmonary arterial endothelial cells lacked detectable STS activity (Milewich et al., 1983). Oestradiol increased glutathione peroxidase (GPx) and manganese-superoxide-dismutase expression and reduced peroxide levels in MCF-7 mammary tumour cells (Borrás et al., 2005). These separate components motivate a local steroid–antioxidant hypothesis, not a demonstrated neonatal pathway or conversion of sulphate into GSH.

Local steroid availability and tissue responsiveness are the proposed modifiers; universally higher circulating oestradiol in female fetuses is not required. A term cord study reported higher male oestradiol with similar DHEA-S, while mass-spectrometric analysis of 860 archived mixed arterial/venous cord samples found no sex difference in four oestrogens (Simmons et al., 1994; Hickey et al., 2014). Placental enzyme activity and cord concentrations cannot substitute for local steroid production, receptor responses or antioxidant effects in the tissue and developmental window of interest. The proposed STS contribution to the redox differences in Section [40.4](#ss_p10_sec_40_4) remains testable and is not required for those observations or the GSH-processing component in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7).

Skin experiments provide a second STS-related route through OXTR expression and redox regulation. STS knockdown reduced OXTR transcript expression in primary keratinocytes derived from neonatal foreskin; reduced OXTR immunostaining was also observed in reconstructed skin models and skin from three people with recessive X-linked ichthyosis ([McGeoghan et al., 2023](#ss_revsyn3_ref_McGeoghan2023)). Separately, OXTR knockdown increased oxidant-sensitive fluorescence in human skin cells. A cellular thiol signal used to estimate reduced GSH fell significantly in fibroblasts but only slightly in keratinocytes at baseline, with further depletion after ultraviolet exposure ([Deing et al., 2013](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Deing2013)). These are compatible component findings rather than a measured STS-to-GSH sequence.

The proposed connection is that reduced STS-dependent OXTR expression could limit a local redox response, whereas higher STS activity could modify resilience where this coupling operates. A discriminating test would ask whether restoring OXTR after STS reduction restores the redox response, while distinguishing steroid availability and other STS-dependent changes. Receptor abundance, ligand responsiveness and GSH availability are separate measurements. Extension from skin to placental, vascular, renal, neural or glial tissue requires evidence in each relevant compartment; skin findings do not establish the renal AVP-processing constraint in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7).

Placental STS deficiency offers a separate candidate route into birth-window demand through altered steroid availability and labour course. [Dreyer et al. (2018)](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Dreyer2018) described two affected male births with slow labour progress despite oxytocin and subsequent caesarean delivery; one pregnancy had very low maternal oestriol. These histories motivate investigating whether placental steroid metabolism modifies labour exposure and subsequent recovery. Uterine OXTR, sodium–water balance and AVP were not measured, so the skin expression result cannot supply the obstetric mechanism.

Genetic observations require a distinction between STS and neighbouring genes. Among 25 boys with X-linked ichthyosis, all five autism-spectrum or related language/communication cases carried larger deletions including NLGN4X; none occurred with typical deletions or presumed STS point mutations ([Kent et al., 2008](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Kent2008)). A later survey found elevated autism-related traits in the broader XLI sample, but self- or parent-reported diagnoses and incomplete genotype information did not isolate an STS effect ([Chatterjee et al., 2016](#ss_revsyn3_ref_Chatterjee2016)). These findings neither establish isolated STS deficiency as an ASD cause nor exclude every possible modifying contribution.

The Sodium-Struggle prediction is that a defined difference in STS activity changes local steroid or OXTR-dependent responses, or the birth exposure, sufficiently to modify compensation and recovery. Higher female activity remains a testable developmental modifier rather than guaranteed protection. A neural developmental explanation still requires the local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery intermediary; skin and other peripheral effects may remain parallel consequences. Preserved recovery through effective buffering would weigh against this proposed contribution under the specified conditions.

#### 34.8 Integrative Sodium-Struggle synthesis: an adrenal memory of defence

This adrenal branch proposes that repeated sodium–water, filling or metabolic defence can leave lasting endocrine reweighting. The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad protects immediate stability; its proposed developmental cost is altered functional or structural capacity after the initiating exposure resolves, without a compulsory osmotic direction or simultaneous hormone signature.

A plastic gland provides the supported starting point for the adrenal proposal. The separate STS branch concerns tissue-specific steroid availability, OXTR expression or birth exposure. Either branch could modify demands on sodium–volume defence or remain peripheral; a contribution to autism still requires the local neural developmental intermediary. Successful restoration of zonal function, maintained endocrine reserve or effective local buffering would constrain the corresponding persistence or modifier claim.

Scope of the potassium proposal: extracellular potassium, dietary intake, aldosterone synthesis and ZG lineage are different measurements. The experiments identify potassium as a regulator of steroidogenic activity; they do not establish developmental lineage damage or an autism treatment.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35"></a>

### 35 Membrane Defence and Sterol Supply: Reconciling Low and High Circulating Cholesterol in ASD

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35_1"></a>

#### 35.1 Membrane Cholesterol, Mechanical Protection and Volume Recovery

Steroid production is one demand on cholesterol; membrane protection and restoration provide another. Cholesterol-dependent membrane adaptation is proposed here as one structural arm of sodium–volume defence. A membrane can be adequate at baseline yet face demands beyond its usual reserve during a rapid change in extracellular tonicity. Its composition and organisation can influence water permeability, available surface area and resistance to rupture. These functions can protect the cell without necessarily accelerating restoration of its volume. The developmental question is whether repeated recruitment and rebuilding of this protection change the conditions under which tissue matures.

At the bilayer itself, composition can alter water movement without changing every mechanical property. In protein-free dioleoylphosphatidylcholine (DOPC) vesicles, increasing cholesterol from 0 to 40 mol% reduced water permeability from 15.8 to 6.8 × 10⁻³ cm/s during hypertonic shrinkage, without increasing the measured bending modulus (Mathai et al., 2008). Reconstituted AQP4 channels also showed lipid-dependent water permeability (Tong et al., 2012). These experiments support a membrane-level influence on water flux. Slower water entry, however, does not remove the osmotic driving force, and neither experiment establishes improved volume recovery in developing neurons or glia.

Protection against rupture has direct experimental support. Manipulating cholesterol changed erythrocyte osmotic fragility: depletion increased it and enrichment reduced it (Sagawa and Shiraki, 1980). In cultured human red cells, cholesterol-rich lipid supplementation improved osmotic resistance despite broadly preserved shear deformability; supplementation was not a pure-cholesterol rescue (Bernecker et al., 2019). Cooper et al. (1975) found that enrichment increased estimated red-cell surface area and allowed greater swelling before lysis, while larger enrichment impaired deformability. Needham and Nunn (1990) likewise found composition-dependent bilayer toughness, with a maximum near 40 mol% cholesterol in their SOPC mixture. Resistance to lysis, deformability and lipid composition therefore describe distinct aspects of protection.

Volume recovery can move differently. In CHO cells exposed to 300→210 mOsm medium, approximately 50% cholesterol depletion reduced peak swelling and increased ten-minute volume recovery from about 41% to 65%; enrichment did not improve recovery (Kowalsky et al., 2011). Depletion increased whole-cell stiffness, and actin stabilisation also facilitated recovery. This result challenges a universal enrichment-to-better-recovery claim. It does not show that cholesterol always increases rupture risk, or that endogenous stress-induced cholesterol accumulation caused a cost. Bilayer mechanics and the mechanics of an intact cell are different measurements.

Caveolae provide a concrete protection-and-restoration mechanism. Sinha et al. (2011) showed that osmotic swelling or stretching flattened these membrane invaginations, supplying surface area and buffering tension without requiring ATP or actin remodelling for the initial response. Reassembly after stress release required ATP and was regulated by actin dynamics. This supports a rapid defence followed by an active reset. It does not demonstrate cholesterol consumption during flattening, a net synthesis requirement, or a quantified cumulative energetic deficit. The osmotic experiments included 30- and 150-mOsm challenges; transfer to developmental exposure remains to be tested.

Osmotic stress can also reach sterol-regulatory machinery. Lee and Ye (2004) found that hypotonic stress inhibited protein synthesis, depleted rapidly turning-over Insig-1 and permitted SREBP-2 processing despite sterol-mediated inhibition. This is a direct link between osmotic conditions and sterol regulation. The authors nevertheless reported no increase in cholesterol or fatty-acid synthesis in their stress experiments, with those data not shown. SREBP activation therefore cannot be treated as demonstrated protective cholesterol accumulation. Induction of a regulatory response and completion of a beneficial membrane adaptation are separate steps.

Membrane vulnerability also depends on the oxidation state of its lipids. Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are normal membrane constituents, but their susceptible acyl chains provide substrates for lipid peroxidation. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) can initiate peroxidation of PUFAs already incorporated into membranes when local oxidative attack exceeds defence and repair; ingestion of pre-oxidised oil is not required. In molecular simulations, specified oxidised linoleate chains bent towards the aqueous interface and altered bilayer structure and water permeability (Wong-Ekkabut et al., 2007). These changes depend on the oxidation product and membrane composition, rather than making every oxidised membrane uniformly leaky.

Cell experiments establish a further connection to osmotic injury. In ferroptosis models, lipid peroxidation preceded membrane damage and calcium entry, while osmoprotectants delayed cell rupture without preventing lipid peroxidation (Pedrera et al., 2021). Oxidative damage can therefore compromise a membrane’s ability to maintain the ionic conditions governing water movement. Increased water permeability alone does not create an osmotic gradient. These severe injury experiments motivate, but do not establish, impaired recovery in surviving developing neurons or glia.

Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) limits this damage by reducing lipid hydroperoxides to lipid alcohols. Each reaction oxidises two reduced-glutathione (GSH) molecules to glutathione disulfide (GSSG); glutathione reductase uses NADPH to regenerate GSH (Stolwijk et al., 2020). Protection therefore requires a maintained supply of reducing equivalents, rather than an inexhaustible GSH reserve. In human airway epithelial cells, inflammatory stimulation increased lipid-hydroperoxide production, lowered intracellular GSH and increased extracellular GSSG (Nagasaki et al., 2022). Sustained limitation becomes possible when antioxidant demand and losses exceed recycling and synthesis. This supplies a conditional connection to GSH-sensitive AVP processing in Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7).

Competition between functions is local and conditional: peroxide removal, conjugation or loss must exceed GSH recycling and synthesis at the relevant site. Endothelial, renal and neural pools are not one shared reserve. A transient challenge could strain more than one compartment, but the vascular and AVP-processing effects in Sections [16.8.2](#ss_p10_sec_16_8_2) and [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) require separate evidence.

The endothelial glycocalyx adds a distinct vascular interface: a hydrated carbohydrate-rich layer on the blood-facing cell surface. Its shear-sensing and water/protein-barrier functions differ from the bilayer’s control of transmembrane gradients. Hydrogen peroxide reduced surface heparan sulphate and increased albumin passage in cultured human glomerular endothelial cells (Singh et al., 2013). In perfused rat microvessels, removing sialic acids reduced glycocalyx depth and changed water and albumin permeability (Betteridge et al., 2017). Removing heparan sulphate from cultured endothelial cells also blocked shear-induced NO production while preserving the response to bradykinin (Florian et al., 2003). These findings connect surface structure to vascular function without implying loss of all NO signalling. Local shear transduction does not itself identify an afferent filling-signal defect (Tables [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) and [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1)). Glycocalyx and bilayer injury could interact or occur in parallel; neither must precede the other. Oxidised dietary lipids and circulating oxidised LDL are different exposures. A circulating shedding marker alone cannot identify the tissue source or establish impaired neural recovery. The proposed convergence is conditional: altered vascular permeability or flow regulation must measurably compromise filling or delivery, while cellular membrane dysfunction must impair ionic or volume recovery (Sections [16.3](#ss_p10_sec_16_3), [21.5.2](#ss_p10_sec_21_5_2), and [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)). Direct neural membrane injury need not first produce systemic vascular failure.

Direct glutathione interventions support distinct protective components. In bovine aortic endothelial cells, depletion of total glutathione equivalents increased injury from photoperoxidised human LDL. Selenium-deficient cells were also more vulnerable despite higher total glutathione, showing that pool size cannot substitute for peroxide-processing competence (Thomas et al., 1993). In cultured human adipose microvascular endothelial cells, hydrogen peroxide or the GSH-synthesis inhibitor buthionine sulfoximine caused glycocalyx loss and syndecan-1 shedding (Ali et al., 2019). The latter experiment did not quantify the GSH pool or report donor sex or age. These findings support investigating endothelial protection as a way to limit an upstream filling or delivery disturbance; they do not measure sodium storage, infant sex differences or the separate renal AVP-processing route. The neonatal antioxidant comparisons in Section [40.4](#ss_p10_sec_40_4) provide a developmental rationale for that investigation.

A membrane can survive the first challenge yet remain less ready for the next. The Sodium Struggle proposes that repeated demand becomes developmentally consequential when restoration of membrane organisation, ion balance and signalling capacity remains unfinished during neural and glial calibration. A compensatory response must confer a demonstrated benefit; normal recovery before renewed demand would weigh against this membrane-recovery branch.

#### 35.2 Interpretation of Circulating Lipid Panels

Circulating lipids do not measure sterol available to a particular membrane. Uptake, intracellular delivery and local turnover can diverge from total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C or triglycerides; the developmental question is usable sterol and the capacity to maintain it.

There is a human lipid signal to explain. Benachenhou et al. (2019) reported hypocholesterolaemia in 23% of 79 ASD participants in a retrospective study with 79 matched controls. Tierney et al. (2021) found cholesterol below the age- and sex-specific fifth centile in 131 of 570 affected AGRE participants from multiplex autism families. A broader claims analysis associated ASD with dyslipidaemia even in a within-family comparison of 23,837 families, OR 1.76 (95% CI 1.61–1.92; Luo et al., 2020). These observations support lipid-associated heterogeneity. They did not measure osmotic exposure, membrane delivery or compensatory mediation; the claims composite also does not specify a single lipid direction.

Local sterol handling can affect membrane response without a corresponding change in total cholesterol. Brain synaptosomal fractions from nine-month-old efavirenz-treated 5XFAD mice showed less NaCl-dependent light scattering, interpreted as greater resistance to osmotic shrinkage; Cyp46a1 deletion shifted the response oppositely. Male fraction cholesterol remained unchanged, although female concentrations changed (Petrov et al., 2020). This adult ex vivo result makes local handling a concrete candidate, while leaving volume recovery and developmental consequences untested.

#### 35.3 Three Candidate Developmental Lipid Trajectories

Membrane construction through expansion, synaptogenesis, myelination and signalling organisation could compete with repeated defence and restoration. The additional demand may involve lipid redistribution, surface-reservoir rebuilding or solute recovery rather than cholesterol enrichment. Developmental cost arises only where these combined requirements exceed accessible capacity.

The limiting capacity may be synthesis or local delivery, enterohepatic recycling, or lipoprotein production and clearance, modified by endocrine demand and inflammation. Three candidate trajectories are considered separately: persistent low cholesterol (Section [35.4](#ss_p10_sec_35_4)), persistent high cholesterol with proposed conservation (Section [35.5](#ss_p10_sec_35_5)), and documented low early values followed by high values (Section [35.6](#ss_p10_sec_35_6)). Each requires its own history, functional endpoint and limiting test; a circulating value alone cannot identify a defence state. Complete adaptation without lasting lipid dysregulation remains a valid outcome.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35_4"></a>

#### 35.4 Persistent Low Cholesterol and Limited Tissue Access

Low circulating cholesterol can accompany limited intake, absorption or synthesis, or increased clearance and use. Tissue access can also fail with high circulating values. The following mechanisms locate these supply–demand mismatches.

##### 35.4.1 Steroidogenic Demand and Developmental Sterol Compartments

The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad can recruit steroidogenic demand, but resource competition must be located. Across treatment-to-delivery intervals in preterm infants exposed antenatally to betamethasone, lower cord adrenal steroids were followed by higher cord cholesterol, consistent with adrenal utilisation contributing to the circulating pool; altered synthesis remained an alternative (Parker et al., 1996). This is a human endocrine–sterol connection, not evidence that cortisol production deprives the brain. In a Dhcr7-null mouse origin study, maternal supply contributed early, but local production accounted for about 90% of brain sterols by birth (Tint et al., 2006). The developmental-cost proposal requires a measured limitation in the relevant tissue or a demonstrated transfer or signalling bridge. A shared precursor does not make all tissues one shared supply pool.

##### 35.4.2 Sodium-Dependent Bile-Acid Reclamation Impairment

ASBT, encoded by SLC10A2, reclaims bile acids using sodium-dependent transport. Human ASBT in voltage-clamped cells is sensitive to sodium and membrane potential, with results consistent with two sodium ions per bile acid (Weinman et al., 1998). A disturbed enterocyte gradient or transporter can therefore impair reclamation, but plasma sodium does not measure the apical gradient, and increased pump demand does not itself prove gradient failure. Human SLC10A2 mutations can cause bile-acid malabsorption and low plasma cholesterol (Oelkers et al., 1997). Compensation changes the systemic outcome: Slc10a2-null mice had an approximately 80% smaller bile-acid pool and about 20% lower cholesterol absorption, yet total plasma cholesterol rose slightly through HDL, with VLDL and LDL unchanged (Dawson et al., 2003). This remains a sodium–sterol interface worth testing through uptake, faecal loss, hepatic replacement and lipoprotein flux, rather than an assumed double depletion.

Defence signalling can also support this interface. Methylprednisolone restored impaired ASBT uptake and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity in chronically inflamed rabbit ileum (Coon et al., 2010). That pharmacological rescue does not establish an equivalent endogenous cortisol effect, but it prevents steroid action from being treated only as a drain on sterol availability.

##### 35.4.3 Inflammation and Compartment-Specific Sterol Routing

Inflammation can change sterol routing without uniformly reducing access. IL-6 increased LDLR expression and LDL binding, internalisation and degradation in HepG2 cells (Gierens et al., 2000). Increased hepatic uptake could lower circulating LDL while improving hepatic access; it would not establish delivery to the developing brain. The proposed vulnerability is a mismatch between routing and need in a specified compartment. Receptor abundance, uptake across a cell surface, passage across a tissue barrier and arrival at the target membrane must therefore be distinguished, rather than bundled into an IL-6/VEGF deprivation cascade.

An osmotic contribution to hepatic uptake is experimentally accessible. In cholesterol-deficient C3A culture, 24 h at 27.75 mM glucose or 5.55 mM glucose plus 22 mM mannitol increased fluorescent LDL internalisation 1.66- and 1.91-fold, respectively. With longer exposure, LDLR transcripts fell while total receptor protein remained broadly stable (Wooten et al., 2014). The mannitol comparison supports an osmotic contribution and shows why function cannot be read from transcript abundance. This cancer-derived cell experiment did not test membrane protection, circulating LDL direction or persistence after withdrawal.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35_4_4"></a>

##### 35.4.4 Intrinsic Sterol Constraints: Membrane Recovery and Developmental Signalling

Intrinsic sterol constraints provide a testable susceptibility route. DHCR7 deficiency in Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome changes both cholesterol availability and its precursor, 7-dehydrocholesterol (7-DHC). The phenotype cannot be reduced to a uniformly softer membrane: 7-DHC supported raft formation in model membranes and treated rat brains, while raft protein composition changed (Keller et al., 2004). SLOS skin fibroblasts showed altered caveolar sterols and BKCa channel function despite preserved caveolar morphology (Ren et al., 2011). These findings support altered membrane signalling, not a demonstrated osmotic-recovery defect. The proposed extension is that a specified sterol constraint increases the cost or disrupts the timing of recovery under matched osmotic demand, with consequences for developmental signalling and reserve. More cholesterol need not improve every endpoint.

Sterol metabolism can also alter the timing of neurogenesis through a defined signalling route. Tomita et al. (2022) found that DHCR7 deficiency increased 7-DHC-derived oxysterols and accelerated neurogenesis, depleting cortical precursors in mouse and human models. The oxysterol 3β,5α-dihydroxycholest-7-en-6-one (DHCEO) increased glucocorticoid-receptor (GR) and TrkB phosphorylation in human neural precursors without added GR ligands or neurotrophins. Interventions that inhibited GR or TrkB–MEK signalling, and antioxidant treatment, prevented premature neurogenesis in the tested neural precursors; adding cholesterol as LDL did not. Direct DHCEO binding to GR was proposed with docking support, rather than demonstrated by a binding assay. This connects local sterol oxidation to receptor-dependent developmental timing without requiring an inferred rise in circulating cortisol. It identifies premature differentiation, not persistence of every cell in an immature state, and it does not establish ionic or cellular-volume recovery mediation.

The sterol branch has two separable entry points: membrane-dependent susceptibility during challenge and oxysterol-dependent developmental signalling. The Sodium-Struggle proposal is that altered membrane handling changes recovery and thereby the conditions under which neurogenesis proceeds. Preserved relevant recovery during the causal interval would favour an independent signalling route; an antioxidant or GR-directed rescue alone cannot distinguish these causal orders.

Table [35.1](#ss_p10_table_35_1) extends the susceptibility question from a gene name to an allele and a measured function. It includes positive and negative osmotic results, delivery defects and engineered regulatory perturbations. These are mechanistic comparators, not new ASD-gene assignments or additions to the 42/102 count.

##### 35.4.5 Why Low Circulating Cholesterol Can Persist

Persistent low cholesterol may reflect a continuing supply or utilisation constraint. Acquired persistence instead requires altered regulation after the initiating constraint and acute physiology recover. In either case, the developmental concern is demand exceeding accessible supply in the affected tissue. The test is whether correction of the specified constraint restores usable sterol and relevant membrane recovery. Persistently low circulating values with adequate tissue delivery and recovery would weigh against the proposed membrane limitation, even though the lipid finding itself remains real.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35_5"></a>

#### 35.5 High Cholesterol and Dyslipidaemia: The Conservation Hypothesis

The conservation proposal is that repeated membrane-maintenance demand favours sterol retention or supply, potentially continuing after the need ends. Its defining endpoint is useful local protection, not elevated circulating cholesterol alone.

##### 35.5.1 Membrane Defence Adaptation

The systemic extension requires circulating supply to improve membrane delivery and protection. Higher LDL caused by reduced clearance would not establish that benefit.

Renal acquired cytoresistance provides a functional precedent for protective sterol remodelling: membrane cholesterol rose by 25–50% after injury, and normalising it increased tubular injury susceptibility (Zager et al., 1999). Overnight water withdrawal also increased renal cholesterol esters, especially in the medulla, without increasing free cholesterol; separate injury cohorts retained elevated esters for two weeks while renal impairment persisted (Zager et al., 2001). These findings support local stress-responsive sterol handling, without demonstrating hepatic LDL conservation or persistence after completed osmotic recovery.

Location can determine whether retained cholesterol helps. In tumour-cell ferroptosis experiments, blocking NPC1 increased lysosomal cholesterol accumulation while reducing the protection supplied by LDL (Zhao et al., 2023). This is a delivery and lipid-peroxidation example, not an osmotic experiment: more intracellular cholesterol did not mean more useful cholesterol at the site of protection.

##### 35.5.2 Developmental Hysteresis

In this branch, acquired persistence would be altered membrane composition or sterol handling after challenge and physiological recovery. Permeability, signalling and mechanical effects need not move together; a link to circulating lipid regulation is an additional step. A functional test must relate the candidate change to sterol delivery, membrane protection and recovery, then establish whether it remains after exposure and acute physiology have resolved. High circulating LDL without improved local delivery would weaken the protective-conservation interpretation; normalisation after recovery would favour reversible adaptation.

Developmental sterol regulation can outlast an initiating exposure. Rats exposed to 8% rather than 20% maternal dietary protein through gestation and lactation had approximately 30% higher circulating and hepatic cholesterol in males at day 130 despite return to the control diet at day 21; females lacked the adult elevation. Reduced hepatic CYP7A1 and repressive promoter histone changes implicated cholesterol disposal to bile acids, while restoration of the control diet at birth prevented the phenotype (Sohi et al., 2011). This is a timing-dependent nutritional precedent for lasting regulation. It does not establish osmotic initiation, complete physiological recovery or low cholesterol followed by high cholesterol.

Nor does stronger synthesis-related regulation necessarily produce higher cholesterol. Protein-restricted piglets had lower serum and liver cholesterol at weaning despite increased SREBP2, HMGCR activity and CYP7A1 transcription (Cong et al., 2012). They were not followed after withdrawal into adulthood. Together, these experiments justify testing developmental sterol regulation while requiring net production, disposal and delivery to be measured separately. Whether repeated osmotic challenges leave a hepatic sterol phenotype after exposure and acute physiology have recovered remains untested in the evidence assembled here.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35_6"></a>

#### 35.6 Low Early, Then High Later: Scarcity Followed by Conservation

The low-early/high-later branch proposes that documented shortage or high utilisation recruits conservation that remains elevated after supply improves. The resulting mismatch could raise circulating cholesterol. Different age groups or an assumed earlier shortage cannot establish this within-person sequence.

##### 35.6.1 Longitudinal Test

This trajectory requires serial measurements showing low early values, correction of the proposed supply or demand constraint, and later high values within the same individuals, together with evidence of persistent conservation or reduced disposal. Failure to observe the predicted transition would weaken that trajectory; normalisation of handling after recovery would weaken its persistence component. The later circulating increase must still be related to local delivery and protection rather than assumed to be beneficial.

#### 35.7 Shared Interpretation and Exposure Conditions

##### 35.7.1 A Shared Question, Distinct Routes

The shared question is whether a specified challenge changes local membrane protection or recovery enough to affect development. Supply/access limitation and altered production/clearance are different mechanisms, even when they produce similar circulating values.

##### 35.7.2 Endocrine Modulation and Lipid Measurements

The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad may modify substrate use and sterol demand during compensation; its three arms need not imply one lipid signature. A conservation hypothesis must distinguish production from clearance, measure ApoB separately from LDL-C, and assess function rather than infer reverse transport from HDL-C. In an adult primary study, HDL-C and ApoA1 explained less than 40% of variation in ex vivo macrophage cholesterol-efflux capacity (Khera et al., 2011); that assay is itself distinct from whole-body reverse-transport flux. The proposed trade-off remains protective supply during challenge with possible costs if altered regulation persists. A low-HDL or high-LDL pattern alone cannot identify that history.

##### 35.7.3 Laboratory Interpretive Note

Sufficiently lipaemic samples can yield falsely low sodium with indirect ion-selective electrodes; direct-ISE measurement helps distinguish this analytical effect (Koch et al., 2021). Pseudohyponatraemia does not itself demonstrate hypotonicity. Any proposed lipid–osmotic association therefore needs the sodium method and independent assessment of tonicity, rather than treating an apparent low value as exposure.

##### 35.7.4 Mixed Cohorts and Timepoints

Cross-sectional cohorts differ in age, diet, medication exposure, gastrointestinal disease, endocrine state and genetic background. Such differences can contribute to divergent lipid findings, but they do not show that cohorts represent successive stages of one process. Tierney et al. (2021), for example, compared different participants across age bins; those data do not establish the proposed within-person transition. Persistence, continuing constraint and independent lipid disorders remain distinguishable explanations.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_35_7_5"></a>

##### 35.7.5 Osmotic and Endocrine Exposure Modifiers

The exposure proposal is that more frequent or poorly recovered osmotic challenges could reveal a sterol-dependent limitation that remains quiet under ordinary conditions. This requires measured exposure and impaired protection or recovery at the relevant membrane. It does not establish that modern environments are uniformly more dilutional or that every cholesterol-limited membrane swells more.

A specified endocrine-active exposure can also change lipid regulation. Ke et al. (2016) supplied dams with 2.5 µg/L BPA water from delivery through lactation, then continued the same exposure in male offspring after weaning until assessment at eight weeks or ten months. Hepatic cholesterol increased at both ages; older mice also accumulated triglycerides, with altered Srebf1/Srebf2 expression and promoter methylation. This provides a concrete exposure–regulation connection. Because dosing continued, it does not demonstrate persistence after withdrawal, and neither membrane reinforcement nor an initiating osmotic challenge was measured.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_36"></a>

### 36 Receptor and Signalling Imprinting in Coupled Osmotic–Volume Defence

The Sodium Struggle also proposes a lasting change in response architecture: repeated sodium, volume or perfusion challenges could alter receptor balance, coupling, trafficking, transport commitments or recruitment thresholds. These changes provide candidate persistence mechanisms alongside the membrane adaptations considered above.

The proposed imprint is a different response to a matched later input because earlier defence altered local regulation. It can persist after the initiating disturbance resolves without a continuously abnormal laboratory value. Section [21.6](#ss_p10_sec_21_6) summarises the cross-system read-outs; this section develops the receptor-specific exposure, response and recovery comparisons.

Non-linear trajectories are possible, but gain-up, down-regulation and rebound are different predictions. For each branch, specify the receptor, tissue, exposure, expected direction and post-exposure interval before interpreting the result. An overshoot–recoil account requires the predicted high-response phase followed by the predicted blunted phase in the same trajectory; a later low response cannot retrospectively establish an earlier high one.

#### 36.1 Interpretive Drift and Response Geometry

Receptor imprinting denotes a lasting change in how a tissue translates a ligand, potentially through receptor abundance, subtype balance, surface availability or coupling. Cell-state imprinting is broader and can include altered feedback or recruitment thresholds. The distinction from ordinary desensitisation is empirical: the altered functional response must remain after exposure cessation and sufficient recovery, beyond the prespecified transient-adaptation interval. Receptor abundance alone does not measure functional gain.

Interpretive drift is the predicted change in a tissue’s response curve: disproportionate output under challenge after recovery, rather than continuous activation or a diagnostic resting value.

#### 36.2 Multivariate Fetal Calibration

The proposed developmental calibration is multivariate. Osmotic and ionic conditions, filling and pressure, perfusion, AVP–RAAS–cortisol recruitment, inflammation and sympathetic activity can provide different inputs. The maternal and fetal compartments must be distinguished: maternal thresholds or circulating concentrations do not specify fetal exposure or local receptor response. A multivariate account still requires the particular exposure pattern and its developmental intermediary to be measured.

The proposed memory concerns the pattern of challenge, defence and recovery. Recurrence with unfinished recovery should predict later response beyond the exposure average or current physiology; a hormone fluctuation alone is not a programming event.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_36_3"></a>

#### 36.3 Developmental Persistence and Overshoot–Recoil Dynamics

Lasting developmental regulation has experimental precedents. In rats, early maternal-care differences were associated with hippocampal GR-promoter regulation, GR expression and adult HPA responses; cross-fostering and an adult epigenetic intervention altered the effects (Weaver et al., 2004). In mice, early-life stress left sustained hypothalamic Avp expression and endocrine changes linked to altered regulatory-region methylation (Murgatroyd et al., 2009). The former concerns receptor regulation and feedback; the latter concerns ligand production. These studies support biological persistence and potential reversibility, but do not establish sodium–volume mediation or an autism mechanism.

The specific Sodium-Struggle prediction is a persistent response change after a documented developmental defence or recovery burden has resolved. Altered activation threshold, dose–response slope, maximum response and termination time are different forms of that change. Continuing exposure alone does not establish acquired persistent gain.

Scarcity-calibrated sensitivity is one directional branch: reduced or intermittent effective signalling is predicted to precede increased response to a matched input. Recoil is a second branch requiring a documented subsequent response reduction after a specified signal change. Increased secretion, receptor internalisation, low receptor abundance and weakened feedback can affect system output differently. They must not be treated as interchangeable evidence of the same gain change.

#### 36.4 Tissue-Specific Interpretation of Shared Signals

Endocrine broadcasts are systemic, but response architecture is local. Receptor mixtures, steroid metabolism, downstream effectors and energetic reserve differ among brain, vessels and kidney. The hypothesis predicts that a shared challenge can therefore leave different tissue responses. Neural salience, vascular contraction and renal water conservation are distinct endpoints; evidence in one compartment does not establish imprinting in another.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_36_5"></a>

#### 36.5 Vasopressin as an Archetypal Discordant Ligand

<a name="ss_p10_sec_36_5_1"></a>

##### 36.5.1 Exposure and receptor function

The V1a, V1b and V2 pathways in Section [21.4](#ss_p10_sec_21_4) illustrate discordant demands: pressure may need support while excess free water must be shed, and central salience-related responses may diverge from renal or vascular needs.

The proposed imprint concerns local receptor composition, coupling and exposure timing, including pulsatility and relation to RAAS or cortisol. Ordinary circulating AVP could coexist with altered tissue response curves; uniform central AVP excess is not required.

AVP can also activate oxytocin receptors (OXTR), so receptor occupancy does not by itself imply blockade of oxytocin. AVP acted as a partial agonist at human OXTR in a receptor-mutagenesis study ([Chini et al., 1996](#ss_ref_chini_1996)). A separate study in Chinese hamster ovary cells expressing human OXTR found AVP less potent than oxytocin for calcium mobilisation ([Taylor et al., 2018](#ss_ref_taylor_2018)). Lower potency concerns the concentration needed for a response, whereas partial agonism concerns the maximum response attainable in the tested system. Neither finding establishes that AVP reduces the combined response during simultaneous exposure to both peptides; that requires a functional comparison under the relevant concentrations and receptor context.

Prior AVP exposure could alter subsequent oxytocin responsiveness through homologous OXTR desensitisation. In mouse gonadotrope-derived αT3-1 cells, brief AVP stimulation prevented a subsequent oxytocin calcium response while preserving the GnRH response, which the authors interpreted as rapid homologous OXTR desensitisation ([Evans et al., 1997](#ss_ref_evans_1997)). This supports testing an exposure-dependent reduction in oxytocin responsiveness, but does not establish persistent neuronal receptor loss or a human clinical syndrome. Within the present hypothesis, a lower response to matched oxytocin after documented AVP exposure would need to be distinguished from concurrent ligand competition and reduced oxytocin secretion. Persistence after AVP removal is an additional prediction to test, not a finding established here. Renal V2 interactions do not establish brain OXTR responsiveness.

AVP exposure can also reduce receptor availability at the cell surface in a transfected model. In HEK-293 cells transiently expressing HA-tagged OXTR, 100 nM AVP for 30 minutes at 37 °C reduced surface receptor immunoreactivity ([Smith et al., 2006](#ss_p4_ref_Smith2006)). The same study’s calcium-response and pathway experiments used oxytocin. The AVP result supports a trafficking component, without establishing permanent loss of receptor expression or a lasting response defect. Whether relevant fetal neural or renal tissue responds similarly requires its own exposure and functional measurements.

Neuronal experiments supply a further component of this proposed exposure-response chain. Oxytocin-receptor agonists produced desensitisation in adult mouse brain slices, and TGOT, a selective OXTR agonist, induced receptor internalisation in cultured mouse neurons (George et al., 2024). These experiments used oxytocin or TGOT, rather than AVP. Taken together with the AVP experiments above, they justify testing whether sufficient local AVP exposure changes subsequent neuronal oxytocin responsiveness through receptor desensitisation and trafficking. Desensitisation denotes reduced responsiveness; internalisation denotes redistribution away from the cell surface. Their magnitude, persistence and recovery depend on ligand, cell type and exposure. The STS-associated expression route in Section [34.7](#ss_p10_sec_34_7) is distinct from this ligand-induced trafficking sequence. A developmental contribution would require this response to alter the defined local ionic or cell-volume recovery intermediary during a sensitive window, rather than treating receptor redistribution alone as an autism mechanism.

Developmental animal evidence also separates peripheral from central exposure. In fetal lambs, intravenous AVP raised plasma concentrations without raising CSF AVP, whereas hypoxia increased both compartments ([Stark et al., 1985](#ss_p4_ref_Stark1985)). Peripheral persistence therefore cannot be assumed to supply the local exposure required for an OXTR-response mechanism; CSF itself does not measure synaptic peptide action.

##### 36.5.2 Peptide concentrations and renal findings

Urinary symptoms provide a setting in which secretion, solute handling and organ response require separate assessment. Nocturnal enuresis was more frequent in a small ASD clinic sample, while a population cohort found clearer diagnosed-autism associations with daytime wetting at age nine (von Gontard et al., 2015; Gyamenah et al., 2026). A retrospective ASD comparison reported improvement with pooled desmopressin or anticholinergic therapy, without isolating desmopressin-specific response (Gor et al., 2012).

Separate physiological studies of childhood enuresis distinguish possible contributors. Both very low and very high nocturnal plasma AVP accompanied poor desmopressin response in one study (Devitt et al., 1999). Among selected desmopressin-resistant children, nocturnal polyuria was associated with higher nocturnal sodium and urea excretion and urinary prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) excretion, despite comparable urinary AVP and AQP2 measurements; plasma sodium did not differ between groups (Kamperis et al., 2006). These findings establish neither PGE2 causation nor acquired receptor imprinting. The useful comparison combines secretion and renal solute handling with bladder and arousal factors; wetting alone identifies neither hypo-osmolality nor the proposed developmental recovery mechanism.

Human CSF observations further separate ligand concentrations from receptor function. Oztan et al. (2018) found lower CSF AVP in 36 autistic children than in 36 matched clinical controls; the adjusted concentration was 66% of the control value. In archived samples collected during fever assessment at 0–3 months, AVP was also lower among infants later diagnosed with ASD (9 cases and 17 controls with assay data; Oztan et al., 2020). Neither study found a group difference in CSF oxytocin. These selected cohorts argue against a generalised central AVP-excess account and do not establish a high AVP-to-oxytocin signalling ratio. A small postmortem study further linked CSF AVP to hypothalamic AVP gene expression (n = 9), whereas blood AVP was unrelated to that expression (n = 12; Oztan et al., 2026). These observations distinguish central from peripheral measures; they do not measure receptor gain. The scarcity-to-hypersensitivity sequence in Section [36.5.6](#ss_p10_sec_36_5_6) therefore remains a competing mechanistic proposal, not an established explanation of these findings.

[John and Jaeggi (2021)](#ss_ref_john_jaeggi_2021) pooled 31 studies and found lower average oxytocin in autistic children (25 studies; d = −0.44, 95% CI −0.72 to −0.16), with no significant adult difference (six studies). The evidence was predominantly peripheral: 26 studies measured blood, four saliva and one CSF. Assay-related differences and residual heterogeneity remained. The pooled childhood association can coexist with the CSF null results above, including the 2018 cohort represented in that synthesis. It motivates investigation of the origins and functional importance of lower oxytocin concentrations, without identifying reduced secretion, altered clearance or reduced receptor responsiveness as their cause. The age comparison does not establish longitudinal normalisation.

The developmental sex comparison poses a separate question. No sex association with oxytocin concentration was detected in plasma from 37 extremely preterm infants followed from day 14 to 34 weeks corrected gestational age ([Weber et al., 2017](#ss_p4_ref_Weber2017)), in CSF from 18 newborns undergoing sepsis evaluation, including only six girls ([Clark et al., 2013](#ss_p4_ref_Clark2013)), or in urine from 90 infants at a one-month health check ([Kato et al., 2026](#ss_p4_ref_Kato2026)). These findings constrain a generally higher female oxytocin concentration, while their different specimens, ages, clinical selection and assays prevent treating them as one normal developmental trajectory. Nonsignificant comparisons do not establish equivalence or show that stress masked a difference.

##### 36.5.3 Inherited regulatory variation

Inherited regulatory variation provides a separate entry into receptor-response testing; it is not evidence of acquired imprinting. Short AVPR1A RS1 alleles showed a weak ASD association in an Irish family sample, and shorter RS1/RS3 constructs had lower reporter activity in SH-SY5Y cells (Tansey et al., 2011). In a Korean family study, the rs7294536 A allele was associated with ASD and increased reporter activity in T98G cells (Yang et al., 2017). These are allele- and assay-specific transcriptional effects, not demonstrations of stronger V1a ligand responses or slower desensitisation. The hypothesis predicts that a specified regulatory change alters tissue responsiveness and subsequent recovery under matched challenge.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_36_5_4"></a>

##### 36.5.4 Development, expression and release as sources of low AVP

Low AVP can arise at several distinct steps: specification of an AVP-producing lineage, differentiation, subsequent maturation, maintenance or survival, peptide expression in surviving neurons, and stimulus-linked release. Fewer AVP-labelled cells alone cannot distinguish these explanations because cells may remain present while their peptide falls below detection. A proliferation mechanism must act while the relevant cells are progenitors. After neuronal birth, altered maturation, connectivity, expression, release and survival remain separate possibilities. Progressive postnatal loss in a mutant-AVP mouse model illustrates the survival route, without establishing it in autism (Russell et al., 2003).

The available autism-model findings concern different populations and measurements. The Foxp1 result in Section [6](#ss_p10_sec_6) concerns reduced AVP and oxytocin labelling in hypothalamic nuclei of male mice at postnatal day 10; it leaves the relative contributions of differentiation, maturation, expression and survival unresolved (Berkhout et al., 2026). In adult male Shank3B+/− mice, reduced AVP signalling from the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis to the lateral septum accompanied impaired social behaviour, while AVP-labelled cell counts in the paraventricular nucleus were unchanged (Bortolozzo-Gleich et al., 2025). These findings motivate circuit-specific tests; neither measures endocrine water-regulatory reserve.

Adaptation across compartments supplies another possibility. Constitutive IRAP-null mice had higher circulating AVP alongside lower whole-brain AVP content and transcript abundance (Wallis et al., 2007; Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)). This is compatible with compensatory regulation, but does not demonstrate acquired suppression or loss of an AVP lineage. Likewise, the human postmortem association between CSF AVP and hypothalamic transcript abundance does not establish reduced hypothalamic transcription in autism, neuron loss or impaired secretion (Oztan et al., 2026). CSF, regional tissue, whole-brain content and plasma therefore answer different questions.

Two causal directions remain open within the hypothesis. A primary genetic constraint affecting neurohypophyseal AVP secretion could limit antidiuretic reserve when water conservation is needed, contributing to a measured water-balance disturbance and impaired local recovery. Conversely, the hypothesis proposes that impaired ionic or cellular-volume recovery during active circuit development could alter later AVP-neuron maturation, maintenance, connectivity or function. This acquired route could leave an altered response capacity after the initiating disturbance resolves. Both routes require a measured local neural or glial recovery disturbance during the causal interval and a prespecified developmental consequence. Additional regulatory work with adequate recovery is insufficient. Direct effects on central social circuits with adequate recovery remain a competing explanation. Sections [29](#ss_p10_sec_29)–[31](#ss_p10_sec_31) develop the related questions of translation, developmental signalling and differentiation.

Timing should follow the process being tested. Specification and cell production, maturation and connectivity, and ongoing expression, release and maintenance form overlapping process bands, not fixed human age bins. Birth is no universal completion point, and earlier exposure is not necessarily more damaging. The 11–19 gestational-week tissue sampling range discussed in Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3) identifies neither AVP neurogenesis nor an autism susceptibility window. A study should distinguish the exposure and local-recovery interval, the developmental process active then, the age at measurement, and the age when a functional difference becomes recognisable.

The early-infant CSF observations and later postmortem correlations come from separate cohorts (Oztan et al., 2020, 2026); they cannot be assembled into one developmental trajectory. A finite disturbance should instead be followed prospectively through its withdrawal to a specified developmental endpoint. Physiology may normalise while an earlier developmental consequence remains, or recovery may be complete with normal subsequent development. Lasting effects do not require lifelong hyperglycaemia, GSH limitation or AVP dysfunction. Later normal biomarkers neither establish an earlier episode nor erase a prospectively documented one; normal adult peripheral recovery cannot settle a historical neural mechanism.

Later increases in demand, including the transition to walking, could prospectively test whether an earlier limitation becomes apparent or a new disturbance occurs. Walking is neither an established cause of regression nor an explanation for an AVP difference already measured at 0–3 months. The proposed circuit, compartment, process and endpoint must be specified before testing: a negative differentiation result cannot be rescued by switching afterwards to release, another circuit or a renal explanation. The table summarises these distinctions without assigning unsupported ages.

<a name="ss_p10_table_36_1"></a>Table [36.1](#ss_p10_table_36_1). Conceptual timing of AVP-system effects and their observation

| **Process or interval**                  | **Conditional consequence**                                                         | **Distinct biological endpoints**                       | **Evidence boundary**                                                                                     |
|------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Specification and cell production        | Altered production or identity of the relevant neurons.                             | Lineage identity, cell production and differentiation.  | Proposed route. Human fetal peptide detection does not date cell birth.                                   |
| Maturation and connectivity              | Altered projections or response capacity after cells are born.                      | Maturation, connectivity and evoked-response capacity.  | Mouse P10 peptide labelling is an observation age, not the onset of injury.                               |
| Expression, release and maintenance      | Reversible expression or release changes, or separately demonstrated survival loss. | Cell identity, peptide content, release and survival.   | Animal circuit and mutant-AVP findings distinguish possibilities; they do not establish a human sequence. |
| Withdrawal, later demand and recognition | Full recovery, a persisting consequence, or a new disturbance under demand.         | Recovery after withdrawal and response to later demand. | Human CSF associations identify measurement times; recognition need not date initiation.                  |

Rows describe overlapping processes and observation intervals, not age bins or obligatory progression. The acquired causal connections remain proposed. Full recovery with normal subsequent development remains possible.

Source-specific observations: human fetal tissue, Skowsky and Fisher (1977); human CSF, Oztan et al. (2020, 2026); mouse peptide labelling, Berkhout et al. (2026); adult mouse circuit function, Bortolozzo-Gleich et al. (2025); mutant-mouse survival, Russell et al. (2003).

##### 36.5.5 Treatment results and signalling direction

Treatment results impose a separate constraint. The V1a antagonist balovaptan did not improve the primary socialisation/communication endpoint in the adult V1aduct phase 3 trial (322 randomised; terminated for futility) or the paediatric aV1ation phase 2 trial (ages 5–17; 339 randomised, 167 in the primary analysis). At week 24, the adjusted treatment difference on the Vineland-II two-domain composite was −1.84 (95% CI −5.15 to 1.48) at the adult interim analysis and −0.16 (90% CI −2.56 to 2.23) in the paediatric primary analysis (Jacob et al., 2022; Hollander et al., 2022). Conversely, a four-week pilot in 30 children reported improved social responsiveness with intranasal AVP (Parker et al., 2019). These different interventions do not identify one universal signalling direction. The larger negative antagonist trials weaken the expectation of broad benefit from reducing ongoing V1a signalling. They do not directly test prenatal initiation, but their timing provides no positive evidence for imprinting. A developmental receptor account still requires a measured exposure history, altered local response and a subsequent developmental effect.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_36_5_6"></a>

##### 36.5.6 A conditional AVPR1A influence on heparan sulphate

AVPR1A signalling could modify the extracellular matrix that influences later neural or glial responses. One proposed sequence is that reduced local AVP exposure increases subsequent V1a responsiveness, allowing later pulses to alter HSPG regulation and circuit development. This requires a measured change in functional response, not receptor abundance or low CSF AVP alone. An acquired matrix change could then modify later signalling or recovery, alongside the intrinsic matrix routes developed in Sections [28.2](#ss_p10_sec_28_2) and [28.3](#ss_p10_sec_28_3).
