A vascular experiment provides an AVP-associated HS observation: rabbits with AVP-induced hypertension had increased HS content in the thoracic aorta, while hypercholesterolaemia also increased thoracic HS (Drobnik et al., 2000). Tissue was assessed after prolonged hypertension; this does not isolate a direct receptor effect from pressure-related remodelling or measure HS synthesis.

An indirect growth-factor route has separate experimental components. AVP increased TGFβ secretion and type IV collagen production in cultured human mesangial cells; V1A antagonists inhibited these effects, and a TGFβ antibody inhibited the collagen response (Tahara et al., 2008). In porcine mesangial cultures, TGFβ1 increased HSPG expression and production (Kolm et al., 1996). In separate astrocyte experiments, TGFα or TGFβ increased syndecan-1 and HS2ST expression with increased HS 2-O-sulphation (Properzi et al., 2008). These findings motivate testing a growth-factor intermediary without joining different preparations into one observed neural pathway.

The cellular context matters: a V1 agonist left TGFβ1 and TGFβ3 expression unchanged in embryonic-rat cortical astrocyte cultures while reducing IL-1β and TNFα expression and release (Zhao and Brinton, 2004). Thus, the renal TGFβ response cannot be assumed in astrocytes. The proposed receptor route does not make AVP necessary for HS production or predict one uniform matrix increase.

In appropriate developmental models, a test would pair a defined local exposure history with receptor dose–response and termination, a specified HS endpoint, and synaptic or recovery function. HS abundance, sulphation, shedding and ligand interaction are distinct endpoints. Failure to observe the predicted gain increase, no relevant HS change, or unchanged downstream function after correcting that gain would constrain successive links. A neural developmental contribution through the common intermediary additionally requires altered local ionic or cell-volume recovery (Section [28.3](#ss_p10_sec_28_3)). Peripheral matrix changes may occur in parallel; autonomic indices or perfusion differences alone do not establish this sequence.

The distinction between a shared signal and a local response extends beyond AVP. Dopamine-related action-selection circuits provide a candidate example of how altered response architecture could become altered circuit weighting.

#### 36.6 Dopamine as a Signalling-Imprinting Example of Circuit Bias

Dopamine-related circuits demonstrate that changing the activity of a defined neuronal population can change action selection. Tai et al. (2012) transiently stimulated dorsal striatal D1- or D2-receptor-expressing neurons in adult mice and produced opposing choice biases that depended on recent reward history and stimulation timing. This supports pathway-specific gating, not a global D1-low/D2-high account of autism. Activating D2-expressing neurons is also not equivalent to increasing dopamine action at D2 receptors.

The proposed bridge is that a measured developmental ionic or energetic constraint could alter response or plasticity within a specified corticostriatal circuit, increasing the difficulty of initiating or switching actions. A D1 branch would predict reduced D1-dependent facilitation at matched input in the affected population. Stronger indirect-pathway influence is a separate claim requiring pathway activity and causal perturbation; it cannot be inferred from reduced D1 expression, low dopamine or repetitive behaviour. An Ang II-to-D1-to-indirect-pathway sequence remains unestablished.

There is positive evidence for stress-related circuit reweighting. In rats, chronic stress shifted instrumental behaviour towards habitual control and altered associative and sensorimotor corticostriatal structure (Dias-Ferreira et al., 2009). That experiment did not isolate cortisol as the cause or demonstrate sodium–volume mediation. The hypothesis adds a specific question: does a documented local recovery constraint account for the circuit change, and does correcting that constraint preserve flexible action selection? Cortisol concentration alone does not answer it.

#### 36.7 Timing Layer: Parvalbumin Interneurons and Chloride-Dependent Precision

Parvalbumin interneurons provide a candidate timing layer: fast synchronising inhibition depends on maintained ionic gradients and reliable membrane responses.

The proposed link is that impaired chloride recovery during development reduces temporal fidelity, synchrony or the stability of rapid circuit transitions. This depends on the functional GABA response, not simply NKCC1/KCC2 abundance or a more positive reversal potential (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [26](#ss_p10_sec_26)).

Repolarisation machinery supplies a separate route into timing vulnerability. KCNC1 Ala421Val, reported in infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, reduced Kv3.1 current in Xenopus oocytes (Cameron et al., 2019). Altered repolarisation provides a concrete entry point into firing-pattern and recovery-demand tests. The energetic direction remains open: reduced channel current does not by itself demonstrate increased sodium-pump work, depleted ATP or slower ionic recovery, and the reported clinical phenotype is not an ASD-specific mechanism.

#### 36.8 Extracellular and Intracellular Timing Disruption

Local extracellular geometry could add a timing constraint. Swelling-related compression can amplify concentration changes from fixed solute release; altered diffusion, clearance or spillover is a separate consequence (Section [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)).

Calcium-event timing could also change if local ionic and electrical gradients alter sodium–calcium exchange. Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [26](#ss_p10_sec_26) distinguish this clearance branch from altered entry and successful gradient compensation.

#### 36.9 Autism-Relevant Translation: An Optional Receptor Branch

This optional receptor branch predicts altered response curves, pathway weighting or timing after early defence. Depending on the affected circuit, these changes could influence initiation, switching, reward learning or motor planning.

Similar behaviour can arise through other routes; repetition or reduced spontaneous initiation does not identify a receptor defect.

Its contribution to the common-process conjecture requires the local ionic or volume-recovery disturbance to carry the developmental effect. It requires neither continuing hyponatraemia or AVP elevation nor one fixed receptor signature.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_37"></a>

### 37 Brainstem Volume-Sensing and Autonomic Control Imprinting

This section moves from controller pathways to proposed changes in local recovery and then to motor, speech and arousal applications. Acute signalling or circuit function alone does not establish acquired controller imprinting. That claim requires altered recruitment or recovery under a matched later challenge after the initiating disturbance resolves and sufficient recovery time has elapsed. Inherited response differences and continuing exposure require separate comparisons. Appropriate recruitment followed by complete recovery remains a successful outcome.

#### 37.1 Controller Architecture and Peptide Routing

<a name="ss_p10_sec_37_1_1"></a>

##### 37.1.1 Afferent Volume Signalling and Controller Architecture

Local receptor responses operate within circuits that coordinate defence. Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1), Panel B, distinguishes candidate sensing and regulatory disturbances; Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1) supplies component evidence. Sections [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) and [16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9) separate mechanical transmission, afferent encoding and central interpretation. Brainstem volume-sensing denotes integration of pressure, cardiopulmonary filling, visceral and chemosensory information with osmotic context, rather than a single sensor for bulk volume. The nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) is a major cardiovascular afferent entry point. In rat working heart–brainstem preparations, local angiotensin II altered baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflexes differently, demonstrating that one controller signal can reweight distinct input pathways (Paton and Kasparov, 1999). A complementary stream centred on the subfornical organ (SFO) and organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis (OVLT) conveys hydromineral information. In adult male mice, stimulation of an angiotensin-receptor-expressing median preoptic nucleus (MnPO)/OVLT projection to the PVN increased vasopressin release and blood pressure (Frazier et al., 2021). The proposed dual-stream architecture therefore concerns integration of filling and tonicity signals across connected controllers. It does not require every input to converge on one neurone, and its defended variables include effective perfusion and cellular water balance, not serum sodium in isolation. This is excitation and secretion evidence, not a demonstrated fetal differentiation requirement. Applied to the developmental alternatives in Section [36.5.4](#ss_p10_sec_36_5_4), this motivates a test of whether a defined tonicity disturbance interacts with reduced local Ang II signalling to alter maturation. Appropriate AVP suppression during volume-replete hypotonicity does not itself establish developmental injury.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_37_1_2"></a>

##### 37.1.2 Hypothalamic Integration and Autonomic Routing

The supraoptic nucleus (SON) and paraventricular nucleus (PVN) link endocrine water conservation to autonomic control. The SON is predominantly magnocellular; the PVN additionally contains parvocellular neuroendocrine and descending autonomic populations, whose recruitment must be distinguished (Geerling et al., 2010). Magnocellular vasopressin neurones release peptide from posterior-pituitary terminals into blood and locally from their somata and dendrites. Son et al. (2013) directly demonstrated a coupling mechanism in rats: stimulating PVN vasopressin neurones excited nearby PVN-to-RVLM presympathetic neurones, about 100 μm away, through V1a-dependent signalling. Local vasopressin signalling also contributed to renal sympathetic recruitment during a hyperosmotic challenge. The recipient population was identified by its medullary projection; it was not a demonstrated population of vasopressin-producing or CRH neurones. This is positive evidence that local peptide release can coordinate hormonal and sympathetic defence. Oxytocin has a complementary, compartment-specific route: optogenetic activation of rat PVN projections produced oxytocin-receptor-dependent facilitation of excitation in brainstem cardiac vagal neurones (Piñol et al., 2014). The hypothesis proposes that repeated challenge can alter the relative recruitment and recovery of these channels. A persistent vasopressin-weighted state with reduced oxytocin-mediated buffering remains a directional prediction, not a necessary consequence of either experiment. Circulating peptide levels cannot substitute for measurements of these local pathways.

Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) develops a candidate contribution from prolonged AVP exposure to altered oxytocin secretion. A peripheral secretion change would not establish weaker oxytocin signalling in the local autonomic pathways described here. Developmental relevance would additionally require impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carrying a specified developmental effect.

A human birth comparison illustrates why relative peptide exposure must remain separate from oxytocin suppression. Among 53 term births, arterial cord AVP and copeptin were higher after vaginal than elective caesarean delivery, whereas oxytocin concentrations were similar ([Fill Malfertheiner et al., 2021](#ss_p4_ref_FillMalfertheiner2021)). This supports distinct peptide responses in that setting, without identifying secretion rates, receptor responsiveness or local neural signalling. A higher AVP-to-oxytocin ratio can arise through AVP elevation alone.

The receptor-response branch in Section [36.5.1](#ss_p10_sec_36_5_1) is distinct: weaker oxytocin signalling could reflect altered tissue responsiveness without reduced secretion. Neither branch is established by a circulating AVP-to-oxytocin ratio alone.

Functional developmental evidence is available in a separate experimental setting. In embryonic mouse brain sections, an OXTR-selective agonist increased binding of a labelled GTP analogue, a G-protein activation readout, in cortical and septal neuroepithelium at embryonic day 16.5; no sex difference was detected in this small study ([Sommer and Caldwell, 2025](#ss_p4_ref_Sommer2025)). This supports signalling capacity at that stage, without measuring AVP-induced OXTR internalisation or protection from ionic disturbance.

Human transcript data add a separate timing observation. Across 16 brain regions from 57 postmortem donors, [Rokicki et al. (2022)](#ss_p4_ref_Rokicki2022) described sex-stratified OXTR mRNA trajectories normalised across the lifespan. The female curve peaked around birth, while the male curve showed a pronounced early-childhood peak. These smoothed cross-sectional profiles identify candidate windows rather than a precisely dated neonatal event. They do not measure absolute receptor protein, surface availability or signalling, and the sampled regions did not include the hypothalamus. Their relevance here is a proposed timing modifier: altered peptide responsiveness would need to change local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery during a susceptible developmental process.

#### 37.2 Local Recovery and Developmental Timing

##### 37.2.1 Pontine Integration and Timing Sensitivity

The pons brings homeostatic regulation and motor coordination into anatomical proximity, but its dorsal autonomic nuclei and ventral pontocerebellar relays are distinct systems. Rat tracing identifies PVN projections to viscerosensory parabrachial regions and other brainstem autonomic targets (Geerling et al., 2010). Separately, perturbing pontine nuclei during cued reaching in mice usually preserved movement initiation while degrading movement precision, accuracy, duration or success (Guo et al., 2021). This supplies a concrete precedent for impaired refinement without complete motor failure. The proposed developmental extension is that a measured disturbance of local ionic recovery could destabilise relay timing under load and thereby increase trial-to-trial variability. The missing link is the recovery disturbance itself and its mediation of the timing effect; anatomical proximity does not establish it.

##### 37.2.2 Pontine Vulnerability: Vascular Constraints and Metabolic Demand

Pontine supply varies regionally: dissection of 100 adult human brainstems identified basilar paramedian, circumferential and median branches, with occasional cerebellar-artery contributions (Kwiatkowska et al., 2023). The developmental proposal is a local delivery–demand mismatch with greater or more persistent recovery difficulty than in comparable regions. Adult anatomy, small perforators and defended systemic pressure do not establish reduced developmental reserve.

##### 37.2.3 Microenvironmental Burden and Developmental Maturation

Repeated local recovery difficulty could affect oligodendrocyte maturation, glial buffering and relay precision together. One candidate mechanism is ion-handling work exceeding local metabolic reserve. Hypotonic swelling, hypertonic shrinkage and underfilling are distinct inputs, however, and none alone establishes ATP limitation or delayed recovery. Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)–[27](#ss_p10_sec_27) develop the cellular mechanisms; their convergence in developing pontine tissue remains proposed.

##### 37.2.4 The Brainstem Neighbourhood Effect

The Brainstem Neighbourhood Effect proposes that circuits sharing extracellular conditions, vascular supply or glial support can share a recovery constraint and lose timing precision together. Coupled propagation differs from parallel effects of one systemic exposure; anatomy alone establishes neither. The predicted pattern should follow actual territory, cell type, laterality and developmental stage, potentially producing clustered dysfunction without a discrete lesion or cranial-nerve injury.

##### 37.2.5 Chloride Handling and Inhibitory Timing Precision

Disturbed chloride recovery could make inhibition less repeatable under load without abolishing it. Extracellular compression could amplify fixed solute release, but altered removal and impaired gating require additional functional consequences (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) and [25](#ss_p10_sec_25)–[27](#ss_p10_sec_27)).

##### 37.2.6 Developmental Calibration Versus Adult Lesion Models

Rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia in adult rats caused astrocyte loss before oligodendrocyte and myelin loss (Gankam Kengne et al., 2011). This severe injury sequence is not a developmental dose–response model. The proposed early-life route instead concerns recovery difficulty altering glial support, myelination or circuit timing without compulsory demyelination; injury, altered maturation and reversible adaptation remain distinct outcomes.

#### 37.3 Circuit Applications

<a name="ss_p10_sec_37_3_1"></a>

##### 37.3.1 Functional Translation: Motor Coordination and Apraxia

In cortico–ponto–cerebellar loops, the hypothesis predicts reduced timing reserve: a measured local recovery disturbance could make movement corrections and speech sequencing less reproducible under matched load, with consequences set by circuit, cell type and developmental window. Anatomical coupling does not establish that mediation. Speech motor planning/programming, motor execution, language and cognition must be assessed separately. Childhood apraxia of speech concerns planning/programming, whereas dysarthria concerns execution. Chenausky et al. (2019) found suspected apraxia alongside other speech profiles in low/minimally verbal autistic participants, while Shriberg et al. (2011) found no statistical support for concomitant apraxia in an intelligible-speech cohort. Their different recruitment does not define one speech continuum. The retained proposal is variable timing and sequencing dysfunction, potentially without weakness or cell loss, whose physiological mediator must predict the particular motor or speech outcome.

The Purkinje–glial interface gives this proposal a concrete experimental basis. Purkinje-specific Tsc1 reduction in mice altered excitability, social behaviour, repetitive behaviour and vocalisations; heterozygotes showed these changes without detected Purkinje-cell loss through four months (Tsai et al., 2012). Separately, stimulating Ca²⁺ signalling in Bergmann glia lowered extracellular K⁺ and changed Purkinje membrane states and firing (Wang et al., 2012). These experiments establish cell-specific causal contributions and functional glial control. They do not measure impaired ionic or volume recovery or a human speech outcome. The hypothesis proposes that disturbed recovery in Purkinje cells, supporting glia or both can alter circuit development without obligatory neuronal swelling or death. Atypical prosody, apraxia and minimal speech cannot presently be ranked by Purkinje injury; the osmolyte example in Section [24.3](#ss_p10_sec_24_3) also separates redistribution from complete restoration.

##### 37.3.2 Locus Coeruleus and Arousal Regulation

The locus coeruleus is a candidate route from altered recovery to state-dependent arousal. Optogenetic experiments in mice establish that changing locus-coeruleus firing can alter cortical state and sleep-to-wake transitions (Carter et al., 2010). Its placement in the dorsal pons does not make it interchangeable with neighbouring nuclei: rat tracing found strong PVN input to the pre-locus coeruleus but comparatively little to locus-coeruleus catecholamine neurones (Geerling et al., 2010). The present model predicts altered arousal recruitment or recovery only where a specified pathway or local disturbance reaches this system. Faster recruitment, prolonged recovery and unstable responses are separable predictions. Their direction should be fixed for the chosen exposure, age and task, rather than inferred from attention or sensory differences after the fact.

#### 37.4 Synthesis and Discriminating Predictions

Peptide coordination of endocrine and sympathetic output, specified descending pathways and pontocerebellar movement refinement provide the established components. The proposed Brainstem Neighbourhood Effect connects them through shared local recovery difficulty, potentially reducing timing reserve while gross transmission remains intact. This could contribute to motor, autonomic or arousal variability; speech planning requires the distinct evidence considered in Section [37.3.1](#ss_p10_sec_37_3_1). Repeated defence followed by complete recovery and normal later pathway recruitment would support successful adaptation. Adequate recovery despite the predicted developmental timing disturbance would challenge mediation, while preserved timing after the specified recovery defect would weaken that timing branch. The proposal does not assign all autism to pontine dysfunction.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_38"></a>

### 38 Candidate Placental Vascular Imprinting and Fetal Perfusion Constraint

Alongside controller calibration, vascular responsiveness could retain a history of challenge. A defined osmotic or endocrine history could leave placental vessels more responsive to later constrictor signals after the initiating ligand and physiological disturbance have resolved. Increased AGTR1 or AVPR1A coupling is the high-resistance prediction; lower AVPR1A-related responses in pre-eclamptic fetoplacental vessels caution against blanket gain-up (Gao et al., 2019; Section [14.6.3](#ss_p10_sec_14_6_3)). Such a retained placental response could prolong or renew a fetal perfusion constraint during later demand. Placental persistence during the same pregnancy and a lasting fetal developmental consequence are separate claims. Reduced flow could affect fetal oxygen delivery, endocrine responses and developmental recovery or choroid-plexus function, but neither fetal growth restriction nor normalised maternal hormones identifies that sequence.

#### 38.1 Oxygen Delivery, ATP Supply and Sodium Transport

Where maternal pressure defence raises uteroplacental resistance, reduced fetal oxygen delivery could constrain ATP-supported sodium transport if ATP production and reserve fail to meet demand. Fetal sodium loss requires altered net balance; hyponatraemia additionally depends on water relative to effective solute. Fetal AVP–RAAS–cortisol recruitment follows fetal signals, not maternal hormone concentration alone. Sections [14.7](#ss_p10_sec_14_7) and [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) develop the delivery, ATP-supply and transport-work distinctions.

Sections [14.6](#ss_p10_sec_14_6) and [16.6](#ss_p10_sec_16_6) develop the Ang II–perfusion–energetics and microvascular-flow routes underlying this conditional placental imprint. Section [39](#ss_p10_sec_39) extends the persistence question to systemic vessels, distinguishing retained responsiveness from continuing exposure, ordinary adaptation and structural change.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_39"></a>

### 39 Systemic Vascular Imprinting

#### 39.1 Exposure and the Meaning of Vascular Imprinting

Vascular imprinting denotes a retained change in vascular responsiveness or structure after an early exposure has ended. The proposed functional changes concern response thresholds, gain, reserve, regional allocation or recovery. They may be detectable during a challenge despite adequate resting perfusion. Structural remodelling is a separate possibility; a lasting functional difference does not require an altered vessel count or geometry. Neither abnormal perfusion nor an autism-associated vascular finding alone identifies an imprint.

Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) separates actual filling and delivery disturbances from altered sensing and regulation. Table [16.1](#ss_p10_table_16_1) identifies component sites, while Sections [16.8](#ss_p10_sec_16_8) and [16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9) distinguish local vascular effects from afferent encoding and central interpretation. Here the additional question is what retains a response difference after the initiating conditions resolve, and whether that difference contributes to the local neural or glial recovery disturbance required by Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2).

Exposure is described by independently observed filling and tonicity disturbances, including their direction, magnitude, duration, recurrence and developmental timing. These dimensions are kept separate rather than combined into an unvalidated score. Serum sodium cannot supply a filling measurement, and glucose-corrected sodium is not measured effective tonicity. The neonatal studies in Section [12](#ss_p10_sec_12) illustrate why a sodium range cannot distinguish a sustained disturbance from repeated excursions. Missing episodes remain missing information. Recovery time, response gain and later diagnosis are outcomes or comparison characteristics, not components of the exposure whose consequences are being explained.

#### 39.2 Vascular Responses and Local Effectors

The water-conservation and vascular-support weightings in Section [5](#ss_p10_sec_5) describe continuous, potentially coexisting responses. Urine concentration or free-water clearance characterises antidiuresis; constrictor slopes characterise particular arterial or venous responses. Neither substitutes for measured sodium balance, plasma volume, central filling or tissue delivery. Greater constriction need not imply AVP sparing. A proposed imprint could increase or decrease gain, shift a threshold, limit reserve or alter recovery; its direction must be specified for the vessel bed and stimulus.

Local ionic mechanisms provide concrete ways to change response gain. Inducible Tmem16a deletion in mouse vascular contractile cells abolished measured calcium-activated chloride currents and reduced selected constrictor responses, with substantial differences between vascular beds (Heinze et al., 2014). In rat cortical slices, TMEM16A-dependent chloride efflux amplified pericyte depolarisation, calcium entry and agonist-evoked capillary constriction. Bumetanide attenuated the endothelin-1 response, and changing the external chloride gradient restored it (Korte et al., 2022). These experiments connect chloride gradients to contraction without demonstrating an acquired, persistent chloride elevation after early osmotic stress.

Endothelial signalling supplies an opposing local response. PIEZO1 supported flow-induced ATP release, P2Y2 signalling and eNOS activation; adult mouse endothelial Piezo1 deletion nearly abolished tested flow-mediated dilation while preserving chemical relaxation and contraction (Wang et al., 2016). This identifies a flow-response component, not a neural false-deficit signal. Extracellular ATP therefore has a defined vasodilatory role in this preparation; its direction cannot be transferred unchanged to smooth muscle, pericytes or every stress state.

Repeated stimulation can also recruit protective attenuation. A second Ang II challenge 30 minutes after the first produced less constriction in control resistance arteries, whereas caveolar disruption or Cav1 loss prevented that attenuation (Czikora et al., 2015; Section [14.6](#ss_p10_sec_14_6)). Endothelial caveolin-1 re-expression rescued impaired flow responses in Cav1-null mice, but the accompanying remodelling experiment maintained altered flow throughout assessment (Yu et al., 2006). Section [35](#ss_p10_sec_35) develops membrane organisation and its limits. Receptor trafficking, channel availability and membrane organisation can alter acute responses; retained changes in these components require their own evidence.

Venous capacitance and splanchnic redistribution remain distinct from resistance-vessel gain. Healthy-adult tilt and lower-body negative-pressure experiments produced similar regional flow reductions but opposite splanchnic volume changes (Taneja et al., 2007). Resistance or cerebral perfusion alone therefore cannot identify redistribution. The proposed venous imprint is a retained change in regional venous mechanics or recruitment after early exposure. The acute comparison does not establish that developmental origin. Sections [43](#ss_p10_sec_43) and [44](#ss_p10_sec_44) describe the consequences for later filling.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_39_3"></a>

#### 39.3 Retained Vascular Changes After Early Exposure

A persistence mechanism must identify what remains changed and how it alters later function. Continued hormone excess, residual tonicity disturbance and retained tissue regulation are different explanations for a later abnormal response. Exposure withdrawal strengthens a persistence claim; comparison under characterised current physiology is needed to separate retained regulation from continuing consequences of the original disturbance. Irreversibility is not required.

Prenatal water deprivation provides a regulatory precedent relevant to the present framework. Male rats assessed at 7–8 weeks after three days of late-gestation maternal water deprivation had greater Ang II-evoked pressure responses and reduced challenge-derived baroreflex sensitivity despite similar resting pressure and heart rate (Guan et al., 2009; five independent litters per group). Cardiac AT2-receptor expression was increased. Maternal food intake also fell, however, and the experiment neither located the reflex difference in vascular tissue nor established normal later filling and tonicity. It demonstrates a later response difference, while leaving the responsible retained substrate unresolved.

A more specific expression mechanism was identified after prenatal hypoxia. Following maternal 10.5% oxygen exposure on gestational days 10–20 and return to normal conditions, male rat offspring at 16 weeks showed reduced pulmonary arterial constrictor responses, lower Cav1.2 expression and calcium currents, and increased methylation at selected Cav1.2 promoter sites (Li et al., 2021). In isolated pulmonary artery rings, a broad DNA-methyltransferase inhibitor increased channel expression and responsiveness; Cav1.2 knockdown reduced calcium responses in control myocytes. These convergent results support an expression-linked mechanism, although the inhibitor does not establish locus-specific methylation causality. Resting pulmonary pressure and measured wall dimensions did not differ significantly. Retained functional change can therefore occur without detected structural enlargement or raised resting pressure, and need not mean increased contractility.

Systemic vessels show a complementary developmental effect. In male rats exposed to 13% oxygen during gestation, femoral arteries at four months had impaired relaxation to methacholine and an NO donor; fetal aortic thickening was no longer detected in adult aortic morphology (Giussani et al., 2012). Maternal vitamin C restored total methacholine relaxation through a greater NO-independent contribution, while the NO-donor deficit remained. This study supports lasting vascular dysfunction after gestational exposure, but does not identify a molecular storage mechanism or show restoration of every signalling component. Together, these hypoxia experiments support developmental vascular plasticity in specified male rat tissues. They do not establish the same retained programme after sodium–volume defence or its extension to cerebral and venous beds.

Extracellular matrix offers another possible substrate. In adult mouse mesenteric arteries, 24-hour reducing treatments that enabled transglutaminase-2 cross-linking altered passive pressure–diameter behaviour measured with active tone removed; cross-linking-deficient enzyme did not reproduce the effect (van den Akker et al., 2011). This identifies a mechanism capable of changing vessel mechanics beyond immediate contraction. The pharmacological preparation does not establish developmental memory, and the exact matrix substrate responsible for the mechanical change remained unresolved.

Resetting has a different evidential reach. After reversal of two months of experimental renal hypertension in rats, depressed baroreceptor gain normalised within 90–120 minutes although threshold resetting remained incompletely reversed (Moreira et al., 1990). Acute pressure–response hysteresis also contains mechanical and neural contributions (Studinger et al., 2007). As Section [16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9) explains, a shifted curve or dependence on recent history is not sufficient evidence of a lasting developmental imprint. The present vascular hypothesis requires a specified retained component, response and interval, with continuing exposure and ordinary adaptation distinguished.

#### 39.4 Structural Development and Neurovascular Interfaces

Vascular development responds to local activity and flow. In developing mouse cortex, sensory deprivation reduced vascular density and branching, while moderate stimulation increased them (Lacoste et al., 2014). A separate study found that prolonged excessive activity during an early postnatal window inhibited angiogenesis and, depending on exposure duration, left a vascular deficit after stimulation ended (Whiteus et al., 2014). These results establish developmental sensitivity and a retained structural consequence under particular conditions. They also show why greater recruitment cannot be assigned a single structural direction.

At the level of individual branches, endothelial migration away from low-flow segments contributed to vessel regression in developing mouse retina and zebrafish vessels (Franco et al., 2015). Local flow differences, tissue demand and developmental stage therefore matter to a pruning mechanism. Early filling or tonicity disturbance could alter those conditions, but the resulting density, branching, tortuosity or pruning pattern cannot be deduced from water-conservation or vascular-support weighting alone. Increased resistance does not establish reduced shear in every vessel, and inward narrowing of a vessel is distinct from loss of vessels. Structural claims require direct structural evidence.

The neurovascular interface also has separable functional outcomes. A coupling difference concerns the relationship between neural activity and its haemodynamic response; a perfusion trace alone cannot distinguish altered neural demand from altered vascular coupling. Vascular recovery can be impaired without a striking baseline abnormality: adult endothelial Nfat5 deletion reduced post-ischaemic reperfusion in mice, a challenge-specific finding developed in Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7) (Kunze et al., 2024). The continuing genetic manipulation and ischaemic injury do not demonstrate an acquired developmental imprint.

BBB transport or permeability and perivascular drainage require their own evidence. A change in barrier tracer passage does not establish net systemic plasma loss, and perivascular-space dimensions do not directly measure clearance. Normal resting perfusion, reactive hyperaemia or arterial reserve cannot settle these distinct outcomes. The proposed vascular imprint may involve one interface without the others; Sections [24](#ss_p10_sec_24) and [30](#ss_p10_sec_30) develop the local extracellular and transport context.

#### 39.5 Local Recovery and Limiting Results

A retained vascular change could contribute to the developmental mechanism if delayed or inadequate tissue delivery limits energy-dependent restoration while neurons or glia are recovering from ionic or cell-volume disturbance. Altered vascular mechanics could also change sensory input and prolong endocrine or autonomic recruitment, a separate signalling route developed in Section [16.9](#ss_p10_sec_16_9). Either route requires impaired local recovery and a specified developmental effect. Increased vascular resistance, additional regulatory work or reduced reserve alone does not establish that sequence. Adequate supply and complete local recovery would interrupt it. A regulatory or vascular imprint may precede the local disturbance; a developmental consequence may remain after the initiating physiology later normalises (Sections [2](#ss_p10_sec_2) and [4](#ss_p10_sec_4)).

The functional hypothesis predicts an exposure-related response difference under characterised present conditions, not necessarily chronic vasoconstriction or abnormal resting cerebral perfusion. Precise independent findings that exclude the specified change in gain, reserve, recovery or redistribution would weaken that branch. A non-significant contrast alone is insufficient, while absence of the predicted exposure–response relationship supplies a separate limit. Structural and barrier branches require their own outcomes; one vascular abnormality cannot validate the entire module.

Chloride participates in cell-volume recovery, renal NaCl feedback and vascular excitability, but reuse across tissues does not imply a shared upward chloride shift. Cross-threat consolidation would require a retained, compartment-specific chloride or recovery change linked to responses across the proposed threats. Ordinary transient chloride flux, or endocrine recalibration without that linkage, leaves the separate physiological mechanisms intact without establishing their consolidation. Section [23](#ss_p10_sec_23) develops the candidate local ionic persistence mechanism and its developmental limits.

<a name="ss_p10_part_g"></a>

## Part G Heterogeneity and later expression

<a name="ss_p10_sec_40"></a>

### 40 Sex Differences and Sodium-Struggle Responses

#### 40.1 Diagnosis patterns and liability

Male predominance in identified childhood autism varies with ascertainment, age and associated conditions. [Loomes et al. (2017)](#ss_p1_ref_Loomes2017) reported pooled male-to-female odds ratios of 3.25 with active population screening and 4.56 when studies relied on existing diagnoses. Male predominance remained in both groups, while the difference supports an identification contribution. Their intellectual-disability analysis grouped studies by participants’ IQ distribution; it did not directly compare individual children with and without intellectual disability.

Individual-level Norwegian registry data provide that complementary comparison. Male-to-female ratios were 3.67 among children aged 4–17 and 2.57 among adults aged 18–48; among children, ratios were 2.62 with a recorded intellectual-disability diagnosis and 3.94 without one ([Posserud et al., 2021](#ss_p1_ref_Posserud2021)). These estimates concern diagnoses recorded during 2008–2015, so earlier diagnoses without subsequent specialist contact could be missed. Intellectual disability and the separate construct of profound autism should not be treated as interchangeable.

[Fyfe et al. (2026)](#ss_p1_ref_Fyfe2026) modelled age, calendar-period and birth-cohort effects using Swedish diagnoses recorded through 2022. The model-derived cumulative male-to-female diagnosis ratio was approximately 1.2 by age 20 for the 2022 calendar period; parity in 2024 was an extrapolation beyond follow-up. This is not observed lifetime prevalence in one completed cohort. Intellectual disability was not analysed, so these findings cannot establish the cognitive profiles of later-diagnosed females. The age-dependent pattern retains a childhood male excess.

Biological modifiers remain plausible alongside identification effects. Greater deleterious-variant burden in affected females is consistent with a higher liability threshold (Jacquemont et al., 2014), while relationships between autistic traits, additional difficulties and meeting diagnostic criteria differ between girls and boys (Dworzynski et al., 2012). Neither observation supplies the complete explanation. The Sodium-Struggle proposal is that sex-dependent exposure, developmental timing and regulatory capacity could modify compensatory demand and recovery. Its systemic prediction is greater or longer recruitment of defence, or slower recovery, in the more susceptible group under a defined condition. The direction must be established for the relevant age, tissue and disturbance. Diagnosis ratios alone quantify neither that physiological difference nor the proposed local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery intermediary.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_40_2"></a>

#### 40.2 Exposure and developmental timing

Sex may modify exposure as well as response. In a Dutch registry cohort restricted to singleton births to white European women, male fetuses had greater risk of spontaneous preterm birth, with no corresponding excess in medically indicated preterm delivery (Peelen et al., 2016). Among 11,844 infants born before 28 weeks and admitted to English neonatal units, surviving males born at 24–27 weeks had longer invasive ventilation and more bronchopulmonary dysplasia; neither difference was significant at 22–23 weeks (Dassios et al., 2024). These sex-associated differences could increase exposure to the respiratory and AVP-related demands described in Section [21.5.1](#ss_p10_sec_21_5_1). They do not establish a greater male hormonal response to an identical disturbance.

A separate observation concerns healthy newborns. In a 241-infant cohort born at 35 weeks or later, the 81 infants delivered by primary caesarean before labour had median venous cord copeptin of 5.5 pmol/L in boys and 4.8 pmol/L in girls ([Burckhardt et al., 2014](#ss_p1_ref_Burckhardt2014)). Delivery stress and cord pH also influenced birth measurements in the full cohort, and sex was not independently associated with day-3 copeptin. This supports a time- and context-specific difference in an AVP-related marker. It does not measure active-AVP clearance or demonstrate a fixed sex difference in response to the same challenge.

Positive amniotic-fluid findings support investigating a prenatal androgen contribution to autistic traits. Among 235 children aged 6–10 years, higher amniotic testosterone was associated with higher AQ-Child scores in both sexes; CAST associations were significant in the combined sample and boys, but not girls ([Auyeung et al., 2009](#ss_and_ref_Auyeung2009)). In a later birth cohort, higher amniotic testosterone was also associated with higher Q-CHAT scores at 18–24 months in 129 toddlers, with associations within both sexes ([Auyeung et al., 2010](#ss_and_ref_Auyeung2010)). A separate amniotic-fluid study found no significant association with CAST scores among 92 children aged 3–5 years ([Kung et al., 2016](#ss_and_ref_Kung2016)). In a later cohort largely overlapping the 2009 sample, comprising 97 adolescents and young adults aged 13–21 years, prenatal testosterone showed no direct association with AQ scores; exploratory interactions with pubertal timing had limited statistical robustness ([Dooley et al., 2022](#ss_and_ref_Dooley2022)). These observations concern autistic traits rather than diagnosed ASD and do not identify maternal testosterone transfer or renal mediation. They motivate the fetal question while preserving uncertainty about its consistency and mechanism.

Androgen-sensitive renal development and regulation provide an additional question about susceptibility in both sexes (Section [32.1.4](#ss_p10_sec_32_1_4)). Maternal polycystic ovary syndrome has been associated with offspring ASD (Kosidou et al., 2016), but this diagnosis does not isolate testosterone from metabolic, genetic or other pathways. Direct studies of maternal circulating testosterone did not find significant adjusted associations with offspring ASD in the MARBLES analysis of 196 mother–child pairs at elevated familial likelihood of ASD or the Swedish study of 367 autism cases and 477 controls (Granillo et al., 2022; Kosidou et al., 2024). The proposed maternal/offspring renal route should therefore be investigated without treating high maternal gestational testosterone as an established ASD exposure, or assuming that it explains male predominance.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_40_3"></a>

#### 40.3 Renal and endocrine allocation

Vasopressin physiology offers a concrete example of sex-dependent response architecture. Liu et al. (2011) found renal V2-receptor mRNA and protein expression 2.6- and 1.7-fold higher, respectively, in adult female than male Sprague-Dawley rats. After five days of water loading during desmopressin administration, both sexes showed similar physiological escape from antidiuresis despite different receptor down-regulation. This supports measuring both receptor response and recovery. Greater V2 activity can conserve water but can also increase dilutional liability; it is not inherently female protection. A male shift toward V1a-mediated pressure defence during human fetal development remains a separate prediction, not a result of this experiment.

Renal sodium handling likewise differs by segment and context. Veiras et al. (2017) found lower proximal reabsorption and faster saline-load excretion in adult female rats, alongside greater NCC abundance/phosphorylation and ENaC cleavage. The mouse saline experiment did not reproduce that excretion difference. These findings provide a biological rationale for investigating analogous allocation in humans, while transporter markers do not establish unused downstream reserve and disposal of excess saline differs from recovery after sodium depletion. Whether coordinated differences operate during human infancy and childhood, and influence recovery from mineral or sodium–volume disturbances, remains to be established. The proposed RAAS branch asks whether matched filling deficits recruit a different balance of sodium conservation and vasoconstriction during development. Renin, angiotensin action, aldosterone and net sodium balance must therefore be distinguished, as in Tables [14.2](#ss_p10_table_14_2), [14.3](#ss_p10_table_14_3), and [14.4](#ss_p10_table_14_4) and Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32).

Human newborn findings identify components rather than the complete allocation. Among 104 healthy newborns, boys had higher spot urinary sodium-to-creatinine ratios and girls higher potassium-to-creatinine ratios; these measurements did not establish intake-adjusted balance or the responsible segments ([Cillo et al., 2001](#ss_p3_ref_Cillo2001)). In 123 neonatal intensive-care patients, urinary AQP2 was initially higher in boys but did not correlate with urine osmolality, limiting its use as a direct marker of AVP action at this age ([Zelenina et al., 2006](#ss_p3_ref_Zelenina2006)). The infant phosphate-transporter result in Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) and mineral-hormone observations in Section [33](#ss_p10_sec_33) provide separate developmental comparisons, without establishing a female distal reserve advantage.

Infant mineral-hormone differences provide a specific candidate modifier of compensation. The higher three-month intact FGF23 concentration in girls (Holmlund-Suila et al., 2016), together with experimentally different renal actions of PTH and FGF23, supports asking whether boys and girls distribute sodium transport differently during phosphate disposal. A relatively PTH-weighted response in some boys could increase the downstream adjustment needed to maintain balance if proximal sodium reclamation falls (Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9)). That prediction requires a sex difference in the response to a defined exposure, followed by measured transport or recovery differences; baseline hormone concentrations and within-sex correlations do not establish it. Feeding, growth, acid-base and potassium status could modify either direction of response. Minipuberty provides a candidate timing modifier in both sexes, with hormone-linked growth and possible changes in renal regulation considered separately in Section [32.1.4](#ss_p10_sec_32_1_4). Greater male compensatory demand remains a testable contribution, not an established explanation of the autism diagnosis ratio.

Relevant null findings remain informative. A cohort of 262 clinically stable preterm neonates found no significant sex association with plasma renin concentration or serum aldosterone during the first three weeks ([Xu et al., 2023](#ss_p3_ref_Xu2023)). In 39 healthy children aged 7–15 years, circadian sodium regulation was similar between boys and girls under standardised conditions ([Mahler et al., 2015](#ss_p3_ref_Mahler2015)). Whole-kidney output or circulating hormone similarity neither excludes internal transport differences nor supplies evidence for them. Developmental stage, filtration, intake and the defined disturbance must therefore accompany any comparison of allocation or recovery.

##### 40.3.1 Pressure-dominant defence as a candidate response

Pressure-dominant defence could preserve circulation while changing the support available for growth. Sex-dependent glucocorticoid action, adrenal enzymes and DHEA-S turnover are candidate modifiers (Section [34](#ss_p10_sec_34)). Low aldosterone does not establish cortisol substitution, and low renin can accompany effective retention. Fetal experimental expression differences support a developmental question, while an earlier male shift to cortisol-supported pressure defence or greater female renal glucocorticoid inactivation in human fetuses remains to be established.

Sex-dependent maturation of renal corticosteroid pathways provides experimental grounds for this question. In mice, female kidneys showed a late-gestation expression peak at E17.5 for MR, GR, Hsd11b2 and several target genes, including αENaC; male profiles were steadier or increased towards birth ([Dumeige et al., 2017](#ss_chain_ref_Dumeige2017)). These findings support investigating whether local glucocorticoid metabolism and receptor responsiveness alter sodium handling and recovery. They measure developmental gene expression, rather than unused transport reserve, hormone replacement of one defence pathway by another, or the corresponding human fetal response. Adrenal and DHEA-S-related modifiers remain separate components of the proposal in Section [34](#ss_p10_sec_34).

A longer vasoconstrictor phase or slower withdrawal after challenge could narrow perfusion flexibility. The proposed sex difference concerns this developmental response and recovery pattern, not a male baseline inferred from resting autonomic measures.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_40_3_2"></a>

##### 40.3.2 Renal allocation and recovery predictions

The proposed renal contribution to male predominance in identified childhood autism is conditional but specific. If relevant sex differences in proximal/downstream coordination operate during a susceptible developmental window, they could modify the duration or intensity of compensation following a defined mineral or sodium–volume disturbance (Sections [21.5.1](#ss_p10_sec_21_5_1) and [32](#ss_p10_sec_32)). For phosphate excess, a candidate male susceptibility is greater or more persistent proximal phosphate reclamation at a matched filtered load. This could require a larger reduction in phosphate reclamation while sodium balance is maintained through coordinated proximal and downstream transport. Altered delivery between segments could be fully accommodated, produce inadequate conservation during underfilling, or contribute to excessive retention. A male disadvantage is one prediction to test, rather than an inference from adult transporter abundance. A contribution to neural development additionally requires disturbed local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery; peripheral renal or vascular consequences may occur in parallel and do not establish that intermediary.

Existing cohorts, archived samples and clinical observations could relate age-specific renal function to the onset, persistence and resolution of a naturally occurring disturbance. Appropriate adult, animal and computational comparisons can distinguish cumulative sodium deficit or excess, effective filling, mineral recovery and hormonal recruitment after the disturbance ends. Recovery should be assessed against a defined baseline range, with direct tests of sex-by-time or sex-by-disturbance differences. Earlier male distal exhaustion, slower male recovery and an explanation of the diagnostic ratio remain unestablished; preserved recovery or an absent physiological difference would constrain this proposed contribution while leaving other developmental routes available.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_40_4"></a>

#### 40.4 Antioxidant defence across tissues and stages

Selected neonatal studies support sex-dependent antioxidant defence without a universal difference in glutathione concentration. Female-derived neonatal endothelial cells showed increased glutathione-reductase activity and better viability under tert-butylhydroperoxide challenge; separate tracheal-aspirate samples from oxygen-dependent newborns had higher intracellular total glutathione in females ([Lavoie and Chessex, 1997](#ss_p2_ref_Lavoie1997)). Among 240 infants born before 32 weeks, girls had higher erythrocyte GPx and glutathione-reductase activities within 48 hours, while plasma total glutathione did not differ ([Hamon et al., 2011](#ss_p2_ref_Hamon2011)). GPx uses reduced GSH during peroxide reduction, whereas glutathione reductase recycles oxidised glutathione; neither measurement establishes de novo synthesis or a whole-body reserve.

In 56 healthy term deliveries, girls had lower erythrocyte-membrane hydroperoxides in cord arterial blood and higher erythrocyte antioxidant-enzyme activities; GSH concentration and GPx4-specific activity were not measured ([Díaz-Castro et al., 2016](#ss_p2_ref_DiazCastro2016)). Cysteine uptake increased with maturity in female-derived neonatal leukocytes and tracheal-aspirate cells, while no corresponding age association was detected in male-derived cells. This supports precursor availability as a candidate contributor rather than demonstrating faster recovery after depletion ([Lavoie et al., 2002](#ss_p2_ref_Lavoie2002)). Challenge endpoints can point in different directions: peroxide-perfused human umbilical veins showed sustained increased glutathione release from male tissue and dose-dependent eicosanoid responses in female tissue ([Lavoie and Chessex, 1994](#ss_p2_ref_Lavoie1994)). Release into the perfusate is distinct from intracellular availability or effective protection.

Animal findings add developmental specificity without supplying a universal direction. In rats assessed about 20 hours after a postnatal-day-7 hypoxic–ischaemic insult, female shams had approximately 30% more reduced GSH in brain homogenates. After injury, female homogenate GSH fell in both hemispheres and ipsilateral homogenate GPx activity increased; male homogenate GSH increased contralaterally and was unchanged ipsilaterally, while contralateral mitochondrial GPx activity and GPx4 protein decreased (Demarest et al., 2016). In sheep twins at gestational day 65, however, males had more reduced GSH in skeletal muscle, while females had higher brain and liver malondialdehyde (Al-Gubory and Garrel, 2016). Species, tissue, enzyme activity, available substrate and injury are therefore separate dimensions. These results motivate the proposed membrane/endothelial and local steroid modifiers in Sections [34.7](#ss_p10_sec_34_7) and [35.1](#ss_p10_sec_35_1); they do not establish faster female neural recovery or renal AVP clearance.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_40_5"></a>

#### 40.5 Neural maturation and recovery comparisons

There is a developmental timing signal in chloride-related physiology. In hippocampal cultures prepared from newborn rats, Nuñez and McCarthy (2007) found larger muscimol-evoked calcium peaks in females at two days in vitro but in males at seven days; neither sex showed a significant average rise at 14 days. Separate hippocampal tissue measurements showed higher phosphorylated NKCC1 in males at postnatal days 0 and 7, no sex difference by day 14, and higher KCC2 in females at day 7. These findings motivate a specific hypothesis: a matched ionic perturbation may have different consequences when it overlaps different maturation schedules. They do not establish a general male WNK–SPAK/OSR1 response to hyponatraemia or human renal NKCC2 instability. As Section [26](#ss_p10_sec_26) explains, a depolarising GABA response must also be distinguished from its net effect on inhibition and firing.

Regional findings refine that proposal. In rat mediobasal hypothalamus, [Perrot-Sinal et al. (2007)](#ss_bridge2_ref_PerrotSinal2007) found higher male total NKCC1 at embryonic day 20 and birth, but no sex difference in phosphorylated NKCC1. KCC2 protein was undetectable at those ages and lower in males at postnatal day 5. The hypothalamic phosphorylation result therefore differs from the hippocampal comparison above. Abundance and phosphorylation cannot substitute for measured transport or recovery, and these overlapping-investigator studies are not independent replications of one universal sex effect.

The developmental exposure studies in Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7) make timing a candidate interaction rather than a fixed ranking of vulnerability. The relevant prediction concerns sex, cell type, developmental stage and exposure together: do matched disturbances produce different recovery trajectories, and do those trajectories mediate a specified developmental effect? This requires an explicit interaction comparison and appropriate recovery measurements. A finding in males alone, or significance in one sex but not the other, cannot establish that interaction or a general female protective advantage.

OXTR timing adds another candidate modifier (Section [37.1.2](#ss_p10_sec_37_1_2)). Its relevance is whether a disturbance overlaps a period of altered peptide responsiveness and changes local neural or glial recovery. The birth experiments in Section [23.7](#ss_p10_sec_23_7) and infant concentration findings in Section [36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5) do not establish a universal female protective advantage.

Slower restoration of a specified osmolyte pool could extend overlap between recovery and sensitive maturation. Section [24](#ss_p10_sec_24) develops this mechanism; a general rule of faster male loss or slower male recovery is not established.

Brain-water adaptation provides a positive but distinct comparison. During continuous AVP or desmopressin infusion producing severe hyponatraemia in rats, brain water returned to normonatraemic-control levels after five days in females and ten days in males; no deaths occurred in either infusion group ([Verbalis, 1993](#ss_p5_ref_Verbalis1993)). These sampled timepoints describe volume adaptation during continued hyponatraemia, not post-correction osmolyte restoration; the timepoints alone do not establish a formal sex-by-time difference. They cannot supply an infant recovery timetable. Successful volume adaptation can therefore coexist with an ongoing extracellular disturbance.

Survival findings point in a different direction under another protocol. [Arieff et al. (1995)](#ss_p5_ref_Arieff1995) reported mortality of 62% in adult females and 13% in adult males during chronic hyponatraemia. [Silver et al. (1999)](#ss_p5_ref_Silver1999) subsequently found no deaths or detected sex differences in measured brain water, electrolytes or major osmolytes during a four-hour AVP-and-water experiment in 10-day-old pups. This re-examined the earlier young-rat findings, not the chronic-adult mortality arm. Silver and colleagues identified differences in water administration and sodium severity, including less severe hyponatraemia in the earlier testosterone-treated pups. Those differences limit comparability without resolving the adult discrepancy.

Vascular measurements add another endpoint. After four days of AVP-associated hyponatraemia in adult rats, female cerebral blood flow and oxygen consumption were reduced, while male values were unchanged ([Koźniewska et al., 1995](#ss_p5_ref_Kozniewska1995)). The MRI cerebral perfusion index fell in females, but not with desmopressin-induced hyponatraemia or AVP during normonatraemia. Oestrogen-pretreated hyponatraemic males had perfusion-index values not different from females. These results identify protocol-dependent vascular responses, without isolating sodium from osmolality or explaining the survival disagreement. AVP versus desmopressin alone is insufficient to reconcile the studies because both infusion groups survived in Verbalis’s experiment. The separate glutathione and isolated-vessel findings in Sections [3.3](#ss_p10_sec_3_3) and [24.3](#ss_p10_sec_24_3) do not establish the cause of the reported brain-water timepoints or survival differences.

#### 40.6 Other modifiers and the integrated prediction

Sex-dependent barrier or CSF–interstitial responses could similarly alter exposure or recovery (Section [30](#ss_p10_sec_30)). Adult oestrogen effects do not establish fetal physiology or explain the autism sex ratio.

Thyroid-dependent maturation and ATP-supported transport offer further modifiers where they precede reduced recovery capacity. Neither hyponatraemia-induced thyroid suppression nor greater male dependence is assumed; transport work remains distinct from inadequate ATP supply (Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23), [26](#ss_p10_sec_26), and [27](#ss_p10_sec_27)).

Sex could modify the developmental cost of a challenge through regulatory allocation, recovery and maturation, without one universal hormone signature or protection for every girl. This explanation gains support only where the physiological difference helps account for developmental outcomes beyond genetic liability and identification effects; diagnosis rates alone cannot establish it.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_41"></a>

### 41 Centralisation of Perfusion: Preferential Blood Redistribution Under Sodium–Volume Defence

Centralisation of perfusion denotes a protective redistribution of circulatory support during a measured filling or pressure challenge. The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad, together with autonomic control of vascular resistance and venous capacitance, can support central filling while changing regional delivery. The key distinction is between preserving systemic pressure and matching local delivery to local demand. Healthy-adult tilt and lower-body negative pressure maintained systolic pressure despite reduced regional flows and opposite splanchnic volume changes (Taneja et al., 2007). Reservoir volume, regional blood flow and cellular recovery must therefore be followed separately; Section [43](#ss_p10_sec_43) develops the splanchnic example and Sections [42](#ss_p10_sec_42) and [44](#ss_p10_sec_44) extend the question to autonomic and postural demand.

The splanchnic circulation is a substantial blood reservoir, but its resting contents are not the amount routinely mobilised, and blood volume is distinct from tissue blood flow or total body water. In healthy adults, Taneja et al. (2007) found approximately 18% greater splanchnic segmental volume during 70° head-up tilt (n = 8) and 12% lower volume during −50 mmHg lower-body negative pressure (n = 10), despite similar reductions in regional flow. These impedance estimates refer to change from supine baseline in the regional compartment. They demonstrate why posture, venous capacitance and arterial resistance must be measured separately; they do not establish visceral injury or an autism mechanism.

The developmental proposal begins where successful circulatory defence leaves a demonstrable local recovery cost. If altered delivery constrains restoration of ionic gradients or cellular volume in developing neurons or glia, repeated recruitment could contribute to the lasting changes in reserve and response proposed in Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)–[30](#ss_p10_sec_30) and [38](#ss_p10_sec_38). The same redistribution with adequate local recovery remains successful compensation. For this branch, the discriminating sequence is a defined challenge, a measured redistribution, impaired local recovery and a subsequent developmental effect. Preserved pressure alone supplies none of the intervening measurements. Genetic constraints can instead initiate local recovery difficulty directly, without this systemic sequence (Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_42"></a>

### 42 Autonomic Recalibration: Pressure Defence and Recovery Under Load

(A proposed plastic downstream consequence; functional set-point recalibration)

Normal maturation is the comparison for this proposed recalibration. In term infants, heart-rate and blood-pressure variability changed with age and sleep state during the first six months (Yiallourou et al., 2012; Section [44.2](#ss_p10_sec_44_2)). Recalibration here means a history-dependent change in later responses beyond developmental stage, current state and the matched challenge. Its relation to the local neural/glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery mechanism required by [Section 2](#ss_p10_sec_2) must be measured separately.

The Sodium-Struggle framework links these immediate regulatory responses to a possible lasting change in autonomic control: an adjustable downstream layer of defence. Repeated recruitment to protect pressure and perfusion could alter the thresholds, intensity and termination of later responses. This is proposed to be more reversible than structural developmental changes in the Section [22.1](#ss_p10_sec_22_1) roadmap, a comparison requiring longitudinal evidence. Stability at rest can coexist with a higher cost of maintaining stability during activity; the predicted cost is a physiological measurement, not an inference from an autistic trait.

Section [18](#ss_p10_sec_18) proposes tissue-specific AVPR1A/AVPR1B sensitisation, reduced OXTR responsiveness and altered aquaporin-dependent handling as possible influences on later autonomic thresholds. They are separate receptor hypotheses, not a shared signature supplied by resting hormones or extra-axial CSF. Sections [36](#ss_p10_sec_36) and [37](#ss_p10_sec_37) distinguish receptor-level persistence from controller architecture. Autonomic recalibration can be assessed independently of any one receptor branch.

#### 42.1 Autonomic prioritisation under pressure and perfusion threat

When effective central filling or arterial pressure falls, rapid autonomic adjustments help defend circulation. Human blockade experiments identify a major vagal contribution to the initial heart-rate response to standing, while postural studies distinguish active movement from passive tilt (Ewing et al., 1980; Borst et al., 1982). The hypothesis extends this acute physiology to development: repeated recruitment could favour earlier withdrawal of cardiac vagal restraint or more persistent sympathetic support under a specified challenge. A low sodium concentration alone does not determine that response. Osmotic cues, filling, pressure and the timing of AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence-triad recruitment must be distinguished, as in Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3).

#### 42.2 The proposed imprint: response thresholds and recovery

The proposed imprint concerns vagal set point, baroreflex gain and sensitivity, vestibulo–autonomic integration, sympathetic thresholds and endocrine coordination. Developmental timing and individual plasticity would shape when, how strongly and for how long support is recruited, without requiring a uniform resting signature.

Autonomic calibration provides a candidate connection between cardiac regulation, visceral function and the timing of recovery. The prediction is coordinated change under a defined load: the physiological disturbance should precede or accompany the specific functional difficulty. Extensions to immune, speech or motor function require their own functional measurements rather than cardiac variability as a proxy.

#### 42.3 Cardiac vagal regulation during challenge and recovery

The relevant distinction is between a persistently low resting measure and difficulty regulating or recovering during load. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) indexes respiratory modulation of cardiac intervals; its interpretation depends on breathing and recording conditions. In healthy adults, changing breathing rate and tidal volume altered interval spectra without significantly changing mean intervals (Brown et al., 1993). RSA is therefore neither a direct measure of whole-body vagal activity nor a measurement of cerebral blood flow.

For a specified developmental stage and load, this branch predicts greater cardiac vagal withdrawal or slower recovery after comparable filling reductions. Blunted, exaggerated and oscillating responses cannot all confirm that same prediction.

#### 42.4 Sympathetic recruitment and the cost of recovery

Repeated defence episodes are proposed to make rapid mobilisation easier to recruit and harder to terminate. This would link current load with prolonged arousal and recovery demands, while retaining the short-term protective role of the AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad. The developmental prediction is that earlier measured burden forecasts later response thresholds beyond current illness, medication, anxiety, fitness and sleep; a cross-sectional difference cannot establish that history.

#### 42.5 What ASD autonomic studies establish

The evidence supports context-sensitive autonomic differences, but not one invariant pattern. In 40 autistic children and 34 controls, Kushki et al. (2014) found no baseline RSA difference and a blunted heart-rate response to public speaking. The Eyes-task RSA contrast reached significance only after excluding medicated participants and the overall RSA group-by-task interaction was not significant. In 18 autistic and 18 non-autistic boys aged 8–11, Neuhaus et al. (2016) found similar autonomic change with a novel partner but different responses with a familiar partner. These findings justify measuring task and recovery conditions. They do not demonstrate sodium-driven imprinting, cerebral underperfusion or uniformly exaggerated defence.

#### 42.6 Lifespan expression as context-dependent instability

The proposed lifespan expression is variable capacity under changing demands, including prolonged recovery or reduced engagement after activity. It becomes a physiological explanation only where filling, delivery or recovery accounts for within-person change beyond sensory, emotional and social context; pallor, unusual gait, fatigue or burnout-like experiences alone do not identify the cause.

#### 42.7 Testable predictions and boundary conditions

The walking window is a developmental probe of earlier constraints, not an assumed cause of regression or a required route to autism. Section [47.4.1](#ss_p10_sec_47_4_1) develops the distinction between demand, delivery and engagement.

- Endocrine timing: the volume-defence branch predicts larger or more persistent copeptin responses than controls matched for tonicity, renal function and the fall in effective filling. The mixed-cue prediction of relatively suppressed AVP recruitment in Section [10.3](#ss_p10_sec_10_3) is a separate comparison.

- Regional delivery: the predicted postural disturbance concerns flow or oxygen delivery. Conventional fNIRS measures haemoglobin oxygenation changes, not cerebral blood flow directly; systemic and respiratory CO₂ effects can also alter the signal (Kirilina et al., 2012).

- Motor expression: gait differences are outcomes to explain and potential mechanical modifiers, not clinical proxies establishing vestibulo–autonomic dysfunction.

The adaptive-recalibration branch is weakened when the predicted autonomic or delivery disturbance is absent during the relevant load-related functional change, or when earlier measured burden fails to predict later calibration. A normal resting result does not settle this dynamic claim. Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2) defines the implications for the common-process conjecture.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_43"></a>

### 43 Splanchnic Reservoir Imprinting: Preferential Abdominal Volume Recruitment and GI Consequences

#### 43.1 Splanchnic Volume Defence and Gastrointestinal Function

##### 43.1.1 Definition

The gut provides an organ-level example of the redistribution described in Section [41](#ss_p10_sec_41). The Splanchnic Reservoir Hypothesis concerns coupling among three distinct processes: vascular reservoir recruitment, epithelial sodium and water transport, and neural regulation of motility and secretion. These processes may respond together to effective sodium–volume signalling, but reservoir blood volume, luminal fluid balance and transit are different endpoints (Sections [43.1.3](#ss_p10_sec_43_1_3)–[43.1.7](#ss_p10_sec_43_1_7)). The proposed history-dependent gastrointestinal contribution therefore requires a measured link between circulatory recruitment and the relevant local response.

##### 43.1.2 Sensing and regulatory routes

Volume-related sensing includes gut-wall stretch and signals of effective central filling, but splanchnic pooling or redistribution is a haemodynamic state rather than a single sensory pathway. Enteric and vagal signalling about gut conditions must be distinguished from baroreflex pathways responding to circulatory loading. RAAS-related cues and stress-hormone dynamics can influence vascular and epithelial responses as well as autonomic recruitment. These pathways can converge on gut function without assigning the same direction to perfusion, secretion or motility (Sections [43.1.3](#ss_p10_sec_43_1_3), [43.1.6](#ss_p10_sec_43_1_6), and [43.2](#ss_p10_sec_43_2)).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_43_1_3"></a>

##### 43.1.3 Splanchnic recruitment during circulatory challenge

Sympathetic recruitment could couple central filling to gut function through mesenteric resistance and venous capacitance. In healthy adults, head-up tilt and lower-body negative pressure changed splanchnic volume in opposite directions despite similar reductions in flow (Taneja et al., 2007; Section [41](#ss_p10_sec_41)). Vascular redistribution therefore cannot be equated with intestinal water loss, dry stool or altered secretion.

The reservoir role provides a plausible route for state-dependent coupling between circulatory defence and gut function. Repeated recruitment is proposed to increase variability in perfusion or symptoms only where recovery is incomplete or a local functional cost is demonstrated; ordinary adaptive redistribution need not impair the gut.

###### ***43.1.3.1 Later haemodynamic responses***

The vascular branch predicts exaggerated splanchnic vasoconstriction, redistribution or delayed recovery during later circulatory challenge. Reservoir volume, gut-wall perfusion and visceral sensation remain distinct: altered recruitment becomes consequential only where it changes local function.

##### 43.1.4 Corroborative contexts and natural experiments

Orthostasis illustrates recruitment of the splanchnic reservoir: baroreflex-driven sympathetic output can change venous compliance as well as arteriolar resistance. Coexisting nausea, bloating, constipation or diarrhoea could reflect this coupling, but cannot identify redistribution as the cause or exclude primary gastrointestinal disease.

Digestion and central circulatory support can impose concurrent demands; heat and exercise provide further contexts in which coupling may become apparent. Symptoms alone do not distinguish vascular recruitment from epithelial transport, autonomic signalling or other gastrointestinal mechanisms.

##### 43.1.5 Luminal conditions and gastrointestinal function

Osmotically active agents can change stool water and transit, illustrating a luminal route to altered bowel function. Luminal osmolality, epithelial absorption and secretion, and motility must nevertheless be distinguished. In controlled perfusion of the intact human colon, increasing sodium within isotonic solutions increased net sodium and water absorption, whereas sufficiently hypertonic mannitol solutions drew water into the lumen (Billich and Levitan, 1969). The direction depended on solution composition. This supports a sodium–water interface without establishing that withdrawal of vascular volume produces the same response.

AVP, aldosterone and cortisol can couple effective circulating volume to gut transport, vascular tone and motility. Stress-related endocrine states may suppress or accelerate transit depending on autonomic context; this is not a fixed conservation response.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_43_1_6"></a>

##### 43.1.6 Sodium-dependent epithelial mechanisms

Intestinal sodium transport supplies a concrete interface between endocrine regulation and luminal water balance. Net fluid handling reflects both absorption and secretion; sodium does not move uniformly into the lumen. ENaC-mediated apical sodium entry in the distal colon is coupled to basolateral extrusion by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. In isolated human colon, aldosterone increased the amiloride-sensitive transport component in the distal segment, with no corresponding increase in the proximal segment (Sandle, 1989). The developmental extension is that altered endocrine or autonomic recruitment changes epithelial transport during a measured circulatory challenge. A change in vascular volume alone cannot establish the direction of epithelial flux, stool water or transit.

Small-intestinal sodium–glucose absorption provides a separate epithelial connection. Apical SGLT1 uses the sodium gradient to take up glucose and galactose; facilitative glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2; SLC2A2) supports basolateral sugar exit. Sglt1 deletion in mice markedly impaired intestinal glucose absorption (Gorboulev et al., 2012). Human jejunal perfusion demonstrated glucose-dependent sodium and water absorption, with effects varying by luminal concentration and flow (Modigliani and Bernier, 1971). These observations connect carbohydrate delivery with fluid uptake, but neither carrier abundance nor coupling stoichiometry determines net absorption when secretion and luminal conditions also vary. Renal glucose reclamation and subsequent tissue disposal are considered separately in §[19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7).

A selected human study makes this a candidate gastrointestinal interface in autism. Ileal biopsies from 15 boys with autistic disorder and gastrointestinal disease had lower SGLT1 and GLUT2 mRNA than biopsies from seven boys with gastrointestinal disease alone (Williams et al., 2011). These transcript measurements did not establish reduced transporter activity, sodium depletion or a finding generalisable to autism without gastrointestinal disease.

A separate study found higher small-intestinal SGLT1 and SGLT3 protein signals in male BTBR mice than in C57BL/6J controls (Franco et al., 2021). It did not study SGLT2. Different species, intestinal sampling and transcript-versus-protein measurements do not establish a common direction of altered transport or compensatory instability. A contribution to the proposed developmental pathway to autism requires altered epithelial function to change sodium, water or glucose handling sufficiently to impair local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery during a susceptible interval. Expression differences alone do not establish that route.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_43_1_7"></a>

##### 43.1.7 Neural and endocrine regulation during later challenge

The proposed downstream enteric branch asks whether a measured developmental change in autonomic, vascular or endocrine regulation alters gut function during later challenge. The relevant imprint and its gastrointestinal consequence must be established together.

###### ***43.1.7.1 Autonomic gating of motility and secretion***
