Altered sympathetic or vagal recruitment could slow propulsion, increase sphincter engagement or alter epithelial flux during challenge, with urgency or looser stools during recovery. Direction depends on the gut segment and timing; this proposed contribution neither excludes coexisting disease nor explains alternating constipation and diarrhoea from symptoms alone.

Autism studies report context-dependent differences in cardiac autonomic modulation, including within-study null results (Kushki et al., 2014; Neuhaus et al., 2016). As Section [42](#ss_p10_sec_42) explains, heart-rate variability (HRV) and respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) do not directly measure gut vagal function or establish reduced visceral buffering.

A separate consequence of vagal regulation concerns vitamin B12 handling. In seven duodenal-ulcer patients, proximal gastric vagotomy reduced basal and pentagastrin-stimulated intrinsic-factor output by 19.8% and 41.4%, respectively; the authors attributed the reduction to lower gastric secretory volume (Vatn et al., 1975). This supports neural control of the gastric secretory component. Whether smaller, state-dependent vagal changes reduce B12 absorption remains the proposed functional extension; neither reduced intrinsic-factor output nor a cardiac HRV difference establishes that consequence.

###### ***43.1.7.2 Endocrine coupling to sodium and water handling***

The endocrine branch concerns altered aldosterone or cortisol action on epithelial sodium and fluid handling. Hormone concentration does not identify local receptor action, net transport or stool consistency; structural and inflammatory causes can coexist.

##### 43.1.8 Haemodynamic Selection: A Candidate Contributor to Dysbiosis

Within the Splanchnic Reservoir Hypothesis, repeated changes in perfusion, secretion or transit could alter the conditions in which microbes compete. A direct physiological precedent comes from mice given polyethylene glycol (PEG): caecal osmolality rose from 533 to 810 mOsm/kg while blood osmolality remained unchanged, and microbial community composition shifted. In culture, a Muribaculum intestinale isolate failed to grow above 700 mOsm/kg, while other tested commensals retained growth (Tropini et al., 2018). This demonstrates local osmotic selection under the tested conditions. The proposed haemodynamic extension requires circulatory recruitment to produce a corresponding luminal change; redistribution alone does not establish it.

Relative abundance cannot distinguish microbial expansion from attrition elsewhere in the community. Combining sequencing with cell counts revealed up to tenfold differences in faecal microbial load between healthy individuals and showed that an apparent Bacteroides–Prevotella trade-off was a compositional artefact (Vandeputte et al., 2017a). A relatively prominent Bacteroides population therefore cannot be assigned expansion, competitive replacement or selective survival without quantitative abundance and functional evidence.

Stool water content is also distinct from water available for microbial growth. In 62 fresh human stool samples, water activity remained above 0.97 and correlated with neither moisture content nor stool consistency (Vandeputte et al., 2017b). This argues against ordinary differences in stool firmness acting through desiccation. It leaves measured changes in transit, substrate delivery or substantial luminal osmolality as distinct ecological mechanisms.

The mucus interface offers another measured ecological link. In the mouse PEG experiment, mean colonic mucus thickness fell from 34.2 to 10.0 μm and subsequently recovered, without histological epithelial injury (Tropini et al., 2018). A changed microbial habitat therefore need not imply persistent barrier failure. Hypoperfusion is a separate candidate entry route, considered in Section [43.2](#ss_p10_sec_43_2); attributing microbial change to that route requires evidence of the intervening local perfusion and epithelial response.

Human intervention data connect transit changes with microbial changes. In eight healthy volunteers on a controlled diet, mean transit time was 73 hours at baseline, 47 hours with cisapride and 147 hours with loperamide; the slower-transit period increased methanogen counts and reduced sulphate-reducer counts (El Oufir et al., 1996). Feedback is also possible: methane infusion slowed transit in dogs (Pimentel et al., 2006). These findings support a bidirectional transit–microbial relationship, although the drugs may affect other gut functions. They do not establish a microbial signature of reservoir withdrawal or a shared tolerance to low flow.

Changes in transit, bile acids or secretion could also alter microbial sterol metabolism and delivery to host membranes (Section [35](#ss_p10_sec_35)). This remains a proposed connection; neither its taxonomic direction nor its effect on membrane protection and recovery is established.

Microbial change could be a consequence of altered perfusion, transport or transit, a feedback influence, or an independent process. The reservoir hypothesis concerns the first route; dysbiosis alone cannot establish it.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_43_2"></a>

#### 43.2 Secondary and Tertiary Consequences of Repeated Splanchnic Volume Defence

Repeated recruitment of the pressure-defence configuration in Section [43.1.3](#ss_p10_sec_43_1_3) could preserve central filling while changing local tissue support. Arterial pressure, microvascular flow and inflammatory activity are distinct variables: maintaining pressure does not require inflammation to cease. In 20 adults with septic shock, raising mean arterial pressure from 65 to 75 and 85 mmHg with noradrenaline did not improve mean sublingual microvascular flow index or the proportion of perfused capillaries, despite substantial individual variation (Dubin et al., 2009). This severe inflammatory preparation demonstrates that higher pressure need not restore microvascular delivery; it does not establish intestinal hypoperfusion during ordinary successful defence. The proposed gut cost therefore depends on local delivery relative to workload and recovery, not on pressure defence and inflammation being incompatible programmes.

Immune timing has direct experimental support, although a universal suppression–rebound sequence does not. In 23 healthy adults, hydrocortisone given immediately before and during endotoxin exposure rendered circulating TNF undetectable while leaving IL-6 unchanged; when endotoxin was given 12 or 144 hours after a six-hour hydrocortisone infusion, both cytokine responses were greater than with endotoxin alone (Barber et al., 1993). In a separate randomised study of 36 healthy adults, an intermediate six-hour cortisol infusion increased IL-6 and reduced IL-10 responses to endotoxin the next day; the higher dose did not significantly change those overall responses, and TNF did not differ between groups (Yeager et al., 2009). These results preserve a strong timing principle: an endocrine exposure can alter a later inflammatory response after circulating cortisol has returned to baseline. They demonstrate priming of a subsequent challenge, not spontaneous rebound or gut-specific immune suppression. The proposed extension is that recurrent defence episodes could similarly shift symptom timing where the local endocrine or delivery sequence is demonstrated.

Villus-tip injury provides a concrete tissue-level example of delayed costs and rapid repair. In 30 adults undergoing pancreatic surgery, an isolated jejunal segment underwent 30 minutes of ischaemia. Epithelial injury was followed by shedding of apoptotic villus-tip enterocytes after 25 minutes of reperfusion, and epithelial continuity was restored within 60 minutes (Derikx et al., 2008). Thus, a transient perfusion insult can produce structural injury that repairs rapidly, not only functional disturbance. The proposed extension is that repeated deficits in delivery relative to epithelial workload could cause reversible brush-border or transport dysfunction, with gradient restoration and barrier repair extending the recovery demand. The human experiment establishes injury and repair after vascular occlusion; it does not establish injury from moderate adaptive redistribution, nor quantify the proposed competition for recovery energy.

A separate hepatic experiment supports an energetic constraint on conjugation. In isolated rat hepatocytes, low oxygen inhibited acetaminophen sulphation, and experimentally lowering ATP reproduced the inhibition; ethionine experiments linked the sulphation effect to absolute ATP loss (Aw and Jones, 1982). This is evidence for oxygen-sensitive, ATP-dependent conjugation in that preparation. It does not show that intestinal gradient restoration consumes hepatic ATP or that sulphate becomes depleted. The proposed gut–liver link is a shared limitation of oxygen delivery or metabolic capacity that could constrain both epithelial recovery and hepatic conjugation, with the connection between compartments still unmeasured.

Interoceptive consequences require pathway-specific attribution. In mice, intragastric water inhibited thirst-promoting subfornical-organ neurons before a detectable change in blood osmolarity, whereas hypertonic saline activated them; vagotomy attenuated the gut signal and water-induced satiation (Zimmerman et al., 2019). This supplies a direct gut–fluid-homeostasis bridge, including recorded responses of vasopressin neurons, without showing that sympathetic recruitment silences visceral afferents. In adult female mice, one hour of water-avoidance stress daily for ten days increased urinary frequency without increasing urine production and enhanced bladder afferent activity at physiological filling pressures; activity fell at high, noxious pressures (Mills et al., 2021). Stress can therefore reshape sensory gain rather than simply reduce it. The proposed contribution is altered timing of thirst or bladder signalling during documented defence and recovery. Hunger, pain, sphincter control and sensation are separate endpoints; low drinking, withholding or accidents alone cannot identify the mechanism or establish recovery.

#### 43.3 Scope and competing routes

This is an additional downstream route, compatible with gut-originating disease and gut-to-system feedback. It does not require universal or persistent gastrointestinal symptoms.

#### 43.4 Synthesis

Enteric function may carry the history of how circulation was defended, if a measured change in autonomic or endocrine recruitment predicts the local gut response and its recovery.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_44"></a>

### 44 Mechanical Engagement: The Walking Window as a Conditional Probe of Imprinted Physiology

Crawling, supported standing and independent walking change postural transitions, muscle-pump activity and recovery demands. The locomotor transition could therefore reveal limited reserve that was less apparent earlier. Walking is an expression-stage probe of prior calibration, not a necessary initiating cause of autism; neither regression nor discrete skill loss is required.

The walking window is defined by the child’s actual exposure and experience, not by a fixed birthday. In the WHO longitudinal study, the 1st–99th percentile window for walking alone was 8.2–17.6 months, and supported standing generally occurred earlier (WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study Group, 2006). Thus the manuscript’s approximate 11–18-month focus is a candidate observation period, not a universal onset threshold. Early features before walking remain compatible with this expression-stage proposal.

Its strongest prediction concerns within-child change: as upright exposure increases, children with the proposed limited reserve should show greater transition-related physiological disturbance or slower recovery than expected from age, movement and arousal alone. That prediction can fail even if some other part of the Sodium Struggle remains plausible.

#### 44.1 A changing mechanical workload

Upright posture increases heart-to-head and dependent-bed separation, changing hydrostatic pressures and venous distribution. Muscle activity and reflex responses can compensate, so the new workload combines loading, active pumping and recovery rather than uniformly worsening circulation.

Natural walking supplies many repeated opportunities to observe that balance. During spontaneous free play, 12–19-month-old walkers averaged approximately 2,368 steps and 17 falls per hour, with movement distributed in short, variable bouts (Adolph et al., 2012). These are motor observations, not counts of hypotensive episodes. They establish the frequency and intermittency of the workload that the hypothesis proposes to measure.

Stepping can assist venous return, while stopping removes that assistance; rising also changes muscle activation, resistance and reflex drive. Posture or variable early gait therefore cannot establish the direction of a pressure change or an inefficient pump. Adult measurements show why movement details matter, but the proposed infant shortfall remains unmeasured (Tauraginskii et al., 2023).

<a name="ss_p10_sec_44_2"></a>

#### 44.2 The autonomic challenge: vagal buffering, baroreflex gain, vestibulo-autonomic coupling

Movement recruits cardiac timing, vascular resistance, venous return and breathing together. Vagal withdrawal and sympathetic support can be effective compensation; a lower vagal index alone does not identify impaired recovery or reduced cerebral delivery.

Infants already compensate for postural perturbations well before walking. In nine healthy term newborns, 30° head-up tilt increased heart rate by about 3.25 beats/min; the authors described an effective baroreceptor response (Thoresen et al., 1991). In a separate longitudinal study of 31 term infants, heart-rate and blood-pressure variability changed with sleep state and age over the first six months (Yiallourou et al., 2012). Functional compensation and continuing maturation coexist.

These neonatal findings concern an already functioning system. The proposal is that prior constraints alter its reserve as exposure changes; young age, neonatal tilt responses and sleep-related maturation do not establish a deficit at walking onset.

The predicted abnormality is a transition-related cerebral delivery or recovery difference. A transient systemic pressure change may be buffered locally, and neither HRV nor a normal resting value settles that dynamic question.

Vestibular input supplies a concrete link between movement and cardiovascular regulation. In adult experiments, head-down rotation increased muscle sympathetic nerve activity during lower-body negative pressure, demonstrating interaction between vestibular stimulation and baroreflex unloading (Ray, 2000). This supports a protective contribution to control during movement. It does not show that lateral gaze, infant walking or increased vestibular drive causes perfusion instability.

Reduced effective filling or incomplete recovery could make the same daily transitions require more autonomic and endocrine support. That is the proposed connection to sodium–volume defence; movement or HRV does not assign the direction of AVP, RAAS or cortisol recruitment.

#### 44.3 Hydrostatic load and lever-arm effects as a conditional amplifier

Hydrostatic pressure follows ΔP = ρgh: at an assumed blood density of 1,060 kg/m³, 10 cm corresponds to about 7.8 mmHg. This calculation is not a measured infant pressure fall; actual delivery depends on arterial and venous pressures and compensation (Figure [44.1](#ss_p10_figure_44_1)).

An infant’s shorter column produces a smaller absolute gradient than an adult’s at comparable orientation, without establishing greater reserve. Dependent filling pressure can rise without altered intrinsic vessel compliance. The candidate amplifier is the interaction of actual geometry, venous distribution, pumping and compensation; stature alone identifies none of these limitations.

**Text description of Figure 44.1**

The diagram, titled “Posture, hydrostatic load and compensation”, compares schematic relatively horizontal and upright bodies. Both mark the head, heart and a dependent vascular bed. In the horizontal view, these points have smaller vertical separations. In the upright view, the head lies above a dashed heart-reference plane and the dependent bed below it. Double-headed dimension arrows indicate positive displacement above the heart (Δz \> 0) and negative displacement below it (Δz \< 0); they mark distances, not blood-flow directions.

A formula panel gives the hydrostatic contribution relative to the heart as ΔP = −ρgΔz. At an assumed blood density of 1,060 kg/m³, a 10 cm vertical separation corresponds to a pressure-difference magnitude of approximately 7.8 mmHg. The panel explicitly identifies this as a pressure contribution rather than a measured perfusion fall.

Below, two boxes point with solid arrows to a common measurement box. “Load changes”, comprising geometry and venous distribution, has an arrow labelled “contributes”. “Protective support”, comprising muscle-pump and reflex responses, has an arrow labelled “buffers”. The destination requires separate measurement of filling and pressure, and of regional delivery and recovery.

The legend identifies these arrows as component physiology, not measured developmental mediation. The proposed interpretation appears separately at the bottom: limited reserve may disturb delivery or delay recovery after matched transitions. The diagram therefore distinguishes the physical pressure term and protective responses from the hypothesis about limited reserve.

<a name="ss_p10_figure_44_1"></a>Figure [44.1](#ss_p10_figure_44_1). Posture, hydrostatic load and compensation. The hydrostatic contribution relative to heart height is ΔP = −ρgΔz, where ρ is blood density, g is gravitational acceleration and Δz is vertical displacement, positive above the heart. At 1,060 kg/m³, 10 cm corresponds to a pressure-difference magnitude of approximately 7.8 mmHg. This is a physical calculation, not a measured infant pressure fall or loss of cerebral perfusion. Muscle-pump and reflex responses can preserve filling and delivery despite changing geometry. Solid arrows indicate component physiological contributions; the limited-reserve interpretation is the hypothesis to test. Actual geometry, pressure, regional delivery and recovery require separate measurement. The same physical relation applies during growth, without making walking, stature or adolescence a necessary cause of a neurodevelopmental outcome.

#### 44.4 Why cortex matters here

Locomotor exploration recruits cortical systems that integrate sensory information, predict movement and sustain engagement. The proposed vulnerability is a mismatch between regional demand and available delivery or recovery, not a claim that all association cortex occupies vascular border zones. Section [47](#ss_p10_sec_47) distinguishes actual vascular anatomy from functional network labels.

A systemic perturbation becomes relevant here only if it changes cortical delivery relative to demand beyond normal neurovascular responses or motion artefact. A regional haemodynamic signal alone cannot establish insufficient supply.

Repeated delivery or recovery disturbances could then contribute to the developmental timing mechanisms proposed in Section [37](#ss_p10_sec_37). The two-timescale proposal is that current movements can reveal a limitation, while repeated limitation could influence later circuit calibration. Neither an acute haemodynamic association nor a receptor finding alone establishes the full developmental sequence.

<a name="ss_p10_table_44_1"></a>**Table [44.1](#ss_p10_table_44_1). Conditions, proposed effects and interpretive boundaries**

| **Condition**                            | **Proposed effect**                            | **Interpretive boundary**                                                      |
|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Limited transition-related reserve       | Larger delivery disturbance or slower recovery | HRV alone identifies neither delivery disturbance nor impaired recovery.       |
| Repeated head and postural motion        | More frequent demands on coordinated control   | Motion itself does not establish a recovery limitation.                        |
| Greater vertical separation              | Larger hydrostatic component of load           | The hydrostatic component depends on geometry and pressure, not stature alone. |
| Proposed osmolyte or recovery constraint | Longer local recovery after matched demand     | Network labels do not identify a local osmolyte or recovery constraint.        |

These are prospective contrasts, not established network differences. Preserved delivery and recovery during the predicted vulnerable transitions would weaken the corresponding branch; a difference confined to an unrelated task would not confirm it.

<a name="ss_p10_box_44_1"></a>**Box [44.1](#ss_p10_box_44_1). Movement-Assisted Stability Across Walking Onset**

Section [45.1](#ss_p10_sec_45_1) defines the toe-walking proposal. At walking onset, the proposed benefit is movement-assisted stability during the child’s actual upright exposure, rather than a consequence assigned from the milestone alone.

ECG and HRV describe cardiac timing, not arterial pressure or cerebral perfusion. ECG-to-PPG delay is pulse arrival time, including the pre-ejection period; it is neither pure pulse transit time nor automatically validated blood pressure (Payne et al., 2006).

The branch predicts greater disturbance or slower recovery during upright transitions, and improved recovery preceding or accompanying engagement when a movement compensates for it. Preserved physiology despite the functional change, or no benefit from the proposed compensatory movement, would weaken this account. Even a positive association would not establish earlier sodium–volume defence, a hormonal mediator or lasting developmental change.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_45"></a>

### 45 Motor and Sensory Contributions to Physiological Regulation

Sections [42](#ss_p10_sec_42) and [44](#ss_p10_sec_44) provide the autonomic and postural context for these applications. A movement’s circulatory contribution depends on its measured effect on filling, delivery or recovery alongside its sensory, motor, expressive and pleasurable functions.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_45_1"></a>

#### 45.1 Toe Walking as a Candidate Mechanical Contribution to Perfusion

Movement supplies another potential contribution to circulatory regulation. When upright reserve is limited, a recurring movement could acquire an immediate circulatory benefit alongside its sensory or motor functions. Toe walking is a candidate because it changes calf recruitment and foot loading; its appearance alone cannot identify a circulatory limitation.

The calf pump is a cycle of pressure changes, venous flow and valve action. Direct recordings during adult walking show that contraction and relaxation phases produce different pressures and flow conditions; sustained muscle activation at a fixed ankle angle is not equivalent to cyclic pumping (Tauraginskii et al., 2023). Nor does more calf tension necessarily mean more effective ejection. In 11 adults (22 legs), air plethysmography yielded median ejection-fraction estimates of 59.7% during body-weight transfer and 42.6% during a bilateral tiptoe manoeuvre (Lattimer et al., 2018). These reported estimates make movement and loading relevant without comparing ordinary gait with autistic toe walking or measuring restored central filling.

In 20 healthy adults, the contraction-time tiptoe trace contained muscle-motion artefact as well as venous ejection; the subsequent refilling trace was less affected but was not established as an exact ejection measure (Suehiro et al., 2023). This qualifies interpretation of calf-volume changes without recalculating Lattimer’s results or establishing improved central filling.

The proposed benefit is improved central haemodynamics or regional delivery sufficient to offset the movement’s demand. Adult pump results do not establish that benefit in autistic children; Section [44](#ss_p10_sec_44) considers walking as a repeated challenge to an existing control system, not a necessary cause of autism.

Sensory preference, motor learning, muscle–tendon constraints and a circulatory contribution can coexist. A compensatory interpretation gains support only if the predicted physiological improvement follows the movement and explains additional variation beyond those alternatives. A sensitive comparison showing no benefit, or a greater physiological cost, would count against the pumping explanation.

#### 45.2 Hand Flapping as a Candidate Circulatory Contribution During Arousal

Upper-limb effort can change systemic pressure. In a randomised crossover study of 19 patients with tilt-induced vasovagal syncope, two minutes of handgrip increased systolic pressure from 92 ± 10 to 105 ± 38 mmHg, whereas it fell from 91 ± 11 to 73 ± 21 mmHg in the control condition (Brignole et al., 2002). This is positive evidence for an arm counterpressure effect in that preparation. Hand flapping differs in force, muscle recruitment and timing, so it cannot inherit the same effect size or mechanism.

Sympathetic venoconstriction reduces the volume veins hold at a given pressure (Sumner et al., 1989; Robinson et al., 1989). Limited venous return during arousal therefore cannot be inferred from sympathetic activation alone. Rhythmic forearm, wrist and hand contractions could assist valve-directed flow towards the thorax, but a meaningful contribution from hand flapping remains unmeasured.

Movement-associated cardiovascular activity has been measured directly. In ten autistic children and young adults, Heathers et al. (2019) recorded rocking and hand flapping alongside ECG and found similar heart-rate acceleration and deceleration patterns, without a consistent directional change in heart-rate variability. Lydon et al. (2015) studied five autistic children using ten-second comparisons around movement onset and offset, with non-occurrence periods as controls. Coupling was inconsistent overall, although individual effects included an overall heart-rate decrease in one participant. These observations support physiological coupling in some settings without identifying improved venous return, tissue delivery or the reason a movement is selected.

The hand-flapping proposal is that upper-limb movement during arousal improves filling or delivery enough to offset its energetic cost. A pressure rise alone cannot distinguish pumping from an exercise pressor response, altered breathing or broader muscle recruitment. Equal benefit from another movement would leave the selection of flapping unexplained; voluntary stopping does not exclude intermittent benefit.

Excitement and enjoyment belong in that comparison alongside distress. Arousal is not itself evidence of inadequate perfusion, and movement can be expressive, pleasurable or sensory-regulatory without serving a circulatory purpose. Motor stereotypies also occur in non-autistic children (Harris et al., 2008), so their presence alone cannot identify an autism-specific circulatory mechanism. If the predicted haemodynamic improvement is absent under an adequately sensitive test, this particular account of the movement is weakened.

#### 45.3 Lateral Gaze and Predictable Sensory Input: A Separate Regulatory Proposal

Lateral viewing is a documented behaviour, but its function remains open. Mottron et al. (2007) found lateral glances, often toward moving objects, in autistic children aged 33–73 months and proposed altered sampling of visual detail and motion as an explanation. The Sodium Struggle adds a different, testable question: can predictable self-generated sensory input reduce physiological variability or make engagement easier when reserve is limited? Visual sampling, sensory predictability and circulatory support are distinct explanations and must be compared.

The oculomotor anatomy supports gaze holding, not the proposed rescue by itself. Primate perturbation experiments implicate the prepositus hypoglossi and medial vestibular region in horizontal gaze integration (Cannon and Robinson, 1987); PPRF burst-neuron recordings instead establish a role in generating rapid eye movements (Hepp and Henn, 1983). Recruiting these circuits during eccentric gaze does not demonstrate improved autonomic coordination, cerebral perfusion or reduced metabolic demand.

Predictable visual, tactile or auditory patterns may stabilise experienced state. The proposed physiological contribution is improved autonomic recovery or delivery beyond effects of attention and sensory preference. An object beside the head supplies visual input, but periocular trigeminal input requires contact; specific trigeminal or auditory perfusion effects remain unestablished.

Improved comfort without a delivery change would support a useful sensory effect, but not the perfusion branch. Continued engagement while looking sideways can be an effective way of interacting without establishing cortical energy savings or a physiological motive.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_46"></a>

### 46 State-Dependent Recovery and Clinical Comparisons

The three comparisons address different parts of the proposed physiology. Sleep concerns conditions and time for restoring extracellular buffering and reserve; fever-associated changes concern acute function, demand and recovery capacity; middle-ear fluid clearance concerns peripheral transport and clinical sequence. Each requires its own measured endpoint. An acute functional change or peripheral association does not by itself identify an earlier developmental mechanism.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_46_1"></a>

#### 46.1 Sleep and recovery of extracellular buffering margin

Sleep–wake transitions provide component evidence for state-dependent extracellular regulation. In mice, sleep and anaesthesia were associated with lower extracellular K⁺, higher Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺, and expanded extracellular space. Applying different ionic mixtures changed local cortical activity and extracellular-space volume; expansion could occur while the animal remained awake (Ding et al., 2016). The extracellular environment can therefore influence network state. These acute findings concern ionic composition and extracellular geometry; restoration of an earlier disturbance or of intracellular metabolic reserve requires a separate recovery measurement. Extracellular-space volume, diffusion and solute clearance remain distinct endpoints (Sections [25](#ss_p10_sec_25) and [30](#ss_p10_sec_30)).

The Sodium Struggle hypothesis proposes that sleep can provide conditions for restoring extracellular buffering margin and cellular reserve after daytime demand. Where astrocytic water loading, altered end-foot function or delayed gradient recovery persists, interrupted sleep could shorten that recovery opportunity and increase next-day sensory or autonomic lability. Within this branch, sleep disruption amplifies an existing constraint rather than being assumed to initiate the developmental imprint. The prediction is delayed physiological recovery after comparable demand and a corresponding loss of functional reserve. Successful recovery remains possible; ordinary sleep–wake ionic differences alone do not establish this constraint.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_46_2"></a>

#### 46.2 Fever-Associated Changes: Circuit Modulation, Recovery and Cellular Repair

Temporary changes in function during fever or recovery can reveal modifiable physiological conditions without erasing developmental history. The observation to explain is a reproducible improvement in communication, engagement or comfort in some individuals, rather than reduced activity or an assumed benefit for all autistic people. Temperature, immune signalling, systemic regulation and cellular repair provide distinct candidate routes. The relevant comparison is whether function changes through acute circuit modulation, reduced demand on recovery, or improved recovery capacity itself.

Human observations warrant investigation but differ substantially. Curran et al. (2007) compared 30 febrile autistic children with 30 matched afebrile autistic controls: parent ratings showed transient reductions in irritability, hyperactivity, stereotypy and inappropriate speech, alongside greater lethargy. Severity-stratified analyses suggested that the changes were not confined to the sickest children, so sickness alone might not explain them. In a retrospective Simons Simplex Collection report, parents of 17% of 2,152 children described improvement during fever (Grzadzinski et al., 2018). A later prospective study enrolled 141 autistic and 103 typically developing children; observed fevers were associated predominantly with worse functioning, although three autistic children showed consistent improvement (Byrne et al., 2022). These designs and observation windows do not estimate one common response rate. Reduced activity alone must be distinguished from improved communication, engagement or comfort.

Animal experiments separate routes that ordinary fever combines. In adult maternal-immune-activation offspring, LPS improved sociability through IL-17A-dependent signalling in somatosensory cortex. Blocking that signalling prevented rescue; raising body temperature by approximately 1°C without systemic inflammation did not reproduce it, and the LPS rescue occurred without a detected temperature rise (Reed et al., 2020). This is causal evidence for a cytokine route in that model, rather than evidence for heat-shock-mediated repair.

This adult IL-17A effect does not contradict adverse prenatal effects in Section [18.6](#ss_p10_sec_18_6): circuit construction and acute modulation differ. Neither the adult result establishes vascular or chloride-recovery rescue nor the prenatal result predicts the direction of later sociability change.

Later work refined the cortical route: in adult MIA offspring, IL-17A-dependent social improvement required endogenous IL-17E/IL-25 and neuronal IL-17RB. IL-17E acted through IL-17RA/RB-expressing neurons and reduced somatosensory cortical excitability; tested IL-17A slice exposure did not significantly change firing (Lee et al., 2025). How IL-17A increases IL-17E remains unresolved. This adult modulatory effect does not establish osmotic–volume recovery.

Circuit direction also matters. In adult Fmr1-KO mice, direct cerebellar IL-17A increased Purkinje-cell firing and reduced inhibitory-current amplitude; poly(I:C) improved selected behaviours through cerebellar IL-17A signalling. Baseline IL-17A was already elevated, and tested LPS did not reproduce the cerebellar cytokine increase (Yin et al., 2026). This differs from the cortical firing reduction. Neither study demonstrates thermal rescue or restoration of endogenous chloride gradients.

Heating also produces model- and endpoint-specific effects. Lopez-Rodriguez et al. (2023) found that four hours of whole-body heating reduced selected repetitive behaviours and improved social interaction in C58/J mice, and reduced excessive grooming in heterozygous Shank3B mice. After temperature normalised, reduced backflips persisted at 48 hours in C58/J mice and reduced grooming at 24 hours in Shank3B mice; the C58/J social effect did not persist at 24 or 48 hours. In separate C57 experiments within the same study, heating induced modest, region-dependent brain heat-shock transcripts without the assayed LPS-like inflammatory response; hypothalamic Avp and Oxt transcripts did not change significantly. The molecular and behavioural measurements therefore do not establish HSP mediation in the affected strains, or a peptide-signalling change. Together with Reed, this supports testing temperature, inflammation, model and timing separately. Neither experiment measured the proposed sodium–volume recovery intermediary.

Direct thermal modulation supplies another route. In Scn2a+/− mice, warming without an inflammatory challenge improved performance when an escape exit was relocated and discrimination of textured objects. Recordings linked warming to greater potassium-channel activity, a higher spike threshold and reduced excessive firing in somatosensory pyramidal neurons. Chemogenetic inhibition at normal body temperature reproduced selected behavioural benefits (Shen et al., 2026). Cooling reversed recorded input-resistance and threshold changes, supporting modulation of the current state rather than demonstrating lasting repair. These results do not measure extracellular potassium clearance or the proposed sodium–volume recovery intermediary.

The heat-shock component is experimentally grounded. In 12 healthy adults, experimentally raising body temperature to about 39°C increased leukocyte HSP70, particularly in monocytes (Oehler et al., 2001). Human A549 lung cells exposed to 38.5–41°C showed HSF1 activation and temperature- and duration-dependent HSP72 expression; HSF1 DNA binding alone did not predict the size of the response (Tulapurkar et al., 2009). These experiments support a fever-range response, with cell-specific kinetics, rather than uniform induction of every HSP or demonstrated repair in an autistic brain.

Protein repair and cytoskeletal maintenance have concrete experimental counterparts. Reconstituted human HSP70–HSP40–HSP110 systems disaggregated and reactivated denatured model proteins (Rampelt et al., 2012). In human endothelial cultures, oxidative stress recruited a p38/HSP27 pathway associated with actin reorganisation; inhibiting p38 blocked that response, and increasing HSP27 altered the response of fibroblasts (Huot et al., 1997). In HeLa cells, HSP90 depletion impaired microtubule stability, Golgi organisation and vesicle transport; restoring MAP4 rescued these defects (Wu et al., 2020). The proposed extension is that improved protein quality control or cytoskeletal function could restore a measured transport, membrane-organisation or recovery process relevant to the earlier neural and glial mechanisms. HSP abundance, actin turnover and functional recovery are distinct measurements; their sequence has not been demonstrated in fever-associated autistic behavioural change.

Pyrin is a candidate immune branch, not an established link in that sequence. RhoA activates PKN1/2, which phosphorylate pyrin and permit inhibitory 14-3-3 binding in the studied immune-cell systems (Park et al., 2016). However, microtubule dynamics also support downstream pyrin activation: both microtubule-disrupting and stabilising drugs inhibited the tested response after pyrin dephosphorylation (Gao et al., 2016). Thus, improved cytoskeletal organisation cannot simply be equated with reduced pyrin activity. NLRP3 findings cannot substitute for pyrin measurements. A heat-shock-induced restoration of pyrin restraint, and any resulting effect on neural function, remain separate predictions requiring the relevant cell type and direction to be specified.

Fever does not identify one fluid or peptide response. In a selected sample of children with infections, febrile participants had higher plasma AVP and more hyponatraemia without a significant CSF AVP difference (Sharples et al., 1992). Another paediatric study found no significant plasma AVP difference between groups and lower CSF AVP in febrile nonconvulsive children than in nonfebrile nonconvulsive controls (Kiviranta et al., 1996). These compartment-specific observations do not establish the physiology of autistic fever responders. In the present hypothesis, sodium, glucose and AVP–RAAS–cortisol changes remain conditional modifiers to be measured, not an assumed fever sequence.

Three possibilities therefore remain distinct: circuit modulation may improve function while relevant local recovery remains unchanged; reduced disruptive activity may lower demand enough for existing capacity to keep pace; or a thermal, immune or repair process may increase recovery capacity. Distinguishing them requires separate measures of meaningful function, activity or load, and neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery. Initial disturbance and ongoing demand must be matched or explicitly accounted for: reduced firing or a smaller ionic load does not itself show greater recovery capacity.

Functional benefit with adequately demonstrated unchanged relevant recovery would limit the specified acute recovery-mediated explanation. Conversely, improvement in both function and recovery requires an appropriate selective comparison before recovery can be assigned a mediating role. The repair branch further predicts that its specified protein, cytoskeletal or pyrin change carries the recovery benefit; a pyrin extension requires pyrin-specific effects. These acute comparisons neither establish nor erase an earlier developmental history, which requires its own temporal and causal evidence (Sections [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) and [23.13.1](#ss_p10_sec_23_13_1)). Peripheral HSP measurements cannot establish the neural sequence. This proposal provides no reason to induce fever or alter its treatment.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_46_3"></a>

#### 46.3 Otitis media, epithelial fluid clearance and antibiotic exposure

Middle-ear fluid clearance offers a peripheral setting in which to investigate the proposed recovery framework. A shared vulnerability in epithelial transport or its regulation could favour persistent effusion, with ear disease appearing before autism is diagnosed. Otitis could therefore be a parallel peripheral consequence, or a consequence of an earlier systemic disturbance, rather than the initiating event. These are testable proposals; a preceding ear diagnosis alone does not establish the physiological or developmental sequence.

Local transport has direct experimental support. In cultured normal human middle-ear epithelial cells, dexamethasone increased ENaC-mediated sodium current and fluid absorption; a separate study implicated NHE3 in luminal fluid absorption and its stimulation by dexamethasone ([Son et al., 2009](#ss_ear_ref_Son2009); [Choi et al., 2006](#ss_ear_ref_Choi2006)). In mouse middle-ear inflammation, several ion-homeostasis transcripts decreased, including β-ENaC and Na+/K+-ATPase components ([MacArthur et al., 2011](#ss_ear_ref_MacArthur2011)). Thus inflammation itself can alter local transport machinery. These findings support investigating clearance and recovery, without treating otitis as a validated marker of systemic sodium-transport impairment.

AVP provides a candidate hormonal connection to peripheral ear-fluid recovery. Systemic vasopressin produced cochlear endolymphatic hydrops in guinea pigs and increased AQP2 mRNA in rat cochlea and endolymphatic sac ([Takeda et al., 2000](#ss_chain_ref_Takeda2000); [Sawada et al., 2002](#ss_chain_ref_Sawada2002)). Separately, AQP2 mRNA was detected in inflammatory middle-ear tissue from 81 patients with chronic otitis media ([J. H. Kim et al., 2019](#ss_chain_ref_Kim2019)). These findings support asking whether a systemic disturbance and its hormonal response modify local ear-fluid recovery, producing a parallel peripheral consequence. The middle-ear extension depends on demonstrating AVP-responsive transport in the relevant tissue. Inner-ear endolymphatic hydrops is distinct from middle-ear effusion, commonly called glue ear; neither AQP2 expression nor these AVP experiments demonstrates Eustachian closure. The proposed sequence is altered exposure and local transport, followed by changed fluid recovery.

Epidemiology supports an ear association while limiting a simple antibiotic explanation. Among 780,547 Danish children, secondary-care otitis diagnoses were associated with subsequent ASD diagnosis (adjusted HR 1.83, 95% CI 1.71–1.95). Having both otitis and recorded broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure did not produce a higher estimate than otitis without that exposure ([Wimberley et al., 2018](#ss_ear_ref_Wimberley2018)). The latter category could still include other antibiotics, and the study was not a neonatal treatment experiment. Neither sodium handling nor AVP was measured. Anatomical or inflammatory susceptibility, shared familial factors, developmental differences and healthcare ascertainment remain alternatives to the proposed recovery mechanism.

Prediagnostic records provide a further clinical association relevant to fluid and electrolyte regulation. Among 3,911 ASD cases and 38,609 matched controls, fluid/electrolyte/acid–base diagnoses occurred in 2.71% and 1.51%, respectively, with adjusted OR 1.78 (95% CI 1.43–2.21; [Alexeeff et al., 2017](#ss_bridge4_ref_Alexeeff2017)). This category required at least two diagnoses with the same ICD-9 code within 276.xx. The exposure period preceded the first ASD diagnosis, not necessarily the onset of developmental differences. These records identify a broad clinical category, without specifying sodium direction, net balance, renal origin or recovery.

Within the same study, the category labelled ‘Ear’ under infections had adjusted OR 1.07 (0.99–1.15), while ‘Ear, nose and throat conditions’ had OR 2.47 (2.25–2.72). The original supplement shows overlapping, heterogeneous code groups and different recording rules; the ENT group includes hearing loss, congenital anomalies and external-ear conditions ([Alexeeff et al., 2017](#ss_bridge4_ref_Alexeeff2017)). This is not an outpatient-infection versus hospitalised-clearance-failure comparison, nor evidence that ear and electrolyte findings co-occurred through one mechanism. The useful next question is whether verified fluid disturbances and measured clearance/recovery distinguish trajectories beyond diagnosis codes and healthcare use. Section [14.4.2](#ss_p10_sec_14_4_2) provides the separate infant-UTI and age-window comparison.

Antibiotics could become an initiator or amplifier when a specific treatment produces a consequential intestinal or renal disturbance; their successful treatment of infection could also reduce physiological demand. Prescription histories alone cannot distinguish these effects. In a Korean cohort, the association between antibiotic prescriptions during the first six months and ASD attenuated to HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.96–1.03) in sibling comparisons ([Choi et al., 2024](#ss_ear_ref_Choi2024)). Some timing and duration subgroups retained higher estimates, with residual illness-related confounding possible. This constrains a general antibiotic-to-autism claim while leaving drug-specific physiological questions open.

One candidate intestinal route involves microbial support of epithelial transport. Seven days of broad-spectrum antibiotics reduced NHE3 and other transport/barrier expression measures in 6–8-week-old mice; tributyrin and/or Lactobacillus GG preserved selected measures ([Cresci et al., 2013](#ss_ear_ref_Cresci2013)). The study did not establish reduced sodium flux or net sodium depletion. In adult Clostridioides difficile infection, lower intestinal NHE3 expression and higher stool sodium and pH were observed in separate biopsy and stool cohorts; organoid and culture experiments supported feedback between the organism, transport machinery and luminal conditions ([Engevik et al., 2015](#ss_ear_ref_Engevik2015)). Stool concentration is distinct from daily sodium loss. An analogous infant sodium–volume burden remains to be demonstrated, and the findings cannot be extended to all clostridia.

A renal route has direct neonatal evidence. Among 23 preterm and term newborns treated for suspected infection, gentamicin infusion increased fractional sodium and magnesium excretion and the urinary calcium/creatinine ratio, while potassium and phosphate fractional excretion and serum electrolytes remained unchanged ([Giapros et al., 2004](#ss_ear_ref_Giapros2004)). This identifies a treatment-associated change in handling, not sustained negative balance or neural injury. In a different, high-dose rat experiment, calcium and magnesium losses diminished during continued treatment and urinary sodium was unchanged ([Lee et al., 2012](#ss_ear_ref_Lee2012)). Agent, dose, illness, developmental stage, replacement and recovery therefore matter. Normal serum results alone neither establish pathological compensation nor exclude a measured compensatory workload.

The discriminating question is whether impaired clearance precedes recurrent otitis, follows local inflammation, or accompanies a separately documented systemic disturbance. Existing longitudinal cohorts and clinical records could distinguish those sequences while accounting for infection, antibiotic class and timing, hearing status and healthcare use. A proposed systemic contribution requires measured balance or recovery changes beyond the ear; an interpretation linking these disturbances to autism additionally requires the local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery intermediary defined in Sections [2](#ss_p10_sec_2) and [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13). Successful resolution remains the physiological comparator. Peripheral ear disease and neural developmental effects must not be treated as interchangeable endpoints.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_47"></a>

### 47 Downstream Convergence: From Physiology to Phenotype

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is defined clinically by persistent differences in social communication and interaction, alongside restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, beginning in early development. This section asks **what physiological conditions could contribute to that neurodevelopmental phenotype.**

The physiological proposal considers both lasting developmental organisation and the current cost of sustaining engagement, then asks whether a movement or change in activity reduces a measured current cost. Developmental change, current limitation and useful compensation are distinct causal links. The proposal concerns variation in participation while preserving the person’s agency and experience.

Enduring circuit organisation and current physiological constraint operate on different timescales. Their interaction may make a trait more apparent under load without making it a compensatory act; a peripheral metabolic result alone does not explain social communication or every autistic behaviour.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_47_1"></a>

#### 47.1 Enduring developmental organisation and learning

A developmental recovery disturbance could leave lasting changes in circuit organisation or learning after the disturbance itself has resolved. In the proposed route, impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery changes a defined developmental transition; the resulting organisation could then influence sensory integration, salience and response selection without a continuing systemic delivery limit. Sections [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4) and [31.4](#ss_p10_sec_31_4) distinguish developmental timing and PV-interneuron maturation, with direct genetic and other independent routes retained. The test is whether the specified earlier recovery deficit carries the developmental change; an effect with preserved relevant recovery throughout that interval favours another route.

Quattrocki and Friston (2014) already connected oxytocin, bodily regulation and social development through interoceptive inference, assigning oxytocin roles in signal precision and attenuation. The present proposal adds a possible source of altered input reliability through recovery. Their theoretical account is an antecedent, not evidence of sodium–volume mediation.

If incomplete neural or glial recovery makes responses depend on recent challenges, the same cue could have variable consequences. Where that carry-over is uninformative, a stable-context model with unchanged prior precision predicts lower estimated reliability and less weighting of that channel. This is conditional: predictable carry-over could be learned as state, and stronger signals need not be less reliable. The proposed developmental link is altered salience from recovery-dependent bodily consequences, not a universal autistic weighting direction.

Signal strength, detection, confidence and computational weighting differ. Heartbeat tracking was unimpaired in 46 autistic and 48 comparison adults irrespective of alexithymia, with Bayesian support for the null (Nicholson et al., 2018). This limits a general detection-deficit claim but does not measure thirst, volume classification or prediction-error weighting. Strong sensations or low confidence alone establish neither inaccurate detection nor inappropriate weighting.

The learning proposal requires a recovery-dependent change in response reliability to alter learning, beyond sensory intensity or arousal. A learning difference with normal relevant recovery during the causal interval favours another route. Direct oxytocin effects on learning may bypass sodium–volume physiology, and an acute behavioural improvement cannot establish the developmental origin of autism.

#### 47.2 Current Physiological Constraints and Recovery

Cellular persistence could prolong or localise a disturbance linked to an earlier systemic exposure, including the renal branch in Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32). No particular systemic route is required in every trajectory, and a structural constraint alone does not establish its endocrine or neural consequences.

The later-expression proposal concerns metabolic flexibility, neurovascular matching, network timing and recovery under repeated demand. Chloride-dependent persistence is one possible amplifier alongside systemic and intrinsic neural routes, not an obligatory second stage. The common-process claim still requires local ionic or cellular-volume recovery difficulty to carry the developmental effect (Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2)).

Lasting renal, adrenal, autonomic, vascular and hypothalamic-glial changes could feed back into later systemic physiology. The cellular mechanisms in Sections [23](#ss_p10_sec_23)–[30](#ss_p10_sec_30) could prolong or amplify those consequences where they leave reduced local recovery reserve; chloride weighting alone does not establish that connection.

Expression is expected to vary with illness, sleep, hydration and clustered sensory or metabolic demand. Where a persistent cellular disturbance makes sympathetic or AVP-dominant stabilisation easier to re-enter, it could amplify autonomic lability without becoming a universal readout or a fixed chronic disease state. The metabolic-persistence and immune-memory examples are developed in Sections [21.2](#ss_p10_sec_21_2) and [21.3](#ss_p10_sec_21_3). Sections [23.10](#ss_p10_sec_23_10) and [24.5](#ss_p10_sec_24_5) examine the proposed glial and network connections; Section [46.1](#ss_p10_sec_46_1) considers recovery opportunity during sleep and changing physiological states.

##### 47.2.1 Defended variables under sodium–volume challenge

Earlier incomplete recovery could leave less reserve for later demands through altered thresholds, receptor responses or vascular regulation. The behavioural branch concerns those consequences, without assuming that successful early compensation necessarily leaves impairment.

The relevant margin includes arterial pressure regulation, venous return and cardiac output, and regional delivery relative to demand with recovery after challenge. Table [15.1](#ss_p10_table_15_1) separates actual filling or delivery disturbance from altered sensing or regulation; neither alone establishes the other.

The hypothesis predicts that enduring differences in these components will help explain within-person changes in engagement across contexts. A diagnosis or a behaviour alone cannot identify which component is limiting.

##### 47.2.2 Successful compensation and functional margin

Functional margin may narrow before or without fainting. Absence of syncope neither proves costly compensation nor excludes it; pressure must be interpreted alongside regulatory effort, local delivery and recovery.

Changing posture, movement or activity could reduce compensatory work. The term ‘load-shedding’ applies here only where the change follows a physiological burden and lessens it.

#### 47.3 Adaptive Haemodynamic Support and Its Possible Costs

Central filling and pressure are supported by splanchnic venous recruitment, sympathetic resistance and capacitance control, context-dependent AVP or cortisol, baroreflex adjustment and postural changes in venous return. Their possible cost concerns sustained engagement, not their ordinary protective action. Section [41](#ss_p10_sec_41) gives the physiological redistribution comparison and distinguishes regional blood volume from tissue blood flow.

Recruitment is adaptive; a consequential cost requires a link to impaired tissue function, discomfort, sustained regulatory demand or delayed recovery. The behavioural prediction is that reducing demand sometimes lowers this cost. That benefit must be demonstrated.

##### 47.3.1 Upright posture and motion as a load stack

Posture, motion and engagement can combine redistribution and central-filling changes, the compensation needed to sustain delivery, and visceral consequences. These components of the proposed ‘load stack’ remain distinct.

Sitting may reduce an orthostatic challenge, whereas movement can both add metabolic demand and assist venous return. Thus, stillness and movement cannot be ranked by appearance alone. A posture-related change in engagement supports this branch when the predicted physiological limitation changes with it.

#### 47.4 Regional Delivery Margins: Anatomy and Functional Reserve

A whole-body defence response can have different regional consequences, but a functional network is not a vascular territory. The superior temporal sulcus, temporoparietal junction and prefrontal cortex include subregions supplied by different arterial branches; they cannot all be assigned to one MCA–PCA watershed. D. E. Kim et al. (2019) mapped substantial territorial variation in 1,160 adult large-artery infarcts, with frontal territories distributed mainly between ACA and MCA. Such maps help define an anatomical test; they do not establish reduced reserve in autistic children. The proposed vulnerability must be located using individual anatomy and measured delivery.

Perfusion findings give this question an empirical foothold but not a uniform direction. Yerys et al. (2018) found lower relative perfusion in fusiform and inferior-temporal regions during passive viewing in 33 autistic and 25 comparison males aged 12–17; the study did not demonstrate a whole-brain absolute-flow deficit. Jann et al. (2015), studying 17 autistic and 22 comparison youths at rest, found frontotemporal hyperperfusion alongside dorsal anterior-cingulate hypoperfusion. Lower flow can reflect lower neural demand as well as restricted supply; higher flow does not establish successful compensation. This hypothesis therefore requires a prespecified regional failure of demand matching or recovery, not an arbitrary change in either direction.

There is a physiological precedent for examining timing as well as mean flow. During graded tilt, 11 participants with postural tachycardia syndrome showed declining 2-back accuracy and task-related cerebral flow-velocity responses compared with nine controls, despite similar mean flow velocity (Stewart et al., 2015). This association supports measuring dynamic regulation; it does not transfer the diagnosis, causal pathway or developmental history to autism.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_47_4_1"></a>

##### 47.4.1 When Social Demands Could Expose Limited Reserve

Live interaction combines changing cues, attention, prediction and response selection; social content alone does not establish unusually high energy use. In nine adults, somatosensory stimulation raised local flow by 29% but oxygen consumption by 5% on average (Fox and Raichle, 1986). Thus normal recruitment can exceed metabolic change; the hypothesis concerns inadequate local delivery under particular demands.

A broad social-brain deficit is not an established starting point: Moessnang et al. (2020) found no robust diagnostic-group difference in activation during an animated-shapes mentalising task in 205 autistic and 189 comparison participants aged 6–30 with IQ above 75. This constrains a general claim of deficient social-task recruitment, while leaving the specified demand–delivery test distinct.

The proposed limitation is impaired demand matching or delayed recovery that precedes or accompanies reduced engagement and improves as the limiting load resolves. BOLD or fNIRS amplitude alone does not establish oxygen shortage; scalp and systemic signals can affect fNIRS (Kirilina et al., 2012). Preserved delivery and recovery during the predicted functional change would weaken this account.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_47_4_2"></a>

##### 47.4.2 Developmental history and current task comparisons

The proposed bridge is from a documented developmental constraint to lasting circuit organisation and later state-dependent expression. Sections [41](#ss_p10_sec_41)–[45](#ss_p10_sec_45) consider possible systemic feedback, while Box [47.1](#ss_p10_box_47_1) compares current task demands and local delivery. Direction and timing must be established rather than inferred from the coexistence of cortical and peripheral findings.

Prenatal construction, PV-interneuron maturation and activity-dependent refinement occupy distinct, overlapping windows. The OTX2 and local-support mechanisms in Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4) do not establish prenatal oxygen gating. Physiological recovery may leave circuit organisation shaped during an earlier window, so developmental legacy and continuing impairment remain separate outcomes.

<a name="ss_p10_box_47_1"></a>**Box [47.1](#ss_p10_box_47_1). Association and Sensorimotor Function Under a Local Delivery Constraint (Testable Comparison)**

The proposal is that one physiological disturbance can have different functional consequences across tasks because local reserve and task demands differ. The comparison tests those differences directly; it assigns no vascular or energetic disadvantage to social function from its label alone. Sections [44](#ss_p10_sec_44) and [47](#ss_p10_sec_47) specify the shared tests.

| **Dimension**                                         | **Association-network tasks**                                                                                                              | **Sensorimotor tasks**                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Perfusion topology under transient pressure dips      | Supplying territory and delivery reserve are candidate determinants of vulnerability; association function does not identify a borderzone. | Territory and reserve vary independently of the label; sensorimotor function does not establish vascular protection.   |
| Walking-window task demands                           | Integrative exploration and social tasks may reveal limits in sustained function; comparable nonsocial demands remain relevant.            | Task complexity and postural demands vary; the network label assigns neither lower metabolic cost nor greater reserve. |
| Predicted temporal relation if instability is present | A physiological limitation precedes engagement change, with improvement during recovery.                                                   | A physiological limitation precedes gait or performance change; pacing benefit remains a separate proposed effect.     |

The hypothesis predicts differential consequences where a local limitation is measured. Preserved delivery and recovery during the predicted functional change would weaken this branch.

#### 47.5 Local AVPR1A (V1a) Imprinting: A Gain Constraint, Not a Trait

Consistent with Section [19.4](#ss_p10_sec_19_4), a circulating endocrine signal can be expressed differently across tissues. The proposed imprint concerns a lasting change in local responsiveness after a defined exposure; it must be distinguished from continuing ligand exposure and from an unchanged receptor acting in a different physiological environment.

Increased vascular AVPR1A responsiveness is proposed to strengthen constriction at matched ligand exposure and reduce dynamic reserve. OXTR responsiveness is a separate branch. Either must affect physiology before it can explain behaviour; rigidity, perseveration or reduced eye contact cannot identify a receptor state, and neural, sensory or developmental explanations remain alternatives.

#### 47.6 Functional Expression Under a Current Constraint

One proposed trajectory combines an earlier developmental change with a demonstrable current constraint:

**An early systemic or intrinsic cellular disturbance → impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery → a defined developmental change → measurable limitation under specified later demands → changes in sustained engagement or movement → possible contribution to the observable phenotype.**

A physiological limit can change the cost of participation before it produces overt circulatory failure. To call a behaviour compensatory, however, the behaviour must also be shown to reduce that limit or its consequences. Developmental difference, current constraint and useful compensation are distinct links.

##### 47.6.1 Social-perceptual behaviours

Reduced eye-looking does not identify one mechanism. In 86 two-year-olds, including 26 with autism, Moriuchi, Klin and Jones (2017) found that cueing the eyes did not elicit faster looking-away; the pattern favoured reduced sensitivity to social cues over active aversion in those tasks. In an older sample of 23 autistic participants aged 10.6–40.7 years and 20 controls, constraining gaze to the eye region increased subcortical BOLD responses (Hadjikhani et al., 2017). That study lacked in-scanner eye tracking and did not link activation to concurrent discomfort or inadequate delivery. Age, task, salience and aversion must therefore be separated before testing a physiological explanation.

A current delivery or recovery limit could make engagement less reliable, while earlier physiological burden could alter how cues acquire salience. Gaze alone identifies neither process; sensory, attentional, anxiety-related and communication explanations remain alternatives. Section [47.1](#ss_p10_sec_47_1) develops the distinct learning proposal.

##### 47.6.2 Posture, movement, and rhythmic repetition

Sitting could improve sustained function by reducing an upright haemodynamic limitation. Motor effort, pain and sensory comfort remain alternative benefits; preference alone does not establish circulation as the mechanism.

Rhythmic movement may offer muscle-pump assistance or reduce demand variability (Section [45](#ss_p10_sec_45)). Autistic adults described stimming as sensory and emotional regulation and communication, including positive excitement and both deliberate and automatic action (Kapp et al., 2019). Those functions stand independently of the additional haemodynamic proposal, which requires a meaningful improvement in filling or delivery.

##### 47.6.3 Abrupt changes in engagement

A sudden reduction in engagement could reflect crossing a physiological capacity boundary without obvious panic. The prediction is a reproducible sequence: the specified limitation develops, function changes, and function recovers as the limitation resolves. Anxiety, sensory overload, pain and communication difficulty can produce or accompany similar transitions. Their occurrence or the absence of visible distress cannot identify the physiological sequence.

##### 47.6.4 GI–social coupling: the splanchnic switch

Autonomic changes in gut perfusion or motility could connect demanding contexts with visceral discomfort, which could in turn increase load and reduce engagement (Section [43](#ss_p10_sec_43)). Redistribution, flow and symptoms are separate steps; direction and timing determine whether this splanchnic account applies.

Anticipatory symptoms before school could reflect learned responses to expected demands, including anxiety, sensory conditions and pain. The splanchnic prediction is that the relevant vascular or motility change precedes the symptom and tracks its recovery within the person; the setting itself does not identify the physiological stimulus.

#### 47.7 Proposed Convergence of Social and Repetitive Features

A shared limitation could make sustained engagement unreliable while favouring controllable, repeatable activity when recovery costs are high. The framework proposes this as an explanation for their co-occurrence to test; it does not derive both diagnostic domains from an assumed control solution.

A shared constraint should account for covariation across contexts beyond sensory, attentional and motor differences. Preserved engagement in demanding nonsocial tasks despite the predicted physiological limitation would challenge a general-load explanation; social specificity would need its own physiological basis. One task contrast cannot explain the breadth of autism.

#### 47.8 Clustering, Persistence, and Generalisation

Clustering becomes informative when the same measured limitation predicts changes in engagement, movement and visceral symptoms across settings. Generalisation should follow the relevant load and recovery conditions, rather than the social label of the situation. Different physiological responses across apparently similar activities would narrow the proposed common explanation.

The central proposal is that the cost of sustaining an interaction can differ from the wish to engage. Neither willingness nor physiological cost can be read directly from eye contact, stillness or repetition.

#### 47.9 Conclusion

The proposed contribution links early incomplete recovery to lasting developmental organisation and, in one trajectory, the later cost of using developing circuits. Autonomic recruitment, regional delivery and movement could connect that history to engagement and visceral symptoms where physiology predicts functional change and recovery. Current physiological modulation can also occur without establishing this developmental origin. Behavioural resemblance alone cannot establish the mechanism.

<a name="ss_p10_part_h"></a>

## Part H Wider comparisons and final evaluation

<a name="ss_p10_sec_48"></a>

### 48 Candidate Shared Developmental Constraints Across Autism, Cardiometabolic Disease, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Schizophrenia

The recovery framework also invites comparison across diseases. ASD and cardiovascular disease, insulin resistance/type 2 diabetes and CKD could share constraints on sodium handling, perfusion or recovery while differing in timing, tissue and reserve. Low nephron endowment offers one structural comparison: the Brenner framework concerns susceptibility to hypertension and kidney injury; the proposed neural extension requires a renal limitation to prolong a relevant exposure during circuit maturation (Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32)). Birth history or renal anomaly alone does not establish it. Direct genetic recovery defects, independent developmental mechanisms and unrelated comorbidity remain alternatives, without one required sodium direction or endocrine configuration.

Systemic constraints could leave altered endocrine, autonomic, vascular or water-handling responses. Low-renin/high-gain behaviour and cortisol-heavy support are candidates, not a shared obligatory state. Proposed adrenal drift from CYP11B2-rich zona glomerulosa towards CYP11B1-rich fasciculata-like function remains a separate speculative route (Section [34](#ss_p10_sec_34)), and systemic recruitment is not compulsory for intrinsic neural mechanisms.

Compensatory filtration and growth can preserve output despite fewer nephrons without implying raised intraglomerular pressure, obligatory efferent constriction, continuously high RAAS activity, albuminuria or progression (Section [32](#ss_p10_sec_32)). The proposed cross-organ consequence depends on limited reserve prolonging a water–solute disturbance and altering neural exposure. Autism, hypertension and CKD are not inevitable stages of that course.

#### 48.1 Early exposure comparisons

Table [48.1](#ss_p10_table_48_1) separates ASD associations from other developmental outcomes, childhood cardiometabolic measures and later disease. Maternal versus offspring diagnoses and vascular disease, metabolic disease, placental dysfunction and prematurity remain distinct comparisons. They motivate a shared recovery question without identifying nephron number, endocrine gain or renal-to-neural mediation from birth history alone.
