#### 48.2 Findings across physiological compartments

ASD findings span different compartments and causal timescales. Lower CSF AVP in childhood and archived early-infant samples, with greater social severity at lower concentrations in boys in the childhood cohort, constrains general central AVP excess (Oztan et al., 2018, 2020; Section [36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5)). In 49 autistic children versus 89 with intellectual disability, water-drinking severity was greater but polydipsia frequency was not significantly different (Terai et al., 1999). Dilutional hyponatraemia with inappropriate ADH secretion was documented in two institutionalised autistic males aged 17 and 19 during compulsive drinking (Hiratani et al., 1997). These observations do not constitute one joint central/peripheral AVP phenotype or establish prenatal exposure.

Autonomic and perfusion findings likewise vary by context and region (Jann et al., 2015; Yerys et al., 2018; Sections [42](#ss_p10_sec_42) and [47](#ss_p10_sec_47)); oxidative markers are not direct measures of cerebral endothelial inflammation.

Metabolic evidence distinguishes maternal diabetes associations before birth (Xiang et al., 2018), higher adjusted HOMA-IR after diagnosis in a small treatment-naïve sample (Manco et al., 2021), subsequent type 2 diabetes (Chen et al., 2016) and prospective metabolic change during risperidone treatment (Scahill et al., 2016). HOMA-IR does not measure brain insulin resistance, GLUT4 or IRAP, and these histories cannot be collapsed into one initiating defect (Sections [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7) and [21.2](#ss_p10_sec_21_2)).

Energetic findings also differ: lower lymphocyte NADH oxidase activity was found in an exploratory comparison of ten autistic and ten comparison children aged 2–5, with elevated lactate in only two autistic children (Giulivi et al., 2010). A specialist-clinic series confirmed abnormal acyl-carnitines in 20 of 42 retested initial positives among 213 screened patients (Frye et al., 2013). Neither measures cumulative defence cost or neural recovery.

Mineral findings add another comparison. Among 66 autistic and 1,208 non-autistic Australian children aged 11–12, adjusted distal-tibial trabecular density was about 5% lower and estimated strength lower in the autistic group; activity adjustment partly attenuated differences, while medication and detailed mineral intake were unmeasured (O’Flaherty et al., 2025). Fracture patterns vary by site and ascertainment: US emergency-department data showed higher hip-fracture odds at ages 3–22 and 23–50, whereas UK primary-care data showed lower overall childhood fracture odds in boys (Neumeyer et al., 2015; Furlano et al., 2014). These findings do not identify FGF-23/Klotho mediation; direct ASD measurements remain sparse, and Sections [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) and [33.3](#ss_p10_sec_33_3) distinguish the renal, soluble and vascular mechanisms.

The shared-process question is whether these separately reported findings coexist and arise through a linked recovery disturbance. Biomarker overlap alone establishes neither limited renal reserve nor its developmental consequences.

#### 48.3 Skeletal sodium and hormonal comparisons

Experimental hyponatraemia supplies a specific skeletal comparison. In rats, severe dilutional hyponatraemia sustained for three months reduced bone mass and increased resorption (Verbalis et al., 2010). The same paper’s cross-sectional NHANES III analysis of adults aged 50 years and older associated mild hyponatraemia with osteoporosis at the total hip and femoral neck. Low extracellular sodium also increased osteoclast formation and resorption in culture; restoring osmolality with mannitol enhanced rather than abolished the response (Barsony et al., 2011). This sodium-sensitive resorption is distinct from the tonicity-sensitive FGF23 response in Section [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9), so the skeletal findings cannot all be assigned to hypotonic swelling.

Hormonal signalling provides a second candidate skeletal route. In bone-cell cultures and mice, AVP signalling promoted osteoclast activity and inhibited osteoblast differentiation; V1a-receptor deletion or antagonism increased bone mass (Tamma et al., 2013; see 2014 correction). These experiments support a direct signal-to-bone connection, although they did not establish the skeletal effects of sodium–volume compensation in normonatraemic people. In a small cross-sectional adult study, treated AVP deficiency was associated with lower CTX, a resorption marker, without a significant P1NP formation-marker difference; BMD was not measured (Varaldo et al., 2026). This is consistent with the resorptive component of the experimental findings, while leaving human formation effects and developmental relevance unresolved. Sympathetic β2-adrenergic regulation of RANKL and angiotensin-dependent osteoblast support of osteoclastogenesis provide additional experimental connections, with angiotensin receptor effects differing by model (Elefteriou et al., 2005; Shimizu et al., 2008; Asaba et al., 2009). The resulting hypothesis is that specified endocrine or autonomic responses could carry a skeletal cost even when serum sodium remains normal; their recruitment, duration and skeletal consequences require measurement.

Verbalis et al. (2010) interpreted bone resorption as a possible defence of sodium homeostasis at a structural cost. The experiments did not show that mobilisation restored serum sodium or quantify the proposed protective benefit. The corresponding ASD question is whether documented sodium–water disturbances or specified endocrine/autonomic responses precede altered skeletal turnover or accrual in a defined subgroup, accounting for activity, nutrition, growth and puberty, medication, and renal or endocrine factors. ASD studies have already measured turnover markers and microarchitecture without establishing this exposure pathway (Neumeyer et al., 2013, 2017). Paired longitudinal measurements could test competing explanations, but turnover patterns alone would not identify the responsible signal or reconstruct an earlier defence history. Skeletal and neural developmental effects could be parallel consequences of a shared systemic history. The proposed ASD arm separately requires impaired local neural/glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery to carry its developmental effect.

#### 48.4 Prognostic markers and intervention outcomes

Disease comparisons separate prognosis from intervention. Copeptin predicted 24-month mortality in 786 chronic-heart-failure patients (Neuhold et al., 2008), while tolvaptan improved fluid outcomes and low serum sodium but not mortality or cardiovascular death/heart-failure hospitalisation in 4,133 EVEREST participants (Konstam et al., 2007). Enalapril reduced mortality risk by 16% in symptomatic reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure in SOLVD (SOLVD Investigators, 1991). These results support substantive sodium–water and RAAS physiology without equating a marker, fluid response and survival benefit. They do not establish exaggerated receptor gain, developmental origin or the local neural recovery intermediary needed for a shared ASD route.

#### 48.5 Genetic and functional comparisons across organs

In this expanded cluster view, schizophrenia warrants consideration as another neuro-renal phenotype that may, in a subset, share upstream developmental constraints with ASD and the CVD–IR–CKD triad. A candidate natural comparison is 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11.2DS), in which a recurrent copy-number lesion can affect neurodevelopment and renal development. This motivates the mediation tests in Section [32.4](#ss_p10_sec_32_4) rather than proving a renal cause of the neuropsychiatric phenotype. Rates depend on age, diagnostic assessment and recruitment. In the 1,402-person international consortium, ASD diagnoses were assessed in a 548-person subset: 12/94 children aged 6–12 years (12.8%), 43/162 adolescents aged 13–17 (26.5%) and 47/292 adults aged 18–25 (16.1%). Schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses, a broader category than schizophrenia alone, occurred in 76/323 participants aged 18–25 (23.5%), 62/150 aged 26–35 (41.3%) and 53/127 aged 36 or older (41.7%) (Schneider et al., 2014). These are cross-sectional rates in differently ascertained cohorts, with variable ASD instruments and increasing psychiatric referral with age; they are not population lifetime risks or evidence that autistic traits develop into schizophrenia. In parallel, 22q11.2DS is a recognised genetic driver of congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT), including renal agenesis and renal hypoplasia among reported findings.

Renal agenesis or hypoplasia could modify reserve in affected carriers, but shared deletions can also act on organs in parallel. The 17q12 versus intragenic-HNF1B comparison cautions against renal-to-autism inference from co-occurrence (Clissold et al., 2016; Section [32.4](#ss_p10_sec_32_4)). Renal-to-neural mediation requires an exposure reaching susceptible neural processes, not a prescribed renin or perfusion state.

#### 48.6 Developmental timing and synaptic refinement

Timing provides the proposed link between shared physiological constraints and divergent outcomes: a constraint could have different effects during construction, stabilisation or refinement. These windows overlap: ASD genes cannot be assigned wholesale to construction or schizophrenia genes to adolescent pruning. CHD8, PTEN and SCN2A have distinct actions, and the 102-gene classification does not establish a shared timing intermediary.

Pruning has separable selection and execution steps. Activity and complement influenced microglial engulfment in the developing mouse retinogeniculate system (Schafer et al., 2012). Astrocytic MEGF10/MERTK pathways also contributed to elimination there (Chung et al., 2013), while neuronal autophagy provided a distinct pruning mechanism in the models studied by Tang et al. (2014). The hypothesis proposes that altered ionic recovery could change activity-based selection, cellular capacity to execute elimination, or the timing of either. Greater spine density alone cannot identify reduced elimination: increased formation or altered stabilisation can produce a similar snapshot. Section [31.4.1](#ss_p10_sec_31_4_1) retains the distinction between human cross-sectional findings and experimental model mechanisms.

Tang et al. (2014) demonstrated pathway dependence: rapamycin improved pruning and social endpoints in Tsc2-heterozygous mice, but normalisation failed when neuronal autophagy was disabled through Atg7 deletion. Growth-pathway regulation and functional removal machinery were therefore distinct requirements. Sections [29](#ss_p10_sec_29) and [31.4.1](#ss_p10_sec_31_4_1) propose recovery disturbance upstream of protein production or autophagic function; spine density and static autophagy markers cannot establish those processes.

MIA adds a possible immune interaction. One mouse preparation showed complement changes and increased microglial engulfment, whereas another showed deficient engulfment and excess synapses (Yan et al., 2024; Andoh et al., 2019). These findings do not establish one direction across preparations or developmental windows. Immune exposure could change glial responsiveness while local recovery difficulty changes activity or target-recognition signals. Neither that convergence nor maternal complement transfer follows from offspring complement expression (Table [18.4](#ss_p10_table_18_4)).

The reduced-elimination branch proposes insufficient reserve for timely removal, but energy limitation does not automatically stop microglial work. During acute glucose deprivation, mouse microglia maintained surveillance and damage responses through glutamine use and mTOR-dependent adaptation (Bernier et al., 2020). This does not establish normal developmental pruning or tolerance of combined substrate and oxygen limitation. It does require the proposed branch to identify an actual cellular limitation and its directional effect on refinement.

Increased elimination requires a different mechanism. Human C4A overexpression increased microglial engulfment and reduced cortical synapse density in mice (Yilmaz et al., 2021), without establishing a sodium–perfusion origin or schizophrenia as the opposite of ASD. Adolescent growth could expose limited reserve, but stature changes hydrostatic pressure rather than proving cerebral hypoperfusion (Figure [44.1](#ss_p10_figure_44_1)). The proposed convergence is a directional interaction between susceptibility, physiology and timing; opposite pruning outcomes cannot both confirm the same pathway.

Refinement changes despite preserved relevant recovery, or despite timely prevention of its defect, would challenge this route. Failed late correction is less informative about initiation. Contact, engulfment and completed removal remain distinct, with neuronal and astrocytic mechanisms alongside microglia (Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2)).

Refinement may catch up after recovery or leave lasting circuit organisation. This distinction gives timing its explanatory role: a brief constraint could alter how a circuit is built without lifelong sodium abnormality. Neither trajectory follows from component compatibility alone.

Calcium/magnesium nutrition, total dissolved solids and sodium are distinct exposures. A water–solute interaction with limited renal or vascular reserve remains possible, but neither these associations nor low nephron endowment establishes retained water, dilution or an autism mechanism.

#### 48.8 Scope and tests of a shared recovery process

‘Sodium struggle’ is not a synonym for ASD. Genetic susceptibility, developmental timing, the physiological disturbance and cumulative exposure define the comparison. Different ages and tissues encounter different demands and reserves; sodium loss, relative water retention, impaired perfusion and local recovery difficulty do not prescribe one endocrine pattern (Table [14.3](#ss_p10_table_14_3)). Heat, illness, diet, medications or psychosocial stress may modify an earlier trajectory or leave it unchanged.

Brain, kidney and vasculature may differ in their limiting reserve. A constraint during neural development could affect circuit formation, whereas later renal or vascular challenges could chiefly affect cardiometabolic function. Co-vulnerability could produce overlap, and successful compensation could leave neither outcome. These are candidate trajectories, not histories recoverable from diagnoses alone.

Central AVP, water-balance disturbances, autonomic responses, perfusion and mineral metabolism have largely been studied separately. Their coexistence as a shared defence phenotype remains unestablished, as does one origin for low-renin hypertension, hyponatraemia, FGF23/Klotho findings and stiffness in cardiorenal disease. Table [48.3](#ss_p10_table_48_3) keeps observations distinct from candidate mechanisms; Sections [14.9](#ss_p10_sec_14_9) and [33.3](#ss_p10_sec_33_3) provide the detailed Klotho account.

The shared-process claim is that a particular limitation changes the work or completion of recovery and thereby affects an organ during a susceptible interval. Tables [48.1](#ss_p10_table_48_1), [48.2](#ss_p10_table_48_2), and [48.3](#ss_p10_table_48_3) distinguish exposure follow-up, biomarkers and genetic or functional comparisons. For a proposed ASD route, that connection must reach the local neural or glial recovery difficulty defined in Section [2](#ss_p10_sec_2); protective physiology alone does not establish developmental harm.

The comparison should distinguish response gain and recovery from resting concentrations, and a sodium-centred mechanism from generic stress or independent disease. Its value is the prediction that the same protective physiology can have different consequences according to where reserve is limited and when that limitation is encountered; no single marker or water-composition association establishes the shared history. Section [49](#ss_p10_sec_49) evaluates these comparisons alongside the complete developmental argument.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_49"></a>

### 49 Discussion

#### 49.1 Evidence and the central recovery claim

The strongest support for this framework lies in experiments that measure a defined physiological process and show what changes it. The manuscript brings together sodium and chloride restoration, cellular-volume regulation, vascular and metabolic support, and manipulable developmental processes. These findings make the proposed connections testable. They do not yet establish the central inference: that impaired local neural or glial ionic or cell-volume recovery carries a developmental effect across autistic trajectories. That inference has greater explanatory reach than any individual component result and therefore requires a separate causal test (Sections [2](#ss_p10_sec_2) and [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)).

Direct recovery assays are especially informative because they measure restoration over time. KCC2 R952H and R1049C slowed chloride-sensor recovery after loading in transfected Neuro2a cells (Kahle et al., 2014). In human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons, KW-2449 shortened the chloride-recovery time constant towards the isogenic wild-type value (Tang et al., 2019). These experiments establish defined recovery phenotypes and, in the latter preparation, a modifiable one. Their epilepsy and Rett-model contexts remain important; the mixed ASD association evidence for SLC12A5 does not change the measured cellular result. Neither experiment establishes recovery-mediated development across autism, and KCC2's structural functions and the drug's other actions prevent a broad rescue from identifying the mediator by itself (Section [6.4](#ss_p10_sec_6_4)).

Successful restoration supplies the necessary positive comparator. Cultured postnatal rat hippocampal neurons restored intracellular sodium after chemical anoxia and reoxygenation, whereas sodium-pump inhibition prevented that recovery (Sheldon et al., 2004; Section [14.7.2](#ss_p10_sec_14_7_2)). In primary rat cortical astrocytes, LRRC8A knockdown markedly impaired regulatory volume decrease during hypotonic exposure (Formaggio et al., 2019; Section [24.2](#ss_p10_sec_24_2)). The first comparison concerns restoration after an insult; the second concerns volume regulation during continued exposure. Together they show why the measured variable, phase and transport machinery matter. Increased transport work, adaptive solute release or a transient deviation can accompany successful regulation rather than a developmental cost.

Developmental experiments address another part of the argument. Perinatal interventions in valproate-exposed rats and Fmr1-null mice altered juvenile neural physiology and early pup vocalisations, providing a precedent for developmental effects after a brief intervention (Tyzio et al., 2014; Section [23.7.2](#ss_p10_sec_23_7_2)). Those experiments did not measure recovery after matched ionic loading or isolate selective neural recovery mediation. Likewise, the vascular, oxygen-signalling and lineage-timing experiments in Section [31](#ss_p10_sec_31) establish consequential developmental interfaces while leaving the proposed recovery connection open. The evidence is therefore strongest for particular components and experimental recovery phenotypes; it is less complete at the step linking that recovery to a defined developmental transition, and cannot establish universal participation.

This ranking concerns what the selected findings establish, not a systematic estimate of the literature. The narrative selection described in Section [1.1](#ss_p10_sec_1_1) is illustrative. Reusing one experiment in an early explanation, a mechanism chapter and this evaluation does not provide independent replication, and the frozen genetic component classification does not establish enrichment or mediation.

#### 49.2 Entry routes and developmental conversion

The systemic and intrinsic routes explain different starting points. A maternal, placental, renal or vascular disturbance can alter the conditions supporting local restoration. An intrinsic transport, metabolic or cellular constraint can begin within neural or glial tissue without a preceding systemic sodium deficit. Immune mechanisms can enter at either level. Underfilling, impaired effective filling despite fluid expansion, hypertonic exposure and genuine overfilling need their own exposure and response descriptions. The AVP–RAAS–cortisol triad organises context-dependent protective responses; it does not assign one hormone direction to every route (Sections [3](#ss_p10_sec_3), [6](#ss_p10_sec_6), [7](#ss_p10_sec_7), [9](#ss_p10_sec_9), [10](#ss_p10_sec_10), [15](#ss_p10_sec_15), and [18](#ss_p10_sec_18)).

A measured initiating disturbance can justify a place in this account before its full developmental sequence is demonstrated. The additional work is to connect that disturbance to delayed, incomplete or unstable local recovery and then to a specified developmental effect. More pump turnover, lower reserve or prolonged protective recruitment can be fully accommodated. Conversely, a local transport defect can matter without a large systemic abnormality. The explanatory distinction is between the effort needed to restore conditions and whether restoration succeeds at the time development depends on it. Exposure associations, circulating hormones and resting ion concentrations address parts of that sequence rather than substituting for it (Sections [1.1](#ss_p10_sec_1_1), [2](#ss_p10_sec_2), and [4](#ss_p10_sec_4)).

The same distinction applies to persistence. Renal structure, vascular responsiveness, receptor action and controller thresholds could change later exposure or recovery, while continuing ligand exposure could maintain a response without an acquired change in gain (Sections [21](#ss_p10_sec_21), [22](#ss_p10_sec_22), [32](#ss_p10_sec_32), and [34](#ss_p10_sec_34)–[39](#ss_p10_sec_39)). The proposed glucose contribution to extracellular osmotic support and the insulin-associated AVP-clearance route are separable questions; either can be tested without making the other compulsory (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)). Identifying a sustaining mechanism gives these branches explanatory content beyond the continued presence of a biomarker.

#### 49.3 Lasting organisation and current function

The developmental accounts in Sections [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4), [31.4](#ss_p10_sec_31_4), and [31.5](#ss_p10_sec_31_5) distinguish physiological recovery from lasting changes in circuit organisation. Section [46.2](#ss_p10_sec_46_2) considers fever-related changes as acute functional comparisons, and Section [46.3](#ss_p10_sec_46_3) considers middle-ear fluid clearance as a peripheral comparison. Neither identifies the developmental mechanism on its own.

The enduring-developmental proposal concerns a transition that occurs while restoration is constrained: differentiation, inhibitory maturation, synapse stabilisation or circuit refinement. Once that transition has changed, its consequences may remain after the initiating exposure and local physiological disturbance resolve. The continuing-state proposal instead concerns a present limitation in delivery, transport, buffering or recovery that changes current function. Both can operate in one person, but evidence for either does not establish the other. Later recognition, including during the additional demands of upright locomotion, need not identify the timing of origin (Sections [30](#ss_p10_sec_30), [31](#ss_p10_sec_31), and [47](#ss_p10_sec_47)).

This distinction changes the interpretation of behaviour and short-term improvement. A physiological explanation becomes informative when a specified limitation precedes a functional change and that function improves as the limitation resolves. Sensory comfort, communication, pleasure, attention, learning and individual agency remain independent explanations of movement and engagement. The cost of participation cannot be inferred from a person's wish to engage, eye contact or repetition. Acute modulation during fever, ordinary recovery during sleep or resolution of a peripheral fluid problem can clarify present function without reconstructing the earlier developmental cause (Sections [45](#ss_p10_sec_45)–[47](#ss_p10_sec_47)).

#### 49.4 Alternative mechanisms and cross-disease specificity

The proposed intermediary adds a particular causal requirement to chloride-state, metabolic-signalling, neuroimmune and direct developmental accounts. A resting chloride difference can change signalling without demonstrating impaired restoration; a recovery defect can occur despite similar starting values. Protein production, cytoskeletal signalling, extracellular developmental signals and altered lineage timing could influence development independently, or could act upstream or downstream of recovery. Their relationship must be resolved within a defined model. A broad upstream rescue that improves several processes cannot determine which one carried the developmental effect (Sections [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13), [26](#ss_p10_sec_26), [29](#ss_p10_sec_29), [31](#ss_p10_sec_31), and [35](#ss_p10_sec_35)).

Cross-disease comparisons sharpen that question when they identify a shared lesion or function precisely. Table [48.2](#ss_p10_table_48_2) distinguishes a same-variant multisystem channel lesion from different CUL3 lesions in different tissues and from neural and renal transporter paralogues. Those comparisons have unequal evidential strength. A shared gene name, biomarker or developmental exposure does not establish a common causal path. For a recovery mechanism to explain divergent neural, renal, vascular or skeletal outcomes, its predicted direction must depend on a specified tissue, developmental interval and limiting reserve rather than being chosen after the outcome is known (Section [48](#ss_p10_sec_48)).

Parallel organ effects remain valuable comparisons in their own right. A skeletal cost of sodium-sensitive resorption or endocrine signalling could coexist with a neural effect, occur without it, or reflect a different exposure history. Reduced nephron reserve may constrain later renal recovery while compensation preserves function elsewhere. Similarly, prognosis, a fluid response and a survival benefit are different outcomes in the cardiorenal intervention comparisons. The proposed neural route requires its local recovery intermediary in addition to any shared systemic history; unrelated comorbidity and successful compensation remain possible (Tables [48.1](#ss_p10_table_48_1) and [48.3](#ss_p10_table_48_3)).

#### 49.5 What contrary findings change

Contrary findings should narrow the claim they actually test. Preserved GABA driving force and inhibition in the tested Shank3B-null preparation constrain an obligatory chloride-state explanation for that model (Chiesa et al., 2019). They do not establish that every relevant local recovery process was normal. Conversely, attributing the result to another unmeasured compartment would not support the hypothesis. The claimed variable, cell type and developmental interval must be specified before testing. An adequately demonstrated developmental route with preserved relevant recovery, or an effect persisting despite timely prevention of the required disturbance, would challenge universal participation while leaving possible contributions elsewhere (Section [23.13.1](#ss_p10_sec_23_13_1)).

Other negatives constrain broader interpretations. The recurrent-hyponatraemia model in Section [23.6](#ss_p10_sec_23_6) showed a slower, less pronounced ADC decline on subsequent water challenge, rather than the predicted amplification (Tejedor et al., 2026). Lower CSF AVP in selected childhood and early-infant cohorts constrains general central AVP excess, while leaving peripheral and local circuit signals separate (Oztan et al., 2018, 2020; Section [36.5](#ss_p10_sec_36_5)). The sex comparisons in Section [40](#ss_p10_sec_40) include preserved renal regulation, null endocrine differences and opposing tissue- or protocol-specific responses. Similar renal outputs neither exclude internal transport differences nor demonstrate them. The modifier claim requires a physiological difference under specified developmental conditions, rather than a universal female reserve advantage or a diagnosis-ratio explanation inferred from adult physiology.

Developmental direction also matters. Section [30.4](#ss_p10_sec_30_4) retains delayed, accelerated and unchanged findings across distinct OTX2, PV and matrix models. They constrain a universal immaturity account. Opposite outcomes can test a timing-dependent hypothesis only when the relevant preparation, interval and expected direction are specified beforehand; they cannot both confirm an unspecified shared defect. Direct genetic and extracellular-signalling explanations remain available until the recovery connection is measured.

Human associations also change with exposure definition and comparison design. In the neonatal cohorts reviewed in Section [12](#ss_p10_sec_12), the fully adjusted glucose-corrected sodium-range result was nonsignificant, and the grouped psychiatric/developmental endpoint in the asphyxia cohort was also nonsignificant (Gervais et al., 2022; Viitaharju et al., 2026). Neither endpoint was an autism-specific recovery test. Maternal infection associations attenuated in the sibling comparison retained in Table [48.1](#ss_p10_table_48_1) (Brynge et al., 2022). These results limit the corresponding exposure inferences without erasing the separate experimental component mechanisms. They also show why collecting compatible associations cannot establish a shared physiological history.

The two phase 3 bumetanide trials did not meet their primary clinical endpoints in established ASD, and treatment produced more thirst, polyuria and hypokalaemia (Fuentes et al., 2023; Section [23.7.3](#ss_p10_sec_23_7_3)). These findings constrain therapeutic claims and do not favour a recovery account over a chloride-state account. Later treatment failure cannot settle an earlier developmental mechanism when the relevant interval and mediator were not tested; equally, it supplies no evidence for an otherwise unobserved earlier disturbance. The same discipline applies to a positive acute response: improved function does not identify the developmental cause.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_49_6"></a>

#### 49.6 Three discriminating comparisons

Three comparisons would resolve different joints in the argument. They are priorities within the existing experimental and observational approaches developed in [Table 2.1](#ss_p10_table_2_1) and Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13), rather than three obligatory steps for every route. Each needs a defined preparation or population, developmental interval, recovery variable, alternative explanation and outcome. Normal serum sodium, larger initial loading and altered resting biomarkers cannot substitute for the recovery measurement.

First, an intrinsic recovery comparison can build on the human stem-cell-derived Rett-model neurons and dynamic chloride assay described in Section [6.4](#ss_p10_sec_6_4). Compare recovery time, residual deviation and stability under matched initial loading and ongoing demand, while measuring inhibitory maturation or synapse development separately. Then assess whether timely correction of the recovery defect changes that developmental endpoint, with transport-related effects distinguished from KCC2's structural or other intervention effects. Better recovery alone establishes a physiological rescue. A developmental improvement attributable to correction during the relevant interval would support mediation in that route; persistence of the developmental effect despite adequate, timely prevention of the proposed disturbance would count against it (Sections [4](#ss_p10_sec_4) and [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13)).

Second, a systemic clinical comparison can ask whether measured salt-wasting and recovery trajectories add information beyond an illness diagnosis. Existing records, cohorts or archived samples may permit comparison of similarly ill infants with impaired conservation and those with preserved conservation, considering serial blood and urine measurements, intake, replacement, output, prematurity, illness severity and treatment. The question is whether the defined physiological trajectory precedes and predicts a specified developmental outcome. A sufficiently precise null would weaken that clinical prediction; a positive association would still require temporally relevant local neural or glial recovery evidence to support the proposed developmental intermediary. Renal or peripheral outcomes alone cannot complete that inference (Sections [14.4.2](#ss_p10_sec_14_4_2), [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13), [32](#ss_p10_sec_32), and [40.3.2](#ss_p10_sec_40_3_2)).

Third, the valproate-exposed rat model in Section [23.7.2](#ss_p10_sec_23_7_2) provides an existing preparation for a developmental-history comparison across the perinatal chloride-regulation interval and later circuit function. Its GABA and behavioural findings would need to be related to a measured recovery trajectory, distinguishing a retained developmental consequence from continuing physiological impairment. Compare later function after the exposure and relevant disturbance have resolved, at the same chronological age and comparable current physiological and task conditions; record maturation separately so that matching does not remove the timing effect under investigation. Timely selective prevention of the earlier recovery disturbance would test its contribution to the retained difference. The existing broad bumetanide intervention does not provide that selective test. A history-dependent effect reduced by such prevention would support the proposed connection; differences explained by continuing exposure or current load would favour present-state modulation. Normal later physiology and failed late reversal cannot decide this comparison alone ([Table 2.1](#ss_p10_table_2_1); Sections [21](#ss_p10_sec_21), [31](#ss_p10_sec_31), and [47](#ss_p10_sec_47)).

#### 49.7 Scope of the proposed contribution

The framework's contribution is a common causal question across otherwise different physiological and developmental accounts: does a defined limitation impair local restoration at a consequential time, and does that disturbance carry the developmental effect? The breadth of possible entry routes makes this question useful only if its required intermediary remains specific. One supported route would establish a contribution in that setting; several supported routes would strengthen convergence without proving participation in every autistic trajectory. A well-characterised bypass would challenge that universal conjecture. The proposed value therefore lies in comparisons that distinguish successful compensation, incomplete recovery and recovery-dependent development, while allowing parallel peripheral outcomes and independent causes. This physiological synthesis does not establish an intervention or assign an individual's developmental history from diagnosis.

<a name="ss_p10_sec_50"></a>

### 50 Conclusion: The Sodium Struggle as a Physiological Framework

The Sodium Struggle proposes a common developmental process: diverse initiating conditions converge on disturbed local neural or glial ionic or cellular-volume recovery during sensitive fetal or early postnatal windows, changing the conditions under which circuits mature. Maternal, placental, renal and vascular physiology can supply systemic entry routes, including altered sensing or regulation; genetic influences can act through systemic regulation, direct cellular constraints, or both. Local routes can begin with impaired transport, energetic support or recovery itself. Maternal immune activation can act through circulatory or local immune mechanisms. Clinical hyponatraemia and preceding systemic defence are not compulsory. Whether this process participates across all autistic trajectories remains a demanding, unestablished conjecture.

Its organising insight concerns compensatory physiology and its developmental consequences: protective responses can preserve apparent systemic stability while local restoration remains constrained. The AVP–RAAS–cortisol defence triad, autonomic support and renal sodium–water responses defend tonicity, effective filling and perfusion. Their recruitment can be appropriate and successful. The sodium paradox concerns the possible coexistence of limited systemic support and substantial cellular restoration work: sodium entry can increase pump demand, while impaired chloride extrusion supplies a distinct recovery constraint. Increased ATP turnover need not deplete ATP, and increased effort with adequate recovery does not satisfy the hypothesis. The developmental claim begins where restoration becomes delayed, incomplete or unstable and changes maturation.

The hypothalamic layer connects this physiology to regulatory calibration. Systemic AVP supports water and circulatory regulation; local dendritic AVP can recruit nearby presympathetic neurons in the rat PVN (Son et al., 2013). These are distinct compartments, not evidence for uniform AVP elevation or recruitment of a shared AVP-producing or CRH population. The proposed shift towards AVP-linked recruitment or weaker oxytocin-mediated modulation concerns a specified circuit and developmental interval. Repeated protective recruitment, together with local recovery difficulty, could alter controller thresholds, receptor weighting or recovery kinetics. A more AVP-weighted, sympathetic and cortisol-supported profile remains a prediction rather than an assigned signature.

Distributed imprinting could involve vascular responsiveness, renal handling, autonomic gain, hypothalamic balance, astrocytic buffering, extracellular-space regulation or cellular transport. These are alternative or interacting sites. Their relevance to this core requires a local recovery disturbance that changes a defined developmental process, potentially affecting inhibitory maturation, synaptic stabilisation or refinement. Enduring circuit organisation may remain after physiology normalises; continuing regulatory differences can separately modify its expression. Later demands, including upright locomotion and its circulatory, sensorimotor and buffering requirements, may expose a limitation that was partly compensated earlier. The timing of recognition need not identify the timing of origin.

Glucose’s possible osmotic support and insulin-associated AVP clearance exemplify separable metabolic proposals (Section [19.7](#ss_p10_sec_19_7)). Redox-dependent vascular dysfunction, membrane injury and endocrine constraints offer other entries or amplifiers. Each candidate contribution requires its own physiological evidence and, for the developmental claim, the specified local recovery effect.

Schrier’s effective arterial blood volume, Guyton’s sodium–volume–pressure physiology, Sterling and Eyer’s allostasis, and Barker’s developmental programming provide the framework’s physiological foundations. They explain functional adequacy, coordinated compensation, adaptive reweighting and lasting calibration; they do not establish a sodium–volume cause of autism. The additional claim here is that different demands or intrinsic constraints converge on local recovery difficulty that carries a developmental effect. Cross-disease comparisons ask whether similar protective physiology operates at other times and sites, without establishing a shared cause.

This contribution connects ion handling, vascular regulation, endocrine control and neural maturation around a defined causal question. The selected evidence is strongest for physiological components and directly measured recovery in experimental preparations; whether the recovery disturbance carries a developmental effect remains unresolved. Genetic and immune findings may support that intermediary or reveal routes that bypass it. Exposure associations, altered resting biomarkers and increased workload cannot decide between those possibilities. Nor can later challenge responses retrospectively establish an unmeasured developmental episode. The framework assigns neither blame nor an intervention. Its explanatory value depends on distinguishing component physiology, recovery mediation and developmental consequence.

Three comparisons give that question practical priorities: recovery and a separate developmental endpoint in human Rett-model neurons; naturally occurring salt-wasting and preserved-conservation trajectories in existing clinical material; and developmental history versus current physiology in the valproate-exposed rat preparation. Section [49.6](#ss_p10_sec_49_6) specifies their alternative explanations and informative outcomes.

Section [23.13](#ss_p10_sec_23_13) states the decisive unresolved boundary. A well-characterised developmental route proceeding despite adequately demonstrated absence, or timely selective prevention, of the relevant recovery disturbance would challenge universal participation, even if the process contributes elsewhere. Normal routine serum sodium is not that demonstration, and an unmeasured intermediary is not evidence for the hypothesis. Conversely, an unsupported earlier episode cannot rescue an informative negative result. The hypothesis stands or falls on whether impaired local recovery actually carries the developmental effect, not on how many otherwise compatible observations can be assembled.
